t: Mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles required ERK phosphorylation.
Mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles required p38 phosphorylation.
Mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles was not dependent on PI3 kinase activity.
Mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles was mediated specifically by the S1P1 receptor rather than S1P2.
The S1P2 receptor was not found to mediate mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles, in contrast to S1P1.
Mast cell migration induced by activated T-cell microvesicles was also mediated by sphingosine kinase 1.
Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and seasonal allergic rhinitis frequently co-occur, with up to 71% of SAR patients reporting conjunctival symptoms and 75% of SAC patients experiencing rhinitis.
In children, 42% of those with allergic rhinitis also have perennial allergic conjunctivitis.
The review notes recent studies suggesting shared genetic and metabolic contributors underlying both nasal and ocular allergic diseases.
Oral and intranasal antihistamines remain the mainstay treatment for seasonal allergic rhinitis.
Combination intranasal corticosteroid-antihistamine regimens offer enhanced control for perennial allergic rhinitis compared to monotherapy.
Topical dual-action antihistamine-mast cell stabilizers are commonly used in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and serve as first-line therapy for perennial allergic conjunctivitis.
Novel ocular delivery systems such as dexamethasone intracanalicular inserts show promise as a treatment for perennial allergic conjunctivitis.
Skin histopathology in CSU shows mast cell degranulation along with a perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and basophils.
Mast cells and basophils act as key effector cells driving CSU pathogenesis and severity and can be activated via both IgE-dependent and IgE-independent mechanisms.
In the type I (autoallergic) endotype of CSU, IgE autoantibodies target autoantigens such as thyroid peroxidase.
In the type IIb (autoimmune) endotype of CSU, IgG autoantibodies target IgE or its high-affinity receptor FcεRI, driving mast cell/basophil activation.
Some CSU patients co-express both the type I and type IIb autoimmune endotypes simultaneously, though the clinical implications of this co-expression remain unclear.

Diagnostic tools including the autologous serum skin test, basophil histamine release assay, and detection of circulating autoantibodies help identify CSU autoimmune endotypes but lack standardized assay protocols.
Beyond IgE-dependent pathways, complement and the mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2) are implicated in non-IgE-mediated mast cell activation in CSU.
Endotype classification predicts therapeutic response in CSU, with type IIb (autoimmune) patients often showing lower responsiveness to antihistamines and omalizumab compared to other endotypes.
In both healthy and ischemic groups, blood volume was highest in the proximal MCA segment and decreased progressively toward the distal segment.

The maximum pressure and maximum/average energy loss measured across the entire M1 segment (proximal-to-distal) were higher than those measured across either individual sub-segment alone, in both groups.

No statistically significant differences were found in peak blood flow velocity, axial WSS, circumferential WSS, maximum/average 3D WSS, and average pressure between the proximal, curved, and distal MCA segments within either group.

Peak blood flow velocity in the proximal and curved segments of the non-stenotic MCA was significantly lower in patients with anterior circulation cerebral ischemia than in healthy individuals, with no significant difference in the distal segment.

Circumferential WSS in the curved and distal segments of the non-stenotic MCA was significantly lower in the cerebral ischemia group than in the healthy group, with no significant difference in the proximal segment.

Maximum and average viscous energy loss across the entire non-stenotic MCA M1 segment were significantly lower in the cerebral ischemia group compared to healthy individuals, consistent with the lower flow rate observed in these patients.
Two independent radiologists showed good to excellent inter-observer agreement (ICC 0.70-0.86) for 4D flow MRI-derived hemodynamic parameters of the MCA.
In the LOAEL BPA-exposed group, testicular PAR2 expression was increased via mast cell tryptase activation, promoting fibroblast proliferation.
α-Smooth muscle actin, a myofibroblast activation marker, was increased in testes of the LOAEL BPA-exposed group.
Collagen accumulation was observed in seminiferous tubules adjacent to blood vessels in the LOAEL BPA-exposed group, indicating fibrosis.
BPA exposure resulted in increased testicular germ cell apoptosis in the LOAEL group.
Sperm concentration and motility were decreased in the LOAEL BPA-exposed group.
BPA exposure led to excessive mast cell activation and overproduction of histamine in the testis.
BPA exposure at the LOAEL dose caused excessive testicular mast cell activation and overproduction of histamine.
Histamine overproduction resulting from BPA-induced mast cell activation reduced expression of steroidogenic enzymes in the testis.
Testosterone levels were decreased in mice exposed to BPA, linked to histamine-driven suppression of steroidogenesis.
At the NOAEL dose (5 mg/kg-BW), BPA exposure did not produce the adverse testicular immune and reproductive effects observed at the higher LOAEL dose.

Allergen-specific IgG treatment markedly reduced inflammatory cell recruitment around airways and blood vessels in OVA-sensitized/challenged wild-type mice, but not in mice lacking FcγRIIb on mast cells.
IgG treatment significantly reduced alveolar macrophage and eosinophil influx in FcγRIIb-sufficient mice but had no effect in mice lacking FcγRIIb on mast cells.

Allergen-specific IgG attenuated OVA-induced elevations of IL-5, CCL2, and CCL24 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and this suppression was almost entirely dependent on FcγRIIb expression on mast cells.
Allergen-specific IgG blunted the OVA-induced increase in PAS-positive goblet cells only in mice expressing FcγRIIb on mast cells.
Muc5ac mucin gene expression, elevated in OVA-sensitized/challenged mice, was reduced by allergen-specific IgG treatment, correlating with decreased PAS staining, in an FcγRIIb-dependent manner.
IL-4 and IL-13 transcript induction in lung tissue of OVA-sensitized/challenged mice was suppressed by IgG treatment only in mice with FcγRIIb-sufficient mast cells.
The increased frequency of Gata3+ CD4+ Foxp3− Th2 cells following OVA sensitization and challenge was attenuated by IgG treatment in an FcγRIIb-dependent fashion.

Strong OVA-specific IgE responses induced by sensitization/challenge were suppressed by allergen-specific IgG treatment only in mice with normal FcγRIIb expression on mast cells, while FcγRIIb-deficient mice still mounted robust IgE titers despite IgG treatment, indicating IgG acts via FcγRIIb to regulate Th2 tone/IgE isotype switching rather than blocking antibody responses generally.
OVA sensitization and challenge caused marked expansion of lung mast cell numbers, which was blunted by allergen-specific IgG treatment in an FcγRIIb-dependent manner.

Serum MCPT1, a marker of mast cell activation, was elevated after allergen challenge in sensitized mice and was decreased by allergen-specific IgG treatment in an FcγRIIb-dependent manner; FcγRIIb-deficient mast cell mice retained elevated MCPT1 despite IgG treatment.

Allergen-induced airway hyperresponsiveness to methacholine, most evident at 40 mg/mL dose, was significantly blunted by IgG treatment in FcγRIIb-sufficient mast cell mice but not in FcγRIIb-deficient mast cell mice.
81% of patients with IBS-D completing 4 weeks of a low-FODMAP diet met the prespecified responder criterion of a ≥100-point decrease in IBS-SSS.
PROMIS scores for abdominal pain and diarrhea severity improved significantly with LFD among responders but not among nonresponders.
Cumulative 8- to 24-hour urinary mannitol excretion, reflecting colonic barrier function, was significantly lower after 4 weeks of LFD compared with baseline among responders.
Colonic mucosal transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a measure of barrier integrity, significantly increased post-LFD among responders.
Colonic mucosal mRNA expression of the leak-pathway tight junction proteins ZO-1, occludin, JAM-A, and claudin-1 significantly increased post-LFD among responders.
mRNA expression of pore-pathway claudins (claudin 2, 3, 8, and 15) did not change significantly post-LFD.
Quantitative immunostaining showed increased epithelial tight-junction localization of occludin and claudin-1 post-LFD among responders but not nonresponders.
Despite increased ZO-1 mRNA/protein levels, ZO-1 and JAM-A localization at the epithelial tight junction was not increased post-LFD.
Levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain and long myosin light chain kinase did not change significantly post-LFD among responders or nonresponders.
Colonic mucosal mast cell counts per high-power field significantly decreased after 4 weeks of LFD among responders.
Colonic mucosal levels of the mast cell mediators histamine, PGE2, and tryptase all significantly decreased post-LFD among responders.
Changes in physiological parameters (barrier function, tight junction proteins, mast cell counts/mediators) did not significantly differ between responders and nonresponders in sensitivity analyses.
The magnitude of change in physiological barrier/mast cell parameters did not correlate with the magnitude of change in IBS-SSS.

Intracolonic administration of fecal supernatant from pre-LFD IBS-D patients decreased colonic TEER and increased leak-pathway (4 kDa dextran) but not unrestricted-pathway (70 kDa dextran) permeability in mice compared with healthy control fecal supernatant.
Fecal supernatant from the same IBS-D patients collected post-LFD no longer disrupted colonic leak-pathway barrier function in mice.

Germ-free mice humanized with pre-LFD IBS-D feces developed a dysfunctional leak pathway compared with those humanized with healthy control feces, whereas mice humanized with post-LFD feces did not, establishing a microbiome-dependent effect.

Pharmacological TLR4 antagonism (LPS-RS) or removal of LPS from IBS-D fecal supernatant abolished the fecal supernatant-induced decrease in TEER and increase in 4 kDa dextran leakage, identifying fecal LPS as a key mediator.
LPS isolated from pre-LFD IBS-D feces caused significantly greater TEER reduction and 4 kDa dextran leakage in mice than LPS isolated from the same patients post-LFD.
In Tlr4-knockout mice, IBS-D fecal supernatant no longer altered TEER or 4 kDa dextran plasma concentration compared with healthy control fecal supernatant, confirming TLR4-dependence of the effect.
IBS-D fecal supernatant did not significantly change TEER in human colonoid monolayers (which lack immune/mast cells) compared with healthy control fecal supernatant.

Pretreatment with the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn sodium completely abolished the pre-LFD IBS-D fecal supernatant-induced decrease in TEER, decrease in tight junction mRNA, and increase in 4 kDa dextran leakage, indicating mast cell activation is required for barrier dysfunction.

Mast cell-deficient (KitW/W-v) mice showed no difference in TEER or 4 kDa dextran leakage between pre-LFD IBS-D and healthy control fecal supernatant, but reconstitution with wild-type mast cells restored the IBS-D-specific effect, whereas reconstitution with TLR4-deficient mast cells did not, establishing that mast cell TLR4 is required for the barrier dysfunction.
Fecal LPS levels were significantly lower post-LFD compared with pre-LFD.
No significant change in fecal microbial alpha- or beta-diversity was observed with LFD, overall or when responders and nonresponders were analyzed separately.
Change in fecal LPS levels with LFD positively correlated with change in relative abundance of gram-negative bacteria and trended toward a negative correlation with gram-positive bacteria abundance.
Responders to the low-FODMAP diet had a much larger mean decrease in IBS symptom severity score than nonresponders.
PROMIS-measured severity of diarrhea and abdominal pain improved significantly in responders after the low-FODMAP diet but did not change in nonresponders.

After excluding patients with contaminated baseline lactulose/mannitol urine samples, cumulative 8- to 24-hour lactulose excretion showed a significant decrease post-LFD, suggesting improved paracellular permeability.
Alpha-diversity of the fecal microbiome did not change significantly after 4 weeks of the low-FODMAP diet.
Beta-diversity of the fecal microbiome showed no overall compositional differences pre- versus post-LFD at the amplicon sequence variant or phylum level.

Diet-induced changes in fecal LPS levels positively correlated with changes in relative abundance of gram-negative bacteria and showed a trend toward negative correlation with gram-positive bacteria abundance.

Change in fecal LPS levels with the low-FODMAP diet was significantly negatively correlated with the relative abundance of Firmicutes and showed a trend toward positive correlation with Bacteroides abundance.
Unlike in mouse colon, IBS-D fecal supernatant applied to human colonoid monolayers did not cause significant TEER changes compared with healthy control fecal supernatant over 24 hours.
The magnitude of change in physiological barrier/mast cell parameters did not correlate with the magnitude of change in IBS symptom severity score.
Of 42 patients with IBS-D who completed the study, 34 (81%) were classified as responders to the low-FODMAP diet using a stringent ≥100-point IBS-SSS reduction threshold.
All 8 nonresponders to the low-FODMAP diet were non-Hispanic White women.
The provided low-FODMAP meals were significantly lower in FODMAP content than participants' baseline diets but did not reduce total or soluble fiber intake.
Treatment with S. miltiorrhiza extract (SME) significantly reduced β-hexosaminidase release from IgE/antigen-activated RBL-2H3 mast cells, indicating suppression of mast cell degranulation.
SME did not induce cytotoxicity in RBL-2H3 cells at concentrations up to 100 µg/mL, the range used for the degranulation assays.
Oral SME administration dose-dependently reduced Evans blue extravasation in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, indicating suppression of IgE/antigen-induced vascular permeability.
SME treatment (100 µg/mL) significantly inhibited Syk phosphorylation in IgE/antigen-activated mast cells, suggesting suppression of upstream mast cell activation signaling.
SME treatment inhibited ERK phosphorylation in activated mast cells, suggesting suppression of MAPK-mediated allergic mediator release.
SME treatment suppressed AKT phosphorylation in activated mast cells, implicating this pathway in SME's anti-allergic mechanism.
SME treatment suppressed JNK phosphorylation in activated mast cells, further supporting modulation of MAPK-driven allergic inflammation.

In a DNCB-induced atopic dermatitis-like mouse model, topical SME treatment reduced dorsal skin severity scores (erythema, crusting/oozing, scratching, erosion, lichenification) beginning after the fifth treatment.
SME treatment significantly alleviated DNCB-induced ear swelling and inflammatory symptoms in the AD-like mouse model.
Histological analysis showed SME treatment significantly reduced epidermal keratinization and skin thickening caused by excessive keratinocyte proliferation in the AD-like mouse model.
SME treatment significantly reduced serum IgE levels in the DNCB-induced AD-like mouse model, indicating modulation of Th2-mediated allergic responses.
SME treatment significantly suppressed spleen hypertrophy (spleen-to-body weight ratio) in the AD-like mouse model, indicating reduced systemic immune activation.
Sensitive skin is associated with a thinner stratum corneum and increased transepidermal water loss, facilitating penetration of irritants and allergens.
The authors' own prior study found a significant difference in TEWL between sensitive-skin and control groups.
Individuals with sensitive skin have reduced natural moisturizing factors and lipids such as ceramides, leading to decreased hydration and compromised barrier integrity.
Individuals with sensitive skin show low-grade inflammation marked by elevated CCL17, sustaining mild skin inflammation without visible signs.
Individuals with sensitive skin show low-grade inflammation marked by elevated interferon-γ, sustaining mild skin inflammation without visible signs.
Reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density is linked to hyperesthesia in sensitive skin, resembling small fiber neuropathy.
Research identified a decreased number of peptidergic C-fibers in sensitive skin, likely contributing to heightened reactivity in remaining nerve endings.
Excessive CGRP release in sensitive skin overstimulates pain receptors via TRP channels, causing neuropathic inflammation and sensitivity mirroring small-fiber neuropathy features.
Overexpression of TRPV1 in sensitive skin leads to calcium influx and neurogenic inflammation upon activation by acidic pH, heat, and chemicals.
Overexpression of ASIC3 in sensitive skin leads to calcium influx and neurogenic inflammation upon activation by acidic pH, heat, and chemicals.
Transcriptomic studies show reduced PIEZO2 mRNA levels in sensitive-skin patients, suggesting PIEZO2 dysfunction contributes to hypersensitivity.
DOCK9, which encodes a protein regulating dendrite growth, is downregulated in sensitive skin, correlating with decreased nerve fibers and increased sensitivity.
Recent transcriptomic research shows patients with sensitive skin exhibit upregulated genes associated with inflammatory pathways.
Cosmetics exposure is the most significant trigger associated with sensitive skin, with an odds ratio of 7.12, meaning exposed individuals are over 7 times more likely to report symptoms.
A cutoff score of 12.7 on the SS-10 questionnaire achieved 72.4% sensitivity and 90.3% specificity for diagnosing sensitive skin.
Approximately 50-60% of women and 30-40% of men self-report having sensitive skin according to survey-based studies.
A 2019 meta-analysis found 71% of respondents reported some degree of sensitive skin and 40% reported moderate to severe SS globally.
Von Frey Filament Test assessments show decreased mechanical pain thresholds in sensitive-skin-affected areas like the cheeks, suggesting peripheral sensory neuropathy as a key pathogenic factor.
Previous patch-testing studies showed high sensitivity to fragrance mix 1 in sensitive-skin patients.
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus, tacrolimus) help manage sensitive skin by reducing inflammation and neurosensory sensitivity without causing skin thinning, suitable for long-term use.
Intradermal botulinum toxin injections show promise for sensitive skin by inhibiting neurotransmitter release and reducing pain.
Antihistamines, beta-blockers, SNRIs, and GABA analogs (pregabalin, gabapentin) are reported to relieve sensitive skin symptoms by reducing sensitization and nociceptive signaling.
Topical capsaicin desensitizes TRPV1 channels to reduce burning and stinging in sensitive skin, and cannabinoids may relieve inflammation and pain, as emerging treatments.
Neurogenic rosacea, a proposed condition sharing a neuropathic basis with sensitive skin, is resistant to conventional therapies but partially responsive to anticonvulsants and antidepressants.
Corneal nerve fiber length was reduced and was the most pronounced corneal confocal microscopy abnormality, being outside normal range in 34% of IBM patients.
Corneal nerve fiber density was abnormal (outside normative range) in 18% of IBM patients.
Corneal nerve branch density was abnormal in 24% of IBM patients, an intermediate finding between CNFD and CNFL abnormalities.
Skin punch biopsy of the thigh showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, abnormal in 61% of patients.
Skin punch biopsy at the shank (distal leg) showed a more pronounced, length-dependent reduction in IENFD, abnormal in 71% of patients.
Among corneal immunological cell subtypes, intermediate cells were the most abundant, with only moderate overall CIC numbers observed in the IBM cohort.
Quantitative sensory testing of both feet showed a leading impairment of the vibration detection threshold, with only slight impairment of thermal and mechanical detection thresholds.

Z-tests comparing QST parameters to an ideal healthy population showed significant abnormalities in warm detection threshold, thermal sensory limen, mechanical pain threshold, and vibration detection threshold.

Chi-square testing showed significantly elevated rates of abnormal sensory loss values in mechanical and vibration detection thresholds, and sensory gain in mechanical pain threshold, mechanical pain sensitivity, and paradoxical heat sensation.

QST findings indicated predominant large fiber sensory impairment (61%) with only a small proportion of patients showing functional small fiber impairment (12%), contrasting with the higher rates of structural small fiber loss on biopsy/CCM.
Nerve conduction studies revealed abnormal findings in two-thirds of IBM patients, with predominantly motor rather than sensory involvement.
The main electrophysiological finding was motor axonal damage of the peroneal nerve, reflected by reduced compound motor action potential amplitude.
Absence of the sural nerve sensory nerve action potential was found in 3 of 18 patients, interpreted as axonal sensory nerve damage; four patients showed reduced sural nerve conduction velocity.
CNFL correlated moderately and significantly with the SF-36 energy subscale, suggesting a link between corneal small fiber morphology and perceived vitality.
CNFD correlated moderately and significantly with both the SF-36 energy and pain subscales.
CNFL and CNFD showed a moderate correlation trend with the IBM Functional Rating Scale, but this did not reach statistical significance.
The SF-36 questionnaire showed reduced overall quality of life in IBM patients, primarily attributable to physical limitations rather than to pain.
Pain questionnaires (SFNSL, PainDETECT, BPI) indicated only mild pain-related restrictions in the IBM cohort, consistent with the disease being usually painless.
Ocular Surface Disease Index scores suggested dry eye in two of the IBM patients, a potential confounder for corneal nerve parameters.

The authors interpret the combination of structural small fiber damage without corresponding functional QST abnormality or significant pain as suggesting the observed small fiber pathology may not represent a typical small fiber neuropathy, but rather reflect a broader neurodegenerative process, as seen in Parkinson's disease, dementia, and ALS.
Prior literature cited indicates that IBM patients are up to three times more likely to develop large fiber neuropathy compared with population controls.
Women made up 76% of the Harlequin syndrome cohort.

Idiopathic etiology was the most common cause of Harlequin syndrome (37%), followed by postsurgical, neoplastic, traumatic, small fiber neuropathy, systemic, autoimmune, pure autonomic failure, and multiple sclerosis-related causes.
Small fiber neuropathy was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 4 of 51 patients (7.8%).
Neoplasm was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 5 of 51 patients (9.8%).
Trauma was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 4 of 51 patients (7.8%).
Small fiber neuropathy was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 4 of 51 patients (7.8%).
Systemic causes accounted for Harlequin syndrome in 3 of 51 patients (5.9%).
Autoimmune etiology was identified in 3 of 51 patients with Harlequin syndrome (5.9%).
Pure autonomic failure was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 2 of 51 patients (3.9%).
Multiple sclerosis was identified as the underlying cause of Harlequin syndrome in 1 of 51 patients (2%).
Pupil abnormalities were found in 13 of 51 patients (25.5%) with Harlequin syndrome.
Pupil abnormalities were identified in about a quarter of patients with Harlequin syndrome.
About a third of patients with Harlequin syndrome had abnormal muscle stretch reflexes.
Headache was a common comorbidity, present in about 39% of patients with Harlequin syndrome.
Onset was acute or subacute in the majority of postsurgical Harlequin syndrome patients, whereas insidious onset predominated in nonsurgical patients, a statistically significant difference.
Thermoregulatory sweat testing showed a median anhidrosis extent of 9% of body surface area among tested patients, with wide variability.
The median composite autonomic severity score among tested patients was low, indicating generally mild overall autonomic impairment in this cohort.
Women with FMS reported significantly higher orofacial pain intensity on the VAS compared to healthy controls.
Women with FMS had significantly lower facial pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) at all measured points compared to healthy controls, indicating heightened facial pain sensitivity.
Women with FMS demonstrated significantly reduced mouth opening (mandibular range of motion) compared to healthy controls.

Craniofacial Pain and Disability Inventory (CF-PDI) total, pain, and jaw functional scores were significantly higher (worse) in women with FMS than in healthy controls, indicating poorer orofacial quality of life.
There were no significant differences in facial skin surface temperature (TMJ, distal temporal, proximal masseter, distal masseter ROIs) between women with FMS and healthy controls.
Axillary temperature was significantly higher in women with FMS compared to healthy controls, whereas tympanic (core) temperature did not differ.
Higher peripheral distal temporal (DT) facial skin temperature was significantly associated with lower masseter proximal left (MPL) pressure pain threshold in women with FMS.
Higher temporomandibular joint (TMJ) skin temperature was significantly associated with lower masseter distal right (MDR) and masseter proximal right (MPR) pressure pain thresholds in women with FMS.
No significant association was found between proximal masseter (PM) facial skin temperature and any oral symptomatology variable (VAS, PPTs, mouth opening, CF-PDI) in women with FMS.
Distal masseter (DM) skin temperature was significantly associated with CF-PDI total, CF-PDI pain, and CF-PDI jaw functional scores in women with FMS.
Women with FMS reported significantly greater use of analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, anxiolytics, and antidepressants compared to healthy controls.
Among 272 T2DM patients, 33.09% (90/272) were found to have diabetic gastric motility disorders (DGMD) based on electrogastrogram (EGG) results.
Duration of diabetes was significantly longer in the DGMD group compared with the non-DGMD group and remained an independent risk factor for DGMD in multivariate logistic regression.
Fasting blood glucose (FBG) was significantly higher in patients with DGMD and remained an independent risk factor for DGMD in logistic regression.
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels were significantly lower in the DGMD group than in the non-DGMD group, and low 25(OH)D was an independent risk factor for DGMD.

Presence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) was significantly associated with DGMD and remained an independent risk factor for DGMD after adjustment for other variables.
A composite predictive model combining FBG, diabetes duration, 25(OH)D, and MASLD achieved an AUC of 0.777 for predicting DGMD, greater than any single risk factor alone.
DGMD prevalence increased progressively with longer diabetes duration: 24.37% (<5 years), 26.58% (5-10 years), and 54.05% (>10 years).
DGMD prevalence increased with rising fasting blood glucose: 13.33% (<6.1 mmol/L), 16.98% (6.1-7.8), 30% (7.8-10.0), and 46.27% (>10.0 mmol/L).
DGMD prevalence increased as 25(OH)D levels decreased: 13.33% (>30 ng/mL), 24.05% (20-30 ng/mL), and 44.44% (<20 ng/mL).
DGMD prevalence was substantially higher in T2DM patients with MASLD (58.33%) than in those without MASLD (18.86%/19.32%), with a positive correlation between MASLD and DGMD incidence.

Patients with MASLD showed significantly higher postprandial bradygastria, postprandial tachygastria, and pre-meal rhythm disturbance ratios, and significantly lower pre-meal and postprandial slow-wave ratios, compared with non-MASLD patients.

Across non-MASLD, mild, moderate, and severe MASLD subgroups, postprandial slow-wave proportion decreased and postprandial bradygastria, tachygastria, and pre-meal rhythm disturbance increased progressively with increasing MASLD severity.

BMI, fasting C-peptide, 2-hour postprandial C-peptide, and HbA1c, although higher in the DGMD group in univariate comparisons, were no longer significantly associated with DGMD risk after multivariate logistic regression adjustment.
The prevalence of MASLD among hospitalized Chinese T2DM patients in this study was 40.57%, somewhat lower than a previously reported rate of 42.1%.

The authors propose, as an unverified hypothesis, that 25(OH)D may influence DGMD pathogenesis through modulation of tryptophan metabolism and downstream serotonin (5-HT) signaling, which is closely linked to gastrointestinal motility.
A more intense intermittent fasting regimen (16:8 TRE plus weekly 1-2 day water fasting) reduced Long COVID Symptom Severity Score (LC-Score) more than a milder 14:10 TRE regimen over 4 weeks.
The more intense Fasting regimen also reduced the number of Long COVID symptoms (numLCsym) more than the TRE regimen over 4 weeks.
Across the full 10-week trial (baseline, TRE, and Fasting phases combined), mean LC-Score decreased substantially for all participants.
Number of Long COVID symptoms decreased significantly over the full 10-week trial.
Female participants had greater baseline Long COVID symptom burden than male participants, consistent with prior LC literature.
Younger participants (age <47.5 years) had a substantially greater 10-week reduction in LC-Score than older participants.
Greater baseline daily step count (>4500 steps) was associated with better 10-week symptomatic response to the fasting intervention.
Participants whose Long COVID symptoms began soon after COVID-19 vaccination had better 10-week responses to the intervention.
Participants whose symptoms began during the Omicron wave or later had better 10-week responses than those with earlier-onset Long COVID.
Absence of baseline leg weakness and lower baseline insomnia severity were associated with better 10-week responses to the intervention.
Treatment response over 10 weeks was not significantly associated with sex, baseline BMI, initial LC-Score, initial numLCsym, or Long COVID duration.
Longer total fasting duration (23-60 hours per week) was not correlated with better 4-week Fasting response.
Mean BMI decreased modestly over the 10-week trial.
Fasting-related adverse events occurred in a minority of participants and were generally tolerable, including two severe adverse events requiring hospitalization.
Most participants experienced at least one symptom flare-up during the trial, commonly attributed to overexertion or water fasting.
Fatigue, PEM, blurry vision, and tinnitus were the most treatment-resistant symptoms, resolving in only about 20-24% of participants over 10 weeks.
Fatigue, post-exertional malaise, difficulty concentrating, and brain fog were the most frequent baseline symptoms in this Long COVID cohort.

Among the top-half of responders, mean severity across 28 common Long COVID symptoms decreased by 80.6%, with light sensitivity and headache improving the most and tinnitus and nerve pain improving the least.
The overall frequency of the 28 common Long COVID symptoms decreased significantly across the 10-week trial.

The authors hypothesize that fasting-induced autophagy decreases inflammation and increases viral clearance, potentially unmasking persistent SARS-CoV-2 to the immune system and contributing to symptom improvement.
The rate of treatment-emergent adverse events from baseline to day 28 was higher but not statistically significantly different between the rovunaptabin group and placebo group.
Rovunaptabin significantly increased INR two hours after infusion, consistent with its known anticoagulant activity, but the effect resolved by the next day.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved self-reported fatigue as measured by the FACIT Fatigue Scale compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved severity of fatigue as measured by the Bell score compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved fatigue severity as measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved SF-36 vitality subscale scores compared to placebo, indicating improved quality of life.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved SF-36 general health subscale scores compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved SF-36 social role functioning subscale scores compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin significantly improved the SF-36 mental component summary score compared to placebo.
Rovunaptabin showed no significant effect on post-exertional malaise (DSQ-PEM), 6-minute walking distance, or perceived exertion/dyspnoea (Borg scales) compared to placebo.

At screening, all PCS patients enrolled were seropositive for β2-adrenergic receptor autoantibodies (β2-fAAb, 100%) and M2 muscarinic receptor autoantibodies (M2-AAb, 100%), with a minority also positive for AT1 receptor autoantibodies (7%).
Rovunaptabin neutralised GPCR-fAAbs in all treated patients, with both quick (within days) and delayed effects observed.

In the cross-over analysis, a significant improvement was observed under rovunaptabin in fatigue (FACIT), fatigue severity (Bell score), and ME/CFS diagnostic criteria status (Canadian Consensus Criteria, CCC).
In the cross-over phase, rovunaptabin significantly increased aPTT, confirming its anticoagulant activity, with the effect no longer detectable the following day.
One serious adverse event (hospitalisation after a wasp sting due to known venom allergy) occurred during the trial and was judged unrelated to the study treatment.

A subgroup of participants showed disappearance of GPCR-fAAbs without receiving rovunaptabin (placebo-first), but this was not accompanied by fatigue improvement, unlike participants whose GPCR-fAAbs were neutralised by rovunaptabin, suggesting low-titre fAAbs below assay detection may retain pathogenic activity.
Younger age (<55 years) was associated with increased risk of Long COVID compared to age ≥75 in adjusted analysis.
Obesity was associated with increased risk of Long COVID in adjusted analysis.
Living in more socio-economically deprived areas was associated with increased risk of Long COVID.
Female sex was associated with increased risk of Long COVID.
Higher baseline C-reactive protein was associated with increased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, but attenuated after multivariable adjustment.
Higher triglyceride levels were associated with increased Long COVID risk in both crude and adjusted analyses.
Higher HDL-cholesterol was associated with decreased Long COVID risk in both crude and adjusted analyses.
Higher IGF-1 levels were associated with decreased Long COVID risk in both crude and adjusted analyses.
Higher sex hormone-binding globulin was associated with decreased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, an effect observed in females only in sex-stratified analysis.
Higher HbA1c was associated with increased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, attenuated after adjustment.
Higher cystatin C was associated with increased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, attenuated after adjustment.
Higher urate levels were associated with increased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, attenuated after adjustment.
Higher alanine aminotransferase was associated with increased Long COVID risk in crude analysis, attenuated after adjustment.
Higher vitamin D levels remained associated with increased Long COVID risk after adjustment.
Pre-existing chronic kidney disease was associated with increased Long COVID risk.
Pre-existing COPD was associated with increased Long COVID risk.
Pre-existing metastatic cancer was associated with a lower risk of Long COVID.
Older age (≥75) was associated with a substantially increased risk of PACS compared to age <55.
Obesity was associated with increased risk of PACS.
Living in more deprived areas was associated with increased risk of PACS.
Male sex was associated with increased risk of PACS.
Smoking was associated with increased risk of PACS.
Higher C-reactive protein was strongly associated with increased PACS risk in crude analysis.
Older age (≥75 years) was associated with a higher adjusted risk of PACS compared to those under 55 years.

The physical component score (PCS) of the SF-36 significantly improved from baseline to 3-month follow up after HBOT.

ME/CFS affects an estimated 17 to 24 million people worldwide, with an average of 60% of European patients remaining undiagnosed.

In the US, ME/CFS affects an estimated 836,000 to 2.5 million people, with fewer than 20% formally diagnosed, and NHANES data suggest 1.3% of US adults may have contracted the disease with an annual economic cost of approximately $51 billion (a second estimate cites $24 billion).
Decreased cerebral blood flow may contribute to symptoms in as many as 90 percent of adults with ME/CFS.
ME/CFS has a demonstrated genetic susceptibility, as shown by multiple twin concordance studies finding higher disease rates in monozygotic versus dizygotic twins.
IL8 has been identified as upregulated in ME/CFS patients, with relevance to inflammation, circadian, metabolic, and mitochondrial pathways.
NFKBIA has been identified as upregulated in ME/CFS patients, with relevance to inflammation, circadian, metabolic, and mitochondrial pathways.
TNFAIP3 has been identified as upregulated in ME/CFS patients, with relevance to inflammation, circadian, metabolic, and mitochondrial pathways.
Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, particularly the joint hypermobility subtype, frequently co-occurs with ME/CFS, supporting a possible genetic link.
ME/CFS patients show increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, likely contributing to fatigue and autonomic symptoms.

ME/CFS patients have a reduced TH1 response with an overactive TH2 response, indicated by increased IL-10 and a decreased IFN-γ/IL-10 ratio, resulting in suppressed cellular immunity with persistent low-grade inflammation.
Elevated pro-inflammatory mediators including TNF-α, IL-1, PMN-elastase, lysozyme, and serum neopterin may point toward a diagnosis of ME/CFS.
MRI studies have found reductions in brain white and gray matter volume in ME/CFS patients, with degree of reduction correlating to symptom severity in some patients.
PET imaging has found impairments in brain blood perfusion in some, but not all, ME/CFS patients.
Doppler studies showed an approximate four-fold decrease in internal carotid and vertebral artery blood flow in ME/CFS patients upon going from supine to head tilt, compared to healthy controls.
BOLD fMRI and EEG studies have found functional differences in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, including increased brain activity and disrupted brain waves during sleep.

A prospective study of individuals with mononucleosis found that those who progressed to ME/CFS had greater physical symptoms and immune abnormalities but no increase in psychological symptoms compared to those who recovered, contradicting a psychosomatic explanation.

A study of 169 ME/CFS patients found that 90.5% felt their disease was misunderstood, 88.2% reported mental distress, 71% reported sadness, 66.9% hopelessness, and 39.3% had suicidal thoughts, primarily driven by feeling their condition was dismissed as psychological, lacking strength, or misunderstood.

Analysis of U.S. healthcare data found that ME/CFS-related appointments last approximately 23.6 minutes compared to approximately 19.4 minutes for other visits, indicating greater time burden on providers.
SF-36 general health (GH) scores were significantly lower in ME/CFS cases than in controls for both male and female subjects.
The proportion of mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) reads in plasma cfRNA was significantly lower in ME/CFS cases than in controls.
Differential abundance analysis of plasma cfRNA identified 743 features differing significantly between ME/CFS cases and controls, with 608 elevated in cases and 135 elevated in controls.
IL18R1 (along with CCR7, FCRL5, PRF1, and IFNLR1) was more abundant in cfRNA from ME/CFS cases than controls.
TGFB2 (along with CCL3, CD109, and COL1A1) cfRNA was more abundant in controls than in ME/CFS cases.

The mitochondrial ribosome assembly factor MTG1 was significantly increased in ME/CFS case cfRNA, while several mitochondrial tRNA/rRNA-related transcripts (MTND1P23, MT-TL1, MT-TV, MT-TH, MT-TS2, MT-TT, MTATP8P1, MTND6P3, MTRNR2L3) were significantly decreased, supporting a role for mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS.

A GLMNET Lasso machine-learning classifier built on 21 cfRNA features achieved a training AUC-ROC of 0.86 and a testing AUC-ROC of 0.81, with 77% test accuracy, 84% sensitivity, and 68% specificity for distinguishing ME/CFS cases from controls.
HNRNPLL, a regulator of alternative splicing and mRNA stability in immune pathways, was the strongest contributor to the 21-gene GLMNET Lasso classifier's performance.

Deconvolution of cfRNA cell-of-origin using a ME/CFS PBMC scRNA-seq reference showed plasmacytoid dendritic cell (pDC)-derived cfRNA was the most significantly elevated cell type in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Monocyte-derived cfRNA fraction was significantly increased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, consistent with sustained immune activation.
Platelet-derived cfRNA fraction was significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, supporting baseline platelet dysfunction in ME/CFS.
Naive CD8+ T cell-derived cfRNA contribution was significantly increased in ME/CFS cases, an unexpected finding for this typically quiescent cell type suggesting altered T cell homeostasis.
Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell-derived cfRNA was significantly different between ME/CFS cases and controls.

Effector/memory (E/M) CD8+ T cell-derived cfRNA was significantly elevated only in female ME/CFS cases versus female controls, not detected when both sexes were combined, suggesting sex-specific immune alterations.
Classical monocyte-derived cfRNA fraction was elevated in both female cases and female controls compared to their male counterparts, indicating a sex-based rather than disease-based difference.

Ingenuity Pathway Analysis identified top canonical pathways enriched in ME/CFS cases including focal adhesion kinase signaling, NFKBIE signaling, lipid antigen presentation by CD1, IL-4 signaling, neural cell adhesion molecule signaling, and T cell exhaustion signaling.

CTLA4 signaling in cytotoxic T lymphocytes, an immune checkpoint pathway, showed the most decreased activity in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, suggesting altered immune tolerance/suppression mechanisms.
Network analysis identified a cytokine signaling theme driven by CSF2, IFNG, IL2, IL21, and TNF among genes differentially abundant in ME/CFS cases.
Network analysis identified JAK-STAT pathway involvement, with STAT1 and STAT4 highlighted as key immune regulators dysregulated in ME/CFS.
ADAM12, TGFB2, and MMP2 cfRNA levels were significantly reduced in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, among pathway-related marker genes analyzed.
Seventeen pathway-related genes, including TNFSF15, ITGA10, IL18R1, and several T cell receptor genes, were elevated in cfRNA of ME/CFS cases compared to controls.

cfRNA metagenomic analysis found no significant differences in total viral RNA burden, or burden of individual viral families (including Retroviridae, Herpesviridae, Flaviviridae), between ME/CFS cases and controls.
No significant difference in Picornaviridae (which includes enteroviruses, a genus previously suspected in ME/CFS onset) signal was detected between cases and controls.
Variability in individual sample classification accuracy across the ~1,500 machine learning models was driven by the fraction of platelet-derived cfRNA rather than by clinical phenotype or test site.
Self-reported disease severity metrics (GH scores for all samples, MFI-20 fatigue scores for cases) were not correlated with cfRNA classifier performance.

One ME/CFS case and one control showed unusually high total viral cfRNA reads, mapping primarily to Pegivirus hominis (HPgV), a common, typically asymptomatic virus not previously linked to a specific disease.

Among the most significantly different pathway-related genes, ADAM12, TGFB2, and MMP2 transcript abundance was significantly reduced in ME/CFS cases relative to controls, suggesting dysregulated tissue repair and inflammation pathways.
Seventeen of the top pathway-related genes analyzed, including IL18R1, TNFSF15, ITGA10, and several T cell receptor genes, were elevated in cfRNA from ME/CFS cases compared to controls.

cfRNA metagenomic analysis found Retroviridae, Herpesviridae, and Flaviviridae to be the most abundant viral families in plasma, but total viral RNA burden did not differ significantly between ME/CFS cases and controls.
No significant differences were observed in the burden of individual viral families between ME/CFS cases and controls.
Detectable signal from the Picornaviridae family, which includes enteroviruses previously suspected as an ME/CFS trigger, did not differ significantly between cases and controls.
One ME/CFS case and one control exhibited markedly elevated total viral cfRNA reads mapping primarily to Pegivirus hominis (HPgV), a virus not previously associated with a specific disease.

Variability in how consistently individual samples were correctly classified by machine learning models was associated with the fraction of platelet-derived cfRNA rather than phenotype or test site, indicating a true biological difference in platelet-derived cfRNA between cases and controls.

Deconvolution using the Tabula Sapiens single-cell reference showed that solid-tissue-derived cfRNA contributed minimally to the plasma cfRNA pool and did not differ significantly between ME/CFS cases and controls.

Immune checkpoint disruption has been reported in ME/CFS patients.
Neuroinflammation has been documented as part of ME/CFS immune dysfunction.
Mitochondrial abnormalities have been documented in ME/CFS patients.

TGF-β1 is elevated in patients with chronic inflammatory response syndrome (CIRS) as part of the diagnostic biomarker panel.
MMP-9, a marker of systemic inflammatory activation, is elevated in the majority of CIRS patients and normalizes with cholestyramine therapy.
MSH was found to be consistently low in patients with chronic exposure-related illness, linked to downstream ACTH/ADH dysregulation.
Elevated leptin levels were reported in over half of CIRS patients in Shoemaker's 2005-2006 studies and typically declined with treatment.

The Shoemaker Protocol has demonstrated efficacy in treating CIRS, including objective biomarker normalization and symptom resolution in published studies, in contrast to non-curative ME/CFS interventions.
VCS deficits were common among Pfiesteria/biotoxin-exposed individuals and reliably improved with cholestyramine treatment.
Certain HLA DR/DQ haplotypes were disproportionately represented across fungal, dinoflagellate, and tick-borne illness cohorts, suggesting genetic susceptibility to CIRS.

The 2005 formal CIRS case definition required exposure criteria, symptoms in four or more of eight physiological systems, abnormalities in at least three of six core biomarkers (MSH, MMP-9, ACTH/cortisol, ADH/osmolality, VCS, HLA DR/DQ), and improvement in at least two of three treatment-response indicators.

Between 2001-2017, CIRS treatment literature comprised two RCTs (n=21), two case-control studies (224 cases vs. 134 controls), five case-series/open-label trials (n=118), and seven case reports, mostly of cholestyramine or VIP, consistently showing symptomatic improvement and inflammatory marker normalization.
A symptom-cluster screening model found that eight or more of 13 symptom clusters indicated >95% likelihood of CIRS-WDB, rising to 98.5% diagnostic accuracy when combined with VCS deficits.
Forebrain parenchymal volume showed a significant inverse correlation with VEGF levels in CIRS patients, supporting a blood-brain barrier injury/capillary hypoperfusion mechanism.

NeuroQuant volumetric MRI showed statistically significant caudate nucleus atrophy and enlargement of the pallidum, left amygdala, and right forebrain parenchyma in CIRS patients, absent in matched controls.

In an open-label study of 20 treatment-refractory CIRS patients, VIP therapy reduced symptoms to control levels, normalized C4a/TGF-β1/MMP-9/VEGF, and increased T regulatory cells from 8.9% to 22.5%, with no significant adverse events over 18 months.

Serial MRI showed that higher-dose intranasal VIP therapy was associated with volumetric increases in multiple grey matter nuclei, with overt atrophy in under 1% of structures and reversal of nearly half of volumetric deficits, an effect not seen in controls.

Transcriptomic profiling revealed broad suppression of ribosomal subunit genes and downregulation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial/mitoribosomal genes in untreated CIRS patients, termed molecular hypometabolism (MHM).

A 'proliferative physiology' transcriptomic profile characterized by IRS2 upregulation and translocase downregulation redirects pyruvate to aerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acidosis and reduced ATP.
Upregulation of tubulin genes TUBB1 and TUBA4A was associated with mitochondrial membrane pore closure and correlated with grey matter nuclear atrophy on imaging.
Downregulation of IKZF1 and VIPR1 was associated with poorer clinical response to VIP therapy and increased grey matter atrophy.

An early case-control study by Grattan et al. found that individuals exposed to Pfiesteria-contaminated waterways had significant impairments in verbal learning, divided attention, and fine motor coordination compared to unexposed controls.

A 13-symptom-cluster screening tool was reported to identify CIRS-WDB with over 95% likelihood when 8 or more clusters were present, rising to 98.5% diagnostic accuracy when combined with visual contrast sensitivity (VCS) deficits.

Across 2001-2017, the CIRS treatment literature comprised two RCTs (n=21), two case-control studies (n=224 cases vs 134 controls), five open-label/case-time series (n=118), and seven case reports, most showing symptomatic improvement and normalization of inflammatory markers with cholestyramine or VIP.

A 2016 RNA-Seq study of 14 CIRS patients found that intranasal VIP therapy significantly reduced symptom burden (mean 12.9 to 3.3), improved TGF-β1 and C4a, and produced coordinated downregulation of inflammatory/innate immune genes alongside upregulation of Ikaros transcription factors, coinciding with NeuroQuant imaging improvement.

GENIE transcriptomic profiling identified a 'triple-positive' gene expression fingerprint—co-activation of tubulin genes (TUBB1, TUBA4A), clusterin (CLU), and coagulation-related genes (GP6, GP9, PF4, ITGA2B)—in a subset of CIRS patients, proposed as an early risk indicator for neurodegeneration.

Mechanistic analysis linked MAPK pathway activation with upregulation of tubulin genes and elevated clusterin (CLU) in the same CIRS patients, mirroring cytoskeletal and oxidative injury patterns seen in ALS and Alzheimer's disease.

Transcriptomic research identified upregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1A) in CIRS patients following water-damaged building exposure, reflecting a shift toward proliferative physiology with impaired mitochondrial metabolism, increased glycolysis, and heightened inflammatory signaling.

GENIE-tracked HIF1A upregulation and associated proliferative physiology abnormalities normalized following VIP therapy, alongside improvements in surrogate markers of pulmonary hypertension and mitochondrial function.

EnviroBiomics, Inc. developed commercial qPCR-based tools (Actino Skin® and Actino Plasma®) to quantify skin Actinobacteria such as Corynebacterium tuberculostearicum and Cutibacterium acnes and evaluate host immune reactivity to mycolic acids, though formal peer-reviewed validation is pending.

Mycolic acids, long-chain fatty acids in Actinobacterial cell walls, were proposed as candidate biomarkers for indoor Actinobacteria exposure, analogous to endotoxin testing for Gram-negative organisms.

The 2018 Consensus Statement established a standardized CIRS diagnostic process combining symptom clusters, exposure history, VCS testing, HLA haplotypes, a laboratory biomarker panel, NeuroQuant brain volumetrics, and the GENIE transcriptomic platform.

Among five competing longitudinal models, the fully bidirectional model, in which all internalizing disorders (MDD, GAD) and functional disorders (FM, ME/CFS) at Wave 2 predict all conditions at Wave 3, provided the best fit to the data.
Within-condition autoregressive associations from Wave 2 to Wave 3 were the largest cross-time effects for all four conditions, exceeding any cross-condition associations.
Cross-time within-domain effects (IDs predicting later IDs, and FDs predicting later FDs) were larger than cross-domain effects between IDs and FDs.
Functional disorders at Wave 2 predicted internalizing disorders at Wave 3 somewhat more strongly than internalizing disorders at Wave 2 predicted functional disorders at Wave 3.

The prospective association from earlier fibromyalgia to later major depressive disorder was significantly stronger than the association from earlier major depressive disorder to later fibromyalgia, with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
In the follow-up cross-lagged SEM, fibromyalgia showed greater temporal stability than major depressive disorder.
In the cross-lagged SEM, earlier major depressive disorder did not significantly predict later fibromyalgia after accounting for fibromyalgia's own stability.
Earlier fibromyalgia significantly predicted later major depressive disorder in the cross-lagged SEM, and this cross-time effect was significantly larger than the reverse (MDD to FM) path.
Participants with more ID symptoms and FD criteria at a given wave were less likely to respond to the subsequent follow-up assessment, indicating differential attrition.

Measurement models for MDD, GAD, FM, and ME/CFS showed statistically significant sex differences in factor loadings and thresholds, but the resulting factor scores were nearly identical whether or not sex differences were modeled.

A prior study by the same research group found substantial comorbidity between internalizing disorders (MDD, GAD) and functional disorders (FM, ME/CFS), with tetrachoric correlations ranging from 0.48 to 0.56.

Familial co-aggregation was also observed between MDD, ME/CFS, and fibromyalgia with cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
Hypertension co-aggregated within families with all studied functional and internalizing disorders except MDD, for which the association was not significant.
Atopy showed the strongest familial co-aggregation with functional disorders and generalized anxiety disorder.
Familial co-aggregation between MDD and atopy was small, and the recurrence risk of MDD given atopy in a first-degree relative was not statistically significant.
Autoimmune disease was bidirectionally associated with increased prevalence of all internalizing and functional disorders, including ME/CFS.
Among cardiometabolic diseases, only having a first-degree relative with cardiovascular disease was associated with increased IBS prevalence.
Having a first-degree relative with IBS was associated with increased prevalence of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and obesity, but not type 2 diabetes or MASLD.
Having generalized anxiety disorder in a first-degree relative was associated with increased prevalence of all cardiometabolic disorders except MASLD.

ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and MDD showed significant small-to-moderate familial correlations with all studied cardiometabolic and immune-related disorders, indicating shared genetic and/or common environmental risk.
All internalizing and functional disorders studied, including ME/CFS, showed significant small-to-moderate familial correlations with both atopy and autoimmune disease.
IBS showed significant familial correlations with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, but not with obesity or MASLD.

Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, was added to the patient's regimen and she reported notable improvement in her pain symptoms at six-month follow-up.
Cromolyn sodium, a mast cell stabilizer, was trialed but the patient reported it 'did not help as much as the GI supplements' and it was eventually paused.
Betaine HCl, used to increase gastric acidity, led to near-complete resolution of the patient's diarrhea, suggesting low stomach acid contributed to her GI dysmotility.
Quercetin combined with bromelain, used to stabilize mast cells and inhibit histamine release, provided symptom relief and improved the patient's tolerance to food.
Broad-spectrum digestive enzymes, including a DPP-IV gluten digestion aid, were used to reduce metabolic strain on the GI tract, improve nutrient absorption, and decrease bloating and discomfort.
Traditional antihistamines paradoxically exacerbated the patient's GI symptoms rather than improving them, consistent with an atypical, paradoxical histamine response seen in some MCAS cases.

Following a confirmed CRPS diagnosis and incomplete response to conventional and integrative therapies, the patient is proceeding with spinal cord stimulator (SCS) implantation as an escalation of care.
The patient's mother and sister had both been diagnosed with MCAS, raising suspicion of a familial predisposition contributing to her own MCAS, CRPS, and hypermobility symptoms.
The patient was diagnosed with hEDS using the Beighton score checklist based on joint hypermobility, skin/joint laxity, and history of shoulder dislocation and bilateral pyogenic papules of the heel.
A patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome experienced spontaneous lumenal haemorrhage of the gallbladder that progressed to gallbladder rupture.
Musculocontractural EDS is caused by biallelic mutations in CHST14, which disrupt dermatan sulfate biosynthesis and impair extracellular matrix integrity.

The patient had a lifelong history of severe bleeding tendency with recurrent painful hematomas, requiring more than 90 general anesthesia procedures for hematoma evacuation and vacuum-assisted closure therapy.

Despite CT angiography showing active arterial bleeding, interventional radiology declined embolization due to distal vessel involvement and high risk of iatrogenic vessel rupture from mcEDS-related vascular fragility.

In a previously reported pediatric mcEDS case, conservative management (limb elevation, compression, fluid resuscitation without transfusion, and tranexamic acid) achieved nonsurgical hemostasis and stabilization, discharge occurring after 13 days.
In this adult mcEDS patient, initial conservative management with elastic bandage compression failed to control the expanding lumbar hematoma, and the swelling continued to enlarge despite bandaging.
Tranexamic acid (1 g IV) was administered immediately after CT confirmed active arterial bleeding, as part of initial hemostatic management.
Hemoglobin dropped from 14.0 g/dL to 11.7 g/dL as the hematoma expanded toward the scapular region, signaling ongoing hemorrhage and prompting emergency surgical evacuation.

Emergency surgical evacuation revealed more than 1.1 L of blood/coagula in the subcutaneous cavity, and the patient required four units of packed red blood cells, 2 g fibrinogen, and 20% human albumin to manage blood loss and hemodynamic stability.

Extensive topical application of PerClot (absorbable polysaccharide hemostatic powder) across the wound cavity from the lumbar to scapular region was used to achieve localized hemostasis after electrocautery.
The patient had grade II mitral valve insufficiency associated with a dysplastic mitral valve and prolapse of the anterior leaflet, as a comorbid cardiac manifestation of mcEDS.
The patient had restrictive pulmonary function impairment as part of his mcEDS-related medical history.
Despite congenital anomalies and severe multisystem connective tissue involvement, the patient exhibited excellent cognitive development.
Due to known vascular fragility and history of difficult cannulation, ultrasound guidance was required to successfully establish peripheral venous access in this mcEDS patient.

Extended intraoperative-to-suture-removal antibiotic prophylaxis was used given the extensive wound cavities and hematoma superinfection risk, though the authors acknowledge this increases nosocomial infection risk and is not standard practice.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed refractory stenosis of the gastrojejunal anastomosis following transoral outlet reduction (TORe) endoscopy.
Overall ACL reconstruction survival rate in EDS patients was 85.7% at 50 months of follow-up.
Primary ACLR patients showed substantially higher survivorship than revision ACLR patients, with 93.8% vs 62.5% survival at 50 months and 78.1% survival maintained in the primary group at 150 months.
The cumulative incidence of ACLR failure (competing with conversion to TKA) was significantly higher in the revision ACLR group than in the primary group.
Patients requiring revision ACLR were significantly older than those with primary ACLR, and had shorter follow-up duration.
Three of the five revision ACLR patients required reoperation for medial meniscus tear, treated with meniscectomy.
No clinical or demographic factors, including a reduced model of BMI and age, were significantly associated with risk of ACLR failure in EDS patients.
Age of EDS patients undergoing ACLR differed significantly from age of healthy controls and ACL-injured patients in the Weiler et al. comparator cohorts.
Posterior tibial slope in EDS patients did not significantly differ from ACL-injured or healthy ACL-intact literature controls.
Intercondylar notch width did not significantly differ between EDS patients and healthy or ACL-injured literature comparator groups.
Lateral femoral condyle ratio was significantly higher in EDS patients than in healthy controls, but not significantly different from primary ACL-injury or failed ACLR patients.
Tibiofemoral rotation angle was significantly higher in EDS patients than in healthy controls and intact ACLR patients, but not significantly different from failed ACLR patients.
TT-TG distance was significantly lower in EDS patients compared to both intact and failed ACLR literature cohorts.
BMI differed significantly between EDS patients undergoing meniscus repair versus meniscectomy.
Demographic and anatomical factors did not significantly differ between patients who did versus did not receive chondroplasty or lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET).
Demographic and anatomical risk factors had no significant influence on development of concomitant meniscus or chondral injuries in EDS ACL patients.
No significant differences in ACLR outcomes were detected between graft types (BPTB autograft, hamstring autograft, hamstring allograft) used in EDS patients.
Vascular (Type IV) EDS results from defects in the COL3A1 gene encoding the alpha-1 chain of type III collagen, causing fragility of vascular tissues and hollow organs.
Laboring patients with vascular (Type IV) EDS have been reported to have maternal mortality rates as high as 25%.

A ketamine bolus-and-infusion regimen (two 10 mg boluses 20 minutes apart followed by a 20 mg/hour infusion, total 3 hours) provided effective labor analgesia in a patient with type 4 EDS, opioid contraindication, and malignant hyperthermia family history, resulting in an uncomplicated vaginal delivery.
A prior RCT found that low-dose ketamine (0.2 mg/kg loading dose and 0.2 mg/kg/hour infusion) significantly reduced perceived labor pain compared to placebo in otherwise healthy parturients.
In a study of 73 women, 85% who received ketamine infusion during vaginal delivery reported relief from labor pain, with no significant maternal or fetal side effects.
Ketamine readily crosses the placental barrier during labor and produces transient but significant hypertension in the mother only, not the fetus.
Across two studies totaling 145 neonates exposed to maternal ketamine during labor, all had APGAR scores greater than 4, suggesting low risk of adverse neonatal outcomes.

Neuraxial anesthesia was avoided in this type 4 EDS patient due to a theoretical increased risk of epidural hematoma, consistent with prior recommendations to avoid neuraxial techniques in this population.
A family history of malignant hyperthermia contraindicated the use of volatile anesthetic agents and succinylcholine in this patient, complicating potential emergent cesarean delivery planning.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by heterozygous variants in COL3A1, resulting in tissue and vessel fragility and increased risk of aneurysms and dissections.
Two of the five children with vEDS experienced a childhood vascular event, both involving cerebral vessels.
One patient with vEDS was found to have a mild aortic root dilatation.
One patient died from an aortic dissection in early adulthood despite years of normal MRA surveillance findings, indicating routine imaging surveillance did not predict this fatal vascular event.
The findings highlight variable expressivity of vEDS, including the occurrence of severe vascular events in childhood.
Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage rates did not differ significantly between children with EDS and non-EDS controls.
Children with EDS had a significantly higher rate of a past medical history of easy bleeding compared to non-EDS controls.
Children with EDS had significantly higher use of clotting agents compared to non-EDS controls.
Children with EDS had a significantly higher rate of family history of easy bleeding compared to non-EDS controls.
An association between EDS and concomitant coagulation disorders, including von Willebrand disease and hemophilia, was noted clinically but did not reach statistical significance.

Interpretative phenomenological analysis of interviews with four autistic women living with EDS identified three superordinate themes—'Transformation,' 'Making sense,' and 'The negatives'—describing how co-occurring EDS and autism shaped participants' identity.

Illness identity among participants with co-occurring EDS and autism was found to be dynamic and individually variable, shaped by biopsychosocial factors such as healthcare professionals' attitudes, awareness of the conditions, stigma, community support, and symptom severity.
The study concludes that autistic individuals living with EDS need more individualised, supportive care given the variability in how they experience and integrate their conditions.

Whole exome sequencing achieved a definitive genetic diagnosis in 7 of 24 patients (29.17%) with difficult and complicated pulmonary disease, identifying nine pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants across six genes.
Whole exome sequencing demonstrated diagnostic value in identifying vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) among patients presenting with rare pulmonary involvement.
FB-EVAR achieved 100% technical success in all 15 HTAD patients, with successful deployment of components, patency of all target vessels, and no type I/III endoleaks at completion angiography.
No patients died within 30 days or during the index hospitalization following FB-EVAR.
Midterm patient survival after FB-EVAR was 100% at 6 months and 93.3% at both 1 and 3 years.
One-third of HTAD patients required a secondary intervention during follow-up after FB-EVAR.
The cumulative incidence of secondary interventions at 1 year was estimated at 10.0%.
Endoleaks occurred in one-third of HTAD patients after FB-EVAR, mostly type II with two type IC.
Nearly half of patients showed aneurysm sac shrinkage of more than 5 mm on follow-up imaging after FB-EVAR.
One patient developed delayed spinal cord ischemia (paraparesis) on postoperative day 3 that fully resolved after therapeutic CSF drainage.
One patient treated with FB-EVAR in the native thoracic aorta developed a retrograde thoracic dissection 3 years later, successfully managed with carotid-subclavian bypass and TEVAR.
Intraprocedural complications occurred in 3 patients, including subclavian artery dissection, iliac branch perforation, and a failed percutaneous femoral access requiring conversion to open access.
Among the 15 HTAD patients treated, genetic diagnoses were Marfan syndrome in 9, Loeys-Dietz syndrome in 4, and vascular EDS or ACTA2 mutation in 1 patient each.
In a prior study of 2553 MS and 180 vEDS patients, MS patients were more likely to present with type A aortic dissection than vEDS patients, though HTAD type did not significantly predict mortality.
In the largest multicenter endovascular repair series for connective tissue disease, 5-year survival was 80% for MS/LDS patients but only 40% for vEDS patients.
A cited study found the risk of aortic dissection surgery was highest in LDS (25% by age 38), followed by MS (51% by age 51), while bicuspid aortic valve patients had a much lower risk (~10%).
A cited study reported that ACTA2 mutations are associated with an elevated risk of aortic dissection and death, with presentation varying by mutation type and other factors.
A cited study found that HTAD presence is associated with increased risk of retrograde type A dissection and stent-induced new entry after endovascular stent-graft placement.

A cited series found reoperative open TAAA repair carries high mortality (23%), with age >70 years, eGFR <48 mL/min/1.73m2, and emergency presentation as independent predictors, reaching 80% mortality when all three factors were present.
A large cited series reported overall 7.5% mortality for open TAAA repair across 3309 patients, with only 3.1% mortality among 288 repairs in MS patients.
A landmark cited series of 300 Marfan syndrome patients undergoing open TAAA/dissection repair reported 4% perioperative mortality and 83% 5-year survival.
A 2023 cited retrospective analysis found similar operative mortality for open TAAA repair in Marfan syndrome patients versus those without MS.
Cam morphology is far more prevalent in males (20-30% of the general male population, up to >90% in high-risk athletes) than in females (0-10%).
Hooper et al. found male patients were nearly 40 times more likely than females to present with cam-type morphology.
Nepple et al. reported a greater mean alpha angle in men than women among patients requiring hip arthroscopy.
3D analysis showed male cam lesions had significantly greater height and volume than female cam lesions, even after normalizing for femoral size.
Pincer-type impingement and coxa profunda are more commonly observed in females than males.
Females are two to four times more likely than males to have developmental dysplasia of the hip and borderline dysplasia.
Females tend to have increased acetabular anteversion, while males more often present with relative or true acetabular retroversion.

Fabricant et al. found that patients with relative femoral retroversion (<5° femoral anteversion) experience less improvement after hip arthroscopy than those with normal or increased femoral version.

In a multicenter cohort of over 1,400 patients, males more often underwent femoroplasty, acetabuloplasty, acetabular chondroplasty, microfracture, and loose body removal, while females more often underwent trochanteric bursectomy, gluteus medius/minimus repair, and labral debridement.
Females more often present with insidious-onset, non-specific pain (lateral hip, buttock, back) while males more often report acute traumatic-onset pain localized to the anterior groin ('C-sign').
Clohisy et al. found that females undergoing hip arthroscopy for FAI had significantly lower preoperative Modified Harris Hip Score, HOOS, and UCLA activity scores than males.

A systematic review of over 200,000 patients across 74 studies showed females present with more severe pain and disability on preoperative VAS and patient-reported outcomes despite less severe radiographic FAI.
One study found females had significantly greater internal rotation range of motion in flexion than males.

In a cohort of 2,701 patients undergoing primary hip arthroscopy for FAI and labral tears, generalized ligamentous laxity (Beighton score ≥4) was present in 38.6% of females compared to 13.6% of males.
Females are at increased risk for ischiofemoral impingement due to a wider pelvis with smaller femoral offset.
Females experience greater trochanteric pain syndrome at a 4:1 ratio compared to males.
A meta-analysis of 74 studies (>200,000 patients) found the relative risk of complications for females after hip arthroscopy was 2.34, indicating significantly increased risk compared to males.
Bedi et al. found male patients were at increased risk for developing heterotopic ossification after hip arthroscopy, possibly related to the larger capsular cut and femoroplasty required.

Females are at increased risk for gross and microinstability following hip arthroscopy, possibly related to increased prevalence of generalized ligamentous laxity and acetabular/femoral morphologic differences.

Two large database studies identified female sex as a risk factor for revision hip arthroscopy and conversion to total hip arthroplasty, though more recent studies have not consistently replicated this.

A systematic review of 38 studies with 40,194 hips found no significant sex differences in postoperative PROs overall, but males were more likely to achieve minimal clinically important difference (MCID).
A machine learning model identified female sex as a predictive factor for achieving MCID on patient-reported outcomes after hip arthroscopy, contrasting with other systematic review findings.

McCormack et al.'s systematic review found one-third of included studies determined female sex was a negative predictor of postoperative outcomes, 13% found it a positive predictor, and 58% found no sex-based differences.
Dooley et al. found a 91.9% return-to-sport rate among collegiate/professional athletes after hip arthroscopy for FAI, with 73% of those unable to return being female.
Most surveyed surgeons (69.6%) reported that a comorbid connective tissue disorder is a negative prognostic factor for postoperative pain relief after slipped rib repair.
60.9% of surveyed surgeons reported hypermobility disorder as a negative prognostic factor for postoperative pain relief following slipped rib repair.
A history of trauma or an inciting event was reported by 82.6% of surgeons as a positive prognostic factor for postoperative pain relief after slipped rib repair.
Connective tissue disorder was identified by 58.3% of surgeons as one of the two most common factors associated with recurrence of slipping rib syndrome after repair.
Hypermobility disorder was identified by 45.8% of surgeons as one of the two most common factors associated with recurrence of slipping rib syndrome after repair.
Trauma was also reported by 37.5% of surgeons as a factor associated with recurrence of SRS after repair, though less commonly than connective tissue/hypermobility disorders.
History and physical examination were reported as the most important diagnostic factors for slipping rib syndrome, while CT imaging was rated least important by most surgeons.
There was high variability among surgeons in the use of dynamic ultrasound and intercostal nerve block as diagnostic tools for SRS.
Rib block with lidocaine and rest/ice/heat were the most common conservative treatments offered prior to surgical intervention for SRS, with high variability across all non-surgical modalities.
Failure of medical management was almost universally reported as the indication to proceed with surgical repair of SRS.
Suturing of ribs/cartilage was the most frequently identified integral step in the slipped rib repair operation, followed by cartilage excision and use of a biodegradable plate.

Vertical rib plating with a bioabsorbable plate as an adjunct to costal cartilage excision showed an improved rate of recurrence and reoperation compared to isolated costal cartilage excision, per cited literature (McMahon et al.).

The costal margin reconstruction technique (costal cartilage excision with autograft spacer and overlay bioabsorbable plate) was associated with long-term improvement in symptoms and quality of life, and only a 1% rate of revisional surgery in the largest cohort of SRS patients studied to date, per cited literature (Hansen et al.).

Cryoablation used with cartilaginous rib excision, costal cartilage excision, and vertical rib plating was associated with significantly decreased in-hospital opioid use and length of stay in pediatric patients, per cited literature (Lai et al.).
Most surgeons reported that patients experience the majority of pain relief between 1 and 3 months after slipped rib repair surgery.
HBOT treatment reduced the patient's fibromyalgia symptom severity as measured by the FIQR.
The Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria Questionnaire composite score improved after HBOT despite concurrent medication reduction.
Following HBOT, the patient was able to discontinue pregabalin (Lyrica) entirely and reduce duloxetine (Cymbalta) dosage by 50% while still improving symptomatically.
Sleep quality improved with fewer disturbances after HBOT.

Post-HBOT SPECT imaging showed improved regional cerebral blood flow/perfusion compared with baseline, especially in regions tied to motor function, executive processing, memory, and emotional regulation.

DTI revealed significant post-HBOT changes in white matter integrity (fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity) in pathways related to motor control, memory, decision-making, and sensory processing, interpreted as evidence of neuroplasticity.
Computerized neurocognitive testing (NeuroTrax) showed post-HBOT gains in attention, information processing speed, executive function, and motor coordination.
A minor 4.6% decline in memory domain scores was observed post-HBOT, which the authors attribute to normal single-day testing variability rather than treatment failure.
Functional/mobility testing showed improved gait stability, weight transfer, walking pace, and center-of-pressure control after HBOT.

The authors describe childhood trauma as linked to persistent HPA axis alterations, dysregulated cortisol secretion, heightened stress reactivity, and maladaptive pain processing contributing to fibromyalgia.

HBOT is proposed to act via the hyperoxic-hypoxic paradox, upregulating hypoxia-inducible factors that activate genes for angiogenesis, neurogenesis, and mitochondrial biogenesis, alongside BDNF release and synaptogenesis.
Healthy controls showed statistically significant pain-inhibitory conditioned pain modulation (analgesia) when the test stimulus was set 3°C above their heat pain threshold.
