Healthy controls showed no significant change in pain ratings from conditioning when the test stimulus was set 1°C above their heat pain threshold.
Healthy controls exhibited hyperalgesia (anti-CPM) rather than analgesia when the test stimulus was set 1°C below their heat pain threshold, replicating prior rodent findings.

The subjective perceived intensity of the test stimulus, rather than its objective temperature alone, was found to determine the direction and magnitude of conditioned pain modulation in healthy controls.

Participants with fibromyalgia showed no significant analgesic CPM or hyperalgesic anti-CPM response across the tested stimulus intensities, unlike healthy controls, suggesting dysfunction of the underlying descending modulatory mechanisms.
Fibromyalgia patients showed worse low-contrast visual acuity than controls over the 5-year follow-up period.
Fibromyalgia patients showed worse color discrimination (Lanthony's C index) than controls over the 5-year follow-up.
Fibromyalgia patients had progressive thinning of the nasal inferior macular ganglion cell layer compared with controls over 5 years.
Changes in color vision over time were associated with thinning of the macular ganglion cell layer in fibromyalgia patients.
No correlation was observed between progressive structural/functional visual changes and fibromyalgia disease severity.
Both functional and structural connectivity among DPMS regions collectively explained significant variance in Fibromyalgia Index (FMI) scores across the full UK Biobank sample.

The overall association between structural DPMS connectivity and FMI was driven primarily by participants with chronic pain, while functional connectivity was associated with FMI in both chronic pain and pain-free groups.
Greater PAG-amygdala resting-state functional connectivity was positively associated with higher FMI scores in participants with chronic pain.
A nominal difference in PAG-amygdala functional connectivity's association with FMI between chronic pain and no chronic pain groups did not survive multiple comparison correction.
The overall pattern of structural DPMS connectivity-FMI associations differed significantly between people with and without chronic pain.
In participants with chronic pain, PAG-amygdala structural connectivity was positively associated with FMI whereas PAG-hypothalamus structural connectivity was negatively associated with FMI.
No significant associations were found between structural DPMS connectivity edges and FMI in participants without chronic pain.
Wald tests confirmed that the association of PAG-amygdala and PAG-hypothalamus structural connectivity with FMI significantly differed between chronic pain and no chronic pain groups.
PAG-amygdala functional connectivity's association with FMI was partially mediated by fatigue and widespread pain, with a significant total indirect effect and a robust direct effect remaining.
PAG-amygdala structural connectivity's association with FMI was partially mediated by sleep duration, with the direct effect remaining robust.

Reduced PAG-hypothalamus structural connectivity was associated with greater FMI severity via a negative indirect pathway through depression, brain fog, fatigue and widespread pain, while a smaller opposing positive direct effect was also present.
A sensitivity analysis modeling SPACE symptoms as a single latent factor confirmed a significant negative indirect effect of PAG-hypothalamus structural connectivity on FMI.
Mediation via the SPACE latent symptom factor was not statistically significant for PAG-amygdala functional or structural connectivity after correction.

No significant associations were found between DPMS functional or structural connectivity and either DN4 neuropathic pain scores or average pain intensity, supporting specificity of DPMS-FMI associations to nociplastic rather than general/neuropathic pain.
The association between PAG-dlPFC functional connectivity and FMI reversed direction across the adult lifespan, being positive in younger adults and inverse in older adults.
Unlike functional connectivity, structural DPMS connectivity's association with FMI did not vary significantly across age groups.
Participants with self-reported chronic pain (53% of the cohort) had markedly higher FMI, WPI and SSS scores than those without chronic pain.
A slightly higher proportion of participants with chronic pain were female compared to those without chronic pain.
Among 440 women with fibromyalgia, 163 (37.0%) had documentation of at least one lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS) diagnosis.
Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) was the most commonly recorded LUTS diagnosis in the FM cohort, at 17.0% prevalence.
Urge incontinence (UI) was found in 15.2% of the fibromyalgia cohort, the second most common LUTS diagnosis.
Mixed incontinence (MI) was found in 10.9% of the fibromyalgia cohort.
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) was frequently reported in the fibromyalgia cohort at 13.6%, suggesting overlap between pain syndromes and urologic symptoms.
Interstitial cystitis (IC) was diagnosed in approximately 3% of fibromyalgia patients, a rate the authors suggest may underestimate true prevalence given known underdiagnosis of IC.
Obesity or severe obesity was present in 68.0% of the fibromyalgia cohort.
Depression was present in 42.3% of the fibromyalgia cohort.
Anxiety was present in 34.7% of the fibromyalgia cohort.
In multivariate logistic regression, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) was the strongest independent predictor of having any LUTS diagnosis in fibromyalgia patients, with an odds ratio of 8.53.
Anxiety was independently associated with the presence of any LUTS diagnosis in fibromyalgia patients, with an odds ratio of 4.62.
Depression approached but did not reach statistical significance as a predictor of LUTS after Bonferroni adjustment (OR 1.57, p=0.0855).

Obesity, age, race, and cardiovascular/metabolic comorbidities (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease) were not significantly associated with the presence of any LUTS in adjusted multivariate models.
Negative binomial regression showed IBS was significantly associated with a higher LUTS symptom burden (number of distinct LUTS subtypes per patient), with an incidence rate ratio of 2.86.
Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) was significantly associated with higher LUTS symptom burden in fibromyalgia patients, with an incidence rate ratio of 2.23.
Patients whose race was marked 'Other/Unknown' had a significantly higher LUTS symptom burden (IRR 2.56), though the authors caution this reflects a small subgroup.

IC/BPS patients can be stratified into a non-bladder-centric phenotype (85-90% of patients, non-low bladder capacity >500cc, more co-occurring symptoms) and a bladder-centric phenotype (10-15%, low bladder capacity ≤500cc, older, more Hunner lesions).
Approximately one-third of IC/BPS patients have confirmed small fiber polyneuropathy (SFPN) independent of diabetes mellitus.
Oaklander reported that approximately half of patients with fibromyalgia are SFPN-positive based on skin biopsy.
In a 2019 case series of complex chronic pelvic pain patients, 64% were SFPN-positive, with substantial overlap with fibromyalgia and IC/BPS diagnoses.
In a 2013 case series, corticosteroid treatment improved 67% of SFPN-positive patients, and adding IVIg increased improvement to 80%.
In a 2018 case series of 55 patients with apparent autoimmune SFPN, 77% were classified as IVIg responders with improvement in pain severity and autonomic function testing.
The first double-blind randomized controlled trial of IVIg in idiopathic SFPN found no significant effect on pain, though this trial excluded patients with a non-length-dependent pattern.

In patients with Sjögren's syndrome and SFPN refractory to conventional treatment, long-term low-dose IVIg produced no relapses in 9/12 patients over a mean follow-up of 25 months, with significant improvements in pain and quality of life.

In a subset of fibromyalgia patients with findings suggestive of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, IVIg treatment (n=15) produced significant improvement in pain, tenderness, and strength.

In a 2002 prospective cohort of chronic pain syndromes (largest subgroup fibromyalgia, 48/130 patients), IVIg produced >25% pain relief in about half and >70% pain relief in a smaller subset, but the study lacked a control group and blinding.
A 2022 review found that anti-TNF-alpha therapy was the only immunotherapy showing superiority versus placebo for IC/BPS treatment, based on a single encouraging study.
A 2020 Cochrane review found immune modulators effective versus control for IC/BPS treatment, but rated the certainty of this evidence as 'very low' due to a small number of studies.
The bladder wall in IC/BPS shows increased infiltration by inflammatory cells including mast cells, T lymphocytes, and eosinophils.
IgG autoantibodies targeting bladder epithelium and muscle fibers have been detected in patients with IC/BPS.
Common autoantibodies found in IC/BPS overlap with those implicated in atopic dermatitis and Sjögren's syndrome, supporting an autoimmune theory of IC/BPS.
Preliminary studies suggest the non-bladder-centric IC/BPS phenotype, which has more systemic non-urologic symptoms, contains more SFPN-positive individuals than the bladder-centric phenotype.
Blood-based markers of dysimmunity/inflammation (antinuclear antibodies, elevated ESR, low complement C3/C4, Sjögren's autoantibodies) may predict better response to IVIg in SFPN patients.
The Flow-SuperRCA assay detected KIT p.D816V in a significantly greater proportion of whole bone marrow samples than conventional ASOqPCR (73% vs 53%).
Flow-SuperRCA detected KIT p.D816V in whole peripheral blood at a substantially higher rate than ASOqPCR (59% vs 35%).
Using paired BM/PB samples, Flow-SuperRCA newly detected clonal KIT p.D816V in 18% of patients previously diagnosed with nonclonal MCAS, suggesting reclassification as monoclonal MCAS.
In paired samples, the clonal nature of disease was newly detected in 64% of MMAS and 31% of SM cases using Flow-SuperRCA compared with ASOqPCR.
KIT p.D816V was undetectable by both ASOqPCR and Flow-SuperRCA in all 98 controls (healthy donors and allergic rhinoconjunctivitis patients), confirming assay specificity.
KIT p.D816V variant allele frequency in paired bone marrow versus peripheral blood by ASOqPCR was highly correlated, though generally higher in bone marrow.
With the Flow-SuperRCA assay, KIT p.D816V VAF in bone marrow versus peripheral blood was also highly correlated, with lower median VAF in blood across all diagnostic subtypes.
KIT p.D816V VAF measured by ASOqPCR and Flow-SuperRCA in whole bone marrow were highly correlated with each other despite higher overall positivity by Flow-SuperRCA.
Diagnostic accuracy for KIT p.D816V detection was higher for Flow-SuperRCA than ASOqPCR in both bone marrow (94% vs 87%) and peripheral blood (86% vs 76%).
Among bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM) patients, Flow-SuperRCA detected KIT p.D816V in bone marrow far more frequently than ASOqPCR (97% vs 70%).
Among BMM patients, Flow-SuperRCA detected KIT p.D816V in blood far more frequently than ASOqPCR (80% vs 30%).
In indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM), Flow-SuperRCA detected KIT p.D816V in blood more often than ASOqPCR (98% vs 83%).

Two of ten cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) patients who were KIT p.D816V-negative in whole bone marrow and blood tested positive in purified bone marrow mast cells, suggesting low-level extracutaneous mutant cell infiltration missed by conventional testing.
Serum basal tryptase levels were significantly higher in systemic mastocytosis than in other diagnostic groups, including after hereditary alpha-tryptasemia correction.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) was more prevalent among patients with nonclonal MCAS and cutaneous mastocytosis than among those with systemic mastocytosis.

Patients newly diagnosed with MMAS via Flow-SuperRCA had a distinct clinical profile compared with true nc-MCAS and previously diagnosed MMAS/BMM, including lower REMA scores, lower HαT frequency, more urticaria and pruritus, and fewer cardiovascular symptoms (presyncope/syncope) during anaphylaxis.
None of the 12 patients carrying non-D816V KIT mutations tested positive for KIT p.D816V by either ASOqPCR or Flow-SuperRCA, confirming assay specificity for the D816V variant.
Among 2701 cancer patients with CHIP mutations, DNMT3A was the most common mutated gene (52.1%), followed by TET2 (22.4%) and ASXL1 (13.7%).
Increasing age was associated with higher odds of harboring CHIP mutations in cancer patients.
Compared with current smokers, never smokers and previous smokers had significantly lower odds of harboring CHIP mutations.
Chemotherapy exposure was associated with a greater occurrence of CHIP mutations in cancer patients.
PPM1D, TP53, and SF3B1 CHIP mutations were significantly more frequent in patients treated with chemotherapy than those without.
mCAs, including loss of Y (LOY) and loss of X (LOX) chromosome, were common in this cancer cohort, with expanded mCAs found in nearly a fifth of mCA carriers.
Individuals with expanded mCAs (cell fraction >10%) had significantly higher odds of also carrying CHIP mutations, though overall mCA carriage was not associated with higher CHIP odds.
Mosaic loss of the Y chromosome (LOY) was inversely correlated with the presence of CHIP mutations, while mosaic loss of the X chromosome (LOX) was positively associated with CHIP mutations in women.
Individuals with TET2 mutations had higher odds of also having mCAs.
Patients diagnosed with lung cancer had higher odds of both CHIP mutations and mCAs than patients with other cancers.
Cancer patients with any CHIP mutations had a significantly higher risk of incident cardiovascular disease compared with those without CHIP.
CHIP mutations were also associated with significantly higher overall mortality in cancer patients.
Patients with expanded CHIP mutations (VAF ≥10%) had greater risk for incident CVD and overall mortality than those with lower VAF CHIP.

Patients carrying three or more distinct CHIP mutations had substantially elevated risks across incident CVD, incident CAD, CVD death, CAD death, and all-cause mortality compared with those without multiple mutations.
The elevated incident-CVD risk seen with CHIP mutations alone was not observed when CHIP co-occurred with mCAs, mirroring the null association seen with mCAs alone.
Patients with mCAs alone (without CHIP) had a significantly higher risk of death from coronary artery disease, whereas CHIP alone did not show this elevated CAD-death risk.

Cancer patients carrying both CHIP mutations and mCAs had the highest risk of all-cause mortality, showing a dose-response relationship, although the interaction between CHIP and mCA was not statistically synergistic.
The combination of CHIP mutations with mosaic loss of the X chromosome (LOX) was associated with a more than two-fold increased risk of death from coronary artery disease.

Women with corpus uteri cancer carrying CHIP mutations had a higher risk of both incident cardiovascular disease and incident coronary artery disease compared with corpus uteri cancer patients without CHIP.
Villous atrophy in IBD reduces DAO expression in mature villous cells, impairing histamine degradation in the gut.
Mucosal histamine content and secretion are increased in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis compared to non-IBD tissue.
More than 50 nonsynonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms have been identified in the DAO-encoding gene, with different variants affecting different ancestral populations.
In a cohort of 133 histamine-intolerant patients, the most frequent symptoms reported were abdominal distension, fullness, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation.
H1 and H4 histamine receptor antagonists have been shown to dose-dependently reduce post-inflammatory visceral hypersensitivity.
Mast cell numbers are increased in the intestinal mucosa of IBD patients, particularly in the ileum and colon.
Mast cells from IBD colonic tissue release significantly more histamine than mast cells from healthy controls.
Mast-cell-deficient Ws/Ws rats exhibited altered disease severity in DSS-induced colitis, suggesting mast cells modulate colitis severity.
Histamine-deficient (HDC-/-) mice with DSS-induced colitis showed a marked reduction in IL-10-producing immune cells, indicating a role for mast-cell-derived histamine in immunomodulation.

IBD-associated dysbiosis is characterized by a decline in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, including butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia spp., with an increase in opportunistic Proteobacteria.
A study of histamine-intolerant individuals found a significant gut microbiota imbalance versus healthy controls, with reduced beneficial bacteria and increased histamine-producing species.

Metagenomic analyses of IBD colonic samples show enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae members carrying histidine decarboxylase gene potential, suggesting microbial histamine may contribute to mucosal immune dysregulation.

Analysis of longitudinal stool samples from the iHMP (IBD Multi'omics) cohort showed increased abundance of histamine and histidine decarboxylase genes in the gut microbiome of Crohn's disease patients, with Morganella morganii, some Limosilactobacillus reuteri strains, and Enterobacteriaceae strains identified as histamine producers.
Blockade of the H4 histamine receptor has been proposed to reduce mast cell accumulation and visceral hyperalgesia in a cohort of IBS patients.
Morganella morganii, a potent histamine-producing bacterium, is found in higher abundance in IBD patients, especially those with ulcerative colitis.
Elevated IgG and IgA anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) have been observed in Crohn's disease and other autoimmune conditions, serving as serological markers of immune dysregulation.
Food-derived yeast can directly activate dysregulated CD4+ T-cell responses in Crohn's disease patients, contributing to intestinal inflammation, as shown using PBMCs stimulated with yeast lysate.
An interventional study of yeast exclusion in 19 patients with Crohn's disease reported a significant reduction in mean CDAI (Crohn's Disease Activity Index) during the exclusion period.
The Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet, which eliminates yeast among other components, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in a recent study of pediatric and adult populations with CD.
A high-salt diet exacerbated colitis symptoms in mice by reducing Lactobacillus abundance and decreasing colonic butyrate production, likely via p38/MAPK signaling.

Excess dietary sodium worsens intestinal inflammation by boosting IL-17A and TNF-alpha production in gut immune cells and may cause sodium buildup in colonic tissue, disrupting the epithelial barrier.
A randomized controlled trial comparing the Mediterranean diet with the specific carbohydrate diet in adults with mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease found no diet was superior for symptom control.
The low FODMAP diet improves quality of life and gastrointestinal symptoms in IBD but is not ideal for alleviating mucosal inflammation.
In IBD patients meeting IBS criteria in remission, a 6-week low FODMAP diet improved gut symptoms and diarrhea but did not improve constipation or inflammatory markers.
Ultra-processed food intake is positively associated with urinary 1-methylhistamine (MHA), a potential biomarker for histamine intolerance produced via HNMT methylation of histamine.
The DAO SNP rs1049793 does not appear to influence genetic susceptibility to Crohn's disease, though its role in symptom severity or dietary response remains unclear.

Across multiple fecal metagenome studies (including a 2451-sample analysis), IBD samples consistently show higher abundance of HDC (histidine decarboxylase) gene clusters despite variability in which bacterial phyla are enriched.
Psoriasis patients with allergies had significantly greater disease severity than those without allergies, based on medication usage as a severity proxy.
Co-stimulation of HaCaT keratinocytes with IL-17A and histamine synergistically increased production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6 via activation of the MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway.
Co-stimulation of HaCaT keratinocytes with IL-17A and histamine synergistically increased production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL36G via activation of the MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway.
Co-stimulation with IL-17A and histamine increased IL-17RA expression in HaCaT keratinocytes, as confirmed by immunoblotting.

HDM-sensitized and challenged mice subsequently treated with imiquimod showed aggravated psoriasis-like phenotypes, with higher Psoriasis Severity Index scores and increased epidermal thickness compared to IMQ alone.
HDM-sensitized and IMQ-challenged mice showed enhanced differentiation and activation of Th17 cells compared to IMQ-only controls.
HDM-sensitized and IMQ-challenged mice showed enhanced differentiation and activation of Th2 cells compared to IMQ-only controls.
Skin biopsies from HDM-sensitized, IMQ-challenged mice showed increased mast cell activation compared to IMQ-only controls, indicating amplified inflammation.

Single-cell RNA sequencing identified three mast cell subpopulations in ovarian cancer tissue, with mast cell-2 specifically and highly expressing NR4A3 while mast cell-1 showed markedly decreased NR4A3 expression and mast cell-3 showed no expression.
The proportion of NR4A3-expressing mast cell-2 subpopulation and overall NR4A3 expression in mast cells were significantly higher in metastatic ovarian tumors compared with primary tumors.
Survival analysis using GSE26193 and TCGA ovarian cancer datasets showed NR4A3 expression was positively associated with poor prognosis.

Immunofluorescence showed a significantly increased number of NR4A3-expressing mast cells (co-stained with TPSAB1) in ovarian tumor tissue compared with normal ovarian cyst tissue, and NR4A3 expression in mast cells was associated with distant metastasis status and tumor grade but not lymph node metastasis status in 60 patients.
Overexpression of NR4A3 in bone-marrow-derived mast cells decreased mRNA expression of tryptase alpha/beta 1 (TPSAB1).
NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells released significantly less histamine after Compound 48/80-induced degranulation compared to control mast cells.
NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells released significantly less LTA4 (leukotriene) after degranulation induction compared to control mast cells.

Transcriptome sequencing of NR4A3-overexpressing versus control mast cells found 472 up-regulated and 102 down-regulated genes, including down-regulation of Tpsab1 and Mcpt8, with differential genes enriched in necroptosis, cell cycle, and other pathways.
CXCL16 was significantly up-regulated in NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells, confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting.
IL-8 was significantly up-regulated in NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells, confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting.

Co-culture with NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells increased M2 polarization markers CD163 and CD206 in RAW264.7 macrophages compared with control mast cell co-culture, confirmed by qPCR and flow cytometry.

Blocking CXCL16 and IL-8 signaling with the receptor inhibitors ML339 and Reparixin reduced the mean fluorescence intensity of the M2 marker CD206 in macrophages co-cultured with NR4A3-high mast cells.

Western blotting showed significantly increased STAT6 phosphorylation, increased TGF-β, and decreased IL-6 in macrophages co-cultured with NR4A3-high mast cells compared with control mast cell co-culture, indicating activation of the JAK2/STAT6 pathway; IL-4 and IL-13 levels were not stimulated.

Co-culture with exogenous IL-4 and IL-13-induced M2 macrophages plus NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells did not further increase the proportion of M2-polarized cells, indicating no synergistic effect between NR4A3-high mast cells and IL-4/IL-13 in driving M2 polarization.
Direct co-culture of NR4A3-high mast cells with ovarian cancer cell lines ID8 and OVHM did not directly promote proliferation, migration, or invasion of the cancer cells.
Macrophages pretreated with NR4A3-high mast cells did not significantly promote ovarian cancer cell proliferation in CCK8 and colony formation assays.

M2 macrophages induced by NR4A3-high mast cells significantly promoted the migration and invasion of ovarian cancer cells in wound healing and Transwell assays, an effect that was reduced by CXCL16/IL-8 pathway inhibitors ML339 and Reparixin.

In a subcutaneous xenograft model, mice co-injected with ID8 ovarian cancer cells and NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells developed significantly larger tumors than controls, with higher CD206 expression by IHC.

In a mast-cell-deficient mouse peritoneal metastasis model, mice injected with ID8 plus NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells developed significantly more abdominal wall metastases and greater ascites volume than mice injected with ID8 alone or ID8 plus control mast cells.

Flow cytometry of ascites showed that the proportion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was significantly reduced in mice bearing ID8 tumors with NR4A3-overexpressing mast cells compared with control mast cells, indicating impaired anti-tumor immunity, alongside increased M2 macrophage content.

KEGG gene set enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes from ovarian granulosa cells identified 'regulation of mast cell activation' as one of the significantly enriched pathways in the PCOS group, linked via network analysis to stress-induced inflammatory responses and sex hormone signaling.
Two double-blind randomized controlled trials found that IVIG did not significantly differ from placebo in reducing neuropathy severity or pain in patients with painful small fiber neuropathy.
Retrospective cohort studies of IVIG for painful small fiber neuropathy varied in quality and produced mixed results, with some reporting significant pain reduction and others not.

IVIG appeared to show potential efficacy in autoimmune-associated SFN subtypes, particularly those positive for TS-HDS/FGFR-3 antibodies, with some retrospective studies reporting pain and functional improvements.
Adverse events, including infusion reactions, were commonly reported with IVIG treatment across the included studies.
The effect of IVIG on intraepidermal nerve fiber density was inconsistent across studies, with some reporting improvement and others showing no significant change.
The review authors concluded that standardized protocols, biomarker-based patient selection, and large well-controlled trials are needed to establish definitive efficacy of IVIG for painful SFN.
Peak sensory latencies of the median and sural nerves were significantly longer in males than in females.
Sensory median nerve peak latency increased and amplitude decreased with advancing age across decades.

Subjects in their 50s showed significantly delayed sensory median nerve peak latencies compared to those in their 20s and 40s, and significantly reduced median amplitude compared to those in their 30s.
Sural nerve sensory NCS values did not differ significantly among the different age decades.
Left median nerve CSP end latency and left sural nerve CSP onset latency differed significantly across age decade groups.
Subjects in their 50s showed significantly delayed left median CSP end latency compared to those in their 20s and 30s, and delayed left sural CSP onset latency compared to those in their 20s.
CSP onset latencies of the bilateral median nerves and the ulnar nerve were significantly delayed in males compared to females.
Left median and ulnar nerve CSP end latencies were significantly delayed in males compared to females.
CSP end latencies of both sural nerves were significantly delayed in males compared to females.
Males showed a significantly longer CSP duration in the right sural nerve compared to females.

Males were significantly taller and had longer upper limb lengths than females, which the authors propose as the likely explanation for observed sex differences in CSP/NCS latencies rather than sex per se.
The onset latency difference between sural and median nerves positively correlated with age on both the right and left sides.
Side-to-side (right vs left) variability in CSP parameters was not statistically significant, supporting the clinical suitability of unilateral CSP testing.
In a small cohort of acute-onset SFN patients, about one-fourth had FGFR3 antibodies and 70% had IgG immunoreactivity against nerve tissue, supporting immune-mediated pathophysiology.

Autoantibodies against TS-HDS, FGFR3, and Plexin D1 were found in 37-44% of idiopathic SFN patients and were significantly associated with female sex, nonlength-dependent distribution, and acute onset.

Mice injected with IgG from Plexin D1-antibody-positive patients, but not from negative individuals, showed transiently increased mechanical and thermal sensitivity, supporting a pathogenic role for anti-Plexin D1 antibodies.

Autoantibodies against LGI1 and CASPR2, usually linked to autoimmune encephalitis, are also associated with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, dysautonomia, neuropathic pain, and reduced IENFD, suggesting a pathogenic role in SFN.
In a retrospective study of 91 pure SFN patients, 11 of 12 patients treated with IVIg showed IENFD recovery, especially those with Plexin D1 autoantibodies.

In a cohort of 54 idiopathic SFN patients, 44.4% had TS-HDS, FGFR-3, or Plexin D1 antibodies, and those who completed IVIg treatment showed improvement in clinical examination, questionnaire scores, and IENFD.
The only double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of IVIg in TS-HDS/FGFR-3 autoantibody-associated SFN showed no benefit on pain, clinical examination, or IENFD over 6 months.
Among patients with painful long COVID, nearly half showed a nonlength-dependent pattern of skin denervation on biopsy.
An association was reported between natural killer (NK) cell genetic variants and both long-COVID-associated and prepandemic small fiber neuropathy.
POTS, characterized by orthostatic intolerance and exaggerated heart rate rise, has been reported among autonomic symptoms in long-COVID/SFN patients.
Individuals of Native American ancestry carrying a Neanderthal-introgressed SCN9A haplotype (M932L, V991L, D1908G) exhibited lower mechanical pain thresholds after mustard-oil sensitization.
The SCN9A variant W1538R, located within the Neanderthal-introgressed region, was significantly enriched in chronic pain patients in association with the archaic haplotype.

Lacosamide, a sodium channel blocker, showed efficacy in reducing pain in SFN patients carrying SCN9A variants in an RCT, though effect was influenced by specific variants that can inhibit its pharmacological action.
Gain-of-function variants in SCN9A, SCN10A, or SCN11A were found in 12% of pure SFN patients, rising to 18% when SCN7A, SCN3A, and beta-subunit genes SCN1B-SCN4B were included.
The frequency of SCN gene variants was similar between painful (18.5%) and painless (18.8%) SFN, indicating SCN variant burden alone does not distinguish pain phenotype.
SKAT-O aggregate rare-variant analysis in chronic pain patients versus healthy elderly controls found SCN genes less enriched than TRPA1 and PTPRZ1.
The TRPA1 p.Ala172Val variant is linked to an episodic widespread chronic pain phenotype and causes a gain-of-function of the channel in response to agonists.
Whole-exome sequencing in early-onset (<45 years) painful SFN cases showed enrichment of variants in TRP genes, suggesting a role in pain modulation alongside sodium channels.
Gene burden analysis found significant associations between rare OPRM1 variants and neuropathic pain, likely via abnormal mu-opioid receptor signaling.
A variant in the ANK2 gene, involved in cytoskeletal anchoring, was linked to the 'irritable nociceptor' phenotype.
Four miRNAs expressed in keratinocytes of SCN-related SFN patients correlated with NEDD4 transcription level, implicating NEDD4 in Nav1.7 regulation.

Distinct DNA methylation signatures discriminated painful from painless neuropathy phenotypes in type 2 diabetes, with GCH1, MYT1L, and MED16 emerging as promising differentially-methylated therapeutic targets.

Patients with painful diabetic neuropathy showed accelerated epigenetic aging (DNA methylation clocks, telomere length, immune cell composition, methylation-based plasma protein surrogates) compared with painless phenotype and healthy controls.

In fibromyalgia, some studies show coexisting peripheral small nerve fiber involvement demonstrated by skin denervation, abnormal C-fiber microneurography, and increased thermal thresholds on quantitative sensory testing.

In fibromyalgia, skin denervation typically shows a nonlength-dependent pattern accompanied by morphological abnormalities such as thinner nerve fibers and increased peptidergic innervation of glabrous skin arteriole-venule shunts.

SFN has been linked with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome; about half of these patients experience pain and dysautonomia, with higher thermal thresholds and small fiber morphological abnormalities including fiber tortuosity at corneal confocal microscopy.
Up to 21% of SFN patients have underlying immune-mediated diseases including Sjogren syndrome, sarcoidosis, or lupus erythematosus, or harbor pathogenic autoantibodies.
In sarcoidosis-associated SFN, there is a higher prevalence of symptoms beyond pain, including fatigue, restless leg syndrome, and cognitive impairment.
A B-cell-depleting monoclonal antibody has been proposed as a treatment for antibody-associated SFN, particularly for patients not responding to IVIg or corticosteroids.

Some studies show fibromyalgia patients have coexisting peripheral small nerve fiber involvement, evidenced by skin denervation, abnormal C-fiber function on microneurography, and increased thermal thresholds on quantitative sensory testing.
In fibromyalgia, skin denervation typically follows a nonlength-dependent pattern accompanied by thinner nerve fibers and increased peptidergic innervation of glabrous skin arteriole-venule shunts.

Syndromic small fiber pathology, lacking classic SFN clinical features, has been described in fibromyalgia, chronic visceral pain, irritable bowel disease, bladder pain syndrome, and complex regional pain syndrome type 1.
Fibromyalgia symptoms can overlap with those of other clinical entities such as IBD, particularly in cases with multisystem involvement including dyshidrosis and urogenital dysfunction.

Recent studies have linked small fiber neuropathy with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, a condition marked by fatigue, cognitive impairment, muscle pain, headache, and tachycardia, potentially triggered by infection or stress.

About half of ME/CFS patients experience pain and dysautonomia along with higher thermal thresholds and small fiber morphological abnormalities including corneal nerve fiber tortuosity on corneal confocal microscopy.
POTS is a recently described example of syndromic small fiber pathology occurring without the typical chronic pain features of classic SFN.
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is a recently described syndromic condition associated with small fiber pathology in the absence of typical chronic pain features.
Parkinson's disease is among the neurodegenerative disorders recently associated with small fiber pathology.
ALS is included among the neurodegenerative disorders linked to small fiber pathology in the absence of typical peripheral neuropathy features.
Current diagnostic criteria require the combination of compatible clinical symptoms/signs and objective evidence of small fiber involvement via skin biopsy and/or quantitative sensory testing.

Skin biopsy with quantification of intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) is considered the gold standard, providing structural confirmation of small fiber loss and additional information on fiber distribution and regenerative sprouting.
QST diagnostic accuracy in SFN is significantly enhanced when using combined limit and level methods, particularly combined cold and warm detection thresholds.
Corneal confocal microscopy's diagnostic yield appears lower than that of skin biopsy in idiopathic SFN, despite its noninvasive validated structural profile for small fiber damage.

Corneal confocal microscopy provides markers of systemic inflammation and small fiber pathology through decreased corneal nerve fiber density, increased tortuosity, and increased dendritic cells, allowing longitudinal monitoring of disease progression or recovery.

Perception threshold tracking (PTT), a psychophysical method introduced in diabetic neuropathy, shows high diagnostic concordance with both corneal confocal microscopy and thermal detection thresholds.

Autonomic testing, including heart rate variability analysis, QSART, and thermoregulatory sweat testing, provides valuable information on autonomic fiber integrity, especially useful when first-line investigations are inconclusive.

Microneurography allows direct recording of individual C-fiber activity, offering unique access to nociceptive processing not assessable by QST or skin biopsy, and has proven valuable in analgesic clinical trials and characterizing sodium channelopathies.

Cold-evoked potentials show enhanced sensitivity for cold-specific abnormalities but have limited utility in lower limb recordings due to low signal-to-noise ratio and habituation, and none of the evoked-potential modalities reliably activate C-fibers in the lower extremities.
Current guidelines recommend SNRIs (e.g. duloxetine), gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin), and tricyclic antidepressants as first-line pharmacological agents for SFN-related pain.
Treatment of SFN-related pain remains challenging, with fewer than half of patients achieving clinically meaningful relief and tolerability often limited by adverse effects.
Topical formulations including 5% lidocaine patches and high-concentration capsaicin plasters are considered second-line treatment options for SFN, supported by moderate-quality evidence.
Tramadol and botulinum toxin A may be used in selected SFN cases, although botulinum toxin A has only weak recommendation support from limited RCTs in SFN populations.
Spinal cord stimulation may be considered for refractory SFN cases, though cost-effectiveness and patient selection require careful multidisciplinary assessment.
Physical therapy remains a useful adjunct to maintain mobility and functionality in SFN despite limited supporting data.
Emerging precision medicine frameworks incorporating molecular and neurophysiological biomarkers may enable tailored therapeutic strategies for SFN patients.
CNFD showed a statistically significant but negligible correlation with warm detection threshold, and no significant correlation with other QST measures.
Neither CNFL nor CNBD correlated significantly with any of the quantitative sensory testing (QST) measures.
CNFT correlated negligibly with warm detection threshold and vibration detection threshold.
IENFD correlated moderately with warm detection threshold and mechanical pain threshold, and weakly with cold detection threshold, mechanical detection threshold, and vibration detection threshold.
Across the correlations examined between structural (CCM/IENFD) and functional (QST) measures, r2 values ranged from 0.03 to 0.15, meaning at most 15% of variance was explained.
In diabetic neuropathy patients, CNFD correlated weakly with warm detection threshold and CNFT correlated weakly with mechanical pain threshold.

In diabetic neuropathy patients, IENFD correlated moderately with warm detection threshold, mechanical pain threshold, and mechanical detection threshold, and weakly with vibration detection threshold.

In non-diabetic etiology patients, CNFT correlated negligibly with warm and vibration detection thresholds, while IENFD correlated moderately with warm detection threshold and mechanical pain threshold, weakly with cold detection threshold and vibration detection threshold, and negligibly with mechanical detection threshold.
Post hoc sex-stratified analysis showed warm detection threshold correlated significantly with CNFD and CNFT in women, but not in men.
Post hoc sex-stratified analysis showed cold and mechanical detection thresholds correlated significantly with IENFD in men but not in women.

Age-stratified analysis showed mechanical pain, mechanical detection, and vibration detection thresholds correlated significantly with CNFT in patients under 60, while warm detection threshold correlated with CNFT in older patients.
Correlations between QST variables and IENFD were overall stronger in younger patients than in older patients.

Symptom-duration-stratified analysis showed warm, mechanical pain, mechanical detection, and vibration detection thresholds correlated significantly with CNFT in patients with short (<24 months) symptom duration, while warm detection threshold was associated with CNFD in patients with long symptom duration.
Correlations between QST variables and IENFD were overall stronger in patients with a long duration of neuropathy symptoms.

After multivariable adjustment for sex, age, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and BMI, CNFT remained significantly correlated with warm detection threshold, and IENFD remained significantly correlated with warm detection threshold, mechanical pain threshold, and mechanical detection threshold.

Overall, IENFD (skin biopsy) correlated more strongly with clinically relevant functional peripheral nerve tests (small and large fiber QST) at the foot than corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) measures, suggesting CCM may be less suitable than skin biopsy for evaluating functionally relevant peripheral nerve pathology.

The review notes that comorbid small fiber neuropathy, alongside depression, fatigue, and pain, may exacerbate or mimic cognitive dysfunction in systemic autoimmune and inflammatory diseases such as ANCA-associated vasculitis, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, sarcoidosis, and Behçet's disease.

Among 18 GRADE-based clinical guidelines on chronic pain, irritable bowel syndrome was identified as one of the target populations for which Integrative and Complementary Practices (ICPs) such as acupuncture and mind-body practices are recommended.
Fibromyalgia was also identified as a target chronic pain condition addressed by ICP recommendations across the reviewed clinical guidelines.

In the most methodologically robust guidelines, acupuncture, osteopathy, chiropractic, yoga and tai chi received strong recommendations for low back pain, though even these were noted as being underpinned by generally limited evidence.

Only 8 of the 18 included guidelines demonstrated high methodological quality by AGREE II criteria, with most recommendations for ICPs in chronic pain being weak and based on low-to-moderate quality evidence.

Fibroblast-specific knockdown of MEOX1 in mice protected against bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, reduced CTGF expression and lung fibroblast activation, and reversed mitophagy deficiency and senescence.
In lung fibroblasts, MEOX1 knockdown abolished TGF-β1-induced mitophagy deficiency by downregulating CTGF expression, thereby inhibiting senescence, over-activation, and collagen production.
TGF-β1 treatment upregulated MEOX1 expression in lung fibroblasts via the NOX4-ROS-Smad signaling pathway.
RNA-sequencing of TGF-β1-treated lung fibroblasts and IPF lung tissue identified MEOX1 among the differentially expressed genes implicated in pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis.
Diabetic gastroparesis affects approximately 40% of patients with type 1 diabetes and up to 30% of patients with type 2 diabetes, especially those with long-standing disease.
Pre-intervention scintigraphic gastric emptying scan showed a markedly delayed T1/2 of 699 minutes versus a normal value of 62±11 minutes.
Metoclopramide, ondansetron and domperidone were all trialled but proved ineffective at improving this patient's gastroparesis and glycaemic control.
A single 100U pyloric botulinum toxin injection markedly improved gastric emptying, reducing T1/2 from 699 minutes pre-procedure to 100 minutes four months after the procedure.
HbA1c improved from 7.8% pre-procedure to 7.4% post-BTX, though not reaching the target of <7%.

One year after BTX injection, continuous glucose monitoring showed increased time in range from 44% to 57% and reduced time above range from 54% to 40%, with similar CGM wear time, coefficient of variation and time below range before and after.

Botulinum toxin injected into the pyloric sphincter is proposed to temporarily relax pyloric smooth muscle by inhibiting acetylcholine release, potentially improving gastric emptying in patients with pylorospasm.

Randomised controlled trials have not demonstrated a significant clinical advantage of pyloric BTX over placebo in gastroparesis, and no causal link between pyloric dysfunction and symptoms has been established.
The authors postulate that improved glycaemic control resulting from the BTX procedure may have allowed the patient's underlying autonomic neuropathy to improve.
Despite this case's positive outcome, current data and case studies show no established association between pyloric BTX injections and blood glucose control in type 1 diabetics generally.
GLP-1 receptor agonists are contraindicated in diabetic gastroparesis because they further reduce gastric emptying.

Endoscopic manometry studies have identified periods of unusually prolonged and intense tonic pyloric contractions (pylorospasm) in gastroparesis patients, supporting the pylorus as a potential therapeutic target.
LTGF-beta1 content per unit tissue volume in bovine cartilage decreased significantly from fetal to skeletally mature stages of development.
LTGF-beta2 content per unit tissue volume in bovine cartilage decreased significantly from fetal to skeletally mature stages of development.
When normalized per cell number, LTGF-beta1 and LTGF-beta2 content in bovine cartilage did not change across developmental stages, indicating conserved availability per chondrocyte.
LTGF-beta1 content in human articular cartilage varied by roughly an order of magnitude across donors aged 13 to 80 years.
Donor age was not predictive of LTGF-beta1 content in human cartilage.

The review notes that up to 11% of patients discharged after severe COVID-19 infection were found to have residual interstitial lung abnormalities, with the underlying mechanisms still poorly characterized.
Although peripheral pulmonary infiltrates from COVID-19 typically resolve spontaneously, the review reports that some COVID-19 patients go on to develop restrictive-type pulmonary fibrosis.
The KIR3DL3*002 allele was more frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
The KIR3DL1*020 allele, known to be highly expressed, was more frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
The KIR3DL2*009 allele, reported to have lower expression than other KIR3DL2 allotypes, was more frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
The KIR3DL3*013 allele had a reduced frequency among ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
The KIR3DL2*010 allele had a significantly reduced frequency among ME/CFS patients compared to controls, and this was the only association surviving Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.
A telomeric KIR haplotype combining the two positively associated alleles (KIR3DL1*020 and KIR3DL2*009) was more prevalent in ME/CFS patients than in controls.
Carriers of the Bw480I HLA-B motif (a KIR3DL1 ligand) were significantly more frequent among ME/CFS patients than controls.
Co-carriers of the Bw480I HLA ligand together with KIR3DL1 were more frequent among ME/CFS patients than controls, indicating a KIR-HLA ligand pairing association.
No significant differences in KIR gene content (presence/absence) were found between ME/CFS patients and controls.
No significant differences were observed in copy number variation of any KIR genes, though KIR2DL4 showed the highest variation.

No significant differences were found between ME/CFS cases and controls in KIR haplotype A and B motif groups, for either centromeric or telomeric regions, nor in A/A, A/B, B/B haplotype combination frequencies.
No significant associations were found between the number of KIR HLA ligands (Bw4, C1, C2, A3/11) and ME/CFS.
The previously reported higher carrier frequency of KIR3DS1 in CFS patients (Pasi et al.) was not replicated in this larger study.

This is the largest KIR genetic study in ME/CFS to date, characterizing KIR gene, allele and haplotype frequencies in a Norwegian healthy control population that can serve as a reference for future studies.
ME/CFS patients showed a significantly higher coefficient of variation (CV) of repeated maximal handgrip strength trials compared to healthy controls, across both sexes and both testing sessions.
After excluding participants with abnormal within-session fatigability, female ME/CFS patients still showed significantly higher CV than female healthy controls in both sessions.
In male participants, after excluding those with abnormal fatigability, the difference in CV between ME/CFS patients and controls did not reach statistical significance (p≈0.06).

CV and the index of fatigability were moderately correlated in both healthy controls (r=0.49) and normal-fatigability ME/CFS patients (r=0.35), with no significant difference between the correlation strengths of the two groups.

Adjusting for IF as a covariate reduced the magnitude of the group (HC vs ME/CFS) correlation with CV substantially more in males (60.1% and 19.4% reduction across sessions 1 and 2) than in females (13.4% and 7.8% reduction), indicating fatigability contributes more to the CV group difference in men than women.
In the original validation study, ME/CFS patients had lower mean and maximum handgrip strength and a steeper decline across trials compared to healthy volunteers.

In a separate cross-sectional study of 272 ME/CFS patients, patients showed a significantly larger drop in strength after the first of three handgrips compared to healthy controls, multiple sclerosis patients, or people with chronic fatigue not meeting ME/CFS criteria.
In a deep phenotyping study, impaired ability of ME/CFS patients to sustain grip strength correlated with the tendency to avoid effort in a behavioral effort-expenditure task.
Sustained grip strength decline in ME/CFS was not correlated with arm muscle mass, histological markers of disuse-related muscle atrophy, or an electromyographic index of peripheral muscle fatigue.

Objective electrophysiological measures of peripheral muscle fatigue after sustained maximal contraction were actually lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls, arguing against a peripheral fatigue explanation for grip strength deficits.

In fibromyalgia syndrome, hand grip strength is similarly reduced as in ME/CFS, with a characteristic peak-to-sustained strength discrepancy and higher test-retest discrepancy, linked in other studies to incomplete motor unit recruitment via superimposed electrical stimulation.

A study of 12 male ME/CFS patients using superimposed transcutaneous electrical stimulation found no abnormalities in maximum voluntary contraction, but the small preselected sample achieved >95% voluntary activation and had no measurable strength deficit.

Twitch interpolation was required to record maximal quadriceps contraction in 35% of ME/CFS patients versus 20% of sedentary controls and 13% of depressed controls, a difference that was not statistically significant in this small sample.

During repeated handgrip strength testing, ME/CFS patients showed abnormal temporoparietal junction activation changes analogous to sense-of-agency network abnormalities seen in functional neurological disorder, which were absent in healthy volunteers.

In the original study, the peak-to-average strength ratio in the second session ('Fatigue Ratio2') correlated with self-reported post-exertional malaise independent of gender, though this was not corrected for multiple comparisons.

In a systematic review using individual patient data (n=959), low self-efficacy (≤17 points on the Self Efficacy Scale) was the only patient characteristic predicting nonresponse to cognitive behavioral therapy in ME/CFS.
Female ME/CFS patients had significantly lower dolorimetry pressure-pain thresholds (more tenderness) than female sedentary controls.
Female GWI patients had significantly lower dolorimetry pressure thresholds than female sedentary controls.
Male ME/CFS patients had significantly lower dolorimetry pressure thresholds than male sedentary controls.
Male GWI patients had significantly lower dolorimetry pressure thresholds than male sedentary controls.
Across the whole cohort, males had significantly higher (less tender) dolorimetry pressure thresholds than females, requiring sex-stratified analyses.
Thumb-pressure tender point counts were strongly inversely correlated with dolorimetry pressure thresholds, validating both as measures of central sensitization/tenderness.
McGill Total Pain scores were strongly correlated with CMSI interoceptive complaint scores in both females and males, supporting a shared nociplastic/interoplastic mechanism.
Dolorimetry correlated moderately with pain (McGill) but only weakly and non-significantly with fatigue and disability, suggesting central sensitization mechanisms have limited influence on fatigue.
GWI men had more tender points and more widespread pain meeting 1990 fibromyalgia criteria than ME/CFS or sedentary controls.
Irritable bowel syndrome (Rome I) was progressively more prevalent from sedentary controls to CIF to ME/CFS to GWI.
Migraine prevalence by IHS criteria was stratified in the same pattern as IBS, being highest in GWI, intermediate in ME/CFS, and lowest in controls.
A majority of GWI veterans met criteria for PTSD by history or questionnaire.
Generalized anxiety disorder inferred by GAD7 score was elevated in ME/CFS and GWI.
The 1990 fibromyalgia criteria (widespread pain plus ≥11/18 tender points) were met by roughly half of ME/CFS and GWI patients but almost none of controls or CIF.
Chronic Multisymptom Illness (CMI) criteria were met by a high proportion of CIF and ME/CFS subjects, not just GWI, showing CMI lacks specificity for GWI.
Most GWI subjects also met the Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS, demonstrating substantial diagnostic overlap between the two illness definitions.
The Kansas GWI criteria were met by a large majority of ME/CFS subjects, further indicating overlapping symptom profiles between GWI and ME/CFS diagnostic frameworks.
Male CIF subjects had an intermediate dolorimetry mode between sedentary controls and ME/CFS/GWI, suggesting CIF carries some element of central sensitization.

Chronic idiopathic fatigue was characterized by significant fatigue, impaired vitality, sleep, and cognition, but pain, tenderness, and interoceptive scores were not significantly different from sedentary controls.
In females, orthostatic dolorimetry correlated strongly with cognitive/lightheadedness/dizziness/fatigue symptom clusters while standing.
In men, tenderness (dolorimetry) correlated with PEM, interoceptive complaints, and irritable bowel syndrome, linking central sensitization to gut-related interoceptive distress.
About one third of study subjects had elevated CRP, which the authors link to a possible motivational anhedonia/neuroinflammatory phenotype and propose infliximab as a candidate experimental therapy.

The authors propose that a descending PAG-to-rostral ventromedial medulla opioid-responsive pathway, via BDNF-expressing 'pain-OFF' neurons acting on TrkB-GABA-galanin interneurons in the dorsal horn, normally suppresses pain transmission and that its dysfunction underlies central sensitization in ME/CFS and GWI.
Women overall showed greater nociplastic sensitivity (lower dolorimetry thresholds) than men across diagnostic groups, even though subjective questionnaire scores were similar between sexes.
Pre-exercise SEB-stimulated whole blood from ME/CFS patients showed elevated levels of CXCL5, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, IL-23, and TNF-α compared to HC.
IFN-γ, IL-13, and IL-17 showed similar borderline elevations after SEB stimulation in ME/CFS versus HC (padj < 0.10).
SEB-induced cytokine responses were greater in females than males, and female ME/CFS patients under 45 years of age had significantly higher CXCL5, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 than age-matched female HC.
Plasma testosterone levels were negatively associated with age in female subjects, with no comparable age-hormone association observed in males after BMI adjustment.
HKCA-stimulated whole blood from ME/CFS patients showed elevated pre-exercise IFN-γ and TNF-α compared to HC, with a similarly elevated but non-significant IL-1β trend.
After exercise, HKCA-induced levels of GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α decreased in females with ME/CFS but not in males, with similar reductions across younger and older female ME/CFS.
TruCulture cytokine responses to LPS and poly I:C were higher than unstimulated in both groups but showed no case-control differences between ME/CFS and HC.
In a small PBMC substudy, IL-6 responses to LPS and poly I:C were dose- and time-dependent, with case-control differences most evident at lower stimulant concentrations and at 24 h of incubation.
Baseline plasma levels of CSF1 and LRP8 were lower in ME/CFS than in HC, consistent with prior reports.
Plasma levels of protein C (proC) and BATF3 were elevated in ME/CFS both before and after exercise.
Post-exercise plasma levels of endogenous retrovirus group V member 1 (ERVV1) were elevated in ME/CFS.

Integrative pathway analysis of plasma metabolomic and proteomic data showed reduced analyte levels in integrin cell surface interactions, VEGF signaling, and leukocyte adhesion/diapedesis pathways before exercise in ME/CFS.
Baseline levels of CD93 and COMP were lower, HTRA1 was higher, and CLEC3B (tetranectin) was lower both before and after exercise in ME/CFS, indicating disrupted ECM homeostasis.

Levels of L-selectin (SELL) and ADGRD1 were reduced both before and after exercise, and baseline CDH5 (VE-cadherin) and KDR (VEGFR2) were reduced in ME/CFS, suggesting impaired immune surveillance and endothelial-mediated leukocyte trafficking.
Plasma DAP, a bacterial peptidoglycan component, decreased after exercise in HC but showed no decrease in ME/CFS.

Plasma leucate was reduced pre- and post-exercise in ME/CFS, baseline citrulline trended toward reduction, and baseline TFF1 (a mucosal barrier protein) was reduced, together suggesting compromised GI barrier and dysbiosis.

CALCR levels were higher in ME/CFS both before and after exercise, and RAMP3 and S100A8 were higher after exercise, reflecting abnormalities in calcium signaling that may contribute to inflammation and PEM.
Complement components C1R and CFHR4 were elevated in ME/CFS after exercise, indicating complement activation via classical and alternative pathways.
Plasma GDF15, a biomarker of mitochondrial dysfunction and integrated stress response, was higher in ME/CFS after exercise than in HC.
Higher post-exercise GDF15 levels positively correlated with MFI scores of general fatigue, physical fatigue, and reduced activity in ME/CFS.
Plasma citrate increased after exercise in ME/CFS but decreased after exercise in HC, suggesting a TCA cycle lesion and reduced mitochondrial flux in ME/CFS.
ChemRICH analysis revealed higher plasma triglycerides and diglycerides in ME/CFS before and after exercise, consistent with prior reports.

Plasma acylcarnitines, particularly CAR(12:0), were lower after exercise in ME/CFS, consistent with previously reported reduced baseline acylcarnitines in two independent cohorts, indicating impaired fatty acid β-oxidation.
Baseline 12,13-diHOME was lower in ME/CFS than HC, but after exercise both 12,13-diHOME and its precursor linoleic acid were increased in ME/CFS relative to HC.
Lower baseline 12,13-diHOME correlated with higher MFI physical fatigue and reduced activity scores in both ME/CFS and HC.
The KYN:TRP ratio was lower in ME/CFS before exercise but increased after exercise, suggesting post-exercise overactivation of the kynurenine pathway diverting tryptophan from serotonin synthesis.

The KYNA:KYN ratio was higher in ME/CFS before exercise and decreased after exercise, consistent with a prior report of higher resting KYNA:KYN in ME/CFS serum, indicating reduced kynurenine aminotransferase activity post-exercise.
Baseline plasma indole-3-lactate, a commensal bacteria-derived metabolite important for regulating inflammation, was depleted in ME/CFS.
Plasma propionic acid, a short chain fatty acid, was elevated after exercise in ME/CFS, potentially contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation.
Baseline plasma levels of the neuronal proteins EPHA4 and CNTN4 were lower in ME/CFS, and reduced CNTN4 correlated with higher general fatigue scores.
Post-exercise ELAVL2 was elevated while NRXN1 (synaptic adhesion molecule) decreased in ME/CFS, potentially contributing to PEM-related cognitive impairment.
ORN:CIT and ARG:CIT ratios were elevated in ME/CFS before exercise, consistent with an earlier report, and decreased after exercise, suggesting impairments at different stages of the urea cycle.
Female ME/CFS subjects showed amino acid abnormalities indicative of glutathione depletion both before and after exercise, a sex-specific subgroup effect not seen in males.
Male ME/CFS subjects had lower plasma levels of plasmalogens, suggesting peroxisomal dysfunction as a sex-specific subgroup effect.
An independent study (Shankar et al.) found cellular and systemic oxidative stress in PBMCs from both ME/CFS and long-COVID patients, resulting in inflammation and mitochondrial damage.
In the cited Shankar et al. study, female ME/CFS subjects had elevated reactive oxygen species and depleted glutathione, consistent with the present study's female-specific findings.
The same cited study reported male ME/CFS subjects had biomarkers of lipid peroxidation, a distinct sex-specific oxidative stress signature.
In the cited external study, metformin mitigated ROS-triggered T-cell proliferative responses in PBMCs, suggesting a candidate for reducing oxidative-stress-driven immune activation in ME/CFS.
A cited review proposes that ME/CFS pathogenesis involves 'trained immunity,' in which prior infection lowers the threshold for inflammatory responses to subsequent, unrelated microbial exposures.
The authors propose IL-37 and the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin as candidate treatments for ME/CFS individuals with evidence of enhanced innate immunity or microbial hypersensitivity.
Patients with evidence of gut dysbiosis may benefit from prebiotic (inulin) and probiotic (F. prausnitzii) supplementation to enhance GI barrier integrity and regulate immune responses.

Individuals with low baseline 12,13-diHOME and high post-exercise GDF15, indicating pronounced metabolic disruption, may be more likely to respond to 12,13-diHOME supplementation or GDF15-neutralizing antibody treatment.
Individuals with tryptophan metabolism abnormalities may respond to supplementation with 5-hydroxytryptophan or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
In patients with low carnitine levels, carnitine supplementation may restore carnitine shuttle function and enable use of lipids as an energy source.
Estrogen supplements may modulate the inflammatory response in older women with ME/CFS.
Reduced pre- and post-exercise plasma leucate levels in ME/CFS are consistent with a prior report that fecal levels of R. torques correlated with MFI symptom scores.
Fecal levels of Bacteroidetes are reported to be elevated in ME/CFS, consistent with increased β-glucuronidase activity and elevated plasma glucuronic acid observed in this study.
Butyrate, an SCFA important for GI mucosal integrity, and butyrate-producing bacteria are reported to be lower in fecal samples of ME/CFS subjects.

Baseline mitochondrial dysfunction, including impairments in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and oxidative phosphorylation, was found primarily in subgroups of ME/CFS, consistent with previous reports.
Inter-analyte correlation network analysis revealed distinct correlation patterns between significantly altered metabolomic/proteomic analytes in ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
No differences were found between ME/CFS and HC in plasma protein levels of TLR-3 or TLR-4, or their transcripts in bulk PBMC preparations.

Among individuals with active opioid use disorder recruited from a syringe exchange program, the prevalence of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome was significantly higher than global prevalence estimates.
Chronic migraine headache prevalence was significantly higher than expected among the syringe program sample of individuals with active opioid use disorder, compared to global prevalence estimates.
Fibromyalgia prevalence was significantly higher than expected among individuals with active opioid use disorder recruited from a syringe exchange program, compared to global prevalence estimates.

Chronic low back pain prevalence was significantly higher than expected among individuals with active opioid use disorder recruited from a syringe exchange program, compared to global prevalence estimates.

A transdiagnostic ALE meta-analysis of 46 neuroimaging studies (2603 subjects, 856 foci), including Post-COVID-19 condition among the represented diagnoses, identified three spatially distinct clusters (frontal-striatal-limbic, frontal-cingulate, parietal) associated with mental fatigue across multiple disease categories compared to healthy controls.

A disease-specific ALE meta-analysis restricted to 14 CFS/ME studies (630 subjects, 217 foci) showed a widespread cortical-subcortical activation network sharing the frontal-striatal-limbic, frontal-cingulate and parietal clusters found in the pooled transdiagnostic analysis, with some CFS-specific patterns.

In CFS/ME and Gulf War Illness, the frontal-cingulate cluster (a central executive network node) plays a more prominent role in fatigue-related dysfunction than in other conditions, linked to impaired top-down cognitive control and motivation.
Resting-state connectivity disruptions between the Default Mode Network and other brain regions have been observed in CFS/ME, and are strongly correlated with depression and fatigue symptoms.

CFS/ME patients reported relatively low fatigue severity effect sizes compared to controls in the included studies, which the authors found surprising given fatigue is a hallmark CFS symptom, and attribute partly to use of the Chalder Fatigue Scale which is prone to ceiling effects.

Persistent cognitive fatigue in Post-COVID-19 patients has been associated with prefrontal, basal ganglia and insular activations during effort-reward tasks such as the N-back task, alongside impaired motivational/interoceptive processing.

Post-COVID-19 condition (PC) studies contributed foci to the frontal-striatal-limbic cluster but, along with insomnia disorder, did not contribute any foci to the frontal-cingulate or parietal clusters in the pooled ALE analysis.

Fatigue may result from reduced dopamine availability in striatal structures, leading to reduced firing of striatal dopaminergic neurons and impaired effort-reward decision-making, in line with the dopamine imbalance hypothesis of fatigue.

The dual regulation system model posits that mental fatigue arises from the interplay of a thalamic-striatal-frontal facilitation system and an insular/cingulate-driven inhibition system, with chronic fatigue reflecting overactivation of the inhibition-limbic system over time.

The praecuneus, an essential DMN hub involved in visual perception, episodic memory, self-processing and consciousness, shows over-recruitment during cognitively demanding tasks that acts as a compensatory factor and is proposed as a driver of self-perceived fatigue via increased inner thoughts about one's own fatigue.
Angular gyrus activation, related to visuospatial/attentional mechanisms and sense of agency, is commonly reported to relate to self-reported levels of fatigue across studies.
Fibromyalgia and hepatitis C virus infection were each represented by only one eligible study, and neither contributed any foci to the pooled ALE fatigue-network results.

Overall methodological quality (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) of included studies ranged from 3 to 8, with most classified as moderate risk of bias (scores 4-6); TBI studies had the highest average quality and contributed the most foci, while MS studies had among the lowest quality and fewest contributed foci.

The commented-upon meta-analysis of six RCTs reported that Xiaoyao San significantly reduced fatigue, anxiety, and depression symptoms in CFS patients with few adverse events, though this commentary argues the underlying trial evidence is of low methodological quality.

Chai Hu, a principal herb in Xiaoyao San, has been reported to modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis via corticotropin-releasing hormone and glucocorticoid receptor signalling, a mechanism proposed as relevant to CFS pathophysiology.

Dang Gui, another component herb of Xiaoyao San, contains phthalides and polysaccharides shown in preclinical models to have immunomodulatory and gut microbiota-altering effects, proposed as a candidate mechanism relevant to CFS.
Acupuncture significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control interventions in CFS patients.
Moxibustion significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control interventions in CFS patients.
Tuina (Chinese therapeutic massage) significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control interventions in CFS patients.
Diet therapy (polyphenol-rich chocolate) produced the largest reduction in depression scale scores compared with control among all interventions tested.
Electrical stimulation therapy (tDCS/TENS) significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control in CFS patients.
Combined acupuncture plus moxibustion (Ap+Mox) significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control in CFS patients.
Combined acupuncture, moxibustion, and acupoints embedding (Ap+Mox+Ae) significantly reduced depression scale scores compared with control in CFS patients.
Relaxation therapy, aerobic exercise, resistance training, and Qigong did not significantly improve depressive symptoms compared with control in CFS patients.
Acupuncture and moxibustion produced significantly greater reductions in depression scores than psychotherapy in CFS patients.
Moxibustion, diet therapy, and Ap+Mox produced significantly greater reductions in depression scores than aerobic exercise (AER) in CFS patients.
SUCRA ranking identified diet therapy as the most effective intervention for reducing depression scores in CFS, followed by moxibustion, Ap+Mox+Ae, Ap+Mox, and Mox+MT.
Increased expression of activated microglia translocator protein in the hippocampus of CFS patients was positively correlated with depression scores.
CFS patients with comorbid major depression show mixed immune responses and neuroinflammation across widespread brain regions, associated with severity of neuropsychological symptoms.
CFS patients show reduced tricarboxylic acid cycle activity, mitochondrial energy metabolism dysfunction, and systemic metabolic dysfunction, a mechanism also implicated in depression.
CFS and depression patients show abnormalities in HPA axis regulation with disrupted cortisol secretion feedback, and depressed/physically inactive CFS patients may present with hypocortisolemia.
CFS patients show significantly reduced central 5-HT1A receptor binding potential and lower levels of serotonin transporters/receptors, mechanisms also implicated in depression.
Both CFS and depression patients exhibit significant reduction in gray matter volume in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.
CFS patients exhibit reduced heart rate variability and cerebral blood flow; decreased whole-brain average cerebral blood flow is associated with more depressive episodes in adulthood.
CFS patients have greatly elevated plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which may induce or exacerbate depressive symptoms.
CFS patients with comorbid depression may have more severe endocrine disorders compared with CFS patients without depression.
Higher depression scale scores are associated with an increased overall risk of CFS, with each one-point increase in the depression scale associated with a 49% increase in CFS risk.
Maladaptive perfectionism is associated with depression levels in CFS patients.
Peak oxygen consumption during invasive CPET was lower in both PASC and CFS/ME patients compared with healthy controls.
Peak exercise cardiac index was significantly reduced in both PASC and CFS/ME patients relative to healthy controls.
Mixed venous oxygen saturation at peak exercise was significantly higher in CFS/ME patients compared with both controls and PASC patients.
The systemic oxygen extraction ratio was significantly decreased in CFS/ME patients relative to controls.

Right atrial pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure at peak exercise were lower in PASC and CFS/ME than controls, but the difference was not statistically significant, consistent with preload insufficiency rather than heart failure.

Excluding hemoglobin, all oxygen pathway parameters (lung diffusion, muscle diffusion, alveolar ventilation, mitochondrial oxidative capacity) were lower in both CFS/ME and PASC groups compared with controls.
DM and Vmax further distinguished PASC from CFS/ME, with CFS/ME patients showing greater impairment in these two peripheral oxygen pathway parameters.
DM, DL, and alveolar ventilation were reduced to similar degrees in both PASC and CFS/ME, indicating a shared pattern of multisystem oxygen pathway impairment.

Sequential normalization analysis showed that correcting skeletal muscle O2 diffusion (DM) produced the greatest theoretical improvement in peak V̇O2, followed by lung diffusion (DL), with a similar pattern in both PASC and CFS/ME; normalization of other parameters contributed <10% to reduced V̇O2peak.

Skin biopsy in six PASC patients referred for suspected small fiber neuropathy showed reduced epidermal and sweat gland nerve fiber density consistent with small fiber neuropathy in five of six patients.
Standard nerve conduction studies and electromyography were normal in all patients who underwent skin biopsy, despite biopsy-confirmed small fiber neuropathy in most.
Resting hemodynamics and standard tests (pulmonary function, echocardiography, CT) were comparable across PASC, CFS/ME, and control groups, indicating functional limitations are not evident at rest.
BMI was statistically higher in both the CFS/ME and PASC groups compared with controls.

The lack of a rise in right atrial pressure with exercise in PASC and CFS/ME patients is consistent with 'preload insufficiency,' potentially linking exercise hemodynamics to orthostatic symptoms via dysautonomia or deconditioning.
POTS is described as a frequent complication of both CFS/ME and PASC, potentially representing a pathophysiological link to preload insufficiency.

This study failed to replicate an abnormally reduced systemic oxygen extraction ratio in PASC and CFS/ME that had been reported in prior studies, likely because combined reductions in cardiac output and extraction confound Fick-based interpretation.

The study's findings, together with prior reviews, argue against deconditioning as the primary driver of exercise limitation in PASC and CFS/ME, instead supporting multifactorial mechanisms including dysautonomia, preload insufficiency, and muscle abnormalities.
Double filtration plasmapheresis significantly reduced plasma lipid levels in the 24 male patients when comparing post-treatment to pre-treatment samples.
Apheresis significantly reduced circulating inflammatory markers in the patient cohort after treatment.
Apheresis reduced autoantibodies associated with long-COVID in treated patients.
The authors' prior research indicated that apheresis alleviates symptoms, including fatigue, in patients with long-COVID and chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetic testing in a subgroup of patients found no mutations in LDLR, APOB, APOE, PCSK9, LIPA, or LDLRAP1, the genes associated with monogenic lipid disorders.
All genetically tested patients showed an intermediate to high likelihood that their elevated lipid levels have a polygenic rather than monogenic basis.
The authors propose that the MENA region's extreme temperatures worsen cardiovascular disease by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, dehydration, and blood viscosity.
Nearly all participants with chronic low back pain reported pain outside the upper and lower back region, indicating widespread pain co-occurrence.
45% of participants with chronic low back pain had exactly one additional chronic overlapping pain condition.
24% of participants with chronic low back pain had two or more additional chronic overlapping pain conditions.
Irritable bowel syndrome was the most common co-occurring COPC among participants with chronic low back pain, present in 20% of the sample.
Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome was present in 19% of participants with chronic low back pain, the second most common co-occurring COPC.
Fibromyalgia was present in 15% of participants with chronic low back pain, making it the third most common co-occurring COPC.
Having an additional chronic overlapping pain condition was associated with a 7.6-point higher fatigue T-score compared to chronic low back pain alone.

Compared to people with chronic low back pain alone, those with additional overlapping pain conditions reported more severe pain symptoms, higher anxiety and depression, and worse physical functioning.
Participants with cLBP plus additional chronic overlapping pain conditions reported higher anxiety scores than those with cLBP alone.
Participants with cLBP plus additional chronic overlapping pain conditions reported higher depression scores than those with cLBP alone.
Participants with cLBP plus additional chronic overlapping pain conditions scored worse (lower) on measures of physical functioning compared with those with cLBP alone.
Participants with cLBP plus additional chronic overlapping pain conditions reported more severe pain symptoms overall compared with those with cLBP alone.
Nearly all participants (95%) reported pain outside the upper and lower back region, indicating widespread pain beyond the primary cLBP diagnosis.
The 2017 international consortium classification describes 13 subtypes of EDS, 12 of which have an identified genetic etiology, while hypermobile EDS remains molecularly uncharacterized.
There is no specific treatment for non-vascular EDS, so care management is symptomatic, multidisciplinary, and personalized.
Vascular EDS is caused by mutations in COL3A1, encoding type III collagen alpha 1, typically inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

Conservative management with close hemodynamic monitoring and defined blood pressure/heart rate targets successfully resolved a massive retroperitoneal hematoma and pseudoaneurysm without angiographic or surgical intervention.

The existing retroperitoneal hematoma spontaneously ruptured into the peritoneal cavity on hospital day 9 without contrast extravasation or hemodynamic instability, suggesting rupture of an already-sealed hematoma rather than active rebleeding.
