Celiprolol was prescribed to the patient following his vEDS diagnosis, consistent with standard pharmacologic management aimed at reducing vascular event risk.

Life-threatening complications of vascular EDS, such as arterial dissection/rupture, intestinal perforation, and uterine rupture, develop in more than 25% of patients by age 20 and in more than 80% by age 40.
The average life expectancy for patients with vascular EDS is estimated at approximately 50 years, largely due to vascular collapse.

In a multicenter cohort of connective tissue diseases, survival after aortic intervention was lower for vascular EDS patients than for those with Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndromes, with 1- and 5-year survival rates of 75.0% and 43.8% in vEDS.
Invasive diagnostic procedures such as angiography and endoscopy should be avoided whenever possible in vascular EDS patients owing to tissue fragility and high procedural risk.

The patient was diagnosed with vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome based on a ruptured splenic aneurysm, recurrent idiopathic colorectal perforation, and family history of similar perforation on the maternal side.
The patient presented with extensive intra-abdominal hemorrhage due to a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm, requiring emergency transport, conservative management, and later coil embolization.

The patient had recurrent idiopathic colorectal perforation, first requiring a Hartmann procedure five years prior, then a second emergency colon resection a month after discharge due to perforation at the colostomy mouth, followed by colostomy reconstruction six months later.
There was a family history of idiopathic colorectal perforation on the patient's maternal side, supporting a heritable connective tissue disorder.
Despite initial improvement and discharge, the patient developed fatal aortic dissection about two and a half months after his initial presentation.
Blood biochemistry testing during emergency transport showed a decreased hemoglobin level of 10.2 g/dL, consistent with intra-abdominal hemorrhage from the ruptured splenic aneurysm.

In female football players with ACL reconstruction, having a Beighton score of ≥5 (generalised joint hypermobility) was associated with a 67% increased risk of a second ACL injury compared with those with a score <5.
Knee hyperextension greater than 5 degrees in the non-reconstructed (contralateral) knee was associated with a 67% increased risk of second ACL injury in ACLR players.
Knee hyperextension greater than 5 degrees in the ACL-reconstructed knee more than doubled the risk of re-rupture.
Increased knee laxity, measured by KT-1000 side difference, Lachman test, and pivot shift test, was not associated with the risk of a second ACL injury in players with ACLR.
Visually graded static standing alignment (varus/neutral/valgus) was not associated with second ACL injury risk in players with ACLR.

None of the baseline anatomical variables (generalised joint hypermobility, knee hyperextension, knee laxity, static standing alignment) were associated with risk of a primary ACL injury in knee-healthy female football players.
A moderate correlation was found between KT-1000 measured anterior tibial translation and Lachman test results in players with ACLR.

A weak to moderate correlation was observed between the Beighton score and knee extension range of motion among players with ACLR, indicating hypermobility and knee hyperextension capture partly distinct anatomical features.
In healthy children and young adults, a small mitral annular disjunction (MAD) distance of up to 3.6 mm can be observed and appears not to be indicative of adverse outcomes.
Across all standard CMR views, the MAD distance was larger in patients with connective tissue disorders compared to healthy controls.

Height-indexed maximum systolic MAD distance was an independent predictor of the composite outcome (significant ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, or death) in a covariate-adjusted logistic regression model.
A height-indexed maximum systolic MAD threshold of 0.033 mm/cm best discriminated patients with versus without the composite adverse outcome, with high negative predictive value.
In a bivariate model, height-indexed maximum systolic MAD remained a stronger predictor of the composite outcome than mitral valve prolapse, which was not statistically significant.
The height-indexed maximum systolic MAD distance was longer in CTD patients who also had mitral valve prolapse compared to those without.
Patients with early onset, severe ("neonatal") Marfan syndrome had longer height-indexed MAD distances and a higher composite adverse outcome rate than all other CTD patients.

Patients with a nonspecific (non-vEDS) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnosis who met the composite adverse outcome all had atypical connective tissue disorder presentations without a specific genetic mutation identified.
The single patient in the 'other CTD' category who died had multi-system smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome caused by an ACTA2 mutation.
The height-indexed systolic MAD distance did not change significantly between the initial and most recent CMR examinations over a mean interval of 7 years.

Gross and histopathologic examination of a heart specimen from a girl with early onset severe Marfan syndrome who died confirmed the presence of MAD as fibrous separation of the mitral valve hinge point from the ventricular myocardium.
Nearly half of the patients with connective tissue disorders had mitral valve prolapse, compared to none in the healthy control group.
MAD measurements showed a weak positive correlation with age and height but no correlation with body surface area, and a moderate positive correlation with mitral valve size.
Only a small minority of CTD patients imaged for late gadolinium enhancement had detectable left ventricular fibrosis, limiting analysis of fibrosis as a mechanism for arrhythmia in this cohort.

The 4-chamber CMR view had the lowest odds ratios for predicting the composite outcome and is considered a suboptimal view for measuring MAD distance because it visualizes the mitral valve near the commissures.

Interobserver reliability for systolic MAD measurement was good to excellent across all three CMR views (LVOT ICC 0.89, 4CH ICC 0.81, 2CH ICC 0.76), while diastolic measurement reliability was lower, particularly for the 4CH and LVOT views.

Overall, 8.3% of CTD patients met the composite adverse outcome (significant ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, or death), with patients meeting the outcome being significantly younger at CMR than those who did not.
RUNX2, located on chromosome 6p21, is the gene responsible for cleidocranial dysplasia, though genetic abnormalities in RUNX2 are found in only about 70% of patients.
RUNX2 is described as responsible for osteoblast differentiation and both intramembranous and endochondral ossification.
The child's EEG showed epileptic activity, confirming a seizure disorder in a patient later diagnosed with cleidocranial dysplasia.
Skeletal survey chest radiograph revealed bilaterally absent clavicles and a bell-shaped thorax, a hallmark radiological feature of cleidocranial dysplasia.
Pelvic radiograph showed absent bilateral pubic bones with pseudo-widening of the pubic symphysis.
Skull imaging showed multiple wormian bones, a persistent metopic suture, frontal bossing, absent nasal bones, a wide-open sagittal suture and anterior fontanelle, and multiple supernumerary teeth.
Aplastic/hypoplastic clavicles and abnormal scapular development in CCD cause excessive mobility of the shoulder girdles, allowing shoulder approximation across the chest.
Oral valproic acid at 20 mg/kg/day controlled the child's seizures, with no further episodes reported at one-month follow-up.
Prior literature reports associations between CCD and epilepsy/seizure disorders as well as syringomyelia, possibly indicating chromosomal abnormalities involving genes beyond RUNX2.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher odds of separation anxiety compared to non-hypermobile controls.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher odds of social phobia compared to controls.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher odds of panic disorder/agoraphobia compared to controls.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher odds of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) compared to controls.
ADHD prevalence showed no significant difference between children with generalized joint hypermobility and controls.
Specific phobia prevalence showed no significant difference between children with generalized joint hypermobility and controls.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) prevalence showed no significant difference between children with generalized joint hypermobility and controls.

Unsupervised k-means clustering of scapular marker displacement identified a subgroup (Cluster 1) with restricted acromion marker displacement and elevated y/x displacement ratios during scapular upward rotation, consistent with a hypomobile phenotype.
A second subgroup (Cluster 2) exhibited excessive acromion marker displacement with normal y/x ratios, consistent with a hypermobile scapular movement phenotype.
Pain intensity did not differ between the hypomobile and hypermobile clusters, indicating that clinical pain severity alone does not distinguish these movement phenotypes.

Healthy control participants' scapular displacement values fell between the values of the two patient clusters, suggesting both hypomobile and hypermobile patterns represent deviations from normal movement in opposite directions.

Surveyed spine surgeons identified hypermobility/connective tissue disease as a clinical factor that deters use of cervical disc replacement (CDR) in favor of anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF).
Severe myelopathy was cited by surveyed surgeons as a clinical deterrent to performing cervical disc replacement.
Segmental instability and significant kyphotic deformity on imaging were reported as radiographic determinants favoring ACDF over cervical disc replacement.
Private-practice surgeons adopted CDR for more than 25% of primary cases at a much higher rate (50%) than academic surgeons (13%).
CDR adoption rates varied significantly by geographic region, with the Southwest (71%) and Southeast (57%) regions having the highest proportion of surgeons using CDR in more than 25% of cases.
The most commonly cited barrier to adopting cervical disc replacement was perceived risk-benefit trade-offs, cited by 28% of respondents.
Surveyed spine surgeons reported severe myelopathy as a clinical deterrent to choosing cervical disc replacement over fusion.
Segmental instability on imaging was identified as a radiographic factor favoring anterior cervical discectomy and fusion over cervical disc replacement.
Significant kyphotic deformity on imaging was identified as a radiographic factor favoring anterior cervical discectomy and fusion over cervical disc replacement.

Whole-exome/targeted gene panel sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense mutation in RUNX2 (exon 4, Runt domain, affecting amino acid 155), confirming the molecular diagnosis of cleidocranial dysplasia.

Bilateral hypoplastic clavicles with poor articulation to the sternum resulted in narrow, drooping shoulders with marked hypermobility allowing approximation of the shoulders to the midline of the chest.

CBCT confirmed approximately 45 impacted permanent and supernumerary teeth in various orientations with cystic degeneration around several teeth, an unusually severe dental presentation compared to the 6-20 supernumerary teeth typically reported in CCD literature.

A large dentigerous cyst was identified in the right maxilla measuring 23.29 mm (superoinferior) x 30.28 mm (mesiodistal) x 28.98 mm (buccopalatal), with cortical plate breaches and nasal cavity involvement.
Serum alkaline phosphatase was mildly elevated in the patient, interpreted as consistent with active bone remodeling, while calcium and vitamin D levels were normal, helping exclude hypophosphatasia.

Citing Yoshida et al., the authors note that RUNX2 mutations affecting the Runt domain (critical for DNA binding) are associated with both short stature and greater disease severity, whereas patients with mutations sparing the Runt domain had normal height.

Citing Jensen's study of 17 Danish CCD patients, males with CCD had heights predominantly between the 5th-50th percentiles while all females with CCD had heights below the 5th percentile, indicating a sex difference in growth retardation severity.
None of the six drag queens who completed the physical examination met the Beighton criteria for generalized joint hypermobility.
Cardiovascular fitness varied widely among drag queen participants, with half rated excellent and two rated below average or very poor.
Most drag queens examined showed bilateral hip flexion tightness.
All examined drag queens showed bilateral hip internal rotation tightness.
The lower abdominal and hip extensor muscle groups were the weakest on bilateral testing, with left-sided weakness greater than right.
More than half of drag queen participants reported a current or prior musculoskeletal injury.
Fewer than half of drag queen performers had health insurance.
More than half of drag queens surveyed felt they would benefit from psychology counseling.
Four of seven drag queen participants reported binge drinking at least three times in the past year.
Four of seven drag queens had not seen a primary care physician in over 24 months, indicating potential gaps in routine healthcare access.
Fibromyalgia disease impact (FIQR) was positively correlated with chronic pain intensity in patients with fibromyalgia.
No significant association was found between fibromyalgia disease impact (FIQR) and respiratory variability parameters (respiratory rate and tidal volume variability).
Fibromyalgia disease impact (FIQR) was not significantly correlated with anxiety or depression scores (HADS).
Higher depression scores (HADS) were associated with reduced variability in tidal volume among fibromyalgia patients.
Depression scores were not significantly associated with variability in respiratory rate.
No significant association was found between anxiety scores (HADS) and respiratory variability.
Chronic pain intensity (NRS) was not significantly associated with respiratory variability.
Lower pain pressure thresholds (indicating heightened pain sensitivity/central sensitization) were associated with higher variability in respiratory rate.
Lower pain pressure thresholds were associated with higher variability in tidal volume.
No significant associations were found between respiratory variability and other pain sensitivity measures, including wind-up pain and aftersensation.

Respiratory rate variability appeared higher in this fibromyalgia cohort (0.201 ± 0.039) than in previously reported healthy individuals (0.164 ± 0.072), though the authors note this cross-study comparison is speculative.

Pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, and TNF-alpha have been reported as elevated in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, and linked in some studies to pain, anxiety, and fatigue.
PET imaging studies have shown increased glial cell activation in the brains of fibromyalgia patients, indicating ongoing neuroinflammation.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibit disruption in the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity, which may be reflected in altered respiratory variability.
Fibromyalgia patients show elevated sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic cardiac modulation, reflected in altered heart rate variability.
Heart rate variability has been associated with quality of life, physical function, and perceived stress in fibromyalgia.
Reduced heart rate variability is less evident in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome than in fibromyalgia, suggesting the HRV deficit in fibromyalgia is not simply due to deconditioning.

Two prior studies found that hyperventilatory, deep forceful breathing exercises increased pain thresholds to standardized electrical stimuli compared with control groups who did not perform the exercises.

The authors note a limitation across clinical trials of VNS in musculoskeletal diseases: inconsistent use of physiological biomarkers like heart rate variability to confirm that VNS is actually engaging the vagus nerve.
Isoxanthohumol reduces MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation, thereby lowering inflammation associated with rosacea.

The authors argue that SARS-CoV-2-induced mast cell activation intersects with bradykinin-mediated pathways to produce a pseudoangioedema phenotype that can be forensically confused with true anaphylaxis in COVID-19 deaths.
The authors note that differential diagnosis between anaphylaxis and pseudoangioedema in postmortem COVID-19 cases has important forensic implications.

Other neurotic disorders (neurasthenia, depersonalization syndrome, other neurotic disorders) were more prevalent in acute urticaria patients than controls.

Cluster C personality disorders (compulsive, dependent, avoidant) showed no significant difference between acute urticaria patients and controls.

Overall prevalence of any adjustment reaction was significantly higher in acute urticaria patients than controls.
Bruxism was significantly more prevalent among acute urticaria patients than controls.
Teeth grinding was significantly more prevalent among acute urticaria patients than controls.

The authors cite literature proposing that psychological stress activates the HPA axis, increasing CRH secretion, which can directly stimulate skin mast cells via CRH-R1 receptors to cause degranulation and histamine release, a hypothesized mechanistic link to AU.

The authors cite literature proposing that mast cell-derived IL-6 and TNF-alpha can cross the blood-brain barrier or signal via peripheral nerves, promoting neuroinflammation and modulating limbic anxiety circuits, a hypothesized bidirectional immune-affective link.

A sensitivity analysis excluding patients with documented oral corticosteroid purchases showed that the associations between acute urticaria and anxiety, personality, and nonpsychotic mental disorders remained consistent, suggesting corticosteroid use did not confound the findings.
Among 600 AERD patients surveyed, alcohol-induced upper respiratory, lower respiratory, and skin-flushing symptoms were reported by 79.6%, 45.1%, and 38.8% respectively.

AERD patients who experienced alcohol-induced respiratory reactions had faster postoperative sinus polyp regrowth and worse baseline sinus disease and asthma control than those without alcohol reactions.
AERD patients with alcohol-induced respiratory reactions had higher urinary leukotriene E4 and prostaglandin D2 levels than those without such reactions.
Treatment with dupilumab improved alcohol-induced symptoms for most AERD patients.
Daily aspirin therapy improved alcohol-induced symptoms for most AERD patients.
Nasal polyp ALDH2 protein levels were lower in AERD patients than in aspirin-tolerant controls.
Treatment with dupilumab improved alcohol-induced respiratory symptoms in most AERD patients.
Daily aspirin therapy also improved alcohol-induced respiratory symptoms for most AERD patients.
ALDH2 protein levels in nasal polyp tissue were lower in AERD patients than in aspirin-tolerant controls.
ALDH2 transcript levels in sorted sinus epithelial cells were lower in AERD patients compared with aspirin-tolerant controls.
In vitro stimulation of cultured respiratory epithelial cells with IL-4/IL-13 decreased ALDH2 expression.
In vivo blockade of IL-4Rα with dupilumab increased nasal ALDH2 transcript levels in AERD patients.

The authors propose that acquired ALDH2 deficiency in the AERD respiratory tract, likely driven by local IL-4/IL-13, impairs acetaldehyde degradation and thereby triggers mast cell activation underlying alcohol-induced respiratory reactions.
A retrospective analysis found that 10.9% of patients referred to a tertiary diabetic neuropathy clinic over 5 years met diagnostic criteria for treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes (TIND).

The magnitude and rate of decline in HbA1c levels positively correlates with the severity and distribution of neuropathic pain and degree of autonomic dysfunction, independent of the glucose-lowering agent used.

One proposed mechanism for TIND is that hyperglycemia-driven proliferation of arteriovenous shunts fails to remodel quickly enough during rapid glucose lowering, diverting blood away from the endoneurium and causing acute neuropathy.

An alternative mechanism proposes that rapid glycemic correction induces transient relative hypoglycemia and a stress response that upregulates proinflammatory cytokines, which damage myelinated nerves and drive neuropathic pain.
In this patient, transition from metformin to a basal-bolus insulin regimen caused an abrupt HbA1c drop from 15.0 to 7.1, after which she developed treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.

On admission, the patient exhibited a large orthostatic blood pressure drop (168/83 to 95/68 mmHg) from lying to sitting with essentially no compensatory heart rate increase (81 to 82 bpm), consistent with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
EMG two months prior to the syncopal admission showed a length-dependent, mixed axonal and demyelinating sensory-motor peripheral neuropathy with axonal degeneration in distal muscles.

Bladder catheterization that relieved over 600 cc of retained urine transiently improved the patient's orthostatic hypotension, suggesting urinary retention/autonomic bladder dysfunction contributed to her hemodynamic instability.
Neuropathic pain management was escalated with an increased gabapentin dose and initiation of duloxetine, alongside optimization of the insulin regimen for glycemic stabilization.

Some research proposes permissive hyperglycemia (deliberately reestablishing looser glycemic control) as a strategy to mitigate the inflammatory response from glycemic fluctuations and potentially reduce TIND-related painful neuropathy, though this must be weighed against the end-organ damage risk of chronic hyperglycemia.

Current recommendations to reduce TIND risk suggest limiting the rate of glycemic correction to a target HbA1c change of less than 2 percentage points over 3 months, though no formal consensus exists.
Overall complement protein levels (C3, C4, C5, C7) and CH50 activity did not differ between COVID-19 survivors with versus without post-COVID-19 condition.
Survivors reporting post-COVID fatigue had significantly lower C3 levels than those without post-COVID fatigue.
Survivors reporting post-COVID dyspnea had significantly lower C3 levels than those without post-COVID dyspnea.
Survivors reporting post-COVID dyspnea had significantly lower C5 levels than those without post-COVID dyspnea.
Survivors reporting post-COVID dyspnea had significantly lower C7 levels than those without post-COVID dyspnea.
Electroacupuncture at Baliao acupoints significantly reduced visual analogue scale pain scores in IBS patients compared to sham acupuncture.
In the IBS rat model, EA at Baliao lowered abdominal withdrawal reflex scores compared to sham acupuncture, indicating reduced visceral hypersensitivity.
EA treatment increased the abundance of beneficial gut bacterial taxa Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia in the IBS rat model.
EA treatment suppressed pathobiont taxa Helicobacter and Prevotella in the gut microbiota of the IBS rat model.
Electroacupuncture at Baliao points enhanced intestinal barrier integrity by upregulating the tight junction proteins ZO-1 and occludin in the IBS rat model.
Electroacupuncture at Baliao suppressed TRPV1-positive neuron activation in both the colon and dorsal root ganglia of IBS model rats.
EA at Baliao disrupted mast cell-neuron crosstalk by modulating the TRPV1/MAPK signaling pathway in the gut-microbiota-mast cell-TRPV1 axis underlying visceral hypersensitivity.
CLIC4 protein levels were increased in dermal fibroblasts, keratinocytes and endothelial cells of SSc skin biopsies compared to healthy control skin.
CLIC4 transcript levels were 1.5-fold higher in isolated SSc keratinocytes compared with healthy control keratinocytes.
Analysis of a public scRNA-seq dataset confirmed CLIC4 was elevated in SSc terminal keratinocytes and endothelial cells compared to healthy control.
siRNA knockdown of CLIC4 blocked expression of the pro-fibrotic markers α-SMA and CTGF in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
CLIC4 knockdown reduced β-catenin, phosphorylated SMAD3, and GLI2 levels in SSc fibroblasts but had no effect in healthy fibroblasts.
CLIC4 was elevated in fibroblasts, keratinocytes and endothelial cells of the skin of TβRIIΔk-fib transgenic mice (a fibroblast-directed TGF-β activation model of SSc) compared to wildtype mice.
TGF-β stimulation increased CLIC4 protein levels in HaCaT keratinocytes and HUVEC endothelial cells.
TGF-β stimulation reduced E-Cadherin expression in HaCaT keratinocytes, confirming induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.

HaCaT keratinocytes and HUVECs grown in transwell co-culture or exposed to conditioned media from SSc dermal fibroblasts expressed higher CLIC4 than those exposed to healthy fibroblasts, suggesting paracrine induction.
Chloride channel inhibitors NPPB and IAA-94 reduced POLY I:C (TLR3 agonist)-induced STAT1 (Y701) phosphorylation in HaCaT keratinocytes without affecting IRF3 phosphorylation.
Blocking CLIC4 activity reduced MX1 and CXCL11 interferon-stimulated gene expression in POLY I:C-stimulated keratinocytes.
CLIC4 inhibitors did not affect IRF3 phosphorylation after POLY I:C stimulation, indicating CLIC4 acts downstream of IRF3 to regulate STAT1.

siRNA knockdown of CLIC4 (45-50% reduction) attenuated STAT1 activation by 30% and reduced CXCL10 and CXCL11 (35% reduction) expression in POLY I:C-stimulated keratinocytes, without affecting IRF3 activation.

Chloride channel inhibitors blocked STAT1 activation induced by the cytosolic DNA sensor agonist Poly dA:dT without affecting STING expression, indicating CLIC4 acts specifically on STAT1 regardless of upstream stimulus.
Chloride channel inhibitors blocked TLR9 agonist (ODN2216)-induced MX1 expression in keratinocytes.
Chloride channel inhibitors partially blocked IFN-α2-induced MX1 and IFIT1 expression in keratinocytes.
CLIC4 siRNA depletion in HaCaT attenuated IFN-α2-induced STAT1 activation by 15% compared to scramble control.
TGF-β-induced STAT1 activation in keratinocytes was reversed by chloride channel inhibitors and by CLIC4 siRNA.

SSc fibroblast conditioned media increased STAT1 phosphorylation and induced MX1/CXCL10 in keratinocytes compared to mock or healthy fibroblast media, and this was reversed with a 75% reduction in MX1/CXCL10 by the CLIC4 inhibitor NPPB.
SSc fibroblast conditioned media induced a 1.5-fold increase in CLIC4 protein and transcript levels and increased nuclear translocation of CLIC4 in keratinocytes.

CLIC4 siRNA blocked the ability of SSc fibroblast conditioned media to significantly increase pSTAT1 and pSMAD3 in keratinocytes; increases were significant in scramble-transfected cells but not significant with CLIC4 knockdown.

CLIC4 expression levels were unaffected in keratinocytes stimulated with healthy or SSc fibroblast-derived exosomes, suggesting exosomes and CLIC4 induce type-1 interferon signalling through independent pathways.
The TGF-β receptor/ALK5 inhibitor SD208 reversed SSc fibroblast media-induced increases in pSTAT1, CLIC4 and pSMAD3 in keratinocytes, and reduced downstream CXCL10 and IFIT1 expression.

The JAK inhibitor Tofacitinib reversed TGF-β-induced STAT1 activation in HaCaT but did not block TGF-β-mediated SMAD2/3 activation or CLIC4 expression, indicating STAT1 activation by TGF-β is JAK-dependent while CLIC4 induction is SMAD-dependent.
In ex vivo cultured healthy skin biopsy explants, TGF-β induced expression of MX1, IFIT1 and CLIC4, and this ISG induction was attenuated by the CLIC4 inhibitor NPPB.
IBS model rats (induced by water avoidance stress) showed significantly reduced body weight gain compared to Normal rats.
Both ST36 electroacupuncture and Sham EA groups showed increased body weight gain compared to the IBS group.
Fecal pellet output was significantly increased in the IBS group compared to the Normal group.
IBS rats exhibited significantly higher Abdominal Withdrawal Reflex (AWR) scores at 40 mmHg and 60 mmHg colorectal distension compared to Normal rats, indicating visceral hypersensitivity.
Electroacupuncture at ST36 significantly reduced AWR scores compared to the IBS group at both 40 and 60 mmHg, whereas Sham EA showed similar improvement.

EMG AUC (abdominal muscle electromyography response to colorectal distension) was significantly increased in IBS rats compared to Normal rats, confirming visceral hyperalgesia, and was reduced by EA treatment.
In the open field test, IBS rats showed significant anxiety-like behavior versus Normal rats, with decreased total distance traveled, reduced average speed, and fewer central area entries.
EA at ST36 significantly improved OFT anxiety-like parameters (distance, speed, central entries) compared to IBS group, whereas Sham EA showed no significant improvement in any OFT parameter.

In the elevated plus maze, IBS rats showed decreased open arm entry %, open arm time %, and total arm entries compared to Normal rats, indicating increased anxiety-like behavior; EA at ST36 reversed these changes while Sham EA did not.
IBS rats showed autonomic imbalance with elevated LF power and LF/HF ratio and reduced HF power on HRV analysis compared to Normal rats, indicating sympathetic predominance.

EA at ST36 restored autonomic balance by decreasing LF power and LF/HF ratio and increasing HF power versus IBS group; Sham EA reduced LF power and LF/HF ratio but had no significant effect on HF power.
c-Fos expression (marker of neuronal activation) was significantly increased in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) of IBS rats compared to Normal rats.
c-Fos expression was significantly increased in the anterior insular cortex (AIC) of IBS rats compared to Normal rats.
EA at ST36 significantly suppressed the elevated c-Fos expression in both the ACC and AIC compared to the IBS group.

IBS rats exhibited significantly increased mean firing rates and coefficient of variance (CV), with reduced asymmetry index (AI), in both ACC interneurons (ACC I) and pyramidal neurons (ACC II) compared to Normal rats, indicating irregular, hyperexcitable discharge.
EA at ST36 normalized ACC neuronal firing abnormalities, significantly decreasing firing rates and CV while increasing AI values compared to the IBS group.

In IBS rats, AIC II (pyramidal) neurons showed significantly increased mean firing rates and CV with decreased AI compared to Normal, while AIC I (interneurons) showed similar but non-significant trends.
EA at ST36 selectively normalized AIC II neuronal firing rate, CV, and AI versus the IBS group, with no significant change observed in AIC I neurons after treatment.
LFP analysis showed significantly enhanced power across 0.5-35 Hz in the ACC of IBS rats compared to Normal, with particular increases in delta and theta bands.
EA at ST36 significantly attenuated the elevated delta and theta band power in the ACC compared to the IBS group.

LFP analysis showed significantly enhanced power across 0.5-35 Hz in the AIC of IBS rats compared to Normal, particularly in delta and theta bands, and EA at ST36 significantly reduced this elevated power.

IBS rats exhibited significantly increased LFP coherence and phase coherence between the ACC and AIC in delta and theta frequency bands compared to Normal rats, indicating enhanced oscillatory synchronization between these regions.

EA at ST36 significantly reduced both coherence values and phase coherence between ACC and AIC in delta and theta bands compared to the IBS group, with more dispersed phase angle distributions after treatment.

Retrograde transsynaptic viral tracing (PRV-CAG-mRFP) demonstrated direct neural projections between the ACC and AIC, supporting these regions as an interconnected circuit involved in visceral hyperalgesia.

Punicalagin and ellagic acid dose-dependently increased fibronectin gene expression in cultured human dermal fibroblasts.
FBN1 mutations account for approximately 90% of Marfan syndrome cases.
An 8-year follow-up study found that ARB (losartan) therapy decreased aortic events in MFS patients without causing side effects.
Mutations in FBN1 disrupt fibrillin-1's anchoring of TGF-β via LTBPs in the extracellular matrix, resulting in free and active TGF-β that initiates downstream signaling.
Mutations in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, or SMAD2/3 cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome, while SKI gene mutations are linked to Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, both sharing TGF-β pathway dysregulation with MFS.
Increased nitric oxide levels, driven by iNOS under inflammation, are found in aortic sections of MFS patients and animal models, contributing to aortic pathophysiology.
Oller et al identified mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA depletion in Fbn1 mice and MFS patients, contributing to impaired aortic repair and aneurysm formation.
Meta-analyses confirm that combined beta-blocker/ARB therapy is superior to monotherapy in mitigating aortic pathology in MFS.
Wang et al found no statistically significant differences in number of aortic procedures, adverse effects, or cardiovascular mortality among MFS patients treated with a single pharmacologic agent.

Lacro et al found that adding ARBs to beta-blocker therapy further prevented or slowed aortic root dilatation and reduced aortic arch dilatation in MFS patients who had undergone aortic root replacement, compared to beta-blocker monotherapy.
The Marfan Treatment Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis (2022) found that combined ARB and beta-blocker therapy cuts the aortic root enlargement rate by at least half compared to monotherapy.
While CCBs demonstrated efficacy in slowing aortic growth in some MFS patients, they may increase the risk of aortic dilatation and rupture in Marfan mice and patients in other studies.
Van Andel et al found that resveratrol aids aortic repair in rodent aneurysm models of MFS.
Huang et al showed that a novel vitamin B complex reduced aortic aneurysm volume and increased collagen deposition, stabilizing aneurysms in Fbn1C1039G/+ mice.
Some studies note that men with MFS have a higher aortic disease risk than women, possibly attributable to differences in estrogen levels.
Saddic et al showed that 17β-estradiol reduced aortic root dilatation and rupture in male Marfan mice by inhibiting the TNFα-NF-κB pathway and lowering MMP-2 and MMP-9 levels.
Inhibiting the complement C3a receptor reduced macrophage infiltration and elastic fiber breakage in a mouse model of Marfan syndrome.

Administration of histidyl-cobinamide, a cobalamin (vitamin B12) derivative and antioxidant, to Fbn1C1041G/+ mice significantly reduced DNA, lipid, and protein oxidation in the proximal aorta and prevented pathological aortic changes.
Intraperitoneal rapamycin in Fbn1mgR/mgR mice significantly inhibited mTOR downstream targets including p-RPS6, TNF-α, MMP-2, and MMP-9.
Rapamycin inhibited key oxidoreductase enzymes in smooth muscle cells of MFS mice, reducing SMC proliferation and migration and preventing thoracic aortic aneurysm development.

Oral administration of the small-molecule PP2A activator DT-061 restored PP2A activity, inhibited mTOR signaling, maintained smooth muscle cell phenotype, and mitigated aortic aneurysm progression in mice.
PIEZO1 knockout in a Marfan syndrome mouse model increased inflammation, ECM remodeling, and TGF-β pathway activation, indicating PIEZO1 acts as a protective molecule against aneurysm progression.

Injection of the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda 1 inhibited TGF-β pathway activation, enhanced ECM integrity, protected vascular smooth muscle cells from apoptosis, and reversed TAA progression in mice, with no significant side effects on long-term use.
Over 80% of individuals with Marfan syndrome developed aortic root dilatation or mitral valve prolapse by age 18.
In 109 MFS patients undergoing intraocular lens fixation via modified capsular tension ring, postoperative best-corrected visual acuity was significantly improved compared to preoperative levels.
In a follow-up of 66 MFS patients after modified capsular tension ring implantation, older patient age was associated with more significant decline in best-corrected visual acuity after surgery.
Surgical scoliosis correction with posterior internal fixation fusion was safe and effective for treating MFS-related scoliosis, with no observed neurological complications or spinal derangements.
Using an iPSC-derived model, p38 and KLF4 were found to be engaged in regulation of apoptosis in aortic smooth muscle cells of MFS patients.

Integrin α-v was confirmed to have a pathological role in aneurysm development using an iPSC-derived smooth muscle cell model, and in vivo integrin blockade reduced related molecular activity and aneurysm formation in Fbn1C1039G/+ Marfan mice.
iPSC-derived endothelial cells from MFS patients showed significant dysfunction and accelerated senescence associated with TGF-β and NF-κB signaling pathways.
Using an iPSC smooth muscle cell model, Iosef et al identified new protein markers connected to the MFS aneurysm phenotype, supporting genotype-phenotype correlation studies.

Screening of 1022 small molecules using an iPSC vascular smooth muscle cell model identified GSK3β as a recurring target; GSK3β inhibitors and gene knockdown enhanced cell function and were tested in three MFS patients.
Decoy oligodeoxynucleotides neutralizing AP-1 activators successfully reduced MMP expression in mgR/mgR Marfan mice.
AAV-delivered AP-1 neutralizing RNA hairpin decoy oligonucleotide prevented aortic elastolysis in Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, with decreased ROS production, MMP expression, and monocyte infiltration.

AAV-mediated delivery of the TGF-β inhibitory peptide P144 in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice prevented aortic dilatation when given prophylactically, whereas palliative treatment after aneurysm formation did not fully prevent aneurysm development.

AAV-based overexpression of Regnase-1 reduced inflammation and prevented aortic aneurysms, with improved elastic fiber structure, reduced aortic diameter, and lower circulating pro-inflammatory markers and TGF-β in mice.

CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing and somatic cell cloning were used to generate cloned pigs carrying FBN1 mutations that exhibit MFS-like phenotypes including skeletal curvature, decreased bone density, and aortic elastic fiber rupture.
CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing was used to generate an FBN1+/- zebrafish model mimicking human FBN1 defects.

CRISPR-Cas9 technology was used to repair FBN1 mutations in iPSCs derived from MFS patients, with genetically corrected cell lines exhibiting normal karyotype and maintained trilineage differentiation capabilities.

Aalders et al generated iPSC lines carrying a heterozygous FBN1 c.7754T>C variant from MFS patients and successfully repaired the pathogenic variant using CRISPR-Cas9 homology-directed repair, confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

A base editor system was microinjected into fertilized eggs to correct an FBN1 T7498C mutation via C-to-T conversion, with no off-target mutagenesis or insertion-deletions detected in repaired embryos.
Individuals with Marfan syndrome exhibit a notably higher incidence of aortic surgery compared to other patients undergoing vascular procedures.

Integrated bioinformatics and machine learning analysis identified four potential biomarkers relevant to Marfan syndrome pathogenesis, providing a basis for future investigation of key candidate genes.
Knockdown of Gata2 in bone marrow-derived mast cells significantly increased Itgae mRNA and surface CD103, revealing an opposite regulatory role for GATA2 compared with its activation of Mcpt1/2.
TGF-β stimulation of BMMCs induced surface CD103 expression and significantly increased Itgae mRNA but not Itgb7 mRNA.
TGF-β stimulation significantly increased mRNA levels of the mucosal mast cell proteases Mcpt1 and Mcpt2 in BMMCs.
Itgae mRNA showed a time-dependent increase after TGF-β stimulation, rising approximately five-fold at 4h, eight-fold at 6h, and eighty-fold at 24h, sustained through 48h.
Knockdown of Smad3 or Smad4 significantly suppressed the TGF-β-induced increase in Itgae mRNA, confirming the involvement of canonical Smad signaling.
Gata2 knockdown markedly and significantly increased Itgae and Itgb7 mRNA levels respectively, along with strongly induced surface CD103, while decreasing Gata2 and Mcpt2 mRNA and protein.
Gata2 knockdown abolished the TGF-β-induced transactivation of Mcpt2 while amplifying TGF-β-induced Itgae transactivation, demonstrating opposite roles of GATA2 in these two MMC genes.
Gata1 knockdown reduced Gata1 and Mcpt2 mRNA and produced an approximately two-fold increase in Itgae mRNA, with no effect on Itgb7 mRNA.
Gata1 knockdown alone did not affect baseline surface CD103, but potentiated the TGF-β-mediated increase in CD103, though less strongly than Gata2 knockdown.
Spi1 (PU.1) mRNA levels were significantly increased following Gata2 knockdown in BMMCs, indicating GATA2 normally suppresses PU.1 expression.
Spi1 knockdown, but not Irf4 knockdown, significantly decreased Itgae mRNA levels, indicating PU.1 transactivates Itgae in an IRF4-independent manner.
Double knockdown of Gata2 and Spi1 significantly abrogated the Gata2-KD-induced increases in Itgae mRNA and CD103 surface expression, showing that PU.1 mediates the effect of GATA2 loss.
ChIP assays showed that PU.1 binding to region3 of the Itgae gene was significantly increased following Gata2 knockdown, demonstrating enhanced PU.1 chromatin occupancy at this locus.
Overexpression of Spi1 (PU.1) in BMMCs generated CD103+/GFP+ cells absent in mock transfectants and significantly increased Itgae mRNA, confirming PU.1 is sufficient to induce CD103/Itgae expression.

TGF-β stimulation increased PU.1 binding to the Itgae gene without altering PU.1 or GATA2 expression at mRNA or protein levels, indicating TGF-β enhances PU.1 chromatin recruitment rather than expression.

Spi1 knockdown significantly suppressed the TGF-β-induced increase in CD103 surface expression and Itgae/Itgb7 mRNA, and also abrogated the TGF-β-induced increase in Mcpt2 transcription, indicating PU.1 is required for TGF-β-driven mucosal mast cell gene induction.

In peritoneal mast cells (connective tissue mast cells), TGF-β stimulation increased Itgae and Mcpt2 mRNA without affecting Spi1, Gata2, or Itgb7 mRNA, and induced surface CD103, similar to but distinct from BMMCs.

In peritoneal mast cells, Gata2 knockdown increased Itgae mRNA and amplified TGF-β-mediated Itgae upregulation, but did not increase Spi1 mRNA, unlike in BMMCs, indicating a distinct GATA2-Spi1 relationship in connective tissue mast cells.

The requirement of PU.1 for Itgae and Itgb7 expression, and its involvement in the TGF-β-induced increase in Mcpt2, was also observed in peritoneal mast cells, extending the BMMC findings to connective tissue mast cells.

In conventional dendritic cells, TGF-β markedly increased surface CD103 expression, and this induction was suppressed by Spi1 (PU.1) knockdown, establishing PU.1 as essential for CD103 expression on DCs.
Knockdown of Irf8 did not decrease Itgae mRNA levels in mast cells, indicating PU.1-dependent Itgae transactivation occurs independently of IRF8, despite IRF8's known role in CD103+ DC development.
SARS-CoV-2 infection of Calu-3 lung epithelial cells increased SMAD3 phosphorylation, an effect blocked by the TGF-β receptor inhibitor SB-431542.
SARS-CoV-2 infection induced PAI-1 expression in Calu-3 cells, and this induction was blocked by the TGF-β receptor inhibitor SB-431542.
Recombinant SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein and its RBD induced TGF-β expression by ELISA, and this induction required ACE2 expression, mapping the activity to the RBD.
S protein activated the SMAD3/4 (CAGA12-Luc) luciferase reporter with an optimal concentration of 105 ng/mL, a 10-fold lower concentration than previously reported to activate TGF-β signaling.
Both full-length S protein and RBD stimulated SMAD2/4 (ARE-Luc) and SMAD3/4 (CAGA12-Luc) reporter assays in an ACE2-dependent and TβRI-dependent manner (blocked by SB-431542).
TGF-β, S protein, and RBD all induced PAI-1 protein expression measured by immunofluorescence and immunoblot, an effect that was ACE2-dependent and inhibited by SB-431542.
S protein pseudotyped lentivirus (LentiS-Anc) induced PAI-1 expression in ACE2-expressing cells, whereas VSV.G pseudotyped control lentivirus did not, and induction was blocked by SB-431542.

CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of SMAD3, but not SMAD2, strongly attenuated PAI-1 induction by TGF-β, S protein, or RBD, and SMAD3-specific inhibitor SIS3 blocked both pSMAD3 activity and PAI-1 induction by S protein.
Mutating the Spike RGD motif to RGN (D405N) or to AAA abolished SMAD3 phosphorylation induced by S protein pseudovirus, mapping TGF-β pathway activation to an intact RGD motif.
ATN-161 potently suppressed SMAD2 and SMAD3 luciferase reporter activation and SMAD3 phosphorylation induced by recombinant S protein, RBD, and S protein pseudotyped lentivirus.
RT-qPCR confirmed that PAI-1 (SERPINE1) transcript induction by Spike pseudovirus required an intact RGD motif and was inhibited by ATN-161 and SB-431542.
TGF-β and S protein pseudovirus (LentiS-Anc) suppressed Poly(I:C)-induced IFN-β gene expression, an effect sensitive to SB-431542 and ATN-161 and abolished by the RGD-mutant LentiS-D405N.
SMAD3 was required for S protein-induced suppression of IFN-β, as the SMAD3 inhibitor SIS3 reversed this suppression.

TGF-β and RBD treatment increased Vaccinia virus (WR-VACV) plaque size (1.5-fold and 1.3-fold respectively), a proviral effect abolished by co-treatment with ATN-161 or SB-431542, demonstrating S protein RGD-mediated proviral activity independent of ACE2 entry.
SB-431542 treatment rescued Calu-3 cell viability from SARS-CoV-2-induced cytopathic effect, shifting the EC50 by 4.8-fold; the SMAD3 inhibitor SIS3 trended similarly, increasing EC50 by 4.5-fold.

In an air-liquid interface primary bronchial epithelial cell (ALI-PBEC) RNA-seq dataset, basal cells (a minor population of infected cells) showed strong induction of TGF-β1 expression and a TGF-β transcriptional signature following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In SARS-CoV-2-infected ALI-PBEC cultures, TGF-β1 expression correlated significantly with narrow (ATN-161-sensitive) RGD-binding integrins, and TGF-β1 transcriptional signature correlated strongly with both broad and narrow RGD-binding integrin subsets.

The authors note that with nearly one in five patients experiencing long COVID sequelae, TGF-β signaling and the Spike RGD motif represent potential therapeutic targets, and circulating Spike protein/antibodies have been reported in COVID-19 patients up to 6 months post-infection, potentially contributing to long COVID.

Across CRPS patients treated with cannabis-based medicinal products (CBMPs), all pain-specific PROMs (BPI Pain Severity, BPI Pain Interference, SF-MPQ-2 subscales, Pain VAS) showed statistically significant improvement from baseline to 6 months.
SF-MPQ-2 Continuous Pain and Intermittent Pain subscales only showed significant improvement at 3- and 6-month follow-up, not at 1 month, suggesting a delayed treatment effect.
EQ-5D-5L Self-Care domain showed no significant difference between baseline and 6-month follow-up despite improvements in other quality-of-life domains.
Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC) scores did not show a statistically significant change over time despite subjective improvement trends.
GAD-7 anxiety scores and Sleep Quality Scale (SQS) scores improved significantly from baseline at each follow-up time point, although mean anxiety severity remained classified as 'mild' throughout.
A minority of CRPS patients achieved a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) at 6 months: 28.10% for BPI Pain Severity, 40.6% for SF-MPQ-2 Overall Score, and 37.50% for Pain VAS.
Prior illicit cannabis use was associated with significantly higher odds of achieving a clinically important improvement in Pain VAS scores at 6 months on both univariate and multivariate regression.
Age over 40 years was associated with significantly higher odds of achieving a clinically important improvement in BPI Pain Severity on multivariate analysis.
Five of 64 patients (7.81%) reported adverse events, accounting for a total of 50 AE reports, with severity classified as mild (30%), moderate (30%), and severe (40%).
The most commonly reported adverse events were nausea and headache, each occurring in 4 patients (6.25%).
No psychosis-related adverse events (e.g., paranoia, hallucinations) typically associated with illicit cannabis use were reported by any patient in this monitored CBMP treatment cohort.
Median prescribed daily THC dose increased substantially from baseline to 6 months in CRPS patients treated with CBMPs.
Median prescribed daily CBD dose nearly doubled from baseline to 6 months in CRPS patients treated with CBMPs.

The study cohort had a higher proportion of male patients than expected for CRPS, despite epidemiological data indicating CRPS is roughly four times more common in females; this mirrors sex skew seen in other CBMP-prescribed cohorts.
People with multiple sclerosis and related disorders (pwMSRD) had significantly higher adjusted odds of overall NASEM-defined long COVID than controls.
pwMSRD had substantially higher adjusted odds of long COVID when defined by worsening pre-existing symptoms compared to controls.
When long COVID was defined based only on new-onset symptoms, the association between MSRD status and long COVID was attenuated and no longer statistically significant.
Overall NASEM-defined long COVID prevalence was significantly higher in pwMSRD than controls.
Long COVID prevalence based on new symptoms was significantly higher in pwMSRD than controls.
Long COVID prevalence based on worsening symptoms was markedly higher in pwMSRD than controls.

Worsening dizziness, weakness, muscle spasms, altered sensation, speech/language issues, difficulty concentrating, brain fog, fatigue, bladder control issues, muscle aches, and joint pain persisting >3 months post-COVID were all significantly more likely in pwMSRD than controls after adjustment.

New-onset brain fog, fatigue, and speech/language issues after acute COVID were significantly less likely in pwMSRD than controls, likely reflecting pre-existing symptom overlap masking new symptom detection.
Long COVID (overall, new, or worsening) was significantly associated with decreased PROMIS physical function scores.
Long COVID was significantly associated with decreased PROMIS cognitive function scores.
Long COVID was significantly associated with increased PROMIS depression severity scores.

MSRD status modified (synergized with) the association between long COVID and patient-reported outcomes, with pwMSRD experiencing greater physical function decline and depression severity from long COVID than controls.
In pwMS, long COVID (overall, new-symptom-based, or worsening-symptom-based) was associated with greater patient-reported disability accumulation on the PDDS scale.
Female sex and moderate-to-critical acute COVID-19 severity were consistently associated with higher odds of long COVID across all three definitions (overall, new, and worsening symptoms).
Using the more stringent RECOVER scoring criteria, long COVID prevalence declined substantially in both pwMSRD and controls but remained higher in pwMSRD.
The elevated odds of worsening-symptom-based long COVID in pwMSRD versus controls remained robust under the RECOVER definition.
RECOVER-defined long COVID was also associated with worse patient-reported outcomes and greater disability accumulation in pwMS.

Among pwMS, female sex, worse pre-COVID disability, and worse acute infection severity were significant contributors to long COVID development, while MS onset age, MS subtype, and disease-modifying therapy use were not.
The 2016 modified fibromyalgia criteria (FM2016) had high specificity but low sensitivity and low case-finding utility for identifying self-reported fibromyalgia diagnoses in UK Biobank participants.

A simplified criteria set (WPI≥4, SSS≥4, PSD≥12) conditional on self-reported chronic pain all over the body improved case-finding utility while retaining high screening ability compared to the standard FM2016 criteria.
Alternative definitions of widespread pain other than the single 'pain all over the body' item performed less well in case-finding for fibromyalgia.
In the USA, ME/CFS prevalence is estimated at 0.42% of adults, corresponding to about 1.09 million adults.
The prevalence of ME/CFS in high-income countries is estimated to range from 0.2% to 1%.
The prevalence of ME/CFS in Europe is estimated to range from 0.1% to 2.2%.
In Germany, ME/CFS prevalence is estimated at 140,000-310,000 individuals (0.17-0.37% of the population).
ME/CFS is estimated to affect approximately three times as many women as men.
A Norwegian study found lower ME/CFS prevalence in children aged 5-9 years, with the highest prevalence occurring in the 10-19 year age group.
A review indicated most individuals with ME/CFS have an age of onset between 20 and 45 years.
Estimated DALYs for ME/CFS in the US population aged 13+ increased from 0.714 million in 2013 to 0.733 million in 2017.
DALYs for ME/CFS in the US population aged 5+ increased from 0.921 million in 2020 to a projected 3.35-5.77 million in 2022, depending on an assumed 5% or 10% post-COVID ME/CFS onset rate.
ME/CFS DALYs were higher than those reported for multiple sclerosis, autism and HIV/AIDS.
Inflation- and PPP-adjusted per-patient costs of ME/CFS across studies ranged from USD 2,916 (direct costs only, Latvia) to USD 119,611 (indirect costs only).
Direct costs of ME/CFS ranged from USD 2916 in Latvia to USD 37,615 in the USA.
Outpatient costs of ME/CFS ranged from USD 1666.93 in Australia to USD 4833.30 in the USA.
Inpatient costs of ME/CFS ranged from USD 0 in the UK (no hospitalisations during study period) to USD 1383.07 in Australia.
Drug costs for ME/CFS patients ranged from USD 137.10 to USD 8158.34 across studies.
Indirect costs (mainly productivity losses) accounted for 66-94% of total per-patient costs, the largest cost category in all countries studied.
Unemployment among US individuals with ME/CFS was reported at 35-37%, higher than fibromyalgia (34-35%) and substantially higher than the general US population (5-6%).
Children with ME/CFS attended school less often and achieved lower educational qualifications than children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis and emotional disorders.
ME/CFS research funding in the USA would need to increase from USD 15 million/year to USD 472-600 million/year to match funding for similarly burdensome diseases.
Studies from the UK and USA found ME/CFS costs to be 50% to three times higher than costs for the general insured population with comparison to other chronic diseases such as MS or lupus.
Direct costs of undiagnosed ME/CFS patients in Latvia were estimated at USD 2498, lower than direct costs reported for diagnosed patients in other studies.
SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with subsequent ME/CFS or ME/CFS-like illness: one study reported 2.6% ME/CFS incidence post-infection, and another found 14% developed an ME/CFS-like illness.
Studies reported inconsistent gender differences in productivity losses: two studies (UK, USA) found slightly higher losses for women, while a UK-based review found higher losses for men.
Two Australian studies and one US study reported high costs for non-prescription medications/natural remedies, with one Australian study finding these exceeded prescription drug costs.

A US military claims-data study found the most frequently prescribed medications for ME/CFS in 2010 were esomeprazole, duloxetine, pregabalin, escitalopram and venlafaxine, three of which are antidepressants used off-label for symptom management.
Early FDG-PET imaging in ME/CFS patients showed significant glucose hypometabolism in the right medial frontal cortex and brainstem compared with healthy controls.

In a study of 26 ME/CFS patients, only half showed hypometabolism (cingulate gyrus and adjacent regions, with subsets showing orbitofrontal, cuneus/precuneus deficits), indicating heterogeneity in glucose metabolic abnormalities.

A case report of a 21-year-old woman with ME/CFS found FDG-PET hypometabolism in posterior cortical regions, amygdalo-hippocampal complexes, and cerebellum, with no structural MRI abnormalities detected.
A retrospective FDG-PET study of 143 Long-COVID patients found that 47% showed hypometabolism (21% mild-to-moderate, 26% severe), particularly affecting the brainstem and cerebellum.

Long-COVID patients showed significant bilateral hypometabolism in the rectal/orbital gyrus, pons, medulla, cerebellum, right temporal lobe, and right thalamus compared with healthy controls, with a trend toward greater hypometabolism among those with more symptoms or longer illness duration.

A longitudinal FDG-PET study found significant glucose hypometabolism in frontotemporal cortex, medial temporal cortex, insula, pons, and cerebellum in Long-COVID patients compared with healthy controls, and this hypometabolism remained stable between scans at 7 and 16 months post-infection.

In a study of 22 patients with mild Long-COVID vs 20 healthy controls, initial analysis showed no significant differences in glucose metabolism, though Z-score normalization suggested localized non-significant hypo- and hypermetabolic patterns.

A study of 14 Long-COVID patients with persistent neurocognitive symptoms found no significant difference in pattern expression score compared with 45 healthy controls, and no correlation between metabolic deficits and cognitive impairment measured by MoCA, contrasting with earlier positive findings.
In a preliminary study, Long-COVID patients meeting ME/CFS criteria showed significantly elevated oxygen extraction fraction compared with classic ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

In neurological post-COVID condition, previously hospitalized patients had significantly higher oxygen extraction fraction than both uninfected controls and nonhospitalized neuro-PCC participants, and elevated OEF was significantly associated with impaired locomotor function.
Multiple MRS studies reported significantly elevated ventricular lactate concentration in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy volunteers.
Using MRSI, increased lactate-to-creatine ratios were identified in the right insula, thalamus, and cerebellum of ME/CFS patients, reflecting a shift toward global anaerobic glycolysis.

MRS of the posterior cingulate cortex showed significantly elevated glutamate levels in both ME/CFS and Long-COVID patients compared with healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two patient groups.

Glx levels were increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls but not in Long-COVID patients, and Glx correlated negatively with physical function in Long-COVID while correlating positively with physical function in ME/CFS.
The first report of cortical GABA in Long-COVID found significantly reduced GABA levels in the occipital cortex, suggesting cortical hyperexcitability.
A small MRS study found significantly reduced NAA levels in the hippocampus of ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting neuronal injury or dysfunction.
NAA levels were lower in Long-COVID patients' occipital cortex compared with healthy controls, though not significantly so, and were inversely associated with verbal memory test scores.
In contrast to other studies, elevated NAA levels were found in the posterior cingulate cortex of Long-COVID patients compared with healthy controls, possibly reflecting a compensatory response.

Elevated choline levels were reported in the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex, left middle cingulate, right calcarine sulcus, and right occipital and temporal lobes in ME/CFS patients, interpreted as evidence of abnormal phospholipid metabolism and cell membrane turnover.

MRS revealed significantly reduced occipital lobe GSH levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy volunteers, with GSH inversely correlated with ventricular lactate and associated with physical health and disability indices.

A follow-up study found significantly lower GSH levels in the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (particularly pregenual ACC) of ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, suggesting redox imbalance and neuroinflammation in pathophysiology.
MRS in COVID-19 survivors 3-12 months post-hospitalization found reduced GSH levels in the anterior cingulate cortex, alongside confirmed persistent systemic inflammation.

A case study demonstrated that FDG-PET hypometabolism in the amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus, and cerebellum of a 31-year-old ME/CFS patient normalized after hyperbaric oxygen therapy, coinciding with clinical improvement.

A pilot MRS study found that 4 weeks of daily N-acetylcysteine (a GSH precursor) supplementation significantly increased cortical GSH levels in ME/CFS patients, normalizing them to levels comparable with healthy controls.

Six months after the 2003 SARS epidemic, 60% of survivors reported persistent fatigue and 44% experienced sleep disturbances, and a 4-year follow-up of 233 SARS survivors found 40.3% reported chronic fatigue with 27% meeting 1994 CDC criteria for ME/CFS.
A recent study found that 4.5% of COVID survivors remaining ill for at least 6 months fulfilled criteria for ME/CFS.
Solriamfetol significantly improved Fatigue Symptom Inventory severity scores compared to placebo at Week 8, though not at Week 6.
Solriamfetol improved the BRIEF-A global executive composite score more than placebo at Week 8, indicating improved executive functioning.
The improvement in BRIEF-A global executive composite was driven specifically by improvement in the metacognition index.
Solriamfetol did not significantly improve the BRIEF-A behavioral regulation index compared to placebo.
Solriamfetol was well tolerated in ME/CFS patients, with the most common adverse events being sleep loss and headaches.

Bilateral surgical decompression of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome led to substantial improvement in upper limb TOS symptoms, with near absence of neuralgia, numbness, or tingling one month after the first (left-sided) surgery.
After left-sided nTOS surgery, migraine frequency decreased and occipital neuralgia, vertigo, and brain fog improved, symptoms previously attributed to POTS.
One month after the second (right-sided) nTOS surgery, the patient's occipital neuralgia, arm neuralgia, vertigo, and reversal-of-vision metamorphopsia (RVM) had completely resolved.
Following bilateral nTOS surgery, the patient showed improvement in lightheadedness and cognitive fatigue, with greater cognitive clarity measured on the Wood Mental Fatigue Inventory (WMFI).
Home passive standing testing showed a heart rate increase of more than 40 bpm within 10 minutes of standing without orthostatic hypotension, consistent with a POTS diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score 5/9, elbow hyperextensibility, palms-to-floor, piezogenic papules, hyperextensible eyelids) consistent with hEDS.
The patient was diagnosed with hereditary alpha tryptasemia, confirmed by TPSAB1 copy number analysis, as a comorbid condition.
In a prior study, Hudson et al. found TOS symptoms in 54% of hypermobile patients seen in a rheumatology clinic, with 28% having radial pulse obliteration on arm abduction.
The authors' own recent retrospective review found that 58% of fatigued patients with TOS-suggestive symptoms had a Beighton score of four or higher, and 42% had been diagnosed with hEDS.
In the Sanders surgical series, 73% of 668 TOS patients reported headaches preoperatively, with 94.2% of these being occipital in location.

Cha et al. reported that among 50 patients with combined TOS and chronic migraine, 32 required TOS surgery and 12 experienced complete postoperative headache resolution; visual problems, vertigo, tinnitus, and syncope were also common in this cohort.
Histologic studies of scalene muscles from 45 TOS patients showed increased connective tissue fibers, atrophy of fast-twitch muscle fibers, and increased slow-twitch fibers.

The patient exhibited reversal-of-vision metamorphopsia (a 180° rotation of the visual field) accompanying her worst episodes of vertigo and occipital headaches, a symptom not previously described in the TOS literature.

Doppler ultrasound showed subclavian artery adduction-to-abduction velocities outside normal range on the left side, confirming vascular compression consistent with TOS, prompting left-sided surgery first.
Grip strength testing showed significant improvement after bilateral nTOS surgery compared to preoperative measurements.
Time until symptom onset during the elevated arm stress test (EAST) improved significantly after surgery, with continued improvement on the left side even after the right-sided surgery.

In a series of 30 TOS patients reported by Raskin et al., 21 developed headaches concurrent with TOS symptom intensification, frequently accompanied by nausea, vomiting, teichopsia, photophobia, blurred vision, vertigo, syncope, and tinnitus.

Analysis of PBMC DNA methylomes across three CPET timepoints identified 205 unique differentially methylated fragments (DMFs) specific to ME/CFS patients (not present in controls), reflecting exercise/PEM-induced epigenetic change.

PCA of DMFs captured much less combined variance in ME/CFS patients (49.2% for PC1+PC2) than in healthy controls (92.1%), indicating greater heterogeneity of methylation responses among ME/CFS patients.
Only 211 of the 14,054 control DMFs overlapped with the 5272 significant ME/CFS DMFs, indicating minimal shared methylation change between patients and controls in response to exercise.
Of 205 ME/CFS-specific DMFs, 24 mapped to gene promoters linkable to specific genes, with 19 showing hypermethylation and 5 showing hypomethylation across the CPET timepoints.

Genes linked to hypermethylated DMFs in ME/CFS were enriched for RHO GTPase cycle, JNK cascade, DNA-templated transcription, Wnt signalling, response to steroid hormone, immune response, and tyrosine kinase pathways, suggesting epigenetic silencing of immune, transcriptional and stress-signalling processes after exertion.

Genes linked to hypomethylated DMFs in ME/CFS were enriched for cranial nerve development, endothelium development, Class A1 Rhodopsin-like receptors, and VEGFR2 signalling, suggesting activation of angiogenesis, endothelial and neuro-sensory signalling possibly compensating for reduced cardiovascular performance.

On the second day of the two-day CPET protocol, three of five ME/CFS patients could not achieve the same peak workload as Day One, and cardiopulmonary parameters (heart rate, VO2 peak, anaerobic threshold) showed heterogeneous declines across patients, consistent with onset of post-exertional malaise.

Both healthy controls, despite differing fitness levels, maintained similar heart rate, workload, VO2 peak, and anaerobic threshold across both CPET days, with the fitter control even improving on Day Two, contrasting with the decline seen in ME/CFS patients.

Eight genes (ZDBF2, MSR1, CHD7, RXRA, ACSBG1, CACNA1H, MSI2, KLHL26) with exercise-associated differential methylation in the current PEM study had also previously shown differential methylation in ME/CFS versus healthy controls in a prior non-exertion single-timepoint study, suggesting additional exercise-induced methylation change at these loci.

CACNA1H, encoding a T-type calcium channel subunit important for neural excitability, showed differential methylation in this exercise study and had also been identified in an earlier ME/CFS methylation study, suggesting a potential role for this calcium channel in ME/CFS and PEM.

Five genes (ACOT9, DUSP9, LSM14A, TOP1MT, SEMA6B) linked to methylation changes during the exercise-induced PEM response in this study were also found differentially methylated during a separate stress-related illness relapse in two of the same patients in a prior longitudinal study, suggesting shared epigenetic mechanisms between PEM and relapse.

In healthy controls, 744 genes linked to combined hyper/hypomethylated DMFs showed broad functional enrichment including neuron projection development, chemical synaptic transmission, hemopoiesis, muscle structure development, and cell adhesion, contrasting with the more restricted immune-focused response in ME/CFS.

Promoter-linked DMFs in ME/CFS patients were restricted almost exclusively to genes involved in positive activation of immune and inflammatory responses, in stark contrast to the much more functionally diverse promoter-linked DMFs (axon development, growth hormone response, pancreas development, leukocyte migration, synaptic activity) seen in healthy controls.

The number and functional diversity of genes linked to methylation changes increased over the exercise time-course: 28 genes early (signal transduction, lipid metabolism, neural development, protein modification, metabolism), 53 genes late (adding cytoskeleton, transcription, immune system, ion transport), and 67 genes gradually (adding RNA processing and structural proteins).

MSR1, encoding the macrophage scavenger receptor involved in innate/adaptive immunity and lipid metabolism, showed a pattern of continuous hypomethylation across the exercise timepoints in ME/CFS patients.
All 16 LC-yes patients exhibited post-exertional malaise (PEM), compared to only 4 of 16 LC-no patients (25%).
ME/CFS diagnosis rates did not differ significantly among controls (10.8%), LC-no (6.3%), and LC-yes (18.8%) groups.
Unlike the typical 3:1 female-to-male ME/CFS ratio seen in controls, all three ME/CFS cases in the LC-yes group were male, suggesting a possible sex-specific difference in post-COVID ME/CFS.
A higher proportion of LC-yes patients (68.8%) reported six or more symptoms during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to LC-no patients (31.3%), a statistically significant difference.

LC-yes patients scored significantly higher than both LC-no patients and controls across multiple ICC symptom domains, including PEM, neurosensory/perceptual/motor disturbances, neurocognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, pain, thermoregulatory instability, flu-like symptoms, and susceptibility to viral infections with prolonged recovery.
During the acute infection phase, tiredness and/or fatigue was reported by 93.7% of LC-yes patients compared to 62.5% of LC-no patients.
A cited analysis of 739 long COVID patients found only an 8.4% prevalence of ME/CFS, with a significantly lower prevalence among those infected during the Omicron phase.
A cited study by Tokumasu et al. found that 17.9% of LC cases met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, closely matching this study's own finding of 18.8%.
Independent of ME/CFS diagnosis, fatigue is reported as the most common LC symptom, affecting 50-70% of patients and believed to be of central origin.
A cited pooled analysis reports overall LC prevalence of 43%, higher in hospitalized (54%) than non-hospitalized (34%) patients, with women more frequently affected than men (49% vs 37%).
A cited study found elevated creatine kinase (>200 IU/L) consistent with skeletal muscle injury in 22.4% of patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19.

A cited prior study found normal isolated muscle fiber conduction velocity and jitter parameters in the tibialis anterior muscle of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals with or without LC-related fatigue, suggesting fatigue originates centrally rather than at the neuromuscular junction or muscle fiber level.

Both LC and ME/CFS patients may exhibit sensory or autonomic small-fiber neuropathy, evidenced by impaired heat detection and increased corneal subbasal nerve plexus tortuosity, though this does not distinguish between the two conditions.
Graded Exercise Therapy produced higher recovery rates on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (33%) compared to Adaptive Pacing Therapy and Specialist Medical Care (21-22%).
Graded Exercise Therapy produced higher recovery rates on the SF-36 Physical Function scale (53%) compared to Adaptive Pacing Therapy and Specialist Medical Care (35-41%).
A significantly higher proportion of patients reported symptom improvement after Pacing Therapy (44%) than after Graded Exercise Therapy (12%).
Graded Exercise Therapy resulted in less frequent muscle and joint pain compared to Adaptive Pacing Therapy and Specialist Medical Care.

Graded Exercise Therapy participants scored 4.2 points lower on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire and 6.3 points higher on the SF-36 Physical Function scale than Specialist Medical Care participants, indicating better outcomes.
Adaptive Pacing Therapy and Specialist Medical Care both showed significant improvements in fatigue and physical function at 2.5-year follow-up.
Adverse events were reported across two of the included studies, with more than half of participants experiencing non-serious adverse events (NSAEs).
Adverse events were documented in two of the six included studies, with more than half of participants experiencing non-serious adverse events (NSAEs).
Serious deteriorations in fatigue and physical functioning were noted across all treatment groups (PT, GET, and SMC).
The review concluded that, based on adverse effect profiles, GET and PT appear to be safer treatment options than Standard Medical Care (SMC).

Overall, the systematic review concluded that both Pacing Therapy and Graded Exercise Therapy are more effective than Standard Medical Care for ME/CFS, with GET particularly favoured for improving pain, fatigue, and physical function.
Using ME/CFS classification criteria, 25/51 (49%) of the UofA SSc cohort were classified as fatigued (SSc-F).
In the larger CSRG registry cohort, 45/126 (35.7%) of SSc patients were classified as fatigued (ME/CFS-like) using a FACIT cutoff of <30.
Female sex was significantly more prevalent among fatigued CSRG patients compared to non-fatigued patients.
CRP levels were significantly higher in fatigued CSRG patients compared to non-fatigued patients.
Cognitive failure, anxiety, and depression scores were all significantly higher in fatigued (SSc-F) than non-fatigued SSc patients in the UofA cohort.
Quality of life (SF-36 physical and mental component scores) was significantly lower in fatigued SSc patients compared to non-fatigued.
Disability scores (HAQ-DI) were significantly higher in fatigued SSc patients, and a significantly higher proportion of fatigued patients were unemployed or on disability welfare.
Fatigue (FACIT score) was the strongest correlate of disability (HAQ-DI) in the UofA cohort, outweighing SSc disease-specific indices.
Fatigue (FACIT) was also the strongest correlate of disability (HAQ-DI) in the larger CSRG cohort, outweighing measures of SSc disease severity.
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO SB, % predicted and actual) was significantly reduced in fatigued SSc patients in the UofA cohort.
In the CSRG cohort, both FVC and TLC (% predicted and actual) were significantly lower in fatigued patients compared to non-fatigued patients.

In the CSRG cohort, after controlling for age, disease duration and damage accrual, FVC% predicted and DLCO SB% predicted moderately/weakly correlated with fatigue (FACIT), while disease damage accrual (SCTC-DI) also weakly correlated with fatigue.
In the UofA cohort, no significant correlations were found between fatigue (FACIT) and other parameters when controlling for age, disease duration, and disease damage accrual.
Nailfold capillary density was significantly lower in fatigued SSc patients compared to non-fatigued patients, suggesting increased microvascular remodeling.
Plasma Galectin-9 levels were significantly elevated in fatigued SSc patients compared to non-fatigued patients in the UofA cohort.
Serum Galectin-9 levels were significantly higher in fatigued CSRG patients compared to non-fatigued patients, replicating the UofA finding in an independent cohort.
In the combined cohort (n=174), patients with Galectin-9 levels above the 75th percentile had significantly lower FVC, TLC, and DLCO SB (% predicted) than those below.
Patients with Galectin-9 above the 75th percentile also had greater skin involvement, disease damage accrual, and lower FACIT fatigue scores (indicating worse fatigue).
Plasma levels of LT-α, IL-16, PIGF, and VEGF were significantly elevated in fatigued compared to non-fatigued UofA SSc patients.
CRP, LT-α, and IL-6 (all linked to lung fibrosis) positively correlated with Galectin-9 levels in the UofA cohort.
A FACIT fatigue cutoff of <30 identified ME/CFS-classified patients (per Canadian Consensus Criteria) with 90% accuracy in the UofA cohort.

The frequency of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and interstitial lung disease (ILD) did not differ between fatigued and non-fatigued SSc patients in the UofA cohort, nor did autoantibody status, CRP, TSH, DAT, HbA1c, or vitamin B12 levels.
Hypothyroidism was significantly more prevalent in the long COVID/CFS-ME-like clinical sample than in the pre-COVID community control sample.
Bipolar spectrum disorder was markedly more frequent in the long COVID/CFS-ME-like clinical sample compared to the pre-COVID community sample.
PTSD was significantly more frequent in the long COVID/CFS-ME-like clinical sample than in the pre-COVID community sample.
Major depressive disorder was more frequent in the clinical sample than in community controls by chi-square analysis, though the association only approached significance with Fisher's exact test.
No statistically significant difference was found in the frequency of panic disorder between the long COVID/CFS-ME-like sample and community controls.

Positive screening for depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 (both mean score and proportion above clinical cutoffs) was markedly higher in the long COVID/CFS-ME-like clinical sample than in matched pre-COVID community controls.
Within the clinical sample, hypothyroidism co-occurred with bipolar disorder and other mood disorders at rates far higher than reported in prior literature comorbidity studies.

All cases of bipolar disorder and hypothyroidism in the clinical sample had onset predating the SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infection and the subsequent CFS/ME-like syndrome, supporting their role as pre-existing conditions rather than consequences of infection.

In contrast to bipolar disorder and hypothyroidism, three cases of major depressive disorder and one case of PTSD had onset after the acute COVID-19 respiratory illness, suggesting these arose as a consequence of infection rather than as pre-existing vulnerability factors.
CFS patients show consistently reduced natural killer cell cytotoxicity, considered the most consistent immune abnormality reported in CFS since 1987.
The Th1/Th2 cell ratio was decreased in CFS patients, suggesting a diminished Th1-driven immune response as an intrinsic immune abnormality.
Plasma TNF-alpha levels were higher in CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Increased IL-10 levels were associated with greater somatic symptom severity in CFS patients.
IL-8 levels were reported to be increased in CFS patients.
IL-13 levels were reported to be increased in CFS patients.
