Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity is decreased in CFS patients, potentially contributing to hormonal downregulation and a hypometabolic state.

Booth et al. studied the ATP profile of 138 CFS patients versus 53 healthy controls and found that most CFS patients had mitochondrial dysfunction with an ATP profile associated with disease severity.
DNA methylation differences were found at the PRF1 gene and multiple CpG sites in T cells from CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Some CFS patients (originally described as 'chronic EBV infection syndrome') showed elevated EBV antibody titres, suggesting EBV infection may be associated with CFS development.

Multiple viral infections including HHV-7, parvovirus B19, Borna disease virus, enterovirus, and coxsackievirus group B are described as risk factors for CFS development, with Borna disease virus showing the strongest association.

In an analysis of 10 lncRNAs in PBMCs from 44 CFS patients, the immune-related lncRNAs NTT, MIAT, and EMX2OS were significantly increased, with NTT and EMX2OS levels correlating with disease severity, and an NTT-IFNGR1 axis implicated in CFS.

Children of women with CFS showed similar mental illness conditions to their mothers, whereas this pattern was not observed for fathers, suggesting a possible maternal-linked genetic susceptibility component in CFS.

The lncRNA Erdr1 normally enhances NK-cell cytotoxicity while inducing T-cell apoptosis; the authors hypothesize that dysregulated Erdr1 in CFS may impair NK cell function and contribute to immune surveillance defects, though CFS-specific validation is lacking.

Linc-MAF-4 normally promotes Th1 differentiation and suppresses Th2 differentiation by inhibiting MAF; the authors hypothesize that reduced linc-MAF-4 expression in CFS may contribute to the observed Th1/Th2 imbalance.

GATA3-AS1 upregulates GATA3 and Th2-related cytokines IL-5 and IL-13, promoting Th2 differentiation; the authors hypothesize that its overexpression in CFS could exacerbate Th2 polarization and disrupt immune homeostasis.

THRIL forms a complex with hnRNPL to trans-regulate TNF-alpha expression in TLR1/2-stimulated macrophages; the authors hypothesize that elevated THRIL in CFS may drive increased TNF-alpha and chronic inflammation.

NEAT1 stimulates IL-8 expression by binding the splicing factor SFPQ and inducing its translocation from the IL-8 promoter; the authors hypothesize that NEAT1 upregulation in CFS could enhance IL-8-mediated inflammation and worsen fatigue/pain symptoms.

Decreased HOXA11os in colonic myeloid cells leads to Complex I deficiency, oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction, and mitochondrial ROS production, which the authors hypothesize may contribute to intestinal dysfunction and inflammation in CFS patients with defective HOXA11os.

ROSALIND is a lncRNA that acts as a ROS buffering system protecting mitochondrial translation from oxidative stress; the authors propose that dysregulated ROSALIND without adequate mitochondrial protection may explain persistent fatigue in CFS patients given documented oxidative stress in this population.

LncMtDloop, encoded in the mitochondrial D-loop region, is significantly reduced in Alzheimer's disease patients and its restoration improves AD-like pathology in mice; the authors hypothesize that similar downregulation in CFS patients may contribute to their cognitive deficits.

glycoLINC acts as a scaffold assembling glycolytic enzymes into functional metabolons to enhance glycolytic flux and ATP production under nutrient deprivation; the authors hypothesize its altered levels in CFS may disrupt the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis balance and impair mitochondrial function.

H19 regulates mitochondrial calcium homeostasis, ATP production, ROS levels, and ER-mitochondrial coupling via VDAC1; H19 suppression enhances ER-mitochondrial coupling and upregulates gluconeogenesis genes, and the authors hypothesize altered H19 in CFS may disrupt the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis balance and worsen mitochondrial function over time.

CHROMR is a lncRNA induced during influenza A and SARS-CoV-2 infection that enhances the antiviral immune response by sequestering the transcriptional co-repressor IRF2BP2 and promoting interferon-stimulated gene expression.
LncRNA MALAT1 is proposed to contribute to antiviral responses through interactions with the transcription factors IRF1, IRF4, STAT1, STAT3, and STAT5A.

An unspecified lncRNA was reported to modulate RIG-I signalling and related biological processes implicated in COVID-19 and subsequent disease states, which the authors link conceptually to CFS pathogenesis.
Activin B has been proposed as a candidate biomarker for CFS, but its diagnostic utility remains controversial.
Circulating miRNA expression profiles have been proposed as CFS biomarkers, but recruitment limitations and confounding by age, gender, and motor status have stalled their clinical utility.
In a study examining 10 lncRNAs in PBMCs of 44 CFS patients, the immune-related lncRNAs NTT, MIAT, and EMX2OS were significantly increased.
NTT and EMX2OS expression levels correlated with disease severity in CFS, and the NTT-IFNGR1 axis was identified as potentially playing a role in CFS, though the mechanism remains unclear.

Initial Rasch analysis of the HADS in CFS patients showed suboptimal model fit, but after subtest modifications to address local item dependence, the scale showed acceptable fit, strict unidimensionality, high reliability (PSI = 0.87), and no differential item functioning by demographic variables.

Rasch-converted interval scores yielded a significantly higher mean score than unconverted ordinal scoring in CFS patients, indicating that ordinal scoring systematically underestimates the latent trait level of psychological distress.
Rasch interval scoring of the HADS demonstrated a 45% reduction in measurement error compared to raw ordinal scoring, reflecting improved measurement precision in CFS patients.
Latent class analysis identified a distinct 'psychosomatic' multimorbidity cluster of 527 participants characterized by high prevalence of myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME/CFS), anxiety, and stress.
The elderly multimorbidity cluster (oldest age, high prevalence of chronic kidney disease and hypercholesterolemia) had a higher risk of incident heart failure compared with the young cluster.
The pulmonary disease multimorbidity cluster (high prevalence of respiratory problems) had a higher risk of incident heart failure compared with the young cluster.

The obese/physical inactivity multimorbidity cluster (high prevalence of obesity, hypertension, myocardial infarction and stroke) had the highest risk of incident heart failure among all clusters compared with the young cluster.

Unlike other clusters, the obese/physical inactivity cluster was relatively more likely to develop heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) than heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
Across all six multimorbidity clusters, participants who developed heart failure were more likely to develop HFrEF than HFpEF.
In contrast to the other clusters, the obese/physical inactivity cluster was relatively more likely to develop HFpEF than HFrEF.
Over 110,621 person-years of follow-up, 622 of the 6839 participants developed incident heart failure, comprising 390 HFrEF and 220 HFpEF cases.
Latent class analysis of comorbidities in the PREVEND cohort identified six distinct multimorbidity clusters that differed in age, chronic disease prevalence, and impact on heart failure risk.
TGD individuals had a significantly higher prevalence of hypermobile EDS and hypermobility spectrum disorder than cisgender individuals, with an odds ratio of 18.45.
Among individuals assigned female at birth, TGD individuals had a hEDS/HSD prevalence of 2.62% compared with 0.16% in cisgender females.
Among individuals assigned male at birth, TGD individuals had a hEDS/HSD prevalence of 1.00% compared with 0.04% in cisgender males.
Hormone therapy status among TGD individuals was not significantly associated with differences in hEDS/HSD prevalence.
The common MTHFR C677T polymorphism was not significantly enriched in the hEDS cohort compared to the gnomAD non-Finnish European population.
The common MTHFR A1298C polymorphism was not significantly enriched in the hEDS cohort compared to the gnomAD non-Finnish European population.
Nearly a third (33.5%) of the hEDS cohort carried at least one rare or low-frequency KLK gene variant, with 49 unique variants (79 alleles) identified overall.
The KLK15 p.Gly226Asp missense variant showed perfect phenotype-genotype segregation with hEDS in two independent multigenerational families.
Gene burden testing showed a significantly increased burden of KLK15 variants in the hEDS cohort compared to gnomAD controls.

KLK15 mRNA is broadly expressed across human tissues (highest in thyroid/adrenal glands and GI tissues per GTEx) and was experimentally confirmed by RT-PCR in human ACL, dermal fibroblasts, and mast cells, with conserved expression in mouse thymus, skin, tendon, and adrenal gland.

Yeast two-hybrid screening and co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that KLK15 physically interacts with fibronectin (FN1), binding the amino terminus of mature FN1 required for dimerization and fibrin/heparin binding.

Yeast two-hybrid screening and co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that KLK15 physically interacts with lysyl oxidase (LOX) at its signal sequence and catalytic LOX domain, essential for enzymatic activity.
Achilles tendons from Klk15G224D/+ knock-in mice showed increased displacement, increased strain, and reduced toe modulus compared to wild-type, consistent with a more elastic tendon phenotype.
TEM analysis showed a 20% reduction in Achilles tendon collagen fibril diameter in Klk15G224D/+ mice compared to wild-type controls.
83% (5/6) of Klk15G224D/+ mice exhibited mitral valve prolapse and valve dysfunction on echocardiography, versus none of the 5 control mice.
Movat's pentachrome staining showed myxomatous degeneration of mitral and aortic valves in 75% (3/4) of Klk15G224D/+ mice compared to none of controls.
Klk15G224D/+ mouse tail biopsies showed a significantly reduced soluble-to-insoluble LOX ratio, with a reciprocal increase of KLK15 in the insoluble fraction, compared to control littermates.
Serum cytokine profiling of Klk15G224D/+ mice showed statistically significant downregulation of eleven cytokines involved in inflammation and immune regulation compared to wild-type mice.
WES of 200 hEDS patients revealed rare, predicted-damaging variants across 14 of the 15 KLK genes, indicating potential polygenic involvement of the KLK family beyond KLK15 alone.
Serum mass spectrometry proteomics identified 35 of 478 detected proteins with significantly altered abundance in hEDS patients compared to age- and sex-matched controls.
Complement cascade proteins were the most prominently enriched category among differentially expressed serum proteins, comprising 15 of the 35 altered proteins.
Nine of the 35 differentially expressed proteins (26%) were related to kallikrein activity or clotting cascades.
ECM1 was the only structural extracellular matrix protein found to be differentially expressed in serum between hEDS patients and controls, with most other ECM proteins showing no difference.
No significant differences were found in serum fibronectin or collagen levels, or their proteolytic fragments, between hEDS and control samples, contrasting with prior reports.

Pathway and gene ontology analysis showed that differentially abundant proteins were predominantly localized extracellularly and involved in innate immune responses, complement activation, coagulation cascades, and inflammatory/oxidative stress responses.

Cell type-specific expression analysis indicated that the differentially expressed proteins are predominantly synthesized by hepatocytes and other liver-derived cells, consistent with systemic immune/hemostatic regulatory roles.
ELISA validation in the full cohort showed significantly lower serum C1QA in hEDS patients compared to controls.
ELISA validation showed significantly lower serum C8a in hEDS patients compared to controls in the full cohort.
ELISA validation showed significantly lower serum C8b in hEDS patients compared to controls in the full cohort.
ELISA validation showed significantly lower serum C9 in hEDS patients compared to controls in the full cohort, though this reduction lost significance after excluding males and autoimmune diagnoses.

ELISA showed significantly reduced serum C3 in hEDS patients compared to controls, supporting upstream complement involvement, and remained significant after excluding autoimmune/male samples and across both age groups.
Age-stratified ELISA analysis showed that C1QA reduction in hEDS was most prominent in subjects younger than 37 years.
C8a and C8b reductions in hEDS were significant in both younger and older age subgroups, indicating age-independent dysregulation of terminal complement components.
IGFBP-2 was the only cytokine found elevated in hEDS serum compared to controls in the 105-cytokine array.
Seven cytokines/proteins—MPO, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), TGF-α, Pentraxin 3, transferrin receptor, HGF, and IL-19—were significantly downregulated in hEDS serum, with TGF-α showing the largest fold change.

Correlation matrix analysis showed strong positive correlations between complement components (C3 and C4b, r=0.89; C8a and C9, r=0.85) and between cytokines (MPO and Serpin E1, r=0.85) in hEDS patients.
A proinflammatory cytokine cluster was identified with strong positive correlations between IL-19 and Pentraxin 3 (r=0.89), IL-19 and MPO (r=0.77), and Pentraxin 3 and MPO (r=0.81) in hEDS.
Inverse correlations were observed between C9 and C1QA (r=-0.52), TGF-α and C9 (r=-0.43), and TGF-α and C8a (r=-0.21), suggesting heterogeneity in complement activation within the hEDS population.

Mast cell activation disease-related symptoms were reported by 71% of the hEDS cohort, a prevalence consistent with prior studies, supporting a link between complement dysregulation and mast cell-mediated immune responses.

ADAMTS13, a secreted protein involved in ECM remodeling, blood pressure regulation, and coagulation, was among the differentially expressed proteins identified in the mass spectrometry analysis of hEDS serum.

Disease association mapping of the proteomic dataset showed enrichment for disorders of complement dysregulation and coagulopathies, including complement component deficiencies and thrombotic microangiopathies.

Prior reports indicate an increased prevalence of chronic venous insufficiency in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, mainly affecting vascular EDS but also reported in classic, spondylodysplastic, and kyphoscoliotic subtypes.

EDS patients undergoing vascular surgical or interventional procedures face a markedly increased risk of complications such as vessel tearing, aneurysm formation, arteriovenous fistulas, and severe bleeding, occasionally resulting in limb loss or death.

A 42-year-old man with SLC39A13-associated spondylodysplastic EDS underwent endoluminal laser ablation (1940 nm) of the right small saphenous vein with subsequent foam sclerotherapy of side branches, achieving complete vein occlusion without complications, sustained at one-year follow-up.

A 64-year-old woman with classic EDS underwent endoluminal laser ablation (1940 nm) of the left great saphenous vein with subsequent foam sclerotherapy, resulting in complete vein occlusion without intraoperative complications, sustained at one-year follow-up.

Foam sclerotherapy of side branch varices was effective in both EDS patients but caused mild adverse reactions (painful sclerothrombi in one patient, excessive sclerosing reactions in the other), both managed conservatively without lasting harm.

Long-wave laser systems (1320, 1470, 1500, 1920, 1940 nm) with radial emission fibers are associated with fewer side effects such as pain, ecchymosis, inflammatory reactions, and nerve injury compared with short-wave lasers (810–980 nm).
Bare-tipped laser fibers can cause truncal vein wall perforation due to concentrated heat emission, whereas radial emission fibers diffuse thermal energy and thereby reduce perforation risk.

Arteriovenous fistula formation has been reported as a rare complication of endoluminal laser ablation using short-wave (810 nm) and long-wave (1320 nm) lasers in patients without EDS, suggesting these are general procedural risks rather than EDS-specific complications.
Radiofrequency ablation requires maintaining a 2 cm safety distance from the deep vein, whereas radial laser fibers allow ablation up to the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in COL3A1, which encodes the alpha1 chains of type III collagen, leading to arterial fragility.
Vascular complications in VEDS develop in about 25% of patients before age 20, increasing to 80% by age 40.

Patient 1 had VEDS caused by a pathogenic missense COL3A1 variant (c.970G>A, p.Gly324Ser) and experienced multiple arterial events including celiac artery dissection, hepatic artery aneurysms, bilateral external iliac dissections, and a later spontaneous right coronary artery dissection causing myocardial infarction.

In Patient 1, percutaneous coronary intervention (stenting) for a right coronary artery dissection was complicated by cardiac tamponade, likely due to arterial perforation into the pericardial space, illustrating the risk of interventions in the fragile arteries of VEDS.

Patient 2 was diagnosed with VEDS due to a pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.2302G>C, p.Gly768Arg) after presenting with multiple arterial dissections/thrombosis, and later developed a type B aortic dissection.

In Patient 2, elective splenic artery embolization for an enlarging aneurysm was complicated by a new dissection at the common hepatic/gastroduodenal artery bifurcation, demonstrating the vascular fragility risk of routine interventions in VEDS.

Patient 3 had a COL3A1 splice acceptor variant (c.4255-1G>T) predicted to cause haploinsufficiency, a variant class typically associated with milder VEDS manifestations and delayed onset of arterial dissections, although this patient's disease course was accelerated by coexisting aortic arch anomalies and hypertension.

Aberrant right subclavian artery with a left aortic arch occurs in 0.7%-2.0% of the general population and is associated with Kommerell diverticula that can progressively dilate and rupture, with increased risk of dissection or rupture in patients with heritable aortopathies such as VEDS.

The BBEST open-label trial suggested a potential benefit of celiprolol (up to 400 mg/d) for reducing arterial events in VEDS, but the finding was questioned because many participants lacked genetically confirmed COL3A1 variants.
A randomized clinical trial of the angiotensin II receptor blocker irbesartan (NCT02597361) reported a positive result for VEDS management.
Observational studies suggest that both beta-blockers and angiotensin II receptor blockers reduce clinical vascular events and mortality in VEDS by preventing arterial ruptures.
Median survival in VEDS is significantly shorter than population norms, with arterial rupture being the most frequent cause of death.
Patient 3's right subclavian bypass surgery, performed for VEDS-associated aberrant right subclavian artery/type B dissection, was complicated by right phrenic nerve palsy.
Patients with EDS/HSD had significantly higher rates of revision ankle ligament repair surgery at 2 years compared with propensity-matched controls without EDS/HSD.

At 5 years postoperatively, patients with EDS/HSD showed an even greater relative increase in revision surgery rates compared with matched controls, with EDS/HSD remaining an independent risk factor on multivariable analysis.
Whole exome sequencing revealed a homozygous HBB mutation confirming the diagnosis of sickle cell disease in this child.
A heterozygous COL3A1 mutation was identified, diagnostic of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type IV) in this child.
A homozygous RSPH9 mutation confirmed the diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia in this child.
A heterozygous pathogenic SHANK3 variant established the diagnosis of Phelan-McDermid syndrome, associated with autism spectrum features in this child.

This is reported as the first documented pediatric case of the co-occurrence of four genetically distinct disorders (SCD, vEDS, PCD, and PMS) in a single patient, producing a compounded multisystem disease burden.
The child presented with musculoskeletal manifestations of EDS including hyperextensible skin, joint laxity, and a right knee dislocation at birth that was reduced neonatally.
Generalized hypotonia and ligamentous laxity, attributed to combined EDS and PMS, compromised proper inhaler technique for respiratory therapy.
PCD-related chronic airway inflammation is proposed to act as a continuous pro-inflammatory stimulus that heightens the frequency and severity of acute chest syndrome episodes in this SCD patient.
Splenectomy performed in June 2022 was followed by some clinical stabilization of the patient's hemolytic/anemia crises.
The patient experienced severe hemolytic crises with hemoglobin levels documented as low as 2 g/dL, requiring multiple PICU admissions.
Consanguinity in the Jazan region is proposed as a key risk factor enabling chance co-inheritance of multiple independent pathogenic variants (HBB, COL3A1, RSPH9, SHANK3) in this patient.

Because both parents were clinically asymptomatic for the dominant conditions (vEDS and PMS) and were not genetically tested, the authors suggest the COL3A1 and SHANK3 variants may represent de novo mutations.

A split-thickness skin graft combined with the Recell autologous skin cell harvesting device successfully closed a large complex knee wound in a patient with classical EDS, with intact skin and no complications at 10-month follow-up.
A bilayered dermal substitute (Integra) was applied over the gastrocnemius flap to prime the wound bed and provide a foundation prior to autografting.

A multidisciplinary regenerative medicine team administered testosterone enanthate, human growth hormone, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy to enhance collagen synthesis, angiogenesis, and oxygen delivery to the wound.

Because of compromised cutaneous healing from hyperelastic, narrowed dermis in classical EDS, a thinner confluent sheet of skin than typically harvested for STSG was obtained to promote better donor site healing.
Despite consistent sunscreen use, the skin graft became hyperpigmented, which the authors note is an expected outcome in patients with EDS.

The patient's postoperative course after patellar tendon repair was complicated by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus necrotizing fasciitis and osteomyelitis, necessitating extensive debridement.

Classical EDS is described as featuring joint hypermobility, markedly elastic and friable skin, and poor wound healing due to underlying connective tissue fragility that compromises normal tissue repair.
Up to 30% of patients with Down syndrome have occipitocervical or atlantoaxial instability.
Mucopolysaccharidoses cause accumulation of glycosaminoglycans that can lead to craniocervical instability and cervical spinal canal stenosis.

Connective tissue disorders including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, along with Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1, can cause severe and unstable cervical spine deformities that may remain asymptomatic for a long time.
Cervical X-rays should be performed in patients with connective tissue or neurofibromatosis-related syndromes if there is any suspicion of cervical spine involvement.

For surgical correction and stabilization of progressive cervical deformity or stenosis, instrumentation should have wide limits exceeding the anatomical limits of the deformity by at least 2-3 levels to prevent adjacent segment deformity.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is classified among systemic diseases that disrupt the physiology and integrity of epithelial and connective tissues, leading to periodontal tissue loss considered a distinct form of periodontitis.

A statistically significant association was found between generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) and temporomandibular disorder (TMD), with 85.4% of GJH-positive subjects diagnosed with TMD, although the effect size was weak.
GJH was significantly associated with mandibular asymmetry, with 68.3% of GJH-positive patients being asymmetric compared to 45.5% of GJH-negative patients.
Mandibular asymmetry showed a strong, statistically significant, moderate-effect association with TMD, with 71.2% of TMD patients presenting mandibular asymmetry.
Among participants without GJH, mandibular asymmetry was significantly more common in those diagnosed with TMD, though with a small effect size.
In the GJH-positive group, the association between mandibular asymmetry and TMD reached only marginal significance with a small effect size, indicating a weak relationship in hypermobile individuals.
TMD was highly prevalent in this pre-orthodontic pediatric/adolescent sample, affecting 70.3% of all participants.
No statistically significant association was found between the presence of GJH and sex in this pediatric sample.
Most of the eight patients who underwent non-vascularized toe PIP joint transfer achieved good thumb stability and a functional passive range of motion.
Reconstructed thumbs following toe PIP joint transfer averaged approximately 75% of the length of a normal thumb.
Grip strength of the reconstructed hand measured about 50% of that in the contralateral (unaffected) hand.
Foot donor-site assessment after PIP joint harvest showed toe shortening in most patients but no deficits in ambulation or weight-bearing.
The overall surgical complication rate among the eight patients was 25%, and most patients and parents reported satisfaction with treatment outcomes.

VAS pain ratings were on average higher in FM patient groups than controls but showed high variability, resulting in no statistically significant between-group difference at hand, knee, or foot stimulation sites.
No significant relationship was found between subjective pain rating and the amplitude of the N2 or P2 laser-evoked potential peaks in any group.
Vertex laser-evoked potential amplitude and latency did not differ between controls, all FM patients, or between FM biopsy-defined subgroups.
In healthy controls, hand stimulation elicited a strong synergistic TII cluster near the N2 and P2 components.
FM patients with normal skin biopsy (IENFD-FMN) showed two synergy clusters plus one large redundancy cluster overlapping the N2 and P2 peaks during hand stimulation.
FM patients with proximal denervation (IENFD-FMP) showed a significant synergistic TII effect during hand stimulation.
FM patients with combined proximal and distal denervation (IENFD-FMD) showed a lack of synergistic TII effect and multiple redundancy clusters during hand stimulation.
In controls, knee stimulation elicited a synergy cluster in the temporal interaction information consistent with the N2 wave.
IENFD-FMN patients showed multiple TII clusters at the knee, including one covering a wide time window.
IENFD-FMP patients showed a relatively small redundancy cluster at the knee.
IENFD-FMD patients showed a large positive (synergy) TII cluster at the knee coinciding with the N2 peak and partly P2.
Control subjects showed limited temporal interaction with only two small significant clusters at the foot.
IENFD-FMN patients showed a large synergy TII cluster at the foot overlapping the N2 and P2 components.
IENFD-FMP patients showed several temporal interactions at the foot including one of the largest synergy cluster masses observed in the study.

IENFD-FMD patients showed few TII clusters at the foot, with significantly negative (redundancy) values, indicating reduced additive/synergistic information between late LEP time course and perceived pain.
Between-group comparison at the foot showed significantly higher TII in controls than in IENFD-FMN patients near the P2 peak.

Between-group comparison at the hand showed patients with proximal denervation (IENFD-FMP) had higher T2 TII values than controls near the P2 peak, suggesting a stronger correlation between neuronal activity and pain perception in this subgroup.
Between-group comparison at the knee showed significantly higher TII in controls than in IENFD-FMP patients, associated with the P2 peak.

Between-group comparison at the hand showed markedly higher TII in controls than in IENFD-FMD patients across a large cluster encompassing both the N2 and P2 peaks, suggesting better temporal integration of pain-related information in controls.
Additional significant clusters at the knee and foot showed higher TII in controls than in IENFD-FMD patients, consistent with N2 and P2 peaks but of smaller magnitude than at the hand.

Overall, FM patients with combined proximal and distal small fiber denervation showed the most pronounced pattern of loss of synergy and increased redundancy in temporal interaction information within the vertex LEP complex compared with controls, suggesting a dysfunctional mode of pain processing linked to the degree of small fiber impairment.
Serum malondialdehyde, a marker of lipid peroxidation, was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum vitamin C (ascorbic acid) concentration was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum CRP, a marker of systemic inflammation, was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum zinc levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum magnesium levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum calcium levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum copper levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
In the fibromyalgia group, serum magnesium and copper levels were significantly positively correlated, whereas in healthy controls the same two elements showed a significant negative correlation.
PET imaging shows reduced striatal dopamine D2/D3 receptor availability in patients with fibromyalgia and CRPS, correlating with pain severity and affective distress.
fMRI shows hypoactivation of the nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex during anticipation of pain relief in fibromyalgia, indicating a dysfunctional reward-related pain modulation system.
In rodent models, D2 receptor agonists such as quinpirole reduce mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in neuropathic and inflammatory pain.
Pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of D2 receptors exacerbates pain behaviors in rodent models, underscoring the inhibitory role of D2 receptors in spinal nociceptive processing.
Impaired conditioned pain modulation in chronic pain patients is associated with lower serum or CSF serotonin and norepinephrine and reduced responsiveness to analgesic stimuli.

RCTs and meta-analyses show duloxetine significantly reduces pain intensity and improves function in fibromyalgia, painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and chronic musculoskeletal pain, with an NNT of 5-7 for ≥30% pain reduction.

Greater SNRI-related improvements in pain scores were observed in individuals with initially impaired conditioned pain modulation, suggesting reuptake inhibitors act by restoring deficient descending inhibition.
Elevated BDNF levels are consistently detected in CSF, serum, and PBMCs of patients with fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, migraine, and other persistent pain conditions.

BDNF-TrkB signaling enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation and synaptic trafficking, increasing calcium influx and excitatory synaptic strength in dorsal horn neurons, contributing to LTP-like pain chronification.

BDNF downregulates KCC2 expression/activity in dorsal horn neurons, disrupting chloride homeostasis and rendering GABAergic/glycinergic inhibition less effective or excitatory, exacerbating hyperexcitability.
Intrathecal administration of BDNF in preclinical models induces mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia, mimicking features of central sensitization seen in chronic pain patients.
Blockade of BDNF or TrkB signaling reduces pain behaviors and restores inhibitory tone in animal models of neuropathic and inflammatory pain.

Elevated plasma/CSF Substance P is observed in fibromyalgia, chronic migraine, and CRPS; in fibromyalgia, higher serum Substance P levels are associated with greater pain severity, fatigue, and sleep disturbances.
CGRP levels rise during migraine attacks and normalize following triptan treatment, implicating CGRP in headache initiation and maintenance via the trigeminovascular system.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP or its receptor reduce migraine frequency, intensity, and duration in episodic and chronic migraine with favorable safety profiles and prolonged action.
NK1 receptor antagonists, despite robust preclinical efficacy, failed in multiple Phase III trials for various pain conditions.
Glial modulators such as propentofylline and ibudilast have shown limited clinical efficacy despite strong preclinical rationale for targeting glial activation in chronic pain.

Activated microglia release TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and chemokines CCL2/CXCL1, which enhance neuronal excitability and disrupt inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal dorsal horn, reinforcing central sensitization.
TLR4 is upregulated on microglia following peripheral nerve injury and drives MyD88/NF-κB signaling, leading to cytokine production and sustained neuroinflammation.
P2X7 purinergic receptors, activated by extracellular ATP, are crucial for microglial proliferation and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, facilitating IL-1β release in chronic pain states.

Astrocytes in chronic pain states downregulate the glutamate transporters EAAT1/GLAST and EAAT2/GLT-1 and show impaired glutamine synthetase activity, reducing glutamate clearance and promoting excitotoxicity and central sensitization.

Transcriptomic profiling of DRG neurons and PBMCs shows upregulation of neuroinflammatory genes including TNF, IL1B, and CCL2 in patients with fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, and chronic low back pain.
Transcriptomic profiling reveals upregulation of neuronal excitability genes SCN9A, TRPV1, and CACNA1H in patients with fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, and chronic low back pain.
Transcriptomic profiling reveals upregulation of neuromodulatory signaling genes BDNF, TAC1, and OPRM1 in patients with fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, and chronic low back pain.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of mouse DRG shows selective enrichment of injury-induced markers ATF3 and SPRR1A in nociceptive neuron subsets after injury, alongside dynamic changes in purinergic, peptidergic, and ionotropic receptor genes.

Human and rodent DRG studies show altered histone acetylation and DNA methylation implicated in persistent transcriptional reprogramming of sensory neurons, contributing to long-term changes in pain processing and treatment responsiveness.

Fibromyalgia patients show consistent disruptions in the salience network, default mode network, and executive control network on fMRI/PET, correlating with pain severity, cognitive dysfunction, and affective symptoms.

PET studies using radioligands for glial marker TSPO and dopaminergic/opioid receptors show increased neuroinflammatory signal and reduced receptor binding potential in chronic pain patients' pain-, reward-, and emotion-related brain regions.
Despite robust preclinical efficacy, NK1 receptor antagonists failed in multiple Phase III clinical trials for various chronic pain conditions.
Glial modulators propentofylline and ibudilast have shown limited clinical efficacy in chronic pain despite strong preclinical rationale.

Approximately 80% of preclinical pain studies use exclusively male rodents, overlooking sex-specific pain mechanisms such as T-cell-mediated sensitization in females versus microglial-mediated mechanisms in males.
Studies correlating biomarkers with pain intensity show only modest correlations (r = 0.3–0.5), indicating biological measures capture only part of the pain experience.
Analgesic drug development for chronic pain has a success rate below 10%, reflecting consistent failure of promising preclinical targets in clinical trials.
Female fibromyalgia patients show greater serotonergic dysfunction than males, potentially explaining the higher prevalence and severity of fibromyalgia in women.
BDNF responses to pain stimuli show sexual dimorphism, with females exhibiting greater activity-dependent BDNF release and more pronounced central sensitization following nerve injury.

Estrogen fluctuations lower nociceptive thresholds and weaken endogenous inhibition during low-estrogen phases, progesterone modulates GABAergic tone and descending control, and testosterone confers male protection via anti-inflammatory effects, contributing to sex-specific pain phenotypes and higher chronification risk in women, particularly in fibromyalgia.
CGRP levels and receptor sensitivity vary by sex, with estrogen modulating CGRP expression and contributing to menstrual migraine patterns.
Duloxetine responder phenotypes can be identified based on baseline conditioned pain modulation (CPM) status, suggesting functional biomarkers may improve therapeutic targeting.
Quality of life measures such as sleep quality, physical function, and emotional well-being often predict treatment response in chronic pain more strongly than neuroimaging or molecular markers.
Fibromyalgia is estimated to affect approximately 1-6% of the general population and imposes a substantial healthcare and quality-of-life burden.
Phantom limb pain occurs in an estimated 60-80% of amputees at some point following surgical amputation.
A commonly cited amputee survey found that approximately 78% of respondents reported experiencing phantom limb pain.

Curcuma mangga (CM) water suspension at 10 mg/ml increased basal histamine release from unstimulated rat peritoneal mast cells (RPMCs) to 22.60±5.86%.

In MRGPRX2-transfected RBL-2H3 cells without compound 48/80, CM increased histamine release only at 30 mg/ml; lower concentrations did not significantly increase release.

The highest SA concentration (30 mg/ml) showed the lowest histamine release suppression activity in compound 48/80-stimulated RPMCs compared to other doses.
In MRGPRX2-transfected RBL-2H3 cells without compound 48/80 stimulation, SA treatment did not significantly change histamine release compared to control.
SA at 10 mg/ml produced the greatest suppression of compound 48/80-induced histamine release in MRGPRX2-transfected RBL-2H3 cells, reducing it to 4.88±1.42% versus 35.11±3.10% in control.

Lower SA concentrations (0.1, 0.3, and 1 mg/ml) showed no significant difference in histamine release between groups in both compound 48/80-activated and non-activated MRGPRX2-transfected RBL-2H3 cells.
The anaphylaxis patient had markedly elevated plasma MRGPRX2 concentration compared to the negative control group.
The anaphylaxis patient showed significantly elevated plasma histamine concentration while total IgE remained normal.

Serum from the anaphylaxis patient induced significant release of β-hexosaminidase, calcium, and histamine from mast cells in vitro, exceeding baseline plasma histamine levels.
Rocuronium bromide directly triggered dose-dependent mast cell activation in vitro, causing MCP-1, histamine, and calcium release.
Local paw oedema experiments in mice validated that rocuronium bromide induces local allergic reactions.
Using MRGPRB2-CKO mice and siRNA silencing, the authors determined that rocuronium bromide-induced anaphylactic shock is mediated through MRGPRX2 activation and consequent mast cell degranulation.
The KIT D816V variant was detected at 11.5% variant allele frequency in bone marrow tissue by droplet digital PCR, confirming the somatic activating mutation diagnostic of systemic mastocytosis.
Serum mast cell tryptase was markedly elevated at 810 µg/L, far exceeding the WHO minor diagnostic threshold of 20 ng/mL used for systemic mastocytosis.

Bone marrow trephine biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow packed with spindle-shaped mast cells aberrantly expressing CD2, CD117 and CD25, confirming a neoplastic mast cell population diagnostic of systemic mastocytosis.
The patient met WHO criteria for aggressive systemic mastocytosis based on 'C findings' of bone marrow dysfunction with cytopenias and hepatosplenomegaly with ascites.
Treatment with midostaurin 50 mg twice daily produced a greater than 50% reduction in tryptase within one month along with resolution of fever and dyspnoea, sustained at one year of follow-up.

In the broader population of patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis, midostaurin has demonstrated a 60% overall response rate with generally good tolerability apart from hematologic toxicity, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Avapritinib, a highly selective KIT/PDGFRA inhibitor approved for systemic mastocytosis, is not recommended in patients with platelet counts below 50×10^9/L due to increased risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

The patient's recurrent febrile episodes were attributed to periodic mast cell activation, with pyrogenic mediators (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, histamine, prostaglandin E2) acting on hypothalamic temperature regulation.

Haematologic abnormalities are common in systemic mastocytosis: anaemia affects roughly 30-50% of patients, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia occur in about 15-20%, and eosinophilia may occur in up to 40%.

Diagnostic delay for systemic mastocytosis has been reported as an average of 8.1 years in a Dutch retrospective study and 58.3 months in a US cohort of 116 patients, compared with only 3 months in this case.
A Danish nationwide cohort study (1997-2010) reported a prevalence of systemic mastocytosis of 9.59 per 100,000 inhabitants across all subtypes.
Aggressive systemic mastocytosis carries a poor prognosis, with a median overall survival of 5.7 years reported from the European Competence Network on Mastocytosis (ECNM) registry.
Serum tryptase has only modest diagnostic sensitivity (65%) for mast cell disorders, meaning a significant subset of patients may have normal tryptase despite disease.

Lower tryptase (<90 ng/mL), bone marrow mast cell infiltration under 15%, and indolent SM classification predict hypersensitivity reactions, with new hypersensitivity reactions occurring in 4.8% of all SM patients within four years.

Sclerotic rib lesions visible on CT showed no corresponding FDG uptake on PET-CT, a discordance previously described in systemic mastocytosis where dense osteosclerosis does not necessarily correlate with increased metabolic activity.
A somatic gain-of-function KIT mutation, most commonly D816V, is present in more than 90% of patients with mastocytosis and results in constitutive, ligand-independent receptor activation.
The proliferation and maintenance of mast cell populations is dependent on JAK/STAT signaling.
Mast cell dysfunction can give rise to mast cell activation syndrome and has been implicated in ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and multiple sclerosis.
Mast cells release a broad panel of inflammatory mediators including histamine, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, tryptase, chymase, prostaglandins and growth factors, causing inflammation and vasodilation.
Activated mast cells are proposed to sensitize primary nociceptive neurons via release of histamine, NGF, TNF and IL-8, with IL-8 shown to drive prostaglandin-independent hyperalgesia in vivo.
The authors' own prior work showed increased expression of mast cell markers KIT, CPA3, MS4A2 and MS4A6A in endometriotic lesion tissue compared to control endometrium.
Higher numbers of mast cells located near nerve fibers in endometriotic lesions were positively correlated with pain intensity in patients.

In murine interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome models, MrgprB2-dependent mast cell-neuron circuits drive bladder inflammation and colonic hypersensitivity, and MRGPRX2 antagonism reduced these effects in humanized mice.
MrgprB2-expressing meningeal mast cells respond to compound 48/80 or PACAP with pain behaviors in migraine models, an effect absent in knockout animals and enhanced in MRGPRX2-humanized mice.
Human colonic mast cells express MRGPRX2 and respond to its agonists, with altered receptor/response profiles observed in IBS colonic biopsies.

MrgprB2-expressing mast cells have been shown to be present in the uterus and mammary gland, but no in vivo data currently addresses receptor activation, neuron interaction, or its role in pain or lesion formation in these tissues.

Early treatment with the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen significantly reduced disease severity and prevalence in a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, associated with reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation, rebalanced oxidative stress, and decreased CNS T-cell infiltration.
Randomized controlled trial evidence indicates ketotifen improves asthma control and reduces wheezing in children with mild to moderate asthma.

Sodium cromoglycate stabilized mast cells against degranulation and relieved clinical endometriosis symptoms in a rat model, though no clinical trials of mast cell stabilizers in endometriosis exist to date.

A case report described a 38-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and primary infertility who conceived six months after starting the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib, raising a possible link between JAK pathway inhibition and fertility/inflammation outcomes relevant to endometriosis.
Gain-of-function JAK1 mutations are associated with severe allergic disease, eosinophilia, and Th2-biased inflammation.
Gain-of-function STAT6 mutations increase basal activity and IL-4/IL-13 sensitivity, promoting allergic phenotypes and, in some cases, lymphoma.

As of this review, no gain-of-function mutations in JAK1, STAT3, STAT5B, or STAT6 have been identified in human endometriosis tissues, cell lines, or animal models, leaving this an open area for future study.

Unlike the P2Y14 agonist MRS2905, P2Y14 receptor antagonists 1 and 11 did not cause hypothermia in mice, suggesting the effect is agonist-specific and mast-cell mediated rather than an off-target antagonist effect.

The Psi method and the Method of Limits (MoL) showed similar within-session and between-session test-retest reliability for perception threshold estimation in small cutaneous nerve fibers, with overlapping 95% confidence intervals.
Perception thresholds estimated with the Psi method (1.12 mA) were significantly higher than those estimated with the Method of Limits (0.88 mA), with a bias of 0.24 mA.
Habituation (increase in perception threshold across repeated trials) was greater when using the Psi method than the Method of Limits, though it did not differ between sessions.
Repeated perception threshold estimation showed habituation, with PT increasing by an average of 0.07 mA per trial across the six repeated assessments.

The Psi method required fewer stimuli (37 on average) than the Method of Limits (78 on average, range 50-155) to estimate the perception threshold, and threshold estimates and ICC values stabilized after about 15 trials.

The between-session coefficient of variation of nearly 30% suggests that perception threshold testing can only discriminate small fiber neuropathy from normal thresholds when the neuropathy causes a substantially increased threshold.

In a cited study of type 1 diabetes, rheobase (a nerve excitability measure comparable to perception threshold) was doubled in persons without neuropathy, five-fold higher in pain-free neuropathy, and seven-fold higher in painful neuropathy compared to controls.
The present study found better relative reliability (ICC) of the Method of Limits for small nerve fiber perception threshold than previously reported by Hennings et al., who reported an ICC of 0.64.

Standard quantitative sensory testing (QST) protocols have reported overall test-retest correlation coefficients of 0.86, and thermal pain/perception threshold correlation coefficients of 0.80 and 0.88, in patients with sensory disturbances of varying etiologies.

The anterolateral ligament showed positive immunoreactivity for the pan-neuronal marker PGP9.5, indicating the presence of peripheral nerve fibers throughout the ligament.
Immunoreactivity for VAChT (vesicular acetylcholine transporter) in the ALL suggests the presence of cholinergic/parasympathetic autonomic nerve fibers.
Positive TH immunoreactivity in the ALL indicates the presence of sympathetic (adrenergic) nerve fibers within the ligament.
CGRP-positive fibers were identified in the ALL, indicating peptidergic sensory/nociceptive innervation of the ligament.
NOS immunoreactivity was observed in the ALL, indicating nitrergic nerve fibers with potential vasomotor/neuromodulatory function.
Electron microscopy revealed that the ALL contains both myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers, indicating a neurochemically and structurally diverse innervation.
No encapsulated mechanoreceptors were observed in the ALL samples examined ultrastructurally, suggesting its sensory role does not depend on classical encapsulated receptor types.
The innervation pattern of the ALL was similar to that of the fibular collateral ligament (FCL) used as a control structure.

The authors conclude that the ALL is a richly innervated structure with sensory, autonomic, and neuromodulatory features, indicating an active functional role in proprioception and homeostasis rather than being a passive capsular thickening.

Among 32 symptomatic diabetic patients screened with GCSI, 62.5% (20/32) had objectively confirmed delayed gastric emptying on gastric scintigraphy (GP group), while 37.5% had normal emptying despite symptoms (GP-like group).
Symptom severity measured by both total and average GCSI was significantly higher in the GP group than in the GP-like group.
Total GCSI score was found by multivariate logistic regression to be an independent predictor of delayed gastric emptying on solid gastric scintigraphy.
A total GCSI cutoff greater than 23 showed 80% sensitivity and 66.7% specificity for detecting delayed gastric emptying.
The mean gastric emptying half-time was significantly longer in the GP group compared to the GP-like group.
Serum creatinine correlated positively with gastric emptying half-time (T1/2) across the study population.
AST correlated positively with gastric emptying half-time, suggesting a possible link between fatty liver and delayed gastric emptying.
AST levels were significantly higher in the GP group than in the GP-like group.
Total GCSI score correlated positively with gastric emptying half-time (T1/2).
The nausea/vomiting GCSI subscale correlated positively with gastric emptying half-time.
Vomiting severity correlated positively with gastric emptying half-time.
Hemoglobin levels correlated negatively with gastric emptying half-time, potentially reflecting nutrient deficiencies from poor food intake in gastroparesis.
Diabetic nephropathy was more prevalent in the GP group than the GP-like group, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.

After a 3-month course of medical treatment (dietary modification, glycemic optimization, PPIs/prokinetics, and DPP-4i/metformin discontinuation), 55% of GP-group patients reported symptomatic improvement.

Responders to medical treatment showed a significantly greater reduction in HbA1c than the refractory group.
A higher initial total GCSI score independently predicted a lower likelihood of responding to medical treatment.
An initial total GCSI cutoff below 25 predicted clinical response to medical treatment with high specificity.

No significant differences were found between the GP and GP-like groups in age, sex, DM type, DM treatment/complications, HbA1c, smoking status, or comorbidities.

Repeated FMT produced a large, statistically significant reduction in overall gastrointestinal symptom severity (GSRS-IBS total score) across multiple treatment rounds in 17 participants.
The diarrhoea subscore of the GSRS-IBS decreased significantly after repeated FMT.
The early satiety subscore of the GSRS-IBS decreased markedly after repeated FMT.
The constipation subscore of the GSRS-IBS improved after repeated FMT.
Daily bowel movement frequency decreased significantly two weeks after FMT compared with the preceding week's baseline.
Stool consistency normalised after FMT, with reductions in both hard and liquid stool types on the Bristol Stool Scale.
Participants reported high subjective satisfaction with FMT treatment on a 7-point Likert scale at the 2-week post-treatment follow-up.
Adverse events following FMT were common but mostly mild, with a minority classified as moderate/severe and possibly related to treatment.

A kidney transplant recipient was hospitalised with diarrhoea and vomiting 9 days after FMT, classified as a serious adverse event possibly related to treatment, though no firm causal link was established.
Adverse event frequency did not increase with successive FMT treatments, suggesting no cumulative risk with repeated dosing.
Approximately 10% of the original trial participants (2 of 20) declined the extension study due to perceived lack of symptomatic benefit, indicating a subgroup of FMT non-responders.
In the original randomised FADIGAS trial, FMT reduced GSRS-IBS scores substantially more than placebo, supporting a genuine treatment effect beyond placebo response.

Loss-of-function or dominant-negative FBN1 variants cause Marfan syndrome, presenting with aortic root aneurysm, skeletal overgrowth, lens dislocation, and dural ectasia.
Pathogenic variants in TGFBR1 and TGFBR2 cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome types I and II, leading to widespread arteriopathy and early-onset dissections at smaller aortic diameters.
Despite loss-of-function receptor variants reducing canonical TGF-beta signaling fidelity, downstream pSMAD2 activity is paradoxically elevated in affected tissue.
Pathogenic COL3A1 variants cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, predisposing to spontaneous rupture of arteries, hollow organs, or the uterus.
ACTA2 variants are the most common cause of nonsyndromic familial TAAD, impairing actin polymerization and reducing contractile capacity, leading to early-onset dissection.

LV and RV volumetric and functional CMR metrics were broadly comparable between COVID-19 cases and matched uninfected controls at both baseline and repeat imaging.
Compared to cases, controls had marginally worse global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain at both baseline and repeat imaging visits, though differences were not clinically relevant.
At repeat imaging, LVEF was slightly lower in COVID-19 cases compared to controls, though the difference was not clinically relevant; there was no difference at baseline.
No significant differences were found in myocardial native T1, RV functional metrics, atrial phenotypes, arterial stiffness, or aortic flow measures between cases and controls.

In the subset of cases with COVID-19 hospitalization (n=34), no significant differences were found in average CMR metrics compared to matched uninfected comparators at either baseline or repeat imaging.
At repeat imaging, COVID-19 cases had a significantly faster ventricular rate and longer QTc than controls.
Lead-specific ECG biomarkers including QRS interval, R wave duration, S wave area, T wave area, and T wave amplitude showed significant differences between cases and controls at repeat imaging.
Lower baseline (pre-infection) LVEF and poorer LV strain metrics were associated with higher risk of incident SARS-CoV-2 infection in fully adjusted logistic regression models.
A positive association was found between T wave area in lead V4 and incident SARS-CoV-2 infection, while global ECG biomarkers showed no significant association.

No significant difference was found in the magnitude of interval change (pre- to post-pandemic) in any CMR or ECG phenotype between SARS-CoV-2 infected cases and matched uninfected controls, arguing against causal cardiac effects of mild COVID-19.
Overall, greater nociplastic pain severity (higher fibromyalgia index score) was cross-sectionally associated with worse executive function centile scores.

In minimally adjusted models, higher FMI scores were associated with worse executive function among participants with chronic pain but not among those without chronic pain, showing an interaction effect.

After full adjustment for confounders (ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, BMI, smoking), the association between FMI and worse executive function in chronic pain participants remained statistically significant, though attenuated.

The negative association between FMI and executive function was significantly stronger in males than in females, indicating greater cognitive vulnerability to nociplastic pain in males despite fibromyalgia being more prevalent in females.

In an SEM model adjusted for age and sex only, baseline FMI had a small significant direct effect on follow-up executive function, but after full adjustment for confounders this effect was attenuated and became non-significant, indicating nociplastic pain does not predict longitudinal decline in executive function.

The indirect effect of baseline FMI through baseline executive function on follow-up executive function remained significant, suggesting the effect of nociplastic pain on cognition is primarily cross-sectional rather than driving rate of decline.
Abnormal (short or long) sleep duration partially mediated the cross-sectional association between nociplastic pain severity and executive function at baseline, but not at follow-up.
Anxiety symptoms (GAD-7) partially mediated the cross-sectional association between nociplastic pain severity and executive function, while depressive symptoms did not.
Depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) did not significantly mediate the association between nociplastic pain severity and executive function, unlike anxiety.
Neither subjective brain fog nor fatigue significantly mediated the pain-executive function relationship.
Pain intensity partially mediated the cross-sectional association between FMI and executive function at baseline, but no significant indirect effect was found for follow-up executive function.

Neuropathic pain features (DN4 score, capturing burning/tingling/electric shock-like sensations suggestive of central sensitisation) partially mediated the cross-sectional relationship between nociplastic pain severity and executive function.

After controlling for pain severity and neuropathic features, widespread pain was unexpectedly positively associated with executive function, contradicting prior research suggesting widespread pain is linked to worse cognition.

A marginal indirect mediation effect of tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) use was observed on the FMI-executive function relationship, though its clinical significance is unclear; no significant mediation was found for opioid or gabapentinoid use.

No significant mediation effect of opioid or gabapentinoid use on the nociplastic pain-executive function relationship was found, consistent with recent systematic reviews finding no clear cognitive decline with chronic opioid therapy.
A 200-marker chromosome conformation signature (EpiSwitch CFS test) achieved 92% sensitivity, 98% specificity and 96% overall diagnostic accuracy for ME/CFS in an independent validation cohort.
The top 200 predictive chromosome conformation markers mapped broadly across all chromosomes rather than clustering at a single locus, suggesting a polygenic epigenetic signature of ME/CFS.

STRING network analysis of genes nearest to the top 200 ME/CFS chromosome conformation markers revealed dense connectivity strongly enriched for immune/inflammatory pathways, with IL-2, IL-10, TNF-α and TLR-related proteins as prominent hubs linking cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing, and JAK/STAT and NF-κB cascades.

The ME/CFS gene network derived from EpiSwitch markers showed significant overlap in IL-10, IL-2 and CD4 with the therapeutic knowledge networks of Rituximab and Copaxone (glatiramer acetate), suggesting a subset of patients may be responsive to these immunomodulatory agents.

Hierarchical clustering of the 47 ME/CFS patients based on 765 IL-2-associated chromosome conformation signatures revealed clear stratification into two subgroups (18 and 29 patients), suggesting a potential responder group for IL-2-targeted therapies.
Prior studies cited in this paper report elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, and IP-10 in ME/CFS patients.
Natural killer (NK) cell dysfunction, characterised by reduced cytotoxicity, has been reported in ME/CFS patients in prior literature.
Prior literature identified autoantibodies targeting β2-adrenergic and muscarinic receptors in ME/CFS patients, implicating autoimmunity in disease pathogenesis.
Immune phenotyping of cerebrospinal fluid from ME/CFS patients revealed distinct immunotypes, cited as confirming autoimmune involvement.
Post-COVID patients showed upregulation of JAK/STAT signalling and a prolonged immune response, findings noted to overlap with ME/CFS immune dysregulation.
Upregulation of purinergic receptors (P2X4, P2X5), TRPV1, and ASIC3 has been associated with post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS according to cited literature.
De Vega et al. identified over 12,000 differentially methylated sites in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, mostly hypermethylated and involving immune and metabolic pathways.
Altered expression of miR-21, miR-34a, miR-92a, miR-126, and miR-200c has been reported in ME/CFS patients as potential biomarkers.
Naviaux et al. reported abnormalities in metabolites related to the TCA cycle, amino acid metabolism, and lipid metabolism in ME/CFS, indicating a hypometabolic state.

A large cohort metabolomics study identified hundreds of metabolomic traits differing between ME/CFS cases and controls, but no single trait clearly distinguished cases from controls and no combinatorial diagnostic test was proposed.

Trivedi et al. identified over 17,000 differentially methylated positions across approximately 6,300 genes using the EPIC array, with altered promoter methylation in immune signalling genes in ME/CFS.

De Vega et al. showed that methylation changes at immune and mitochondrial genes correlated with clinical symptoms and physical functioning scores (RAND-36), linking epigenetic changes to fatigue and post-exertional malaise.
Hypomethylation at the NR3C1 (glucocorticoid receptor) promoter has been repeatedly observed in ME/CFS, implying HPA-axis dysregulation.
A larger phase III randomised controlled trial of Rituximab in ME/CFS failed to meet its primary efficacy endpoints, although it confirmed the drug's safety profile in this population.

A six-year follow-up of ME/CFS patients from rituximab/cyclophosphamide trials found that 44.1% of the cyclophosphamide group scored SF-36 physical function of at least 70, and 17.6% scored at least 90, suggesting a beneficial effect in a subgroup.
A recent study of Rapamycin (Sirolimus), an mTOR inhibitor blocking IL-2-mediated T cell proliferation, showed significant improvement in fatigue and post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS patients.
No participants scored at the lowest or highest possible raw sum score on the PROMIS PF-SF, indicating no floor or ceiling effects for the ME/CFS sample.
A single-factor confirmatory factor analysis showed the PROMIS PF-SF fit a unidimensional model well by CFI/TLI criteria, though RMSEA exceeded the conventional acceptable threshold.
The PROMIS PF-SF demonstrated high internal consistency reliability among ME/CFS participants, exceeding the threshold recommended for individual-level clinical use.
ME/CFS participants had a mean PROMIS PF-SF T-score about one standard deviation below the 2000 US Census general population norm, consistent with clinical expectations of impaired physical function.
Participants with ME/CFS scored significantly lower (worse) on the PROMIS PF-SF than healthy controls, with a large effect size.
Among ME/CFS participants, PROMIS PF-SF scores differed significantly by hours of vertical activity per day, though the measure could not fully distinguish medium from high impairment subgroups.
ME/CFS participants who spent more hours in horizontal (recumbent) activity per day had significantly worse PROMIS PF-SF scores, though a ceiling effect in this measure limited group differentiation.

Among ME/CFS participants, PROMIS PF-SF scores decreased monotonically across low, medium, and high functional impairment groups defined by SF-36 Physical Component Summary scores, with a large effect size.
Among ME/CFS participants, higher self-reported physical fatigue (VAS ≥5) was associated with significantly worse PROMIS PF-SF physical function scores, with a medium effect size.

PROMIS PF-SF T-scores were moderately-to-highly correlated (inversely) with EQ-5D-3L physical function items on mobility, self-care, and usual activities among ME/CFS participants, supporting convergent validity.
PROMIS PF-SF T-scores were moderately-to-highly correlated with IPAQ total weekly physical activity scores among ME/CFS participants, further supporting convergent validity.

Endocrinologic testing (triple bolus test) revealed hypothalamic hypoadrenalism as the underlying cause of the patient's persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19, supporting HPA axis dysfunction as a driver of post-COVID ME/CFS.

Treatment with betamethasone and high-dose weekly prednisolone (potent glucocorticoid receptor agonists) for post-COVID ME/CFS precipitated severe mania with delusions of grandeur and auditory hallucinations in this patient with bipolar disorder, requiring hospitalization.

Switching corticosteroid treatment from prednisolone/betamethasone to hydrocortisone, which has relatively stronger mineralocorticoid receptor activity, improved the patient's physical symptoms without exacerbating her psychiatric condition.
Tapering hydrocortisone down to 15 mg/day led to recurrence of hypoxemia attributable to hypothalamic hypoadrenalism, which resolved when the dose was maintained at 20 mg/day.

The authors propose that corticosteroid-induced psychiatric exacerbation results from depletion of endogenous mineralocorticoid receptor ligands caused by administration of steroids with strong glucocorticoid receptor activity.

The patient's pre-existing bipolar affective disorder complicated corticosteroid management of her post-COVID ME/CFS, illustrating a clinically significant interaction between psychiatric comorbidity and endocrine treatment of ME/CFS.
Fatigue severity was the only significant correlate of response inhibition performance among ME/CFS patients.

For cognitive outcomes other than response inhibition (Symbol Digit Test, motor speed, simple and choice reaction time), fatigue severity consistently co-occurred with pain severity, bodily pain, and/or physical functioning as correlates of lower performance.
Restricting analyses to the subset of patients meeting NICE/IOM criteria (n=1072) yielded overall similar results to the full CDC-criteria sample.

Older age (but not symptom duration) moderated the relationships between symptoms and cognition, with stronger associations between cognitive performance and pain severity, physical functioning, and bodily pain observed in older patients.
Symptom duration did not moderate the relationships between symptom severity and cognitive performance, in contrast to age.
Recumbent isometric yoga plus conventional therapy produced a significantly greater decrease in ME/CFS performance status (PS) score than conventional therapy alone over 12 weeks.
The Chalder Fatigue Scale score decreased significantly more in the yoga group than in the control group over the 12-week intervention.
A single session of recumbent isometric yoga significantly reduced acute fatigue (POMS Fatigue subscale) in the overall yoga group.
A single session of recumbent isometric yoga significantly increased vigor (POMS Vigor subscale) in the overall yoga group.
In the severe patient subgroup (PS 7-8), the decrease in PS score showed only a non-significant trend toward greater improvement in the yoga group compared to control.
In severe ME/CFS patients, the Chalder Fatigue Scale score decreased significantly in the yoga group but not in controls, with a greater decrease in the yoga group.
In severe ME/CFS patients, a single yoga session significantly reduced acute fatigue (POMS F score).
In severe ME/CFS patients, a single yoga session significantly increased vigor (POMS V score).
In patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, there was no significant between-group difference in the change in PS score after the intervention.
In patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, the Chalder Fatigue Scale score decreased significantly in the yoga group but not in controls, with greater improvement in the yoga group.
In patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, a single yoga session significantly reduced acute fatigue (POMS F score).
In patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, a single yoga session significantly increased vigor (POMS V score).

Recumbent isometric yoga was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events, including no post-exertional malaise, once patients became accustomed to the procedure; one patient had transient early worsening.

The majority of patients who completed yoga diaries reported subjective benefits of recumbent isometric yoga, including improvements in fatigue, pain, insomnia, brain fog, and enhanced self-efficacy for pacing and PEM avoidance.

The same pandemic-era meta-analyses found CBT and physical exercise interventions associated with significant improvements in anxiety symptoms.

Neuroimaging identified widespread microglial activation in long COVID patients, particularly in the midcingulate cortex, basal ganglia, and thalamus, correlating with vascular dysfunction markers.

Autoantibodies against central and autonomic nervous system targets suggest a potential autoimmune component in both ME/CFS and long COVID.
About half of individuals with long COVID meet the Fukuda ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.

A cohort of over 4,500 adults showed COVID-19 patients had a persistently elevated risk of chronic fatigue over 18 months of follow-up.

A living systematic review found moderate-certainty evidence that CBT reduces fatigue and improves concentration in individuals with long COVID, concluding it probably contributes to recovery and meaningful improvements.

An ongoing single-blind RCT (target n=60) in young adults meeting Oxford CFS criteria is testing graded exercise therapy combined with CBT versus usual care for fatigue severity, aerobic capacity, grip strength, and fall risk.

Generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥6) was markedly more prevalent in children with primary nocturnal enuresis than in non-enuretic controls, with a crude odds ratio of 17.7.

In a phase II open-label study, masitinib produced an overall disability response at 3 months in 56% of KIT-816-mutation-negative patients, sustained into the extension phase.
An international phase III placebo-controlled trial confirmed the benefit of masitinib in indolent systemic mastocytosis patients with disability.
In the PIONEER trial, avapritinib reduced serum tryptase by ≥50% from baseline to week 24 in 54% of treated ISM patients compared to 0% of placebo patients, a highly significant difference.
In an open-label phase II study of midostaurin for ISM, efficacy was noted but digestive tolerability was often poor, with high rates of nausea, vomiting, and headache.
A Danish case-control study demonstrated an increased prevalence of melanoma in patients with mastocytosis, contributing to the recommendation against PUVA phototherapy.
Discontinuation of denosumab carries an increased risk of vertebral fracture with a fracture cascade, a rebound phenomenon also expected in mastocytosis-associated osteoporosis.
Long-term follow-up data (10 years average) from the CEREMAST expert center indicate that cutaneous mastocytosis generally does not progress to systemic mastocytosis.
European cohort registry data show that only 2.5% of indolent systemic mastocytosis cases progress to advanced forms, though this may be an overestimate due to reporting bias toward advanced cases.
Individuals with indolent systemic mastocytosis have a life expectancy comparable to that of the general American population matched for age and sex.

The REMA score uses serum tryptase thresholds (<15 ng/mL or >25 ng/mL) combined with clinical symptoms and gender to predict clonal mast cell disease risk in anaphylaxis patients without an identified allergen, with 86% sensitivity and 94% specificity.
The modified REMA score uses a tryptase threshold of 11.4-20 ng/mL with the same clinical and gender criteria, achieving better sensitivity (93%) and specificity (94%) than the original REMA score.
The NICAS score, incorporating clinical symptoms, gender, serum tryptase >11.4 ng/mL, and blood KIT mutation status, predicts clonal mast cell disease with 75% sensitivity and 100% specificity.

Among 374 patients with grade 3/4 anaphylaxis after Hymenoptera stings, monoclonal mast cell disease was present in 12.7% (28/220) even when serum tryptase was within normal limits, and clonal mast cell disease was found in 9% (34/374) overall; of the 5 who underwent bone marrow biopsy, all 5 had confirmed systemic mastocytosis.
Systemic mastocytosis prevalence differs by tryptase band: 27% of patients with serum tryptase between 11.3-20 ng/mL had SM, compared to 15% of patients with tryptase below 11.3 ng/mL.
Spine MRI identified bone marrow mast cell infiltration in 96% of patients with an advanced form of mastocytosis, whereas this infiltration is much less common in patients with indolent SM.

In the PIONEER trial, avapritinib reduced serum tryptase by ≥50% from baseline to Week 24 in 54% of ISM patients compared to 0% of placebo patients, and reduced mast-cell burden and uncontrolled symptoms.
In a phase II study, open-label masitinib produced an overall response at 3 months in 56% of 25 disabled mastocytosis patients (KIT-816-negative), an effect that persisted into the extension phase.
An international phase III trial comparing masitinib to placebo demonstrated benefit of masitinib in indolent systemic mastocytosis patients with disability.
In an open-label phase II study of midostaurin for ISM, efficacy was notable but digestive safety was often poor, with nausea in 80% of patients, vomiting in 35%, and headaches in 10.5%.
A Danish case-control study demonstrated an increased prevalence of melanoma in patients with mastocytosis, adding to the intrinsic risk of phototherapy (PUVA), which should no longer be offered.

Discontinuation of denosumab is associated with a rebound phenomenon of increased bone remodeling markers, decreased bone mineral density, and risk of multiple vertebral fractures, described in postmenopausal osteoporosis and expected similarly in mastocytosis-related osteoporosis.

The IPSM prognostic scoring system, built from clinical and biological data of a European registry of 1681 patients, identifies age ≥60 years and alkaline phosphatase ≥100 IU/L as factors associated with poorer survival in indolent mastocytosis.
Presence of an ASXL1, RUNX1, or DNMT3A mutation with allele frequency ≥30% was associated with decreased overall survival in patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis.
A study by Lim KH et al. showed that individuals with indolent systemic mastocytosis had a life expectancy comparable to that of the age- and sex-matched American general population.
European registry data show that 2.5% of indolent systemic mastocytosis cases progress to an advanced form, though this figure may be overestimated due to reporting bias toward advanced cases.

CEREMAST follow-up data (average 10 years, unpublished) indicate that cutaneous mastocytosis generally does not progress to systemic mastocytosis, and its prognosis is better than that of indolent systemic mastocytosis.
A 2002 cohort study of 106 adult-onset mastocytosis patients followed for 10 years found regression of urticaria pigmentosa lesions in 10% of patients.

Imatinib is recognized as ineffective in patients carrying the KIT D816V mutation in marrow and/or skin, as demonstrated in vitro, but remains effective for SM associated with hypereosinophilic syndrome with FIP1L1-PDGFRa fusion gene or SM without KIT exon 17 mutation.

A skin-lesion-based scoring system (ranging from -1 to 5, based on serum tryptase level, bone pain/osteoporosis, and constitutional/cardiovascular symptoms) stratifies risk of systemic disease: low risk (score -1/0) 0.7-25%, intermediate risk (score 1-2) 47-71%, high risk (score 3-5) 87-98%.

IBS-D induction (senna + chronic unpredictable mild stress) produced visceral hypersensitivity (lower pain threshold), diarrhea (higher diarrhea index), and anxiety-like behavior (lower OT%) compared to healthy control rats.
Electroacupuncture at ST36, ST25, and LR3 significantly increased visceral pain threshold and OT% and decreased diarrhea index compared to untreated model rats.
Serum DAO, a marker of intestinal permeability, was significantly elevated in IBS-D model rats compared to controls.
Electroacupuncture significantly reduced serum DAO concentrations compared to model rats, indicating restoration of intestinal barrier integrity.
Colonic CRF and CRF-R1 mRNA expression were significantly upregulated in IBS-D model rats compared to controls.

EA downregulated CRF/CRF-R1 expression versus the model group; this effect was abolished by the CRF-R1 agonist Ucn1 and the mast cell agonist C48/80, but not by the exosome inhibitor GW4869, implicating CRF/mast cell signaling upstream of EA's exosomal mechanism.
The percentage of tryptase-positive (activated) mast cell area in colon tissue was significantly increased in IBS-D model rats versus controls.
EA reduced mast cell activation (tryptase-positive area) versus the model group; this was reversed by Ucn1 and C48/80 but unaffected by GW4869.
Colonic tight junction proteins ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1 were significantly lower in IBS-D model rats than in controls.

EA increased tight junction protein expression versus model rats; this restorative effect was blocked by Ucn1 and C48/80 but not by GW4869, which alone mimicked EA's effect on tight junction proteins.
Mast cell-derived exosomal miR-149-5p was significantly elevated in IBS-D model rats compared to controls, identified by sequencing and confirmed by qPCR.
Mast cell-derived exosomal miR-22-5p was significantly elevated in IBS-D model rats compared to controls, identified by sequencing and confirmed by qPCR.
Although miR-1-3p was elevated in sequencing data of the model group, qPCR validation showed no significant difference among groups, so it was excluded from further validation.
EA reduced MC-EXO miR-149-5p and miR-22-5p versus the model group; this reduction was reversed by Ucn1 and C48/80 but unaffected by the exosome antagonist GW4869.
Predicted target genes of differentially expressed MC-EXO miRNAs were significantly enriched in tight junction and actin cytoskeleton regulation pathways.
Transfection of Caco-2 monolayers with miR-149-5p mimics increased FD-40 permeability and decreased ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1 expression compared to negative controls.
