Transfection of Caco-2 monolayers with miR-22-5p mimics increased FD-40 permeability and decreased ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1 expression compared to negative controls.
AAV-mediated overexpression of miR-149-5p abolished EA's beneficial effects on visceral pain threshold, diarrhea index, OT%, and serum DAO in vivo.
AAV-miR-149-5p overexpression reduced colonic tight junction protein (ZO-1, Occludin, Claudin-1) expression and disrupted tight junction/microvillus ultrastructure compared to the EA group.

Administration of the exosome antagonist GW4869 alone produced effects on mast cell activation, CRF/CRF-R1 expression, and tight junction proteins similar to EA treatment, suggesting exosome release inhibition can replicate EA's therapeutic mechanism.
According to cited prior literature, miR-149-5p is significantly upregulated in the serum of human IBS-D patients and its level is reported to be responsive to EA treatment.
Autophagy-related gene 5 (ATG5)-deficient mast cells show severely impaired degranulation in a mouse model of passive cutaneous anaphylaxis.
Decreased mTORC1 activity causes nuclear translocation of TFEB, which enhances mast cell degranulation.
Unstimulated mast cells show protective effects against OVA-induced asthma in rats by decreasing the expression of LC3-B and Beclin 1.
Wnt3a increases the expression of Th2 cytokines and enhances histamine and tryptase release in human mast cells.
IL-33, elevated in a model of allergic rhinitis, inhibits autophagy and promotes mast cell degranulation via the ST2/PI3K/mTOR signaling pathway.
Activation of AMPK negatively regulates FcεRI-dependent mast cell activation in a mouse model of anaphylaxis.
Rotenone, an inhibitor of mitochondrial complex I, inhibits mast cell degranulation and decreases secretion of IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α, and GM-CSF in skin mast cells.
The uncoupler FCCP inhibits mast cell degranulation by blocking the generation of mitochondrial membrane potential.

Inhibition of uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2) enhances histamine release and vascular permeability in mice after allergic and non-allergic stimulation, and its downregulation increases mitochondrial ROS production.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), a key TCA-cycle regulator, is necessary for ATP production and mast cell degranulation, and MITF binds to PDH to mediate mast cell activation.
Inhibiting ERK1/2 suppresses MITF binding to PDH, leading to decreased mast cell activity, and antigen stimulation increases MITF phosphorylation via ERK1/2 in RBL2H3 cells and BMMCs.

IgE and non-IgE mast cell stimulation enhances oxidative phosphorylation through complexes I and III, increasing mitochondrial ATP production and mast cell degranulation; inhibiting the respiratory chain reduces IgE- and non-IgE-mediated degranulation.
Mast cell activation induces mitochondrial fragmentation, morphological changes, and translocation of mitochondria from the perinuclear region to the cell surface.
Mitochondria-targeting curcuminoids inhibit mast cell activation by inducing mitochondrial fragmentation, accompanied by AMPK activation.
Inhibition of mitophagy by sodium metabisulfite promotes mast cell degranulation.

Antigen stimulation increases p62 expression, and p62 mediates allergic inflammation in vitro, in passive cutaneous anaphylaxis, and in passive systemic anaphylaxis models, colocalizing with LC3-II on exosomes of RBL-2H3 cells.
miR-135 binds to the 3′UTR of p62 to decrease p62 expression, suggesting potential as an anti-allergy therapeutic mimic.
The proteasome inhibitor bortezomib abolishes hazelnut allergen-specific IgE and decreases both CD19+ and follicular B lymphocytes in a mouse model of food allergy (anaphylaxis).
TSLP increases the levels of inflammatory cytokines by inducing autophagy, increasing expression of Beclin1, LC3-II, p62, and ATG5 via JAK1/JAK2/STAT5/JNK/PI3K signaling.
Tezepelumab, a fully human monoclonal IgG2 antibody against TSLP, decreases IL-5, IL-13, and IgE levels in severe asthma.
Chloroquine, an autophagy inhibitor, decreases ear thickness, skin damage, mast cell numbers, and the levels of IgE, TSLP, IL-4, and IL-13 in a mouse model of atopic dermatitis.
Bioinformatics analysis shows that patients with severe asthma display higher levels of TP53, SQSTM1/p62, and ATG5 compared to those with non-severe asthma and healthy controls.
ATG5 polymorphism is closely related to the severity of bronchial asthma.
Stanniocalcin 2 (STC2) mediates mitophagy and exacerbates asthma induced by fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and serum STC2 levels in asthma patients are higher during periods of high PM2.5.

Clemastine, a histamine H1R antagonist, inhibits mast cell activation in myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury and attenuates subarachnoid hemorrhage by increasing autophagy-related genes via Nrf2 nuclear translocation.
Peanut allergy results from mitochondrial dysfunction, including increased ROS production in liver cells.

Constitutively active RhoA, activated during mast cell degranulation, induces PINK1 accumulation at mitochondria and Parkin translocation, enhancing PINK1 stability and inducing mitophagy during allergic inflammation.
Ergosterol supplementation alleviated IBS-related symptoms including intestinal motility disturbance, visceral pain, colonic inflammation, gut barrier dysfunction, and mast cell activation.
Ergosterol modulated gut microbiota composition and enhanced tryptophan metabolism, increasing production of the tryptophan-derived metabolite indole-3-lactate (ILA).
Ergosterol treatment increased production of the tryptophan-derived metabolite indole-3-lactate (ILA), which in turn activated aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling.
Antibiotic-mediated depletion of gut microbiota abolished the beneficial effects of ergosterol on IBS symptoms, indicating a microbiota-dependent mechanism.
Direct supplementation with ILA regulated visceral hypersensitivity, intestinal motility, and AhR activity, mirroring the effects of ergosterol.
FcεRI-deficient mice fail to respond to sensitizing stimuli in AD models, implicating FcεRI-mediated IgE-dependent mast cell activation in AD pathogenesis.
High serum IgE titers are associated with higher AD disease activity, and IgE bound in lesional skin cross-links FcεRI on mast cells/basophils to trigger degranulation.
MRGPRX2 expression is upregulated in lesional skin of AD patients and is associated with heightened mast cell responsiveness to non-IgE triggers.
PAR-2 expression is upregulated in AD skin and is activated by mast cell-derived tryptase, mediating histamine-independent itch via a tryptase-PAR-2 axis.
Conditional knockout of IL-4R in dorsal root ganglia sensory neurons significantly reduced scratching behavior in AD mouse models.
Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, has shown mixed but generally positive results in reducing skin lesions, pruritus, and improving quality of life in AD patients with elevated IgE.

In a Phase 2b trial of chronic spontaneous urticaria patients, the BTK inhibitor remibrutinib significantly reduced UAS7 at Week 4 versus placebo across all dose groups, with sustained improvement through Week 12.
In a CSU trial, rilzabrutinib at 1,200 mg/day significantly improved itch and hive scores versus placebo by Week 12, with effects starting at Week 1.
Dupilumab, which blocks IL-4Rα shared by IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, significantly improved eczema severity, itch, sleep, and quality of life in large-scale clinical trials of moderate-to-severe AD.
Nemolizumab, targeting the IL-31 receptor, produced rapid and sustained reduction in itch severity, often within days of starting treatment, in phase 2/3 AD trials.
Avapritinib is a selective KIT inhibitor effective against the D816V mutation and is approved for advanced systemic mastocytosis.
Cromolyn sodium stabilizes the mast cell membrane, preventing mediator release, and can reduce inflammation, itching, and severity of AD flares though it is not a first-line treatment.
In a phase II trial, the histamine H4 receptor antagonist ZPL-3893787 significantly improved AD severity after 8 weeks, with 50% improvement in EASI and 41% improvement in SCORAD from baseline.

Lirentelimab, an anti-Siglec-8 antibody, depletes eosinophils and suppresses mast cell activity, demonstrating clinical efficacy in eosinophilic gastritis, eosinophilic esophagitis, and chronic urticaria in early-phase trials.
Gain-of-function KIT mutations such as D816V drive aberrant mast cell signaling implicated in systemic mastocytosis and gastrointestinal stromal tumors.

Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice exhibit reduced skin inflammation and pruritus compared to wild-type controls under AD-inducing conditions, and reconstitution of mast cells restores the disease phenotype, confirming a critical mast cell role.
Mast cells are strongly implicated as central mediators of cold urticaria, with mediator release activating cutaneous nerves and causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

Historical Prausnitz-Küstner passive serum transfer experiments showed that serum from some ColdU patients could induce cold urticaria in healthy recipients, implicating IgE, IgM, and IgG as candidate transfer factors.
Gruber et al. found IgG anti-IgE antibodies in 55% and IgM anti-IgE antibodies in 22% of ColdU patients, with heating of sera enhancing antibody binding to IgE.
Inganäs et al. reported IgG anti-IgE antibodies in 33% of ColdU patients, a lower rate than reported by Gruber et al.
Kaplan noted that ColdU is primarily associated with IgE antibodies, with IgM and IgG playing only exceptional roles, contradicting reports of frequent anti-IgE IgG/IgM findings.
A 2021 single-center study found high rates of cryoglobulin (46%) and cold agglutinin (27%) positivity among ColdU patients when samples were properly handled by specialized labs.
Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, has proven effective in ColdU patients unresponsive to H1-antihistamines, supporting autoallergy and immune-complex hypotheses.
TRPM8 and TRPA1 cold-sensing ion channels have been proposed as potential contributors to mast cell activation in ColdU, but their role remains speculative and unconfirmed clinically.
EP262, a selective MRGPRX2 receptor antagonist, is currently under investigation as an IgE-independent mast cell-targeted therapy for ColdU.

Acquired ColdU has been linked to infections including Helicobacter pylori, Toxoplasma gondii, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV, mostly reported in case reports, though a direct causal link remains uncertain.
In the COLD-CE cohort, 5% of patients reported a positive family history of cold urticaria.
In COLD-CE phase 1, 412 of 551 patients (75%) had typical ColdU, defined by positive standard cold stimulation testing.
In COLD-CE phase 1, cold-induced anaphylaxis was diagnosed in 37% of patients with typical ColdU.

In COLD-CE phase 2, cardiovascular symptoms occurred in 28% of typical ColdU patients (with syncope or documented hypotension in 12%), respiratory symptoms in 20%, and gastrointestinal symptoms in 10%.
A 2018 case report described a child with ColdU who experienced intraoperative cold-induced anaphylaxis associated with an elevated tryptase level and a normal baseline tryptase.
Basophils from ColdU patients were shown to degranulate upon cold exposure in vitro, supporting histamine release from skin mast cells and blood basophils as a trigger for ColdU and ColdA.

In the COLD-CE cohort, common triggers for typical ColdU included cold air (88%), full-body cold-water immersion (68%), localized cold liquid contact (65%), cold surfaces (59%), and cold food/drink ingestion (34%), with wind (70%) and increased summer humidity (32%) as aggravating factors.
For cold-induced anaphylaxis specifically, cold-water immersion was the most common trigger (27%), while cold ambient air exposure was reported by only 13% of patients.
A 2025 study found that 7% of 92 ColdU patients tested positive for the KIT p.D816V variant, a mutation considered absent in the general population but associated with clonal mast cell disorders.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia was identified in 11% of ColdU patients and 15% of those with cold-induced anaphylaxis, compared to a general population prevalence of 5.7%.
Individuals with cold-induced anaphylaxis had significantly higher total serum IgE levels than those without cold-induced anaphylaxis.
Among 318 COLD-CE patients tested with both ice cube and TempTest, 80.8% were positive on both, 16.7% positive only with the ice cube, and 2.5% positive only with the TempTest.
A strong correlation was observed among shorter critical stimulation time threshold, higher critical temperature threshold, and larger wheal size in ColdU patients.

Approximately one-third of patients with typical ColdU experience mucosal angioedema of the oropharynx triggered by cold foods or beverages, and MAO is associated with greater cold sensitivity and a higher frequency of cold-induced anaphylaxis.
Omalizumab has demonstrated efficacy for cold urticaria in case reports and in one randomized, placebo-controlled trial, though it is not licensed for this indication.
Cyclosporine may be considered for severe and refractory cold urticaria, but supporting evidence is limited to case reports.
Several biologics approved for other indications (anakinra anti-IL-1, etanercept anti-TNF, reslizumab anti-IL-5, dupilumab anti-IL-4/13) have shown benefit in cold urticaria in case reports.

Several investigational therapies are being studied in cold urticaria, including the MRGPRX2 antagonist EP262, the IgE-trap protein YH35324, the BTK inhibitor remibrutinib, and the anti-KIT monoclonal antibody barzolvolimab.

Desloratadine, bilastine, and rupatadine have demonstrated efficacy for cold urticaria in randomized trials and case reports, and second-generation H1-antihistamines can be up-titrated to 4 times the standard dose to achieve disease control.

Cold desensitization, involving gradually increasing cold exposure via showers or baths, has been shown to reduce the critical temperature threshold and cold-induced symptoms but is rarely used clinically due to risk of systemic reactions and need for daily maintenance.

The ColdU Activity Score is the first disease-specific patient-reported outcome measure developed for daily assessment of cold urticaria disease activity, covering wheal/angioedema frequency and severity, symptom frequency and severity, trigger exposure, and avoidance behavior.
The Urticaria Control Test assesses disease control in cold urticaria via 4 questions scored 0-4 each, with a total score of ≥12 indicating controlled disease.

COLD-CE data showed that only a minority of patients received adrenaline during cold-induced anaphylaxis episodes or were prescribed an adrenaline autoinjector, indicating undertreatment of high-risk patients.

Familial cold urticaria (FCU) is an autosomal dominant inflammatory disorder linked to a locus on chromosome 1q44, presenting with systemic inflammatory symptoms, a non-pruritic maculopapular exanthem, extremity swelling, and leukocytosis following generalized cold exposure, distinct from acquired/hereditary ColdU.

Familial cold autoinflammatory syndromes (FCAS1-4) and factor XII-associated cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FACAS) are monogenic disorders linked to pathogenic variants in 5 genes, mediated by interleukin-1 or factor XII, typically presenting in infancy with systemic inflammatory symptoms and negative standard cold stimulation testing.
Negative standard cold stimulation testing has been associated with spontaneous wheals (suggesting cold-exacerbated CSU rather than true ColdU) and with a lower frequency of cold-induced anaphylaxis.

Retrospective measurement of tryptase levels could help support the diagnosis of cold-induced anaphylaxis, with EAACI guidance recommending measurement 30 minutes to 2 hours after symptom onset and again at least 24 hours after complete resolution.

Perioperative management of ColdU patients should include maintaining normothermia with warming blankets, keeping operating room temperature above 21°C, pre-warming intravenous fluids, and caution with cold parenteral medications such as vaccines and biologics, to prevent intraoperative cold-induced anaphylaxis.
Serum EV concentration was approximately 4-fold higher in OVA-induced asthma mice compared to normal mice.
EV size did not significantly differ between normal (mean 158 nm) and OVA-induced asthma (mean 152 nm) serum, both ranging 30-250 nm.
Exosome marker proteins CD9, CD63, CD81, ALIX, and TSG101 were increased by immunoblot in EVs from OVA-induced asthma serum compared to normal serum.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha were significantly elevated in EVs from OVA-induced asthma serum compared to normal serum EVs.
Proteomic analysis identified 21 novel proteins, including a broad distribution of immunoglobulins, unique to asthma-derived EVs.
Kappa and lambda free light chain levels measured by ELISA were increased in asthma-derived EVs compared to normal EVs.
Asthma-derived EVs did not increase proliferation of splenic T cells, B cells, or eosinophils compared to normal EVs.
Neither normal nor asthma-derived EVs induced M1 (IL-1beta, iNOS) or M2 (Arginase 1, Retnla) macrophage marker gene expression by RT-qPCR.
Asthma-derived EVs had little effect on MAP kinase (JNK, p38) phosphorylation in bone marrow-derived macrophages.
Asthma-derived serum EVs significantly increased beta-hexosaminidase release from bone marrow-derived mast cells compared to normal EVs, indicating mast cell degranulation.
Asthma-derived EVs increased phosphorylation of Erk1/2, JNK, and p38 MAP kinases in bone marrow-derived mast cells more than normal EVs.
Asthma serum-derived EVs selectively stimulate mast cell activation via an IgE-independent mechanism, while not activating T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, eosinophils, or macrophages.
A previous report by the authors documented heightened levels of small EVs bearing distinctive mast cell markers in the circulation of individuals with systemic mastocytosis.
Treatment with the glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG completely prevented allergic diarrhea in OVA-sensitized mice, compared to 100% incidence in the untreated FA group.
2-DG treatment significantly decreased levels of allergen-specific IgE compared to untreated allergic mice.
2-DG intervention suppressed systemic and intestinal Th2 cell differentiation in the food allergy mouse model.
2-DG intervention suppressed IL-4 expression as part of dampened Th2 immune responses.
Blockade of glycolysis with 2-DG decreased intestinal mast cell accumulation in the food allergy model.
Serum mast cell protease-1 (Mcpt1) levels were decreased following 2-DG-mediated glycolysis blockade in the food allergy model.
Expression of typical mast cell activation markers Fcer1a, Mcpt1, and Il1rl1 was decreased by glycolysis blockade with 2-DG.
In vitro experiments showed that 2-DG-mediated glycolysis blockade dampened early receptor signaling in mast cell activation and impaired mast cell function.

Hypercapnic challenge produced a significant reduction in the phase shift between blood pressure and cerebral blood flow velocity (measured by Fourier transform) in both middle cerebral arteries in healthy volunteers.
Hypocapnic hyperventilation produced a significant increase in the Fourier-derived phase shift between BP and BFV in both middle cerebral arteries in healthy volunteers.

Using the continuous wavelet transform (CWT) method, hypercapnia significantly reduced the phase shift between BP and BFV in healthy volunteers, similar to but with slightly different magnitude from the Fourier-based estimate.

Compared with the STFT-based approach, the CWT-based cross-wavelet method showed higher sensitivity to changes in cerebral autoregulation rate and better time-frequency localization of Mayer wave coherence changes.

A patient with a cerebral arteriovenous malformation supplied by the right MCA showed a paradoxical (perverse) phase-shift response to hypercapnia, likely reflecting lack of vascular reactivity to CO2 in the pathological vessels.

All examined patients with neurovascular pathology (carotid stenosis/occlusion, AVM) showed asymmetry in cerebral autoregulation indicators between hemispheres and differing phase-shift dynamics during standardized hyper/hypocapnic loads compared with healthy volunteers.

Increasing the study sample size from 3 volunteers/9 patients (prior publication) to 30 volunteers/15 patients substantially increased the statistical reliability of hyperventilation-induced phase-shift differences.
RJA treatment reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release from IgE-antigen-stimulated mast cells, indicating inhibition of mast cell degranulation.
RJA inhibited both MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways in IgE-activated mast cells.
RJA down-regulated RELA transcript expression in IgE-activated mast cells.
RJA down-regulated NFκB1 transcript expression in IgE-activated mast cells.
RJA inhibited cellular H3 lactylation and H3K9 lactylation in activated mast cells.
RJA reduced histone lactyllysine enrichment specifically at RELA and NFκB1 promoter loci, linking H3K9 lactylation to NF-κB transcriptional suppression.

RJA administered by intraperitoneal injection or oral route alleviated allergic symptoms in mouse models of IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) and ovalbumin-induced active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA).

RJA did not affect histamine-induced hypothermia in the passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) mouse model, suggesting its effect is upstream of histamine action rather than on histamine receptor signaling itself.

In murine models under immunological or psychological stress, female mice showed higher serum histamine levels, greater intestinal permeability, and increased mast cell mediator release compared with males.
Tryptase expression in vitro is upregulated by oestrogens and progesterone in the human mast cell line HMC1.
Basal serum tryptase levels are significantly correlated with sex and age, being higher in males and in individuals aged 18-58 years, with this sex difference lost in the elderly.
Familial alpha-tryptasemia (HaT), an autosomal dominant genetic trait, is suspected but not confirmed to be associated with increased risk and severity of anaphylaxis.
Hypersensitivity reactions mediated by MRGPRX2 receptor activation, such as those to radiocontrast media, appear to be more frequent in females, though data are limited.

HMC1 mast cells, normal mast cells, and the RBL-2H3 basophil line express progesterone receptors, oestrogen alpha-receptors, and androgen receptors, suggesting hormonal modulation of mast cell/basophil function.
Systemic mastocytosis prevalence is slightly greater in women, accounting for 55-59.4% of cases compared to men.
Male sex was associated with significantly inferior overall survival and progression-free survival in systemic mastocytosis (both indolent and advanced), per Kluin-Nelemans et al.
Hymenoptera venom hypersensitivity reactions are more prevalent in males and strongly correlate with bone marrow mastocytosis, whose prevalence is also higher among males.
Osteoporosis is a common coexisting condition in systemic mastocytosis in both sexes, with higher incidence and greater fracture risk in young men compared to premenopausal women.

Pregnancy may induce exacerbation of mast-cell mediator release symptoms in systemic mastocytosis due to hormonal influences, though clinical improvement is noted in about one third of expecting women.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) shows a higher prevalence among women, with a female-to-male ratio of 2:1 to 4:1.
Women with chronic spontaneous urticaria report more severe symptoms, including higher urticaria activity scores and increased rates of angioedema, along with higher healthcare utilisation.
Higher pre-pregnancy total IgE levels correlate with more severe chronic spontaneous urticaria course during pregnancy, and CSU worsens in 28.9% of pregnant women.
Omalizumab has been demonstrated as a safe and effective treatment for chronic spontaneous urticaria during pregnancy, with no reported adverse maternal or foetal effects.
Some studies suggest female patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria may experience greater clinical benefit from omalizumab compared with males.

Oestrogen-related angioedema, a rare subtype of hereditary angioedema with normal C1-inhibitor, predominantly affects women (87.5%) and is particularly relevant in those with F12 gene mutations, involving oestrogenic modulation of the kallikrein-kinin system.
A UK study found higher incidence rates of severe anaphylaxis symptoms in women than men (IR 2.55 vs 2.39), a difference more pronounced among those with severe asthma (IR 19.57 vs 7.56).
According to FAERS data from 1999-2019, 62.71% of patients reporting drug-induced anaphylaxis were female, with antibiotics the most frequent causative agent.
Fatal and near-fatal anaphylaxis is reported predominantly in males, despite females accounting for more overall anaphylaxis cases.
Catamenial anaphylaxis is a cyclic anaphylactic presentation occurring at the onset of menstruation, typically presenting in women aged 30-40 but also described in adolescents.

The Swedish BAMSE cohort found allergen-specific IgE levels do not significantly differ between sexes regardless of age or trigger type, though sensitization to airborne allergens was significantly associated with male sex.
All tested bile acids and bile alcohols significantly suppressed degranulation of stimulated RBL-2H3 mast-cell-model cells.
Bile acids and alcohols reduced extracellular Ca2+ influx mediated by store-operated calcium (SOC) channels, a step critical for mast cell degranulation.
Bile acids and alcohols directly interact with Orai1, the key pore subunit of CRAC channels, interfering with its function and thereby blocking SOC-mediated Ca2+ entry and mast cell degranulation.
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has been reported to exert immunosuppressive effects by binding glucocorticoid receptors and inhibiting histamine release from mast cells.
Chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) and deoxycholic acid (DCA) have previously been reported to promote histamine release, in contrast to UDCA's inhibitory effect.
Using the SFN-SIQ cutoff of ≥6, an estimated 37-50% of the 300 diabetic participants met criteria for probable small fiber neuropathy.
Using the DN4 (interview items) cutoff of ≥4, an estimated 31-50% of participants had neuropathic pain symptoms.
Type of diabetes was positively correlated with SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
Duration of diabetes was positively correlated with SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
Current diabetes treatment was positively correlated with SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
Diabetes-related complications were positively correlated with SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
Smoking status was positively correlated with SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
Current diabetes treatment was the strongest correlate of DN4 neuropathic pain scores.
SFN-SIQ scores were positively correlated with DN4 neuropathic pain scores, indicating a close relationship between small fiber neuropathy symptoms and neuropathic pain.
Female participants had significantly higher SFN-SIQ symptom scores than male participants.
Female participants had significantly higher DN4 neuropathic pain scores than male participants.
Patients with confirmed type 1 or type 2 diabetes had significantly higher SFN-SIQ symptom scores than those unsure of their diabetes type.
DN4 neuropathic pain scores also varied significantly by diabetes type, with lowest ranks in patients unsure of their diabetes type.
Patients receiving pharmacological diabetes treatment (oral, insulin, or both) reported significantly higher SFN-SIQ scores than untreated patients.
Patients receiving pharmacological diabetes treatment reported significantly higher DN4 neuropathic pain scores than untreated patients.
In multiple regression, family history of diabetes, smoking, and diabetes-related complications were significant positive predictors of SFN-SIQ symptom burden score.
In multiple regression, family history of diabetes and current treatment were the most significant positive predictors of DN4 neuropathic pain score.
Age was significantly associated with diabetes type, with the highest frequency of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes occurring in individuals over 60 years old.
Age was significantly associated with family history of diabetes, with participants over 60 years showing the highest percentage of positive family history.
Cutaneous silent period onset and offset latencies recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis muscle were significantly prolonged in AIDP patients compared to healthy controls.
Cutaneous silent period onset and offset latencies recorded from the tibialis anterior muscle were significantly prolonged in AIDP patients compared to healthy controls.
AIDP patients showed significantly longer APB onset and offset CSP latencies than patients with other GBS subtypes.
Median CSP duration was shorter in AIDP patients than in healthy controls.
Transcutaneous conditioning electrical stimulation significantly lowered the cold detection threshold in healthy participants compared to no stimulation.
Conditioning electrical stimulation did not significantly change the warm detection threshold compared to no stimulation.
No significant main effect of electrical stimulation frequency (4 Hz vs 250 Hz) was found for either the cold or warm detection thresholds.
The authors propose that a small cathode electrode preferentially activates Aδ fibers over C fibers, explaining why cold but not warm thresholds were altered by electrical conditioning.
Preincubation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells with VIAN-c4551 reduced acetylcholine-induced eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation compared to acetylcholine alone.
A single intravenous bolus of VIAN-c4551 given before acetylcholine reduced acetylcholine-induced eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation in rat lung tissue in vivo.
Acute ex vivo VIAN-c4551 reduced the maximal relaxation (Emax) and increased sensitivity threshold (higher EC50 shift) of acetylcholine-induced aortic ring relaxation compared to untreated segments.

When rats were pretreated in vivo with VIAN-c4551 for 5 days, the ex vivo inhibitory effect of VIAN-c4551 on ACh-induced aortic relaxation seen with acute treatment was no longer observed, with Emax and EC50 similar to untreated rings.
VIAN-c4551 did not alter concentration-response curves to phenylephrine or the thromboxane A2 agonist U-46619 in rat aortic rings, whether given acutely ex vivo or after 5-day in vivo treatment.
In anesthetized intact rats, acute i.v. VIAN-c4551 (1 or 3 mg/kg) did not significantly modify the dose-dependent decreases in diastolic, mean, and systolic blood pressure induced by acetylcholine.

Acute i.v. VIAN-c4551 (1 and 3 mg/kg) did not significantly change resting diastolic, mean, or systolic blood pressure in intact, bilaterally vagotomized, or pithed anesthetized rats, indicating no central or peripheral autonomic cardiovascular effect.
Daily i.v. VIAN-c4551 (1 mg/kg) for 5 consecutive days did not significantly modify diastolic, mean, or systolic blood pressure measured in awake rats.
Daily VIAN-c4551 for 5 days produced no significant changes in heart rate, QRS, QTc, or heart rate variability domains (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF, SD1, SD2) in awake or anesthetized rats.
VIAN-c4551 treatment for 5 days did not alter the Fulton index, cardiomyocyte size, capillary density, or collagen deposition in heart ventricles compared to vehicle.
VIAN-c4551 treatment for 5 days did not modify mRNA expression of the inflammatory markers TNF-alpha and IL-6 or the apoptotic marker caspase-3 in heart ventricles.
VIAN-c4551 did not change body weight or blood glucose levels in awake rats after 5 days of daily dosing.
Maternal separation (MS) stressed adult rats showed increased visceromotor response to colorectal distention at 40 and 60 mmHg compared with controls, indicating visceral hyperalgesia.
MS rats did not show a significant difference in CRD pain threshold compared with controls, suggesting MS induces hyperalgesia rather than allodynia.
MS rats had significantly more MBP-immunoreactive (eosinophil) cells in colonic tissue than controls.
EPO activity, reflecting eosinophil activation, was elevated in the colon of MS rats compared with controls.
Tryptase-positive mast cell counts showed only a nonsignificant trend increase in MS rat colon compared to controls.
Neutrophil (MPO+) and macrophage (Iba-1+) counts did not differ between MS and control rat colons.
Colonic Prg3 (MBP) mRNA, but not Tpsab1 (tryptase) mRNA, was increased in MS rats, supporting a predominance of eosinophil over mast cell activity.
Serum NE concentration was significantly higher in MS rats than controls, indicating sympathetic overactivation.
Chemical sympathectomy with 6-OHDA significantly suppressed colonic eosinophil infiltration in MS rats.
Alpha-adrenergic blockade with phentolamine suppressed eosinophil infiltration in MS rats, and combined alpha/beta blockade prevented significant eosinophil infiltration.
Chemogenetic activation of peripheral DBH-Cre cells with CNO reduced colonic fecal pellet output and elevated serum NE, confirming increased peripheral sympathetic activity.
Chemogenetic CNO activation of peripheral SNS increased MBP-ir eosinophil counts in the colonic lamina propria of DBH-Cre mice, mirroring the MS model.

Flow cytometry confirmed CNO-induced increases in colonic eosinophils (CD11b+SiglecF+) with no changes in neutrophils, basophils, macrophages, or mast cells, while CD4+ T cells decreased; no immune changes occurred with CNO in naive (non-DREADD) mice.
CG-SMG-targeted chemogenetic SNS activation increased VMR to CRD at 60 mmHg without altering serum corticosterone, indicating the effect is independent of HPA axis activation.
Selective chemogenetic activation of colon-innervating (Cartpt-Cre) sympathetic neurons increased colonic eosinophil counts and eotaxin-1 expression compared with mCherry controls.
Norepinephrine colorectal infusion selectively increased colonic eosinophil percentage and absolute number in mice, without affecting other immune cell types.
NE colorectal infusion in rats significantly increased MBP-ir eosinophils in the colon, with no change in neutrophils, macrophages, or mast cells.
Phentolamine significantly reduced NE-induced eosinophil infiltration, while propranolol showed only a nonsignificant trend toward reduction (P=.12).
NE colorectal infusion induced visceral hypersensitivity to CRD at 60 mmHg beginning 6 hours post-infusion.
Ccl11 (eotaxin-1) was specifically upregulated in the colon 6 hours after NE infusion, whereas Ccl24 and Il33 were unchanged and Ccl26/Il5 were undetectable.
Eotaxin-1-immunoreactive cells increased in the colon starting 3 hours after NE colorectal infusion.

Eotaxin-1 colocalized predominantly with vimentin-positive mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts) rather than CD68+ macrophages or CD31+ endothelial cells, and vimentin+eotaxin-1+ cells specifically increased after NE stimulation.
Both alpha-AR antagonist phentolamine and beta-AR antagonist propranolol inhibited NE-induced eotaxin-1 upregulation in the colon.
Blocking the eotaxin-1 receptor CCR3 with SB328437 significantly inhibited NE-induced eosinophil infiltration in the colonic mucosa.

Norepinephrine (10 µM) stimulation of human CCD-18co colonic fibroblasts increased eotaxin-1 (hCCL11) mRNA from 3 hours onward and increased eotaxin-1 protein 13.8-fold at 3 hours and 35.7-fold at 6 hours, while low concentrations/short exposures had no effect.

MS rats showed no change in the distention threshold required to trigger a visceromotor response, indicating that maternal separation induces visceral hyperalgesia (increased response magnitude) rather than allodynia (lowered threshold).
Mast cell numbers (tryptase-positive cells) showed only a non-significant upward trend in the colon of MS rats compared with controls.
Neutrophil (MPO+) and macrophage (Iba-1+) counts in the colonic mucosa did not differ between MS and control rats.
Colonic mRNA for MBP (Prg3), but not tryptase (Tpsab1), was increased in MS rats, indicating a predominance of eosinophil over mast cell activity.
No apparent morphological alterations were observed in the colonic mucosal architecture of MS rats by H&E staining, despite immune cell changes.
Chemogenetic activation of peripheral sympathetic (DBH-Cre) neurons with CNO decreased the proportion of colonic CD4+ T cells.
Basophil percentage appeared elevated at baseline in flow cytometry, which the authors attribute to antibody cross-reactivity rather than a true biological effect.
Chemogenetic activation of the sympathetic outflow via CG-SMG microinjection in DBH-Cre mice did not change serum corticosterone levels, indicating the HPA axis was not affected by this manipulation.
Chemogenetic activation of peripheral DBH-Cre neurons with CNO significantly reduced colonic fecal pellet output, confirming functional peripheral sympathetic activation.
Blocking the eotaxin-1 receptor CCR3 with SB328437 significantly inhibited NE-induced eosinophil infiltration in the colonic mucosa of rats.
SB328437 also suppressed NE-colorectal-infusion-induced visceral hypersensitivity in rats, linking eotaxin-1/CCR3 signaling to pain generation.
Direct colorectal infusion of eotaxin-1 was sufficient to induce eosinophil infiltration into the colorectal mucosa of rats.
Rats given colorectal eotaxin-1 infusion developed hypersensitivity to colorectal distention, directly linking eotaxin-1 to visceral pain generation.
Three days of dexamethasone treatment significantly inhibited eosinophil activation (EPO activity) and reduced visceral pain in MS-model rats.
SB328437 treatment for 7 days significantly suppressed both eosinophil infiltration and visceral hypersensitivity in the MS-induced IBS model.
6-OHDA sympathectomy reduced colonic eotaxin-1-immunoreactive cells and visceral hypersensitivity in MS rats, supporting a sympathetic-eotaxin-1 axis.
In human IBS colorectal biopsies, tryptase-positive mast cells showed a nonsignificant upward trend compared with healthy controls.
Patients with IBS showed a pronounced elevation in MBP-immunoreactive eosinophil counts in cecal or colorectal biopsies compared with healthy controls.
Colorectal biopsies from IBS patients showed increased eotaxin-1-immunoreactive cells, including more cells co-expressing vimentin (fibroblast marker), compared with healthy controls.

Among eosinophil-recruitment genes tested after colorectal NE infusion, only Ccl11 (eotaxin-1) was significantly upregulated; Ccl24 and Il33 were unchanged, and Ccl26 and Il5 were undetectable in colonic mucosa.

After NE stimulation, eotaxin-1 colocalized predominantly with vimentin+ mesenchymal cells (increased) rather than CD68+ macrophages (unchanged) or CD31+ endothelial cells, identifying fibroblasts as the main eotaxin-1 source.
Human colonic fibroblasts (CCD-18co cells) exposed to 10 μM norepinephrine released 13.8-fold more eotaxin-1 protein at 3 hours and 35.7-fold more at 6 hours than vehicle-treated cells.

Sorted mouse colonic fibroblasts (CD45-CD31-CD34+PDGFRα+) and human CCD-18co fibroblasts both expressed α1B and β2 adrenergic receptors, providing a mechanistic basis for fibroblast responsiveness to sympathetic norepinephrine.

AAV2-hSyn-DIO-hM3D-mCherry injected into the celiac-superior mesenteric ganglion produced mCherry-immunoreactive nerve fibers detectable in the distal colon (1-3 cm from the anus), confirming that the chemogenetic manipulation targets colon-innervating sympathetic fibers.

Self-administered non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (nVNS) reduced the average number of anti-nausea rescue medications used per day by half compared to baseline in patients with chronic nausea and vomiting.
The side of initial nVNS stimulation (left or right side of the neck) did not appear to influence the treatment outcome.
Beyond the primary nausea endpoint, nVNS use was associated with robust improvements in abdominal pain, reflux, indigestion, constipation, depression, and some autonomic symptoms.
Daily vomiting episodes paradoxically increased during the first 4-week period after nVNS was initiated, then remained steady thereafter.
BH4 treatment significantly prolonged cardiac allograft survival compared to untreated allogeneic controls in a mouse heart transplant model.
CsA treatment also significantly prolonged cardiac allograft survival compared to untreated allogeneic controls.
Intragraft and serum BH4 concentrations were significantly increased in BH4-treated recipient mice compared with all other groups, confirming drug delivery.
CD3+ T lymphocyte infiltration into cardiac allografts was significantly reduced after both BH4 and CsA treatment compared to allogeneic controls.
CD8+ T cell infiltration was significantly decreased in the allografts of both BH4- and CsA-treated animals compared to allogeneic controls.
Graft-infiltrating CD4+, CD25+, and FoxP3+ cells showed no significant difference between BH4-treated and untreated allogeneic controls, but were significantly decreased with CsA treatment.
Splenic and lymph node CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ Treg and mast cell frequencies were significantly increased in BH4-treated recipients compared to untreated and CsA-treated controls.
BH4 treatment significantly reduced the frequency of myeloid dendritic cells in the spleen compared to untreated allogeneic controls.
Splenic CD3+ T cells, NK cells, and CD11b+CD11c− myeloid cells were unchanged in BH4-treated mice compared to untreated allogeneic controls.
CsA treatment significantly decreased splenic CD3+ T cell and NK cell frequency, while increasing CD11b+CD11c− myeloid cell frequency, compared to untreated controls.
In vitro, sepiapterin treatment increased proliferation of induced regulatory T cells compared to untreated controls.
In a mixed lymphocyte reaction, sepiapterin treatment did not alter the proliferation of CD4+ responder T cells compared to untreated controls.
Sepiapterin increased Treg proliferation in a suppressor assay but did not alter the suppressive capacity of Tregs on responder T-cell activity at any Treg:responder ratio tested.
Sepiapterin treatment significantly increased the proliferation (cell numbers) of peritoneal-derived mast cell precursors after 10 days of culture compared to untreated controls.
BH4-treated mice showed significantly increased IL-10 production in serum and in the transplanted graft compared to allogeneic controls.
IL-4 and IL-5, TH2 cytokines, were significantly increased in the sera of BH4-treated animals, with IL-4 also significantly upregulated in the graft.
IL-9, a cytokine produced by Tregs and TH2 cells, was significantly upregulated in grafts of BH4-treated mice compared to controls.
TNF-α expression was significantly downregulated in the transplanted grafts of BH4-treated animals compared to allogeneic controls, while IFN-γ remained unchanged.
IL-2 secretion in the sera and grafts of BH4-treated mice was significantly downregulated compared with allogeneic controls, with CsA-treated mice showing near-absent IL-2.

GATA-3 mRNA expression, the transcription factor for TH2 cells, was significantly upregulated in grafts of BH4-treated mice, and significantly downregulated in CsA-treated mice, compared to untreated controls.
T-bet and FoxP3 mRNA expression in BH4-treated grafts were in the range of untreated allogeneic controls but significantly higher than in CsA-treated animals.
Sepiapterin-treated pan T cells produced significantly higher levels of IL-4, IL-13, and IL-10 compared to untreated cells in vitro.
IFN-γ was unchanged and IL-5 showed only a non-significant upward trend in sepiapterin-treated pan T cells compared to controls.

In TPH-1 knockout recipient mice, BH4 or CsA treatment increased allograft survival compared to untreated recipients, but the difference was not statistically significant, arguing against MC-derived TPH-1 as the treatment target of BH4.
BH4 treatment resulted in lower, but not statistically significant, ISHLT histologic rejection scores compared to allogeneic controls, whereas CsA significantly attenuated these infiltrates.
Patient-reported neuropsychiatric symptoms were significantly more common in COVID-19 patients than in COVID-negative controls three years after infection.

Abnormal functional status (mRS>0) was significantly more frequent in COVID-19 patients than controls in unadjusted analysis, but the difference was no longer significant after adjusting for age, sex, hospitalization, and mood disorder history.
Rates of abnormal cognitive screening (t-MoCA≤18) were similar between COVID-19 patients and controls three years post-infection.
Rates of ADL impairment (Barthel Index<100) were similar between COVID-19 patients and controls three years post-infection.
Rates of abnormal Barthel Index scores (<100, indicating reduced independence in activities of daily living) were similar between COVID-19 patients and controls three years post-infection.
Rates of abnormal telephone-MoCA cognitive scores (≤18) were similar between COVID-19 patients and non-COVID-19 controls at long-term follow-up.

Among COVID-19 patients with repeated measures over time, no significant changes were observed in cognitive (t-MoCA) or functional independence (Barthel) scores between 6 months and 3 years post-infection.
Modified Rankin Scale functional status significantly improved among a subgroup of COVID-19 patients followed longitudinally from 6 months to 3 years post-infection.

A Taiwanese retrospective cohort study found psoriasis patients had a significantly higher incidence of ME/CFS than non-psoriasis controls (HR 1.48), with an incidence of 0.37 per 100 person-years in psoriasis patients.
In the same Taiwanese cohort, male psoriasis patients had a greater relative risk of ME/CFS (HR 2.05) than in the general population where sex risk was comparable.
Psoriasis patients aged 60 years or older showed a higher relative risk of developing ME/CFS compared with non-psoriasis controls (HR 2.32).

In a 33-year-old male, exacerbation of psoriasis, development of sacroiliitis (right groin pain), and onset of ME/CFS symptoms (profound fatigue, post-exertional malaise, sleep disturbance, orthostatic tachycardia) occurred concurrently.
Treatment with ixekizumab (IL-17A inhibitor) led to complete resolution of psoriatic skin lesions and significant improvement in sacroiliitis-related joint pain after 12 weeks.

Despite complete remission of psoriasis and sacroiliitis with ixekizumab followed by upadacitinib, the patient's ME/CFS symptoms only slightly improved and largely persisted over two years of treatment.
At week 22 of ixekizumab therapy the patient developed paradoxical eczematous lesions on the face, which rapidly improved after switching to the JAK1 inhibitor upadacitinib.
A large study of 186 ME/CFS patients found that symptom severity significantly correlated with serum levels of several cytokines including IL-17F, CXCL1, and leptin.
Another study reported a relationship between serum leptin levels and the severity of ME/CFS.
IL-17F acts on synovial cells and keratinocytes to induce pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines such as CXCL1, promoting joint and skin inflammation.
Serum IL-17F levels are increased in patients with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, exceeding levels of IL-17A.
Polymorphism of the IL17F gene was strongly associated with increased risk of psoriasis.
Leptin promotes Th1 and Th17 immune responses and suppresses regulatory T cells, contributing to psoriasis development, and elevated serum leptin has been reported in psoriatic arthritis.
Leptin mRNA expression levels in subcutaneous adipose tissue correlate with the severity of psoriasis.

A UK/Ireland prospective cohort study found adjusted incidence rates of paradoxical eczema of 1.22 per 100,000 person-years for IL-17 inhibitors, 0.94 for TNF inhibitors, and 0.56 for IL-23 inhibitors.
Two HLA alleles, C*07:04 and DQB1*03:03, occurred at significantly higher frequency in ME/CFS patients than in matched healthy controls in a prior well-powered study.
Two HLA alleles, B*08:01 and DPB1*02:01, occurred at significantly higher frequency in healthy controls, suggesting they are protective against ME/CFS.
In silico predicted binding affinities of ME/CFS-protective HLA alleles to nine human herpesvirus antigens were significantly stronger (lower IC50) than those of ME/CFS-risk alleles.
The log-transformed odds ratio for ME/CFS risk conferred by each HLA allele correlated strongly with the log-transformed mean predicted binding affinity of that allele to the nine herpesviruses.
None of the nine herpesvirus antigens showed strong predicted binding affinity to the ME/CFS risk alleles, whereas the majority showed strong binding to the protective alleles.
The predicted best binding affinity was weak for 100% of the nine HHVs with the ME/CFS risk alleles, whereas strong binding occurred for 78% (7/9) of HHVs with B*08:01 and 67% (6/9) with DPB1*02:01.
Among the nine herpesviruses, HHV6A showed the weakest predicted binding affinity to the ME/CFS risk alleles.
The predicted binding affinity of the ME/CFS risk allele HLA-C*07:04 to SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein peptides was 18.2 times weaker than that of the protective allele HLA-B*08:01.
The predicted binding affinity of the ME/CFS risk allele HLA-DQB1*03:03 to SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein peptides was 114.1 times weaker than that of the protective allele HLA-DPB1*02:01.
The predicted binding affinity of the ME/CFS risk allele HLA-C*07:04 to Borrelia burgdorferi antigen peptides was 20.7 times weaker than that of the protective allele HLA-B*08:01.
The predicted binding affinity of the ME/CFS risk allele HLA-DQB1*03:03 to Borrelia burgdorferi antigen peptides was 14.4 times weaker than that of the protective allele HLA-DPB1*02:01.
A prior meta-analysis found the highest odds of ME/CFS were associated with HHV6 and HHV7 infection, particularly co-infection with both.
Prior research independently found that HLA-C*07:04 is among the weakest binders of the SARS-CoV-2 protein, corroborating the present findings.

Participants receiving OAA showed a significantly greater percent improvement in DANA Brain Vital cognitive efficiency scores from baseline compared to control at Visit 3, with non-significant trends toward improvement at Visits 2 and 4.

A linear mixed model revealed a significant fatigue-by-treatment interaction on cognitive change, such that in the OAA group higher self-reported fatigue was associated with less cognitive improvement, while no such relationship existed in the control group.

The OAA group showed a significantly greater percent increase in UP Time (upright activity) relative to baseline compared to control at Visit 2 (day 30), with numerically higher but non-significant gains maintained at later visits.
Fatigue severity was not a significant predictor of UP Time within either the OAA or control group, though an overall trend-level association was observed across the combined sample.

At Visit 4, responder classification showed the OAA group had a higher proportion of Fatigue Only and Global Responders and fewer Cognitive Only Responders compared to control, but the overall between-group distribution difference was not statistically significant.

A prior randomized controlled trial of OAA in ME/CFS (the primary RESTORE ME outcome study) found the treatment group had more than a 25% reduction in fatigue versus control, with nearly half of treatment participants experiencing an average 63% fatigue reduction.
An open-label pilot study reported that OAA supplementation was safe and reduced fatigue symptoms, with over 80% of participants reporting improvement over 6 weeks.
Preclinical models indicate OAA supplementation improves mitochondrial biogenesis, enhances insulin signaling, reduces neuroinflammation, and increases resistance to muscle fatigue.

Meta-analyses of two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) show that people with ME/CFS reliably exhibit reduced oxygen consumption, work rate, and heart rate at submaximal exertion on the second-day test, a pattern not observed in deconditioned individuals.

In Walitt et al.'s study, healthy volunteers showed no cardiorespiratory impairment on CPET, whereas participants with post-infectious ME/CFS demonstrated moderate to severe cardiorespiratory impairment.

Exercise heart rate was lower in participants with PI-ME/CFS than in healthy volunteers, contrary to the elevated heart rate typically expected with deconditioning, suggesting impaired oxidative metabolism and chronotropic incompetence rather than deconditioning as drivers of fatigue.

The Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task used by Walitt et al. to assess effort preference has not previously been validated in ME/CFS participants, raising concerns given that PEM may worsen during the test itself and confound results.

The original study did not include adequately matched deconditioned control participants, which the commentary authors argue is necessary to differentiate the physiological effects of PI-ME/CFS from those of simple deconditioning.
Only 8 participants with PI-ME/CFS and 9 healthy volunteers underwent CPET in Walitt et al.'s study, a very small subsample that the commentary authors consider likely underpowered.
PI-ME/CFS participants were less likely to select a harder task for greater reward on the Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task, indicating an altered effort preference relative to healthy volunteers.
Maximum grip strength was equivalent between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteers, but the ability to sustain grip force over time was markedly reduced in PI-ME/CFS.

During repetitive grip tasks, the Dimitrov Index (a marker of muscle fatigability from oxidative metabolism) increased as expected in healthy volunteers as performance impairment appeared, but decreased in PI-ME/CFS participants, indicating grip failure was not caused by muscle oxidative fatigue.

As grip approached failure, healthy volunteers increasingly activated their motor cortex while PI-ME/CFS participants showed decreasing motor cortical activation, implicating altered temporoparietal junction function rather than motor cortex fatigue.

Pathologic analysis of vastus lateralis muscle fiber type ratios showed that skeletal muscle deconditioning is not required to have PI-ME/CFS, though only a portion of cardiopulmonary abnormalities correlated with this deconditioning measure.
Correlation analyses showed that only a portion of the cardiopulmonary abnormalities observed in PI-ME/CFS is associated with muscular deconditioning, implying additional independent mechanisms.
Network analysis of RNA sequencing data provided further evidence of muscle deconditioning, suggesting it develops over time as a consequence of the disorder rather than its cause.
PI-ME/CFS participants showed decreased cardiorespiratory capacity, a lower anaerobic threshold, and chronotropic incompetence during CPET, consistent with prior published findings.
Induction of post-exertional malaise (PEM) via a single CPET did not alter total body or immune cell bioenergetics over the following 72 hours in PI-ME/CFS participants.

Comparison of anaerobic threshold with actigraphy-measured daily moderate activity showed that some PI-ME/CFS participants with very low anaerobic thresholds engaged in almost no moderate activity (suggestive of activity avoidance), while others with normal anaerobic thresholds still had lower activity levels than healthy volunteers with similar thresholds.

PI-ME/CFS participants had patient-reported symptom severity approximately two standard deviations greater than healthy volunteers, and severe symptom burden was an inclusion criterion for the cohort.
Nearly half of the X (Twitter) users posting about functional neurological disorder (FND) were also associated with another condition, most commonly ME/CFS or COVID-19, often together.
Posts from self-declared patients with long COVID or ME outnumbered posts from self-declared FND patients and all other subgroups.
In the network graph of FND-related discussion, ME/long COVID-associated users formed a larger and more peripherally connected cluster than FND-associated users.

ME/long COVID-associated network nodes showed stronger connections with otherwise peripheral/isolated users than FND nodes, suggesting greater message exposure and influence on the public FND narrative.

Among the top 10 most influential users by degree centrality in FND-related discussion, only 3 were FND-associated (none professionals/organizations), and the most influential users expressed generally anti-FND sentiment.
The most influential user by closeness centrality in the FND discussion network was a self-identified long COVID patient who was a strong critic of FND professionals.
Among highly-viewed posts (≥5000 views) in the FND dataset, the majority were negatively predisposed toward FND.
Content analysis showed FND was commonly framed online as a misdiagnosis in relation to long COVID or other conditions such as POTS, MCAS, antidepressant withdrawal, and akathisia.
Unlike ME/CFS and long COVID networks, which were mostly composed of patients, the FND-related network showed a comparatively stronger presence of health care professionals relative to patients.

Content analysis identified conflict as a dominant theme, with many users disputing the FND diagnosis particularly in the context of long COVID and ME, describing FND clinicians in adversarial terms and characterizing FND as a threat diverting resources from other conditions.

FND, ME/CFS and long COVID are described in the literature as sharing overlapping core symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and sleep disturbance, and are similarly undiagnosed by objective laboratory or radiological tests, fueling debate about a functional disorder paradigm.
Low-dose rapamycin significantly improved physical activity as measured by the Bell Activity Scale, increasing from baseline to day 90.
Rapamycin treatment was associated with significant reductions in self-reported fatigue, disturbed sleep, PEM, and orthostatic intolerance on the SSS inventory from baseline to day 90.
MFI aggregate fatigue score improved significantly from baseline to day 90 across all fatigue domains (general, physical, reduced activity, reduced motivation, mental fatigue).

Most SF-36 quality-of-life subscales (physical functioning, role-physical, energy/fatigue, emotional well-being, social functioning, bodily pain, general health, PCS, MCS) improved significantly over the 90-day treatment period.
Unlike other SF-36 subscales, the role-limitations-due-to-emotional-problems subscale did not show significant improvement with rapamycin treatment, consistent with ME/CFS not being psychosomatic.
Plasma BECLIN-1, a marker of autophagy flux, significantly increased after rapamycin treatment, with 1.4-fold and 1.5-fold increases at day 60 and day 90 respectively.
Plasma pSer258-ATG13, a marker of impaired autophagy, decreased progressively and significantly following rapamycin treatment, with more than a two-fold reduction by day 90.

Increases in BECLIN-1 from baseline to day 90 positively correlated with improvements in BAS and several SF-36 subscales (physical functioning, energy/fatigue, emotional well-being, general health, MCS).
BECLIN-1 increases were negatively correlated with (i.e., associated with reductions in) MFI physical fatigue, MFI reduced activity, SSS disturbed sleep, and SSS orthostatic intolerance scores.
Reduction in pSer258-ATG13 was significantly and positively correlated with improvement in PEM symptom severity.
Unlike PEM, no significant correlations were found between pSer258-ATG13 reduction and BAS, MFI domains, other SSS symptoms, or SF-36 scores.

The subgroup of clinical responders (N=17) showed the strongest BECLIN-1 upregulation over the treatment course, whereas partial responders (N=18) and non-responders (N=5) showed no significant BECLIN-1 change.
In the viral-onset ME/CFS subgroup (N=36), rapamycin treatment robustly upregulated BECLIN-1 from baseline through day 90, suggesting benefit for post-infectious ME/CFS.
In the viral-onset ME/CFS subgroup, pSer258-ATG13 declined significantly with treatment but its decrease did not correlate with fatigue symptom alleviation, likely due to a dramatic drop at day 90.
A multinomial logistic regression model showed that a higher MFI aggregate score was associated with approximately four-fold increased odds of being classified as a treatment non-responder.
A higher MFI aggregate score was associated with an approximately 80% decrease in odds of being classified as a treatment responder.
Higher SF-36 social functioning scores increased the odds of being classified as a treatment responder.

Once-weekly low-dose rapamycin was well tolerated, with minimal, mostly transient adverse events (GI symptoms, headache, insomnia) that declined over time, and no adverse changes in safety laboratory parameters or increased infection risk.

The authors identified and synthesized 12 evidence sources (1 clinical decision, 3 guidelines, 7 systematic reviews, 1 expert consensus) yielding 27 best pieces of evidence on TCM nursing technologies for chronic fatigue syndrome, spanning acupoint massage, traditional Chinese mind-body exercises, 5-element music therapy, dietetic therapy, acupuncture and moxibustion, and acupoint application.
The 16-year-old male patient was diagnosed with musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS) after fulfilling two major and seven minor criteria of the 2017 International Classification.

The authors note that mcEDS could be definitively diagnosed by identifying mutations in CHST14 (encoding D4ST1) or DSE (dermatan sulfate epimerase), both enzymes involved in dermatan sulfate glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, though genetic testing was not performed in this case.
More than 90% of classical EDS cases are attributed to mutations in type V collagen genes COL5A1 and COL5A2.

The 34-year-old female patient was diagnosed with hypermobile EDS (hEDS) based on a Beighton score of 6, soft velvety skin, increased arm-span-to-height ratio, and history of recurrent joint dislocation requiring surgery, without skin fragility or other rheumatologic conditions.

Head-up tilt table testing in the hEDS patient produced syncope with asystole at 30 minutes, with blood pressure falling from 122/70 to 86/56 mmHg, concluded by cardiologists to represent combined cardioinhibitory and vasodepressor syncope.

hEDS is described as associated with multiple systemic comorbidities including chronic pain, chronic fatigue, anxiety, depression, dysautonomia, dysphagia, constipation, osteoarthritis, and pelvic dysfunction, with overall poor quality of life.
The prevalence of musculocontractural EDS is stated to be less than 1 in 1,000,000.
The prevalence of hypermobile EDS is reported to range from one to five in 10,000, making it more common than mcEDS.

In a cited cohort of 66 mcEDS patients, large subcutaneous hematomas were the most common vascular complication, occurring in 46 of 58 cases with available data, with first episodes typically by age 12.
A summary of multiple prior case reports/series found cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction in 21.6% of hEDS patients, including POTS in 16.4% and orthostatic intolerance in 5.2%.
Within the pooled summary of prior hEDS case reports, POTS was present in 16.4% of patients.

The proposed mechanism for orthostatic intolerance, orthostatic hypotension, and POTS in hEDS is venous pooling in dependent veins due to abnormal vascular laxity and venous distension, reducing venous return and cardiac output, with a compensatory sympathetic reflex tachycardia.

In Case 2, the mixed vasodepressor and cardioinhibitory syncope with reduced heart rate suggested increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic activity, indicating active neurally mediated hypotension as an additional autonomic mechanism.

The authors note that pharmacological options for treating neurally mediated hypotension in this context include midodrine, beta-blockers, and pyridostigmine, while supportive therapy alone is usually sufficient when asystole is absent.
During the tilt-table-induced syncope with asystole, administration of atropine and IV fluids reverted the patient's rhythm to normal.
44% of lipedema patients reported having hypermobile areas of the body and about 60% recalled being hypermobile as children.
Reduced muscle tone was reported in 55% of lipedema patients during childhood, a typical feature of hypermobility spectrum disorders.
70% of lipedema patients reported easy fatigue after physical activity in childhood, another typical HSD feature.
26% of lipedema patients reported frequent childhood pain in legs, knees, back, and cervical spine, compared with 12.7% of lymphedema patients reporting pain.
8.79% of lipedema patients reported frequent abdominal pain during childhood.
5.66% of lipedema patients experienced frequent headaches during childhood.
24.4% of lipedema patients reported thyroid problems (nodules, hypothyroidism, thyroiditis, or thyroidectomy) in adulthood, compared with 14.89% of lymphedema patients.
Childhood overweight was reported in 50% of lipedema patients, in a condition where disease progression is strongly linked to increased body fat percentage.
In adulthood, joint pain was widespread among lipedema patients across multiple regions: 70% ankles, 56% knees, 66% cervical spine, 46% sacrum, and 55% feet.

Abdominal pain was reported in 30% of pediatric lipedema patients and digestive difficulties in 50% of adult patients, suggesting gastrointestinal involvement through connective tissue similar to HSD.
5.4% of lipedema respondents reported being diagnosed with lipolymphedema, i.e., coexisting lipedema and secondary lymphatic insufficiency.

The review notes that generalised joint laxity or acquired capsular insufficiency can act as a systemic contributing factor to symptomatic lateral meniscus hypermobility, though this is less frequently reported than local traumatic or congenital causes.
A participant with insufficient apartment storage/space sustained a skin tear and bruise from cutting her arm on sharp cupboard edges, taking over a month to heal.

An inaccessible toilet height prevented one participant from using his transfer board, and the resulting loss of transferring function was associated with deterioration of his gluteal and other muscles and self-reported progression of his condition.
Delayed installation of a required ceiling hoist led to a fall during a bed-to-chair transfer that resulted in bilateral shoulder dislocation for one participant.

One participant reported a significant reduction in the amount of one-to-one paid support needed after moving to a wheelchair-accessible apartment, describing it as a significant improvement in independence compared to her former housing.
One participant could not access her balcony because of inaccessible egress design, which created a life-threatening safety risk during a building fire, leaving her waiting in bed unable to evacuate.
Most participants lacked automated blinds, resulting in reduced ability to control privacy, temperature, and light, with some describing associated safety and privacy issues.
One participant relied heavily on in-home split-system air conditioning units for temperature regulation because he reported being unable to regulate his own body temperature.
Voice-operated home automation controlling the front door and balcony increased one participant's independence in daily activities.
An automated height-adjustable kitchen benchtop failed to meet one participant's needs, remaining too high for him to see into cooking pots despite adjustment.
Several participants underutilised available assistive technology, such as voice-command features on iPads, because of a lack of awareness or training regarding device capability.
Uneven and warped flooring created manoeuvrability challenges for a wheelchair-using participant, who reported feeling the flex of the floor while moving.

Accessible bathroom features (fold-down shower bench, wide shower space, comfortable toilet with bidet, grab rails, and splash-safe power sockets) supported one participant's independence and safety in self-care.

Participants reported not being adequately informed before moving in about tenancy limitations, such as being unable to choose their own utility providers, which they felt would have affected their decision to sign the lease.

A companion quantitative study (cited, not this study's own data) found a significant increase in health, wellbeing, and home participation among tenants 6-24 months after moving into apartments designed for people with disability.
In an MDR single-locus model, the TT genotype of TRPM6 rs11144134 was associated with high risk of joint hypermobility with strong cross-validation consistency.
A three-locus MDR model combining ADAMTS5 rs229077, ADAMTS5 rs9978597, and TRPM6 rs11144134 was significantly associated with joint hypermobility.
Specific genotype combinations across the three-locus model (TT×TT×CC, TT×TT×CT, CT×TT×CC) were identified as high-risk combinations for joint hypermobility.
A two-factor MDR model of ADAMTS5 rs9978597 × TRPM6 rs11144134 reached nominal significance but had a low cross-validation consistency and was not considered a reliable predictive model.
Entropy-based predictive contribution analysis showed rs9978597 (ADAMTS5) and rs11144134 (TRPM6) had the greatest individual predictive potential for joint hypermobility.
TRPM6 rs11144134 and ADAMTS5 rs9978597 showed a strong antagonistic (redundant) epistatic interaction in the MDR entropy analysis.
ADAMTS5 rs9978597 and rs226794 showed an antagonistic epistatic interaction in the MDR entropy analysis.
TRPM6 rs11144134 and ADAMTS5 rs226794 showed a pronounced synergistic epistatic interaction in the MDR entropy analysis.
ADAMTS5 rs229077 and rs9978597 showed a moderate synergistic epistatic interaction in the MDR entropy analysis.
GeneMANIA network analysis of the candidate JH genes predicted that interactions among them occur mainly via shared protein domains, co-localization, and co-expression.
GDF5 showed predicted co-expression with ADAMTS5, and LUM showed predicted colocalization with ADAMTS5 and GDF5 in the GeneMANIA network.
STRING protein-protein interaction analysis detected an interaction between GDF5 and ADAMTS5 above the medium confidence threshold.
In the expanded STRING network, ACAN and ADAMTS5 showed the strongest predicted protein-protein interaction among the analyzed partners.
In the expanded STRING network, NBL1 and GDF5 showed a strong predicted protein-protein interaction.
In the expanded STRING network, ACAN and LUM showed a strong predicted protein-protein interaction.
Prior single-locus association analysis (from this and previous cohorts by the same authors) found that polymorphic variants of ADAMTS5, BMP, and TRPM6 genes were associated with joint hypermobility.

The authors note that, per GWAS literature, the T allele of TRPM6 rs11144134 is associated with lower serum magnesium levels, supporting a proposed mechanistic link between this marker and connective tissue metabolism in joint hypermobility.
Two weeks of home-based plantar sensory training significantly improved light touch sensitivity in the treatment group compared with controls, exceeding the reported minimum detectable change.

Two-point discrimination improved significantly after plantar sensory training, but the magnitude of change remained below published minimum detectable change thresholds, suggesting the improvement may not be clinically meaningful.
Vibration sensation showed a modest, statistically significant increase in the treatment group following plantar sensory training, though no established MDC exists for interpretation.

Plantar sensory training significantly improved ankle joint position sense (proprioception), with the reduction in plantar flexion joint position error exceeding the published minimum detectable change, indicating a clinically meaningful gain.

Dynamic balance, measured by the Y Balance Test, significantly improved in the treatment group, with the posterolateral reach distance gain exceeding both the minimum detectable change and the minimal clinically significant difference thresholds.

Although some improvements in muscle strength were observed, the group-by-time interaction was not statistically significant for any individual lower-extremity muscle group, indicating no clear treatment-specific effect on strength.

The authors note that individuals with generalized joint hypermobility may have impaired sensory transmission and mechanoreceptor activity attributable to increased connective tissue flexibility, a mechanism proposed to underlie sensorimotor deficits in this population.

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics (age, weight, height, Beighton score, sex distribution, and physical activity level) did not differ significantly between the treatment and control groups, confirming baseline comparability.

The authors note that primary ovarian torsion predominantly occurred in premenarchal patients with hypermobile utero-ovarian ligaments, implicating connective tissue laxity as an anatomical predisposition.

Overall recurrence rate after treatment for primary ovarian torsion was 44%, with no statistically significant difference between laparoscopic ovarian detorsion (LOD) alone (40% recurrence) and LOD plus oophoropexy (LOD+OPX, 50% recurrence).

Oophoropexy fixation to the round ligament resulted in 100% recurrence, a significantly higher rate than fixation at other sites (20% recurrence), identifying the round ligament as an inadequate fixation site.
On follow-up ultrasound after treatment for primary ovarian torsion, 62% of patients showed normal ovarian morphology while 38% showed signs of progressive ovarian atrophy.
Surgically created bilateral L5 pars defects (spondylolysis) significantly increased lateral bending range of motion at the L5/S1 level compared to the intact state.
Spondylolysis significantly increased axial rotation range of motion at the L5/S1 level relative to the intact state.
L5/S1 spondylolysis induced a significant increase in flexion-extension range of motion at the cranial adjacent segment (L4/L5).
L5/S1 spondylolysis increased lateral bending range of motion at the cranial adjacent L4/L5 segment.
L5/S1 spondylolysis increased axial rotation range of motion at the cranial adjacent L4/L5 segment.
L5/S1 spondylolysis did not significantly alter intervertebral disc contact force at the cranial adjacent L4/L5 segment across all six loading conditions.
Contact area at the L4/L5 intervertebral space was not significantly altered by L5/S1 spondylolysis.
Contact pressure at the L4/L5 intervertebral space was not significantly altered by L5/S1 spondylolysis, consistent with prior finite element analyses.
At the C0-C1 segment, flexion-extension range of motion was roughly 60% lower in AAD patients than in healthy controls.
Lateral bending at C0-C1 was also roughly 60% lower in AAD patients compared with controls.
Axial rotation at C0-C1 did not differ significantly between AAD patients and controls.
Primary axial rotation at C1-C2 was markedly reduced in AAD patients compared with controls.
Vertical and anteroposterior translations at C1-C2 were roughly threefold increased in AAD patients relative to controls, consistent with segmental instability.
C2-C3 axial rotation was compensatorily increased in AAD patients compared with controls, indicating adjacent-segment hypermobility.

At the C2-C3 level, translational motion on all three axes was significantly larger in AAD patients than in the reference comparison, consistent with compensatory hypermobility below the primary lesion.
Left- versus right-head rotation produced bilaterally symmetrical motion at the C1-C2 and C2-C3 segments in AAD patients.
In contrast to the lower segments, the C0-C1 joint showed mild bilateral asymmetry in coupled lateral bending and mediolateral translation during head rotation in AAD patients.
Trochlear dysplasia significantly increases the likelihood of recurrent patellofemoral instability and should be considered in evaluation.
Dejour type B and D trochlear dysplasia with trochlear spurs can produce the jumping J sign and are amenable to trochleoplasty.

A lateral patellar glide of greater than 3 quadrants on physical examination is defined as indicating patellar hypermobility, compared with a normal glide of 2 quadrants laterally and 1 quadrant medially.

The moving apprehension test was positive at abnormally high degrees of knee flexion (80° in Case 1, 90° in Case 2) compared with the normal range of 20° to 30°, helping distinguish true patellar instability from pain-related buckling.

Case 2 demonstrated more severe instability with a 4-quadrant lateral patellar shift and positive moving apprehension test to 90° of flexion in the affected knee, compared with a normal 25° reference in the contralateral knee.

Valgus knee alignment with an increased Q angle makes patients more susceptible to lateral patellar subluxation, and long-leg alignment films are recommended to quantify genu valgum since it can be difficult to assess by physical examination alone.

A Caton-Deschamps ratio above 1.2 is considered patella alta, and this ratio is preferred over the Insall-Salvati ratio for elongated patellar poles and the Blackburne-Peel index for abnormal tibial slope.

Key indications for trochleoplasty include supratrochlear spur height and presence of a jumping J sign on physical examination, whereas trochlear flatness alone is better addressed with medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction alone.
In Case 2, trochleoplasty removing the 10-mm trochlear spur and deepening the trochlear groove was expected to eliminate the jumping J sign on subsequent physical examination.

In Case 1, an increased TT-TG distance, a 5-mm trochlear spur, focal chondral damage on the lateral patellar facet, and absence of a jumping J sign led to a treatment plan of tibial tubercle osteotomy with a steeper cut, medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction, lateral retinacular lengthening, and loose body removal (no trochleoplasty performed).
Serum GRP78 levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum PERK levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum CHOP levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum ATF6 levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Total oxidant status was significantly higher in FMS patients compared to controls.
Total antioxidant status was significantly lower in FMS patients compared to controls.
The oxidative stress index, derived from TOS and TAS, was significantly higher in FMS patients compared to controls.
FMS patients scored significantly higher than controls on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, indicating greater disease-related functional impairment.
FMS patients reported significantly higher pain intensity on the Visual Analog Scale than controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher Widespread Pain Index scores than controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher Symptom Severity Scores than controls.
FMS patients had significantly worse sleep quality (higher Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores) than controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher fatigue severity scores than controls.
