FMS patients had significantly higher anxiety scores (Hospital Anxiety Score) than controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher depression scores (Hospital Depression Score) than controls.
The FMS group reported significantly longer pain duration than the demographic profile of the control group at baseline.
Serum uric acid levels differed significantly between FMS patients and controls, though the direction of change was not specified in the text.
Serum total cholesterol levels differed significantly between FMS patients and controls, though the direction of change was not specified in the text.
Platelet count differed significantly between FMS patients and controls, though the direction of change was not specified in the text.
Glucose, albumin, triglycerides, and CRP levels did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
FM patients scored significantly lower than controls on all eight SF-36 quality-of-life domains, with the largest gaps in bodily pain and physical health.
FM patients reported a substantial disease impact, with a mean FIQR score of 65.94 out of 100.
Plasma total antioxidant capacity did not differ significantly between FM patients and controls.
Plasma proteomic profiling identified 30 differentially abundant proteins between FM patients and controls, of which 14 were overexpressed and 7 met a >20% fold-change cutoff for underexpression.
LXR/RXR activation was the most statistically significant enriched canonical pathway distinguishing FM patients from controls, driven by six differentially expressed proteins.
Complement System and Complement Cascade were among the top enriched canonical pathways in FM, involving complement proteins C4A/C4B, C8B, C8G, CFH and IGKC.
S100A8, a component of calprotectin, was overexpressed in FM plasma, consistent with its proposed role as an innate immunity/inflammation biomarker.
Plasma GAPDH (G3P) was reduced in FM patients and is implicated in neuron apoptosis and a proposed gut-brain-mitochondrial axis in FM.
Glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3) was reduced in FM plasma, consistent with deficient oxidative stress defense linked to pain and inflammation.
VDAC1, previously implicated in FM mitochondrial dysfunction, was detected in plasma but did not show a statistically significant difference between groups, possibly due to technical limitations.
Butyrylcholinesterase (CHLE), which regulates cholinergic synapses, was reduced in FM plasma, supporting nervous system disruption.

Dopamine beta-hydroxylase (DOPO), which converts dopamine to noradrenaline, was reduced in FM plasma and correlated with Bifidobacterium abundance, suggesting a gut-brain dopaminergic axis alteration.
Gut microbiota alpha diversity (Shannon and Simpson indices) was significantly lower in FM patients compared to controls, suggesting a worse intestinal environment.

Differential abundance analysis identified 19 zOTUs distinguishing FM patients from controls, with Streptococcaceae, Actinomycetaceae and Mogibacteriaceae increased, and Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and Intestinimonas massiliensis decreased in FM.
Streptococcus salivarius was the most differentially abundant bacterium between FM and control groups, and was the primary contributor to the upregulated microbial enzymatic activities identified.

PICRUSt functional prediction identified 17 significantly altered KEGG pathways in FM gut microbiota, with increased carbohydrate/ascorbate/pyruvate metabolism and folate/carotenoid/flavonoid biosynthesis, and decreased phenylpropanoid biosynthesis and PPAR signaling.

Predicted enzyme activities including HMG-CoA reductase, GAPDH (NADP+), GMP reductase, glutathione reductase (NADPH), and a 16S rRNA methyltransferase were significantly upregulated in the FM gut microbiome, mainly attributable to Streptococcus salivarius.
Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and B. alomucense abundance correlated with plasma proteins PSA7, LX12B, and DOPO, with the correlation pattern consistent across genus and family taxonomic levels.
A cluster of Faecalibacterium zOTUs showed a negative correlation difference with several SF-36 health domains including vitality, physical health, general health, and pain, uniquely in FM patients.
A deep neural network integrating significant proteomic and metagenomic markers achieved a mean AUC of 0.85 for distinguishing FM patients from controls, outperforming either omics layer alone.

DSG1 and IGKC showed strong positive correlation differences with several Firmicutes genera (Clostridium, Eubacterium, Faecalibacterium, Coprococcus, Collinsella, Mogibacterium) uniquely in FM patients, suggesting intestinal barrier breakdown with secondary immune activation.

PRG4 and APOH, both elevated in FM plasma, showed a distinct inverse correlation with Bacteroides cellulosilyticus, linking reduced Bacteroides abundance to altered joint-lubrication/neuroinflammation (PRG4) and antiphospholipid-associated (APOH) protein levels.

CFAH and Faecalibacterium hattori showed the largest correlation differences with health questionnaire scores, with CFAH positively related to physical function and F. hattori negatively related to energy/fatigue, physical health, general health, and pain.

The genus Bacteroides, including species involved in GABA synthesis, was found reduced in FM patients, consistent with two prior independent studies, and is proposed as a possible CNS-imbalance therapeutic target.
The percentage of immature granulocytes (IG%) in peripheral blood was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, and remained significant after age adjustment.
Absolute neutrophil levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, an effect that persisted after age adjustment.
NLR was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than controls, but this became only borderline significant after adjusting for age.
MPV was lower in fibromyalgia patients than controls, but this difference lost significance after adjusting for age.

No significant differences were observed between fibromyalgia patients and controls for several other hematological and inflammatory parameters including CRP, ESR, WBC, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and hemoglobin.
ROC analysis showed IG% at a cutoff of 0.25 had modest diagnostic performance for distinguishing FM patients from controls (AUC 0.610), with low sensitivity but high specificity.
PLCC was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than controls and showed modest diagnostic ability (AUC 0.596) at a cutoff of 0.0103, with high sensitivity but low specificity.
Dichotomizing FM patients by IG% (cutoff 0.25) showed no statistically significant difference in FIQ or FSDC severity scores between subgroups.
IG# and IG% did not correlate with FIQ scores, suggesting inflammatory activity may not directly track clinical disease severity in FM.
Although CRP and sedimentation rate did not differ significantly between FM and control groups, both showed a positive correlation with FIQ disease severity scores within the FM group.

Long-term FMS patients showed 64 significantly reduced white matter-gray matter functional connections compared to healthy controls, with 44 of these involving the left uncinate fasciculus and multiple gray matter regions.
Short-term FMS patients showed no significant differences in white matter-gray matter functional connectivity compared to healthy controls, unlike long-term patients.

In long-term FMS patients, reduced functional connectivity between the left uncinate fasciculus and several gray matter regions correlated negatively with depression, anxiety, pain severity, and pain duration.
Second-generation H1-antihistamines form the first step of the established stepwise therapeutic algorithm for chronic urticaria, requiring continuous administration and periodic evaluation.
Cyclosporine represents a later step in the stepwise therapeutic algorithm for chronic urticaria management.
BTK inhibitors are highlighted as an emerging therapy for chronic urticaria offering a more targeted and personalized treatment option.
Biological therapies and new receptor antagonists are described as emerging, more targeted treatment options for chronic urticaria refractory to conventional therapy.
The review states that recent understanding of molecular mechanisms of mast cell activation and inflammatory cascades has driven the development of novel therapeutic approaches for chronic urticaria.
Activation of MRGPRX2 directly triggers mast cell activation and is linked to allergic inflammatory diseases, making it a potential therapeutic target.

Using an AlphaFold 3-predicted MRGPRX2 structure, virtual screening of a 23,562-compound Bioactive Compound Library identified the top 30 highest-scoring candidate antagonists for experimental validation.
HCH6-1 was validated to inhibit Ca2+ influx in MRGPRX2-overexpressing HEK293 cells, indicating antagonist activity against the receptor.
HCH6-1 inhibited mast cell degranulation, supporting its role as an MRGPRX2 antagonist with anti-mast cell activation activity.
In an in vivo model, HCH6-1 demonstrated a competent curative effect on MRGPRX2-related atopic dermatitis.
Cell membrane chromatography (CMC) was used to confirm the direct binding interaction between MRGPRX2 and the antagonist HCH6-1.
Trypsin at 150 nM increased intracellular calcium in about half of P-STS enterochromaffin-like cells within 10-30 seconds.
Trypsin concentrations of 30 nM or lower failed to produce any visible calcium increase within a 50-second observation window.
Heat-inactivating trypsin abolished the calcium response, showing that enzymatic activity (presumed PAR2 cleavage) was required.
Trypsin-treated chromogranin A-transfected P-STS cells showed a trend toward increased serotonin secretion compared to controls that nearly reached statistical significance.
The PAR2 agonist peptide SLIGRL-NH2 evoked an increase in intracellular calcium in P-STS cells, confirming PAR2-mediated activation.
The PAR2 antagonist I-191 blocked the calcium response to SLIGRL-NH2 and to trypsin, confirming PAR2-dependence of the response.

PAR2-IN-1, a compound marketed by several companies as a PAR2 antagonist, failed to inhibit the calcium response to SLIGRL-NH2, and the authors found no literature or patent evidence supporting its PAR2 antagonist properties.

The trypsin-induced calcium response was strongly inhibited by the T-type VGCC blocker mibefradil, indicating T-type channels mediate most of the calcium entry, while the L-type blocker nifedipine had no significant effect.
Pretreatment with trypsin did not desensitize P-STS cells to subsequent ACh or histamine stimulation, unlike the receptor desensitization reported in other epithelial cell lines.
Histamine pretreatment did not desensitize P-STS cells against subsequent PAR2 activation by trypsin, with some histamine-responsive cells also reacting to trypsin added later.
Neither trypsin alone nor trypsin plus histamine induced detectable NF-κB (p65) nuclear translocation in P-STS cells, unlike the H2O2 positive control.
Trypsin with or without histamine did not induce detectable p38 MAPK phosphorylation in P-STS cells, whereas high-dose H2O2 did.

High-dose H2O2 (10 mM) induced cytoplasmic p38 MAPK phosphorylation and NF-κB p65 nuclear migration in P-STS cells, confirming these stress pathways are functional and inducible in this cell line, unlike with PAR2 agonists.

Because no mutual desensitization occurred between trypsin and histamine and trypsin did not block subsequent ACh-induced secretion, the authors conclude that mast cell-derived tryptase (activating PAR2) and histamine likely have at least additive effects on serotonin secretion from enterochromaffin cells.
Paw TEWL values were significantly higher than ear and abdomen TEWL values, and the ear was chosen as the optimal measurement site due to similarity to human forearm data and measurement feasibility.
TEWL did not differ significantly between male and female mice, supporting sex as not a confound in this model.
Baseline TEWL of control mice remained stable across seven repeated non-reactive food challenges over 17 days.
Heat lamp warming used prior to IV injections increased core temperature but did not significantly alter TEWL, supporting its safe use in the anaphylaxis protocol.
Isoflurane anesthesia significantly reduced TEWL measurements during induction, so anesthesia was avoided during active TEWL measurement in anaphylaxis trials.
Oral gavage of PBS had no significant effect on TEWL, supporting its use as a challenge delivery method without confounding TEWL results.
Tail intravenous injection of PBS had no significant effect on TEWL, confirming this delivery method does not confound anaphylaxis TEWL measurements.

In a non-IgE-mediated histamine anaphylaxis model, TEWL increased markedly by 15 minutes post-injection in histamine-treated mice compared to controls, preceding the more gradual decline in core temperature.

In the histamine model, TEWL change at 15 minutes did not correlate with temperature change but did correlate with anaphylaxis reaction score, indicating TEWL better tracks clinical severity than temperature in this model.

Serum MCPT-1, a marker of mast cell activation, did not differ significantly between control and histamine-treated mice and did not correlate with TEWL change, consistent with the non-IgE-mediated (mast-cell-independent) nature of the histamine model.
In the passive systemic anaphylaxis (DNP/IgE-mediated) model, TEWL and temperature change were greatest at 15 minutes in DNP-challenged mice compared to controls.
In the PSA (DNP) model, TEWL change correlated with both temperature change and anaphylaxis reaction score, supporting TEWL as a proxy for reaction severity in an IgE-mediated model.
Serum MCPT-1 was substantially elevated in DNP-challenged (IgE-mediated) mice compared to controls, but did not correlate with TEWL change.

In the active systemic anaphylaxis (OVA) model, TEWL and temperature change were greatest at 15 minutes in OVA-challenged mice compared to controls, with clear anaphylaxis reaction scores and diarrhea corroborating the reaction.
In the ASA (OVA) model, TEWL change correlated with both temperature change and anaphylaxis reaction score, reinforcing TEWL as a severity correlate in a repeated-challenge IgE-mediated model.

Serum MCPT-1 was markedly elevated in OVA-challenged mice compared to controls and showed a trend toward correlation with TEWL change, suggesting mast cell degranulation may partly contribute to the TEWL increase.

TEWL increased significantly in all three anaphylaxis models tested (non-IgE-mediated histamine, and IgE-mediated DNP and OVA), while anaphylaxis reaction severity and temperature change varied by model, indicating TEWL is a consistent shared cutaneous outcome across differing allergic stimuli.

Butanol extracts of A. lappa dose-dependently suppressed mast cell degranulation in preclinical models, with the highest concentration also inhibiting IL-4/IL-5 expression, NF-κB activation, and MAPK phosphorylation.
Edible Japanese leaf burdock extracts inhibited antigen-stimulated basophil degranulation in vitro.
Oral arctiin inhibited inflammation and pyroptosis in a murine atopic dermatitis model by suppressing TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB and NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD signaling.
Arctiin downregulated P2X7 receptor expression in a chronic stress-induced neuronal injury model, suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation and reducing caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β maturation.
Arctigenin acts as an inhibitor of MAPK signaling molecules ERK1/2, p38 kinase, and JNK.
Arctigenin activates the AMPK pathway, contributing to its anti-inflammatory and antitumor effects.
Arctigenin promotes anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage polarization while inhibiting the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype, aiding resolution of chronic inflammation.
Intraperitoneal arctigenin attenuated systemic lupus erythematosus progression in murine models by inhibiting abnormal germinal center B-cell reactions and downregulating type I interferon signaling.

Arctiin protected human hair dermal papilla cells from H2O2-induced oxidative stress, preserving cell viability, reducing ROS accumulation, preventing cell-cycle arrest, and decreasing senescence markers at 10-30 μM.
A. lappa root extract reduced monocyte infiltration and suppressed VCAM-1 expression in the aortic root in a TNF-α-induced early atherosclerosis/vascular inflammation model.
Arctiin and its aglycone arctigenin act as natural agonists of the adiponectin receptor AdipoR1, potentially enhancing anti-fibrotic AdipoR1/AMPK signaling relevant to systemic sclerosis.
Oral A. lappa aqueous extract at doses up to 250 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks in mice showed no observable organ toxicity or hematological abnormalities.
Stunted (low height-for-age) SCA children had significantly higher mean cerebral artery blood flow velocity than those with normal height-for-age.
BMI category (underweight, normal, overweight) was not significantly associated with mean cerebral artery blood flow velocity.
Children with stunted height-for-age had a significantly higher prevalence of high stroke risk than those with normal height-for-age.
Abnormal BMI (underweight or overweight) subjects had a numerically higher prevalence of high stroke risk than normal-BMI subjects, but this was not statistically significant.
Age was significantly negatively correlated with cerebral artery blood flow velocity, i.e., TAMMV declined as children grew older.
Weight and height were each significantly negatively correlated with TAMMV, while weight-for-age, height-for-age, and BMI showed no significant correlation with TAMMV.
Age and height were significantly negatively correlated with risk of stroke, while weight, weight-for-age, and height-for-age showed no significant correlation.
Higher white blood cell count was significantly associated with, and positively correlated with, greater severity of cerebral artery blood flow velocity abnormality.
White blood cell count was significantly positively correlated with risk of stroke, such that higher WBC counts were associated with greater stroke risk.
Lower packed cell volume (PCV) was significantly associated with, and negatively correlated with, greater cerebral artery blood flow velocity.
Packed cell volume was significantly negatively correlated with risk of stroke, i.e., lower PCV was associated with higher stroke risk.
Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) level was not significantly correlated with either cerebral artery blood flow velocity or risk of stroke in this cohort.
Duration of hydroxyurea use, frequency of blood transfusions, and number of crises showed no significant differences in mean TAMMV or in prevalence of stroke risk categories.
Duration of hydroxyurea use was significantly positively correlated with risk of stroke, likely reflecting that hydroxyurea is preferentially initiated in patients with worsening disease severity.
Frequency of blood transfusion, number of crises, and number of clinic visits in the last 12 months were not significantly correlated with either TAMMV or risk of stroke.
Using a self-established ELISA protocol based only on published methods, seropositivity for anti-FGFR3 was similarly low across SNN, SFN and healthy controls.
Applying a more detailed version of the reference protocol shifted the ELISA cut-off and increased seropositivity rates in SFN patients and healthy controls compared to the self-established protocol.
A subset of fibromyalgia patients tested seropositive for anti-FGFR3 antibodies despite not fulfilling SFN diagnostic criteria.
Anti-FGFR3 ELISA optical densities and cut-off values were substantially higher at center 1 than at center 2 when testing identical sera.
Anti-FGFR3 ELISA optical density values correlated strongly between the two independent laboratories testing the same sera.
The two laboratories showed substantial agreement on positive/negative anti-FGFR3 status across 42 shared sera.
Sera confirmed positive for anti-FGFR3 by ELISA in both centers showed markedly higher rates of binding to small DRG neurons than ELISA-negative sera.
Patients whose sera showed positive DRG binding had significantly higher anti-FGFR3 ELISA OD values than those without DRG binding, at both centers.
Using combined ELISA and DRG binding positivity as a gold standard, ELISA testing alone showed high sensitivity but modest specificity, with a substantial false positive rate.

Tissue-based DRG binding assay did not confirm anti-FGFR3 positivity in any of the fibromyalgia sera tested and confirmed only one of two positive healthy control sera, suggesting many ELISA-positive results in these groups are non-specific.
Two independent, blinded raters showed almost perfect agreement in classifying DRG immunofluorescence staining patterns.
A cell-based assay for anti-FGFR3 using full-length and extracellular domain FGFR3 plasmids could not be reliably reproduced for positive sera and was abandoned as a confirmation method.
Nearly half of the fibromyalgia control cohort had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, indicating small fiber pathology despite not meeting SFN diagnostic criteria.

Two anti-FGFR3-seropositive healthy controls were later found to have developed malignancy or an unrelated autoantibody, suggesting positive results may reflect emerging autoimmune or neoplastic contexts rather than being purely false positives.
Patient serum immunoreactivity on DRG sections showed both cytosolic and membrane localization, whereas commercial anti-FGFR3 and anti-peripherin antibodies stained only the cytosol.
Sera positive for anti-FGFR3 in only one of the two centers showed intermediate DRG binding rates, higher than double-negative sera but lower than double-confirmed positive sera.

Anti-FGFR3 antibodies detected with commercial testing have also been reported in other conditions beyond SNN and SFN, including CIDP, motor neuropathy, trigeminal neuropathy, fibromyalgia and corneal neuropathic pain, questioning their disease specificity.
Prior pilot and retrospective studies found that immunomodulatory treatment did not show a clear beneficial effect in SFN patients with anti-FGFR3 or anti-TS-HDS antibodies.
Autoantibodies capable of binding small sensory neurons have been identified in patients with small fiber neuropathy, supporting an autoimmune mechanism for the disease.

IVIg therapy and plasma exchange, which remove or block circulating antibodies, are correlated with relief of pain and other symptoms in patients with small fiber neuropathy, suggesting a pathogenic autoantibody-driven mechanism.
A regimen of IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days followed by maintenance doses of 0.75-2 g/kg every 3-4 weeks may benefit SFN patients, with improvement in clinical and symptom severity.
IVIg treatment has shown potential efficacy specifically in small fiber neuropathy associated with celiac disease.
IVIg treatment has not shown efficacy in idiopathic small fiber neuropathy or in metabolic forms such as diabetes-related SFN.
Small fiber neuropathy is characterized by severe neuropathic pain, tingling, orthostatic hypotension, dysautonomia, and sensory neuropathy.
Small fiber neuropathy may co-occur with autoimmune conditions such as Sjögren's syndrome, sarcoidosis, and celiac disease, in which autoantibodies target nervous system antigens.
Small fiber neuropathy is idiopathic in approximately 50% of cases, with other cases attributed to vitamin B12 deficiency, diabetes, or sodium channel gene mutations.
IgM natural autoantibodies facilitate phagocytic clearance of cellular debris and apoptotic cells, helping prevent unwanted inflammatory responses.
DNMT3A-dependent CpG methylation controls specific gene expression in B cells, and its deficiency leads to selective expansion of B1a cells, the main producers of natural autoantibodies.
Inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes promotes migration of B1 cells, implicating histone acetylation in regulating natural-autoantibody-producing B cell function.

Natural autoantibody levels are reduced in patients with Common Variable Immunodeficiency compared to healthy subjects and correlate with specific clinical phenotypes; IgG-class NAb levels were restored after IVIg replacement therapy.

Dimeric IVIg preparations contain natural autoantibodies targeting Siglecs along with their corresponding anti-idiotypes, suggesting an idiotype-anti-idiotype mechanism that may suppress excessive inflammatory responses.

Anti-IgE natural IgG autoantibodies, comprising roughly 0.3%-0.5% of total IgG in IVIg, exert dual effects on basophils, with some inhibiting and others activating basophil responses, distinguishing them functionally from the monoclonal antibody omalizumab.
IVIg-derived natural autoantibodies neutralize serum amyloid A, a key inflammatory mediator, reducing IL-6 release and mitigating associated neuronal damage.
In the randomized controlled IgNiTE trial, IVIg therapy significantly improved neurological recovery and reduced long-term sequelae in children with encephalitis.
A novel heterozygous SCN11A variant, c.197A>C p.(Tyr66Ser), absent in controls, cosegregates with small fiber neuropathy in a mother-and-son duo.
Both patients progressively developed positive and negative sensory symptoms and milder autonomic signs over time.
Quantitative sensory testing showed significant thermal hypoesthesia and pinprick hyperalgesia in both individuals.

Rectangle, half-sine, and sine-wave stimulation of hands and feet revealed axonal on/off-like hyperexcitability, possibly due to continuous activation of mechano-insensitive CMi (sleeping) nociceptors.
Nerve conduction studies were unremarkable in both patients despite clinical and electrophysiological signs of small fiber dysfunction.
Pain-related evoked potentials showed pathological responses in both individuals, consistent with small fiber pathway dysfunction.
The intraepidermal nerve fiber density was reduced at the index patient's distal leg, supporting a diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
Patch-clamp analyses showed that p.(Tyr66Ser) shifted the voltage dependence of activation of NaV1.9 to more depolarized potentials.
Patch-clamp analysis showed that the Tyr66Ser variant accelerated the deactivation kinetics of NaV1.9 channels.
The Tyr66Ser variant slowed the inactivation kinetics of the NaV1.9 channel compared to wild type.
Overexpression of the Tyr66Ser variant in mouse sensory neurons shortened the duration of individual action potentials.
Overexpression of the Tyr66Ser variant in mouse sensory neurons enhanced the action potential afterhyperpolarization.
Depleting macrophages partially rescued gastrointestinal dysmotility and enteric neuronal density in a benzalkonium chloride (BAC)-induced enteric neuronal injury mouse model.
In vitro co-culture experiments showed that exosomes derived from M1 macrophages promoted apoptosis of enteric neurons.
MMP8 was identified as enriched in M1 macrophage-derived exosomes and promoted activation of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, inducing enteric neuronal apoptosis.
Inhibiting MMP8 partially mitigated enteric neuronal injury and restored intestinal function in BAC-treated mice exposed to M1 macrophage exosomes.
Elevated serum exosomal MMP8 levels were identified as a potential biomarker for Hirschsprung's disease, a gastrointestinal motility disorder.

A 4-minute abdominal muscle stretching intervention significantly increased frontal alpha band power (8-12.8 Hz) in the immediate post-intervention EEG segment compared with pre-intervention baseline in people with IBS.
Across nine consecutive 1-minute post-intervention EEG segments, alpha power remained significantly elevated in most segments except the sixth and ninth, which showed only marginal trends.
Sensory thresholds measured via peripheral nerve stimulation significantly increased after the stretching intervention compared to baseline, indicating reduced somatosensory hypersensitivity.

Pain thresholds did not show a statistically significant change after the stretching intervention compared to baseline, suggesting selective effect of stretching on sensory but not nociceptive pathways.

Prior literature cited indicates that decreased frontal alpha power and increased occipital beta power during resting-state EEG are characteristic findings in patients with IBS, reflecting default mode network dysregulation.

A prior intervention study cited found that a 4-minute abdominal muscle stretching exercise significantly reduced salivary chromogranin A, a stress biomarker, in patients with IBS, with trends toward improved GSRS and anxiety scores.
Four weeks of active TEA significantly reduced nausea severity by 29.7% compared to baseline, while sham-TEA had no effect.
TEA significantly reduced vomiting severity by 39.3% compared with baseline.
TEA significantly reduced abdominal fullness severity by 21.4% compared with baseline.
TEA significantly reduced bloating severity by 20.6% compared with baseline.
TEA significantly reduced retching severity by 31.1% compared with baseline.
Sham-TEA treatment produced no significant change in any of the gastroparesis symptom scores.
TEA significantly improved the 'pain interfere activity' quality of life score compared with baseline, whereas other RAND-36 domains showed no significant change.
Diabetic gastroparesis patients had a significantly lower percentage of normal gastric slow waves in the fasting state compared to healthy controls.
The percentage of normal gastric slow waves in the postprandial state was not significantly different between DGP patients and healthy controls.
Four weeks of TEA significantly increased the percentage of normal gastric slow waves in the postprandial state compared to baseline.
TEA significantly improved percentage of normal slow waves in channel 1 in both fasting and postprandial states.
The percentage of slow wave coupling among the 4 EGG channels was significantly reduced in DGP patients compared to healthy controls in the fasting state.
TEA showed a non-significant trend toward increased gastric slow wave coupling in the fasting state compared to baseline.

Healthy controls showed a postprandial trend in autonomic (HRV) parameters (LF, HF, LF/HF) that was absent in DGP patients, suggesting impaired autonomic response to food intake in diabetic gastroparesis.
TEA, but not sham-TEA, produced a non-significant trend toward postprandial increase in vagal activity (HF) and decrease in sympathetic activity (LF).
Dominant frequency and dominant power of gastric slow waves did not differ significantly between DGP patients and healthy controls in fasting or postprandial states, and were unaffected by TEA.
Within the treatment group, self-reported hunger VAS scores increased significantly from baseline to week 4 after taking sublingual cannabis oil.
In the placebo group, hunger VAS scores did not change significantly from baseline to week 4.

Comparing between the treatment and placebo groups, mean differences in appetite VAS scores (hunger, satisfaction, fullness, cravings) were not statistically significant despite favoring cannabis oil for several parameters.
Daily caloric intake per kg body weight significantly increased in the treatment group from baseline to week 4.
Daily caloric intake per kg body weight also increased in the placebo group after 4 weeks, but the change was not statistically significant.
Body weight and BMI increased slightly in the treatment group and decreased in the placebo group, but between-group differences were not statistically significant.
Quality of life measured by EQ-5D did not differ significantly between treatment and placebo groups, though the VAS for health trended higher in the treatment group.
TGF-β levels did not differ significantly between the cannabis oil and placebo groups, nor did they change significantly within either group after treatment.
Inflammatory markers ESR and CRP decreased after cannabis oil treatment but increased in the placebo group, though the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
One treatment-group patient developed severe hyponatremia and drowsiness after a single drop of cannabis oil, requiring hospitalization and withdrawal from the study.
Overall incidence of adverse events was not significantly different between the cannabis oil and placebo groups (10 vs 7 patients affected).
At baseline, serum transferrin levels and daily caloric intake per kg body weight were significantly higher in the treatment group than in the placebo group, indicating a baseline imbalance.

In a prior mouse model of SSc cited by the authors, selective CB2 receptor agonist injection reduced skin thickness, collagen accumulation, and skin fibroblast proliferation compared to untreated mice, and reduced lung collagen type I and autoantibody development.
A cited study reported that the synthetic cannabinoid ajulemic acid had antifibrotic effects in SSc-induced mice, proposed to occur via PPARγ activation disrupting TGF-β signaling.
Within the treatment group, VAS scores for satisfaction with eating and being able to eat a lot trended toward increase after 4 weeks but did not reach statistical significance.
Combined subcutaneous treatment with ATZ and losartan reduced mean arterial pressure in L-NAME hypertensive rats to slightly below normotensive levels, an effect greater than losartan given alone.

Hexamethonium-induced hypotension, a measure of sympathetic vasomotor tone, was blunted in ATZ+losartan-treated L-NAME rats compared to saline-treated L-NAME rats, indicating reduced sympathetic activation.
The combination of ATZ and losartan effectively blocked both sympathetic and angiotensinergic activation, abolishing hypertension in the L-NAME rat model.
A systematic review found that most studies reported increased intestinal mast cell numbers or density in IBS patients compared to healthy individuals.
In IBS patients, mast cells were located significantly closer to enteric nerve fibres (within 5-10 µm) than in healthy controls, with evidence of activation on electron microscopy.
Exogenous histamine excites intestinal sensory nerves via H1 receptor activation, an effect blocked by an H1 antagonist but not by H2 or H3 antagonists.
Histamine pre-incubation of DRG neurons augments subsequent neuronal excitation induced by TRPV1, TRPV4, and TRPA1 agonists, indicating TRP channel sensitization.
IBS patients treated with an H1 receptor antagonist reported reduced abdominal pain compared to placebo.
Biopsy supernatants from IBS patients excited spinal afferent neurons via activation of PAR-2.
The serine protease inhibitor nafamostat reduced abdominal pain in a rodent model of post-inflammatory IBS.
In contrast to PAR-2, PAR-4 activation reduced the excitability of colonic nociceptors both in vitro and in vivo, indicating opposing roles of these receptors in pain signalling.
Re-exposure to a food antigen after loss of oral tolerance triggered colonic afferent hypersensitivity in mice, which was blocked by targeting mast cells or IgE.

Germ-free mice colonized with high-histamine-producing microbiota from IBS patients developed visceral hypersensitivity linked to a high-FODMAP diet, which was inhibited by blocking histamine signalling.
In IBS patients, reducing dietary FODMAP intake reduced abdominal pain scores, whereas increasing FODMAPs often worsened symptom scores.
Urine metabolomics showed that histamine levels positively correlated with either increases or decreases in pain scores in a significant number of IBS patients on a FODMAP intervention.
Fecal supernatants from ulcerative colitis patients decreased the visceromotor response to distension in a PAR-4-dependent manner, opposite to the effect of IBS fecal supernatants.
Intracolonic administration of fecal supernatants from IBS-D and IBS-C patients increased the visceromotor response to colorectal distension, with evidence of allodynia and hyperalgesia.

F. prausnitzii, which produces a PAR-4-activating serine protease, reduced abdominal pain in rodent IBS models by reversing increased mucosal permeability, and showed antinociceptive effects on DRG neurons in vitro.

In IBS patients whose abdominal pain improved after a low-FODMAP diet, fecal supernatants collected post-diet had a markedly reduced ability to excite DRG neurons via PAR-2 and histamine receptor activation.

Subthreshold concentrations of trypsin and histamine individually had no effect on nociceptor activity, but their combined application significantly increased afferent mechanosensitivity and nociceptor excitability, demonstrating synergy between protease and histamine signalling.

Prior activation of PAR-2 endosomal signalling by trypsin amplified subsequent histamine-evoked nociceptive responses, whereas pre-exposure to histamine did not enhance subsequent trypsin-mediated PAR-2 excitability, indicating a directional (order-dependent) synergy.

Activation of the δ-opioid receptor triggers compartmentalized endosomal signalling resulting in sustained inhibition of neuronal excitability and prolonged pain relief, in contrast to the short-lived inhibitory signalling of the µ-opioid receptor.

In DRG patch clamp and ex vivo colon afferent recordings, the pH-sensitive opioid NFEPP decreased nociceptor excitability only at acidic pH (6.5-6.8) with no effect at physiological pH 7.4, whereas fentanyl was active at both pH levels.

In conscious DSS colitis mice, NFEPP potently attenuated pain responses to colorectal distension in inflamed colon without affecting nociception in healthy control colon, unlike fentanyl which acted in both.
Repeated dosing of NFEPP in the DSS colitis model showed analgesic activity peaked at the height of inflammation (lowest tissue pH) and waned as inflammation resolved and pH normalized.

At analgesic doses, NFEPP did not affect blood oxygen saturation, unlike fentanyl which caused profound respiratory depression; NFEPP still had no effect on O2 saturation even at fentanyl's LD50 concentration.
NFEPP had no impact on GI transit measured by pellet counting and barium CT imaging, whereas fentanyl caused marked paralysis of GI transit.
Place-preference studies in rats showed a clear reward effect for fentanyl, whereas NFEPP had no effect, suggesting lower addiction potential.
Unlike fentanyl, repeated administration of NFEPP resulted in minimal or no development of analgesic tolerance during progression of acute visceral inflammation.

In ex vivo human colon preparations from surgical specimens, NFEPP did not suppress nerve firing at pH 7.4 but significantly reduced firing when tissue bath pH was lowered to 6.8, supporting translational validity of the pH-sensitive mechanism.
Investigational Na+ and Ca2+ channel blockers (Vertex and Zymedyne compounds) showed modest analgesic benefit in phase II clinical trials for abdominal/visceral pain.
The authors propose stool histamine levels or HDC gene expression as potential biomarkers to identify IBS patients likely to benefit from histamine-targeted therapy.
Inflammation, tissue injury, and tumors cause localized tissue acidification (pH as low as 5.5) driven by reduced perfusion, hypoxia, and glycolytic metabolites, which contributes to pain generation.

NFEPP, a fluorinated fentanyl analogue, was designed with a lowered pKa (6.8) so that it becomes protonated and binds mu-opioid receptors selectively in acidic (inflamed) tissue while remaining inactive at physiological pH.

In patch-clamp recordings from DRG nociceptive neurons, NFEPP decreased neuronal excitability (increased rheobase) at acidic pH (6.5 and 6.8) but had no effect at physiological pH 7.4, whereas fentanyl inhibited excitability at both pH levels.
In ex vivo mouse colon afferent nerve recordings, NFEPP inhibited afferent nerve firing only when tissue pH was acidic, unlike fentanyl which inhibited firing at both acidic and physiological pH.

In conscious DSS-colitis mice, NFEPP potently attenuated colorectal distension-evoked visceromotor pain responses to a degree comparable to fentanyl, but selectively inhibited nociception in inflamed colon without affecting healthy colon, whereas fentanyl acted in both.
In longitudinal DSS colitis studies, repeated NFEPP dosing showed analgesic activity that peaked during maximal inflammation (lowest tissue pH) and waned as inflammation resolved and pH normalized.
At analgesic doses, and even at the fentanyl LD50 dose, NFEPP did not reduce O2 saturation, whereas fentanyl caused profound respiratory depression.
NFEPP had no impact on GI transit (assessed by pellet counting and barium CT imaging), whereas fentanyl caused marked paralysis of GI transit.
Video monitoring showed NFEPP did not affect locomotion in conscious mice, unlike fentanyl which caused profound changes in locomotion.
Place-preference studies in rats showed a clear rewarding effect for fentanyl but no reward effect for NFEPP, suggesting lower addictive potential for NFEPP.
Repeated administration of NFEPP resulted in minimal or no development of analgesic tolerance during acute visceral inflammation, unlike fentanyl.

In ex vivo human colon preparations from surgical specimens, NFEPP did not suppress nerve firing at physiological pH 7.4, but significantly reduced firing when the bath pH was lowered to 6.8, supporting translational validity of the pH-selective mechanism.
The authors propose stool histamine levels or the HDC gene as potential biomarkers to identify IBS patients likely to benefit from histamine-targeted therapy.
The authors propose stool fecal calprotectin as a potential biomarker to identify IBD patients likely to benefit from mechanism-targeted therapy such as pH-sensitive analgesics.
Proximal ciliated cell abundance was reduced in severe compared to moderate PCS nasal epithelium.
Mucous cell abundance was reduced in severe compared to moderate PCS nasal epithelium.
Deuterosomal epithelial cell abundance was significantly reduced in severe compared to moderate PCS.
T-cell abundance increased in severe compared to moderate PCS nasal epithelium.
Basal cell abundance increased in severe compared to moderate PCS nasal epithelium.
Myeloid-dendritic cell abundance increased in severe compared to moderate PCS nasal epithelium.
Bulk-transcriptome deconvolution against a healthy/asthmatic reference cohort showed fewer ciliated cells in severe PCS nasal epithelium.
No detectable SARS-CoV-2 viral genetic sequences were found in the nasal epithelium of PCS patients, indicating viral clearance.
IL6 and CXCL8 expression, markers normally upregulated in acute infection, were not elevated, corroborating an absence of active viral infection in PCS nasal epithelium.
TriNetX analysis of PCS patients versus propensity-matched controls identified 22 comorbidities with significantly increased odds and hazard ratios.
Viral pneumonia showed a markedly increased odds and hazard ratio (>4) in PCS patients relative to controls in the TriNetX registry.
PROGENy pathway enrichment analysis showed inflammation-related pathway activation (TNFα, TGFβ, NF-κB) enriched in severe PCS.
PI3K pathway activity was enriched in moderate PCS, implicating reduced cell proliferation relative to severe PCS.
TGFβ signaling was enriched in severe PCS while cellular migration pathways (indicated by PI3K enrichment) were enriched in moderate PCS.
The IGF signaling pathway, indicative of normal cell differentiation, was absent in cell-cell communication analysis of severe PCS.
MIF ligand-receptor interactions and the MIF-(CD74-CXCR4) signaling axis were specifically enriched in myeloid cells of severe PCS patients.
CXCR4 expression in myeloid cells and CD44 expression in myeloid and basal cells both increased with PCS severity.
TNF and TGFβ1 expression increased in myeloid-dendritic cells and T cells with increasing PCS severity, with TGFβ1 also increased in basal epithelial cells.
GSEA using the Hallmark gene set confirmed TNFα, NF-κB, and EMT signatures as the most upregulated pathways in severe PCS nasal mucosa.

Pseudo-time trajectory analysis showed a more branched differentiation path with more endpoints and lower centrality in severe PCS than moderate PCS, indicating divergent basal-to-ciliated cell differentiation.
In ALI cultures, TGFβ stimulation increased differentiating basal cell abundance and reduced ciliated cell abundance compared to PBS control, mimicking severe PCS epithelium.
In ALI cultures, TNFα stimulation alone resulted in greater basal cell differentiation toward ciliated and secretory cell types compared to PBS control.

Combined TGFβ and TNFα stimulation prevented basal cells from committing to a terminal differentiated state and induced partial epithelial-mesenchymal transition toward a fibroblast/myofibroblast phenotype.
GSEA of ALI cultures showed strong EMT pathway enrichment with TGFβ stimulation alone, while oxidative phosphorylation was reduced with both TGFβ-alone and TNFα-alone stimulation.

The paper cites external research showing metformin significantly reduces TGFβ production in cardiomyocytes in atrial fibrillation, a disease also marked by elevated TGFβ and TNFα, as rationale for a possible PCS therapeutic strategy.
The authors cite a prior study reporting that metformin therapy in diabetic patients reduced mortality by roughly 70% after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Metformin use has also been reported to reduce the hazard risk of developing post-COVID syndrome.

In an allergic rhinitis mouse model, the TNFα inhibitor infliximab reduced cytokine production and immune cell infiltration into the nasal mucosa, supporting TNFα blockade as a plausible strategy for nasal mucosal inflammation.
Pirfenidone, an anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic drug used for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis that suppresses TNFα and TGFβ production, has successfully treated post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis.

A cited murine study found that reduced presence of the transcription factor E2F4 is associated with fewer ciliated cells in mouse nasal epithelium, supporting a role for E2F pathway activity in multiciliogenesis.

A cited study (Roukens et al.) detected CD8+ T cells persisting in the nasal mucosa for at least two months after SARS-CoV-2 viral clearance, supporting a role for prolonged immune cell presence independent of active infection.

Previous findings cited by the authors show that circulating dendritic cells and monocytes remain increased for six months after severe COVID-19 infection, aligning with the persistent myeloid infiltration observed in this study's severe PCS nasal samples.

A cited study links post-COVID exercise intolerance to resident immune cell-induced artery remodeling in skeletal muscle despite viral clearance, supporting long-lasting tissue remodeling as a general feature of PCS.
TGFβ-induced fibronectin was enriched in severe PCS cell-cell communication data, consistent with fibronectin's known role in inducing epithelial proliferation and differentiation.
Laminin B1 was found to be produced more in moderate PCS compared to severe PCS, and is implicated in modulating correct lung development via epithelial cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation.
A cited animal-model study showed that inhibiting MIF and CD74 caused loss of oxidative stress protection, leading to increased inflammatory cytokine production, apoptosis, and higher mortality.
CD74 is reported to signal through activation of the ERK and Akt pathways, providing a mechanistic link to the downstream inflammatory signaling implicated in severe PCS.

G2M and E2F pathway activity was significantly enriched only in PBS control ALI cultures and reduced upon TNFα and TGFβ stimulation, indicating that these cytokines dysregulate normal cell-cycle progression required for basal cell differentiation and ciliogenesis.

The MIF co-receptors CXCR4 and CD44 mediate differential MIF responses related to immune cell infiltration and have been implicated in COVID-19 and acute lung injury, potentially contributing to a new immune cell subset that aggravates PCS severity.

In the ALI in vitro model, GSEA showed strong epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway enrichment with TGFβ stimulation, while oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in both TGFβ-alone and TNFα-alone conditions compared to PBS control.
A systematic review found metformin use was associated with significantly increased relative risk of abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea compared with controls.

In a small pilot study, six fibromyalgia patients treated with metformin 200 mg/day showed normalized IL-1β/IL-18 elevations and a significant reduction in fatigue on the Fatigue Inventory Questionnaire, comparable to an NLRP3 knockout mouse model.
NLRP3 inflammasome protein elevation, linked to impaired AMPK function and hyperalgesia, was observed in fibromyalgia.

Missailidis et al. found that lymphoblasts from 51 ME/CFS patients had significantly reduced ATP synthesis at mitochondrial complex V (15% lower than healthy controls) alongside elevated oxygen consumption at upstream complexes and increased complex V protein transcription, suggesting a hypofunctioning complex V protein.

Missailidis et al. found mitochondrial proton leak associated with mTORC1 hyperactivity in ME/CFS, evidenced by significantly increased phosphorylation of the mTOR substrate 4E-BP1, occurring without change in ATP levels.

Wang et al. demonstrated that increased WASF3 expression reduced mitochondrial complex IV activity through a post-translational mechanism, with higher WASF3 mRNA but lower complex IV protein production.

Wang et al. found an unexpected overabundance of PERK with reduced BiP in ME/CFS-related WASF3 toxicity models, along with discordance between activated PERK and downstream eIF2α, indicating an aberrant ER stress signaling response.

Godlewska et al.'s 7T MRS study of 22 ME/CFS patients versus 13 healthy controls found significant reductions in creatine, glutathione, and myo-inositol, with a non-significant reduction in glutamate (p=0.052) and no change in glutamine.
In vitro, supratherapeutic metformin reduced cellular ROS-buffering demand, maintaining stable glutathione levels while reducing glutamine transport activity and the cysteine/glutamine ratio.
Armstrong et al.'s NMR metabolomic analysis of blood and urine from 46 ME/CFS patients versus 26 healthy controls found reduced glutamate levels alongside disproportionately elevated glucose.

Shankar et al. found significantly elevated oxidative stress markers in ME/CFS and Long COVID cells compared to healthy controls, with sex-specific patterns: males showed greater lipid peroxidation while females showed elevated mitochondrial calcium and hydrogen peroxide; higher reduced glutathione and lower superoxide dismutase were seen in both sexes.
Treating ME/CFS T cells in vitro with 10 μmol/L metformin for 5 days significantly reduced markers of ROS, with no change observed in healthy control cells.

Vizuete et al. showed that methylglyoxal exposure profoundly reduced hippocampal astrocyte glutamate uptake and increased NMDAR1 expression, both of which were reversed by metformin, which also reduced IL-1β and interfered with methylglyoxal-derived advanced glycation end products and RAGE signaling.

Cameron et al. found that 3 hours of metformin exposure at 2 mmol/L activated AMPK and suppressed TNF-α-induced IκB degradation along with reduced expression of proinflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β and CXCL1/2 in vitro.
In a prospective cohort of people with type 2 diabetes, metformin (n=498) reduced the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio by 9% compared with sulphonylureas (n=172).

A randomized placebo-controlled trial found that metformin selectively reduced the proinflammatory cytokines CCL22 and stromal cell derived factor-1αβ in 20 participants at 4 months compared with 12 controls.

Wang and Huang found that metformin suppressed FcεR1-mediated mast cell degranulation and reduced secretion of IL-13, TNF-α and sphingosine-1-phosphate despite provoked Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor activation.

A retrospective cohort study from Hubei province found that metformin-treated patients with COVID-19 and type 2 diabetes had lower rates of heart failure (HR 0.61, p=0.006) and ARDS (HR 0.66, p=0.028) versus non-metformin patients, with no significant difference in mortality, despite higher rates of acidosis and lactic acidosis in the metformin group.

Bramante et al.'s COVID-OUT phase 3 platform trial found that metformin (but not ivermectin or fluvoxamine) reduced confirmed Long COVID incidence by 41% when started within 3 days of COVID-19 symptom onset, among 6602 participants with confirmed cases assessed by day 300.

Reis et al.'s TOGETHER adaptive platform trial found no benefit of metformin (750 mg twice daily for 10 days) on acute COVID-19 hospitalization outcomes (RR 1.14, 95%CI 0.73-1.81), leading to early termination for futility, with higher dropout in the metformin arm.
Metformin reduces the endothelium-specific microRNA miR-34a and enhances GTPCH1, improving vascular nitric oxide availability and vascular responsivity despite underlying endothelial dysfunction.
Kenyon et al. treated ME/CFS and IBS patients with fecal microbiota transplantation delivered transrectally into the sigmoid colon, though the methodology used to measure response was flawed.
Rao et al.'s RCT of Lactobacillus probiotic vs placebo for comorbid anxiety in ME/CFS found an unexpected significant rise in stool Bifidobacteria that correlated with improved anxiety symptoms.

In vitro experiments by Islam and Manna showed that supratherapeutic metformin reduced cellular ROS buffering demand while maintaining stable glutathione abundance and reducing glutamine transport and the cysteine/glutamine ratio.

Shi et al. showed that reduced AMPK from tumor activity upregulated mTOR-driven lymphoma growth, and combining temsirolimus with metformin (3 mg/kg/day) reduced lymphoma growth in vitro and in xenograft models, an effect abolished by the AMPK inhibitor Compound C.
Metformin at concentrations similar to other antiviral studies modulated AMPK to reduce HHV8 (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus) lytic replication, despite enhanced latent RNA transcription.
Islam et al. found metformin (2.5 mM) elevated hypoxanthine, a precursor for de novo purine synthesis, while reducing adenine.
In an animal model, metformin improved leaky gut and intestinal inflammatory markers, increasing bile acids, butyrate, leucine, and taurine while decreasing glutamate and pyruvate.
MCAS has a baseline population prevalence of 17%, with family members of affected individuals 2.7 times more likely to have the condition.

Metformin upregulates miR-26a, miR-34a, miR-146a and miR-200c while downregulating pro-inflammatory miRNAs miR-155, miR-21 and miR-29a, contributing to anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects.
miR-29a-3p has been found elevated in the plasma of ME/CFS patients, potentially contributing to disease pathophysiology.

In Zhang et al.'s animal model, decreased mTORC2 activity corresponded to PPAR-alpha deficiency and increased lipid droplet accumulation, with glucosylceramide acting as the intermediary between mTORC2 and PPAR-alpha.
Metformin has been shown to reduce sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), resulting in reduced tumorigenesis in ovarian cancer.
Metformin activates AMPK directly, independent of AMP, by inhibiting v-ATPase, an effect observed at plasma metformin levels of 5 μmol/L, suggesting a low-dose direct mechanism.
A six-month longitudinal trial by Wu et al. confirmed a persistent metformin-associated reduction in short chain fatty acid-producing gut organisms via pathway enrichment analysis.

Buse et al. found that despite low plasma metformin levels, a delayed-release formulation targeting the distal small intestine achieved 70% of the glycaemic effect of a much higher dose of sustained-release metformin.
Bryrup et al. and Elbere et al. both found metformin reduced Clostridiaceae and increased Escherichia/Shigella abundance in the gut microbiome.

Cameron et al. showed in vitro that metformin (2 mmol/L, 3h exposure) inhibited TNF-α-induced IκB degradation and reduced expression of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β and CXCL1/2 via AMPK activation.
Dengue and Coxsackie B3 viruses required 1 mmol/L metformin in vitro to achieve measurable antiviral activity.

Vizuete et al. found that methylglyoxal exposure increased NMDAR1 expression in astrocytes, an effect reversible by metformin, alongside metformin-driven reductions in IL-1β and interference with methylglyoxal-derived advanced glycation end products and RAGE.
Physical fatigue was the most frequently increased postexertional symptom, reported by 46 of 60 participants with ME/CFS or PASC after a submaximal exercise task.
Anxiety was the least commonly increased postexertional symptom, reported by only 18 of 30 individuals with ME/CFS or PASC after submaximal exercise.
When analyzed individually, none of the eight PESE symptoms showed a statistically significant change across the 7-day period following exercise.

An aggregate score combining 4-5 symptoms (physical fatigue, mental fatigue, physical function, flu-like symptoms, with or without pain) more comprehensively captured maximal PESE changes, which were greatest within 72 hours postexercise and among those with ME/CFS.
A subset of participants showed minimal to no increase in PESE after submaximal exercise: 8 of 30 with ME/CFS and 12 of 30 with PASC.
A minority of participants (6-7 of 30 per group) showed marked PESE increases of greater than 3 points on a 10-point aggregate scale after submaximal exercise.
The weighted proportion of US adults reporting CFS/ME in the 2023 National Health Interview Survey was 1.4%.
Among individuals with CFS/ME, 70.7% (weighted) met study criteria for chronic pain based on pain duration over the past 3 months.
Compared to individuals with chronic pain but without CFS/ME, those with comorbid CFS/ME and chronic pain were significantly more likely to screen positive for depression and anxiety.
Individuals with comorbid CFS/ME and chronic pain were significantly more likely than those with chronic pain alone to report fair/poor general health and life dissatisfaction.

Among those with comorbid CFS/ME and chronic pain, pain was reported across multiple body locations and impacted multiple domains of functioning including life/work activities and family relationships.
Austrian health authorities estimate that at least 300,000 people may have Long-COVID, with 20-30% (about 60,000 individuals) affected long-term.
Current data suggest that approximately 50% of Long-COVID patients recover by 4 months and 75% by 15 months, leaving 25% with persistent symptoms requiring ongoing care.
Austrian national statistics show an exponential rise in ICD-coded chronic fatigue diagnoses between 2021 and 2023, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic.

A randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial of ADAPT-232 (Rhodiola rosea, Eleutherococcus senticosus and Schisandra chinensis) in Long-COVID patients found improved physical performance and renal function.
A dietary supplement combining Rhodiola, Eleutherococcus and Schisandra significantly reduced pain and fatigue in a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
Clinical RCTs using standardized Bacopa monnieri extracts (50% bacoside A and B) show effects relevant to Long-COVID neurological dysfunction, particularly cognitive impairment, at evidence grade Ia.
Case reports from a Long-COVID neurology clinic in Vienna describe treatment of neurological deficits with the Ginkgo special extract EGb 761 (80 mg three times daily) combined with vitamin C.
Silexan showed comparable efficacy to lorazepam and was superior to placebo, with a better side-effect profile than paroxetine, in generalized anxiety disorder.
Glycyrrhizin strongly inhibited SARS-CoV-1 replication in Vero cells in vitro.

Oral combination of glycyrrhizin and a Boswellia extract (66% boswellic acids) led to faster recovery and significantly better CRP and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio values in hospitalized moderately ill COVID-19 patients.
Treatment of 200 patients with an intranasal/oropharyngeal spray combining povidone-iodine and glycyrrhizic acid led to faster recovery, improved lab values, and lower environmental viral load.

A 2022 study found that Long-COVID associated symptoms such as fatigue, anosmia and persistent cough irritation could be significantly reduced with black seed oil and/or vitamin D over 14 days, with a synergistic effect when combined.
ELOM-080 given at 300 mg four times daily for 14 days achieved a 12.3% absolute risk reduction versus placebo in acute bronchitis/cough.
Cineol given at 200 mg three times daily for 10 days reduced the Bronchitis Sum Score by approximately 22% compared to placebo after 4 days.
Polysaccharides from Lycium barbarum inhibit entry of several SARS-CoV-2 variants into host cells by disrupting the spike protein-ACE2 interaction.

A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial found that a Lycium barbarum polysaccharide fraction significantly reduced depressive symptoms in adolescents with subthreshold depression, possibly via lowering IL-17A levels.

A lecithin-based formulation of Curcuma longa (1000 mg/day) and Boswellia serrata (300 mg/day) reduced IBS symptoms in both Long-COVID and non-COVID patient groups, but improved dysbiosis only in the non-COVID group.

A licorice root extract gel applied to the oral mucosa led to viral eradication, from which the authors inferred potential prophylactic use.

The Austrian S1 guideline for Long-COVID recommends olfactory training with essential oils (preferably floral, resinous, and fruity scents, e.g. rose, lemon, clove, eucalyptus) twice daily for about 30 seconds over at least 6 months to regain smell and taste function, with adjuvant intranasal vitamin A and systemic omega-3 fatty acids also suggested.

Statistik Austria data show an exponential rise in ICD-coded chronic fatigue illness diagnoses between 2021 and 2023.
Postviral coagulopathy has been demonstrated and is suspected as a causal contributor to persistent post-viral symptoms.

Muscle compartments can increase in volume by up to 20% during physical activity due to increased blood flow, a change normally reversed at rest.

Between 25% and 80% of certain joint imaging changes occur in asymptomatic individuals, indicating imaging findings do not necessarily correlate with pain.
Treatment of trigger points in shoulder disorders has demonstrated symptom reduction.
In tension-type headache, treatment of trigger points in the neck-shoulder region has shown improved neck posture and a marked reduction in headache frequency.
In plantar fasciitis, a strong correlation has been found between gastrocnemius tightness and pain severity.

In rats, psychological stress produced metabolic changes in muscle similar to physical load, including higher lactic acid levels.

Among the 43-patient cohort, the ISTH-BAT bleeding assessment score was positive in the majority of patients.

Patients recruited from the Haemophilia Unit had much higher rates of positive bleeding scores than those recruited from the Rehabilitation Service.
All patients recruited from the Rehabilitation Service had positive hypermobility criteria, while fewer than half had positive bleeding scores, contrasting with the HU-recruited group.

Whole exome sequencing using a stepwise virtual gene panel approach identified at least one candidate variant in heritable disorders of connective tissue (HDCT) genes in nearly half of the cohort.
Complete genotype-phenotype concordance, explaining both bleeding and joint hypermobility, was achieved in over a third of the cohort, mainly through variants in EDS-associated genes.

A partial genotype-phenotype concordance was reached in about a fifth of patients, where variants explained only the bleeding (via congenital coagulopathy genes) or only the joint hypermobility (via Marfan syndrome-related genes), but not both.
Applying the broader bleeding-gene panel (panel 3) to patients with unexplained positive bleeding scores after panels 1 and 2 did not identify any additional candidate variants.

Of 40 unique candidate variants identified across the cohort, the majority were located in 13 HDCT-related genes, split between eight EDS-associated collagen/complement genes and five Marfan/marfanoid-associated genes.

The remaining candidate variants not located in HDCT genes were found in coagulation factor genes, which were considered to only contribute to the bleeding phenotype without explaining joint hypermobility.
Nearly all candidate variants were missense, with novel variants disproportionately concentrated in HDCT genes compared with coagulation genes.

Under standard ACMG criteria, less than a third of the candidate variants were classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, with nearly half classified as benign or likely benign despite being retained based on phenotype relevance or in silico predictions.
Family segregation analysis supported the pathogenicity of identified candidate variants: variants co-segregated with HDCT symptoms in affected relatives and were absent in unaffected relatives.
A candidate FBN1 variant (p.Arg1170His) identified in one patient (HDCT0035) has previously been described in association with joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, and mitral valve prolapse.

The authors note, citing prior literature, that carriers of a heterozygous F11 variant or haemophilia A carriers can have an increased bleeding tendency despite factor VIII or XI levels remaining within the normal range, supporting the relevance of the CC gene variants identified in their cohort.
An inverse relationship between age and Beighton score was observed, with most patients who had a negative Beighton score being over 40 years old.
No candidate variant was identified in a substantial proportion of patients, particularly in the joint-hypermobility-prone group, consistent with hypermobile EDS having no known genetic basis.

The authors recommend whole-body vascular imaging beyond echocardiography in patients with suspected vascular EDS to identify silent arterial lesions as a risk mitigation strategy.

The authors suggest that reporting pregnancy-associated phenotypes linked to this VUS in variant databases such as ClinVar and LOVD could accelerate reclassification of the variant and improve future genetic counseling.
Among 213 adolescents with genetically confirmed syndromes, 68.08% (n=145) presented with at least one dental anomaly.

Disproportionality analysis showed a significantly elevated rate of occurrence ratio for dental anomalies in Down syndrome relative to the rest of the cohort.
Adolescents with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this cohort showed a relatively low prevalence of dental anomalies (27.27%) compared with other syndromes such as Down syndrome.

Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome showed a significantly reduced rate of occurrence ratio for dental anomalies compared with the rest of the cohort.
Tuberous sclerosis showed a significantly reduced rate of occurrence ratio for dental anomalies compared with the rest of the cohort.

Patients treated with traditional prolotherapy alone showed a smaller but still significant decrease in VAS pain scores from 6.5 to 4.5.

Joint clicking sounds decreased in both treatment groups, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
Transient adverse events including dizziness and temporary facial nerve paresis occurred in a few patients but resolved spontaneously without intervention.

Seven of the ten included RCTs (70%) reported a statistically significant improvement in sleep quality with cervical manual therapy compared to controls, on at least a subset of measurements.

All three RCTs targeting primary/secondary sleep disorders (obstructive sleep apnea and sleep bruxism) reported significant improvements in PSQI-measured sleep quality with cervical manual therapy versus controls.
Despite sleep quality improvement, cervical manual therapy did not significantly improve disorder-specific parameters such as bruxism or OSA symptoms (e.g., AHI/ODI, TMJ function).
Two RCTs of chronic neck pain patients reported significant improvements in sleep quality following cervical manual therapy.
Three of four fibromyalgia RCTs showed non-significant benefit of cervical manual therapy on sleep quality.

Except for one RCT that showed significant pain relief, all fibromyalgia-related RCTs failed to improve other FM symptoms including fatigue, mental health, and pain threshold with cervical manual therapy.
One RCT of post-cardiac surgery patients reported partially significant improvements in sleep quality with cervical manual therapy.

Clinical studies on tuina, an Asian manual therapy, have demonstrated increased peripheral 5-HT levels alongside improved sleep quality.
HPA axis dysregulation, characterized by adrenal insufficiency and cortisol depletion, is frequently reported in fibromyalgia and ME/CFS.
Patients with fibromyalgia exhibit reduced slow-wave sleep (SWS) compared to healthy individuals.

Cortisol-targeted pharmacotherapies have failed to achieve symptom remission in fibromyalgia and ME/CFS.

A systematic review on biochemical effects of spinal manipulation reported that cortisol and inflammatory regulation were influenced by the intervention, with cervical manual therapy eliciting a more pronounced cortisol response than thoracic manipulation.
A recent study identified that non-invasive manipulation of the cervical lymphatics can increase cerebrospinal fluid drainage.
Hypercortisolism disrupts AQP-4 function in the brain's lymphatic and perivascular circulation, which contributes to poor subjective sleep quality.

Fragmented case evidence in ME/CFS suggests patients with cervical spinal stenosis experienced symptom resolution following surgery, indicating a potential organic cervical spinal cord pathology in ME/CFS.
Monovalent reduced IgG1 significantly inhibited degranulation in antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells to a similar extent as intact IgG1.
Reduced IgG1 significantly inhibited IL-4 secretion in antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells similarly to intact IgG1.
Addition of reduced IgG1 caused intracellular SHIP1 to relocalize to the plasma membrane within 5 minutes, mirroring the effect of intact IgG1.

Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (AG) neoadjuvant chemotherapy significantly increased tumor-associated mast cell activation signatures in PDAC compared with naive and FOLFIRINOX-treated tumors, based on multiple single-cell activation-scoring algorithms.

Higher estimated proportions of activated TAMCs (deconvolved from bulk transcriptomes) were significantly associated with worse overall survival, disease-free survival, progression-free survival, and disease-specific survival in the TCGA-PDAC cohort, with validation for OS/relapse-free survival in the E-MTAB-6134 and PDAC_CA_seq cohorts.
Total TAMC infiltration was significantly correlated with shortened disease-free survival in TCGA-PDAC, but similar trends for OS, PFS, and DSS did not reach statistical significance.

Human LAD-2 and murine MC/9 mast cells stimulated with supernatants from AG-treated tumor cells showed increased expression of activation markers FcεRI and KIT, whereas FOLFIRINOX-treated supernatants caused no obvious change.

Conditioned media from AG-stimulated TAMCs, but not FOLFIRINOX-stimulated TAMCs, drove primary CAFs toward an inflammatory iCAF phenotype (increased IL-6+ cells) while reducing the myofibroblastic myCAF phenotype (decreased α-SMA+ cells).

AG neoadjuvant therapy shifted malignant PDAC cells from the aggressive basal molecular subtype toward the less aggressive classical subtype, whereas FOLFIRINOX and other regimens predominantly induced intermediate subtypes.

AG neoadjuvant therapy increased the proportion of interferon-stimulated CD8+ T cells and NKT cells while reducing immunosuppressive exhausted CD8+ T cells, regulatory T cells, and exhausted CD4+ T cells.

iCAF abundance was positively correlated with regulatory T cells, exhausted CD8+ T cells, and exhausted CD4+ T cells across five independent multicenter transcriptomic cohorts, while antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) correlated positively with effector CD8+ T cells and NKT cells.

MIF was significantly overexpressed in PDAC tumor tissues across four large multicenter cohorts, and scRNA-seq data showed upregulated MIF expression specifically in CAFs after AG neoadjuvant therapy.

Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh mice bearing KPC orthotopic tumors showed markedly reduced proportions of PD-1+ and TIM-3+ exhausted T cells and increased infiltration of IFN-γ+, TNF-α+, and GZMB+ effector T cells compared with mast-cell-competent B6 Albino mice, indicating that mast cell deletion alleviates T-cell suppression.

In orthotopic KPC xenografts in B6 Albino and KitW-sh mice, the MIF antagonist ISO-1 combined with TAMC ablation significantly attenuated tumor burden under AG chemotherapy, with the combination showing supra-additive (synergistic) effects, and reduced exhausted T cells while increasing effector T-cell populations.

In a subcutaneous KPC xenograft model, the mast cell stabilizer SCG monotherapy significantly inhibited tumor growth, and the combination of SCG with AG and ISO-1 produced the strongest reduction in tumor burden compared with SCG alone or SCG plus AG.

In an orthotopic PDAC model, combining the MIF antagonist ISO-1 with anti-PD-1 antibody significantly reduced tumor burden beyond AG treatment alone, demonstrating that MIF blockade sensitizes PDAC to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in the AG neoadjuvant setting.

Spatial transcriptomics showed that iCAFs and cytotoxic T lymphocytes exhibited mutually exclusive spatial distribution within PDAC tumors, indicating iCAF-mediated exclusion of cytotoxic T cells from tumor niches despite increased effector T-cell infiltration after AG treatment.

IgG tended to be higher in vaccinated patients compared with unvaccinated patients.
Mean IgE was highest in severe COVID-19, intermediate in moderate, and lowest in mild disease, with IL-10 elevated across severity groups and highest in moderate cases.

Five patients developed new or worsened glomerulopathy two to four months after COVID-19 infection, temporally suggesting a possible causal association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and autoimmune renal disease exacerbation.

All five vaccinated patients, who had pre-existing autoimmune disease, developed either post-COVID lobar pneumonia (n=2) or exacerbation of their autoimmune condition (n=3), including glomerulonephritis, granulomatous polyangiitis, and lupus nephritis.

The authors propose, based on their prior work and cited literature, that IgG4 accumulates in lung parenchyma during acute COVID-19 as a compensatory counter-regulatory response to elevated IgE, potentially blocking IgE-mediated mast cell activation while possibly impairing viral clearance.
High concentrations of free (unbound) IgE can activate mast cells similarly to antigen-bound IgE, amplifying immune responses even without antigen stimulation, per cited literature.

Large-scale electronic health record analyses cited by the authors show asthma confers higher risk of hospitalization and mortality in COVID-19 compared with other allergic conditions such as atopic dermatitis, and new-onset allergic disease risk rises significantly within 30 days post-COVID and persists at least six months.

In delayed pressure urticaria, lesions typically develop 4-6 hours after sustained pressure, peak around 6 hours after onset, and can persist from 8 hours up to 3 days.
More than half of patients with delayed pressure urticaria experience associated systemic symptoms, most commonly malaise and fatigue.
Mast cell activation, histamine release, and eosinophil infiltration, along with multiple other mediators, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of delayed pressure urticaria.
Combined cell membrane chromatography and molecular dynamics analysis showed that agonists and antagonists of MrgprX2 do not compete for the same binding site on the receptor.
Antagonists of MrgprX2 predominantly interact with amino acid residues located in transmembrane domain 2 (TM2) and transmembrane domain 7 (TM7) of the receptor.
Agonists of MrgprX2 preferentially form favorable interactions with residues in transmembrane domain 6 (TM6) and extracellular loop 3 (ECL3).
Calcium imaging confirmed that MrgprX2 antagonists suppress mast cell activation through noncompetitive binding to the receptor, inhibiting agonist-induced calcium influx.
Across 393 case reports of allergic vasospastic angina (Kounis syndrome), the median patient age was 53 years and 64% were male.
46% of patients with allergic vasospastic angina had one or more cardiovascular risk factors.
32% of patients with allergic vasospastic angina had a documented history of atopy.
71% of allergic vasospastic angina patients presented with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction as part of an acute coronary syndrome.
Prescription medications were the precipitating allergen in 55% of allergic vasospastic angina cases.
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation was identified as one of the allergic mechanisms underlying coronary artery spasm in allergic vasospastic angina.
Eosinophil-mediated allergic response was identified as a potential mechanism contributing to allergic vasospastic angina.
Non-IgE mediated mast cell activation pathways were also implicated as mechanisms driving allergic vasospastic angina.
Management of allergic vasospastic angina differs from conventional vasospastic angina and may include allergen avoidance and allergic response-modulating therapies.

Allergic vasospastic angina (Kounis syndrome) is an under-recognised subtype of vasospastic angina in which coronary artery spasm is precipitated by an allergen, often presenting as acute coronary syndrome.
MRGPRX2 is identified as a key receptor driving mast cell activation and IL-17A release that promotes progression of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
Bioinformatics and histopathological analysis showed that activated mast cells are significantly enriched in cSCC lesions and correlate with worse prognosis.
Tumor cell-mast cell crosstalk triggers hyperactivation of the extracellular signal-regulated kinase/protein kinase B (ERK/AKT) pathway, inducing mast cell degranulation and IL-17A secretion.
IL-17A secreted by activated mast cells promoted proliferation, migration, and apoptosis resistance of cSCC cells.
Treatment with the mast cell membrane stabilizer sodium cromolyn abrogated the tumor-promoting effects of mast cell activation on cSCC cells.
MRGPRX2 knockdown abrogated the tumor-promoting effects of mast cell activation on cSCC cells.
Blockade of IL-17A abrogated the tumor-promoting effects of mast cell activation on cSCC cells.
In vivo, MRGPRX2 deficiency reduced mast cell activation and decreased IL-17A production, partially suppressing tumor proliferation and delaying epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
The study concludes that MRGPRX2 acts as the key receptor driving mast cell activation and IL-17A release, establishing a tumor-promoting feedback loop that drives cSCC progression.
Mast cells in the skin exhibit microenvironment-dependent plasticity, contributing variably to cSCC pathogenesis depending on local tumor context.

Vitexin substantially inhibited TRPV4-dependent calcium influx in TRPV4-transfected HEK293T cells and primary mouse dorsal root ganglion neurons, reducing peak responses and the proportion of agonist-responsive neurons.
Vitexin dose-dependently suppressed compound 48/80-induced calcium signaling in HEK293T cells expressing human MRGPRX2.
