Vitexin dose-dependently suppressed compound 48/80-induced calcium signaling in HEK293T cells expressing murine MrgprB2.
Vitexin markedly decreased β-hexosaminidase release from primary mouse peritoneal mast cells upon compound 48/80 stimulation.
Vitexin markedly decreased β-hexosaminidase release from HMC1.2 human mast cells upon compound 48/80 stimulation.
In silico molecular docking showed vitexin occupies binding regions in TRPV4 that overlap with those of known agonists, suggesting direct receptor interaction.
In the MC903-induced murine AD model, VTX treatment reduced the transcriptional upregulation of Trpv4 in skin tissue.
VTX treatment also reduced the transcriptional upregulation of MrgprB2 in the MC903-induced murine AD model.
VTX treatment reduced mast cell activation in the MC903-induced murine model of atopic dermatitis.
The antipruritic effects of VTX were enhanced in Trpv4-deficient mice, indicating that MRGPRX2/MrgprB2 suppression also contributes to VTX's antipruritic action independent of TRPV4.

Expert consensus at the Vulvodynia Therapeutic Research Summit ranked ketotifen fumarate, a mast cell stabilizer, as the top candidate for further research into treating neuroinflammation in provoked vestibulodynia.
Resiniferatoxin, a TRPV1 agonist that causes chemo-inactivation of nerve terminals, was ranked second among therapeutics proposed for further study in provoked vestibulodynia.
Specialized pro-resolving mediators or strategies to boost their levels (e.g., maresin 1 and a TPPU-type compound) were ranked third as candidates for further research on provoked vestibulodynia.
Luteolin, a flavonoid with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroprotective properties, was ranked fourth as a therapeutic target for research into provoked vestibulodynia.
Alpha-lipoic acid, an antioxidant with nerve-specific anti-inflammatory and mast cell stabilizing qualities, was ranked fifth as a candidate for further research on provoked vestibulodynia.

An NGFR121W-SNAP IR700 trimer activated with near-infrared light, designed for photoablation targeting nociceptors while sparing surrounding tissue, was ranked sixth as a therapeutic target for provoked vestibulodynia research.
Primary Atopic Disorders are defined by pathologic mast cell activation/degranulation, persistent Th2- and eosinophil-mediated inflammation, and exaggerated IgE production.
A distinct PAD subgroup, mast cell hyperreactivity syndromes prototypically represented by mastocytosis, is caused by somatic or germline gain-of-function KIT mutations.

Consensus statement #19 proposes that very high total IgE (>10,000 kU/L), extreme eosinophilia (>10,000 cells/mm3), and elevated basal tryptase and/or histamine, combined with severe atopic manifestations including urticaria/angioedema/anaphylaxis, increase the likelihood of PAD once hematologic malignancy is excluded.
Elevated basal tryptase or histamine levels may reflect mast cell hyperactivation and dysregulation occurring in some PAD.

Germline KIT variants, cytokine/receptor gene variants (IL13, IL6, IL6R, IL31, IL4R), and increased TPSAB1 (alpha-tryptase) copy number are increasingly recognized as associated with systemic mastocytosis in adults, beyond somatic KIT gain-of-function alone.
Normal total IgE levels do not exclude a diagnosis of PAD, as some cases present with severe hypereosinophilia without significant IgE elevation.
Low Th17 cell counts can help differentiate hyper-IgE syndrome due to STAT3 dominant-negative loss-of-function mutations from severe atopic dermatitis.

Reduced CD3+CD25+ regulatory T cell counts suggest impaired immune regulation and may point to IPEX or IPEX-like conditions in patients with severe atopic dermatitis or other atopic disease with or without autoimmunity.
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is described as the only curative treatment for Omenn syndrome, a severe life-threatening manifestation of PAD.
Recurrent cold skin abscesses (non-inflammatory, non-painful) are classic in hyper-IgE syndrome due to STAT3 loss-of-function mutations.

Eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders with severe eosinophilia (>5000 cells/mm3) and multiorgan involvement should be considered a potential PAD manifestation, seen in conditions such as STAT3-DN-HIES, DOCK8 deficiency, Comel-Netherton syndrome, ERBIN deficiency, JAK1 AD gain-of-function, STAT5b gain-of-function, and STAT6 gain-of-function.

PAD can be classified by seven pathogenetic mechanisms: skin barrier dysfunction, altered cytokine signaling, impaired TCR signaling/cytoskeletal remodeling, metabolic disturbance, mast cell dysregulation, T cell repertoire restriction, and tolerance failure.
Recurrent/severe infections due to opportunistic pathogens and Herpesviridae (CMV, EBV, HHV-6) are frequent in PAD but may also be absent.
Hypereosinophilia (>5000 cells/mm3) combined with multiorgan dysfunction is uncommon in severe allergic disease and should raise suspicion of PAD.

Good clinical response to a specific targeted therapy supports involvement of the underlying pathogenic mechanism but does not by itself distinguish monogenic PAD from multifactorial atopic disease, since similar responses can occur in non-monogenic conditions.
Systemic SHED-CM treatment significantly reduced clinical dermatitis severity scores compared with DMEM and Fibro-CM controls in OVA-specific allergic dermatitis (OSAD) mice.
SHED-CM treatment significantly decreased epidermal thickness and inflammatory cell infiltration in OSAD mouse skin compared with DMEM.
SHED-CM treatment significantly reduced skin mast cell numbers in OSAD mice compared with DMEM controls.
SHED-CM preserved the Filaggrin-positive stratum corneum layer, which was destroyed in DMEM and Fibro-CM treated OSAD mouse skin.
SHED-CM significantly decreased CD3ε+ and CD4+ T cell infiltration in OSAD mouse skin compared with DMEM.
SHED-CM significantly increased Foxp3-expressing regulatory T cell numbers in OSAD mouse skin compared with DMEM and Fibro-CM.
Thymic-derived Helios+ Treg numbers were reduced by DMEM/Fibro-CM but preserved at Sham-comparable levels by SHED-CM treatment in OSAD skin.
More than 80% of Foxp3-positive Treg cells in SHED-CM-treated OSAD skin co-expressed TGFβ, suggesting a TGFβ-secreting Treg phenotype.
SHED-CM suppressed infiltration of B220+ B cells and CD11c+ dendritic cells in OSAD mouse skin.
SHED-CM treatment reduced skin mRNA expression of Th2-related genes Il4 and Il13 that were elevated in OSAD.
SHED-CM treatment reduced skin mRNA expression of Th17-related genes Il17a and Rorc that were elevated in OSAD.
SHED-CM treatment did not alter skin mRNA expression of Tslp or Th1-related genes Tbet and Ifng.
SHED-CM significantly increased skin mRNA expression of Treg-specific genes Foxp3, Tgfb, and Helios.
SHED-CM treatment inhibited skin mRNA expression of inflammation-related factors Tnf, iNOS, CD206, and Arg1.
SHED-CM significantly reduced OSAD-associated lymphadenopathy in draining lymph nodes compared with DMEM and Fibro-CM.
SHED-CM shifted the Th1/Th2 balance in lymph nodes, decreasing GATA3+ cells and increasing Tbet+ cells by immunohistochemistry.
SHED-CM significantly increased Foxp3-expressing and preserved Helios-expressing Treg cells in OSAD draining lymph nodes by immunohistochemistry.
Flow cytometry confirmed that SHED-CM increased Tbet+ and Foxp3+ cell proportions while decreasing GATA3+ and RORγt+ cell proportions in OSAD draining lymph nodes.
SHED-CM significantly decreased IgE-positive cell numbers in skin (immunohistochemistry) and the proportion of IgE+ cells by flow cytometry, without affecting B220+ or IgM+ cell proportions.
SHED-CM significantly reduced serum total IgE from day 24 and OVA-specific IgE from day 28 compared with DMEM and Fibro-CM groups.
SHED-CM significantly reduced serum IL-2 and IL-6 levels on days 28 and 35 in OSAD mice.

Secretome/LC-MS analysis identified TGFB2, LIF, IGF2, and TGFB1 as proteins with >2-fold enriched abundance in SHED-CM relative to Fibro-CM, among 655 significantly enriched proteins, that are known regulators of Treg induction.

Flow cytometry showed that the proportion of IgE-positive B cells, but not B220-positive or IgM-positive cells, was significantly reduced in the SHED-CM group compared with the DMEM and Fibro-CM groups.
Serum total IgE levels were significantly reduced in the SHED-CM group compared with the DMEM and Fibro-CM groups starting at day 24.
Serum OVA-specific IgE levels were significantly reduced in the SHED-CM group compared with the DMEM and Fibro-CM groups starting at day 28.
Serum IL-2 and IL-6 levels were significantly reduced by SHED-CM treatment at both day 28 and day 35 compared with DMEM.

LC-MS secretome analysis identified 655 of 1,261 membrane-associated proteins with more than 2-fold higher abundance in SHED-CM versus Fibro-CM, among which TGFB2, LIF, IGF2, and TGFB1 were identified as candidate Treg-inducing factors based on prior literature.
In vitro, SHED-CM significantly increased the proportion of Foxp3+ and CD25+ cells among CD3/CD28-stimulated naive splenic CD4+ T cells compared with DMEM.
Dilution of SHED-CM reduced its Treg-inducing capacity in a dose-dependent manner, with no difference between 1:2 and 1:20 dilutions but a significant reduction at 1:40 dilution.

Neutralizing TGFβ, but not LIF or IGF2, significantly inhibited SHED-CM-induced Foxp3+ cell induction, though it did not affect CD25+ induction, indicating TGFβ is essential for the Treg-inducing effect of SHED-CM.

Heat-treated SHED-CM (75°C for 10 min or 95°C for 5 min) lost its ability to promote Treg differentiation, indicating that the bioactive Treg-inducing components of SHED-CM are predominantly proteinaceous.
The magnitude of Treg induction by SHED-CM was not significantly different from that induced by a standard protocol using 5 ng/mL exogenous TGFβ protein with or without IL-2.
Under Treg induction conditions, SHED-CM did not induce RORγt+ Th17 cells.

SHED-CM did not alter the proportion of Tbet+ (Th1), GATA3+ (Th2), or RORγt+ (Th17) cells when naive splenic T cells were differentiated toward these lineages in vitro, indicating no direct effect on Th1/Th2/Th17 differentiation.

NRP1 protein was strongly expressed on macrophages/Kupffer cells, splenic white pulp, lymph node follicular lymphocytes, capillary and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, and renal proximal tubules/glomeruli in fatal COVID-19 tissues.
NRP2 protein expression was more restricted than NRP1, moderately detected in intestinal smooth muscle cells and macrophages of lung, trachea, spleen, lymph nodes, and adrenal gland.
Myocardial small capillaries, arterioles, and postcapillary venules showed strong NRP1 protein expression by IHC in fatal COVID-19, while NRP2 protein was not detected in these vessels.
Single-cell RNA sequencing of fatal COVID-19 hearts showed abundant NRP1 transcripts in vascular endothelial cells and pericytes, whereas NRP2 was mainly restricted to lymphatic endothelial cells.
Despite NRP1 mRNA expression in cardiomyocytes, neither NRP1 nor NRP2 protein was detected in cardiomyocytes by IHC or CODEX, indicating transcript-protein discordance.
scRNAseq confirmed strong NRP1 and NRP2 expression, but not ACE2, in cardiac macrophages from fatal COVID-19 hearts.
ACE2 transcripts were largely confined to cardiomyocytes and pericytes and were barely detectable in vascular endothelial cells.
NRP1-positive myocardial capillaries were numerically more frequent in COVID-19 hearts than in influenza or noninfectious control myocardium, but this difference was not statistically significant.
COVID-19-associated syncytial macrophages with high phagocytic activity in the lung were positive for NRP1 and CD68 by CODEX and IHC.

NRP1 transcripts were significantly upregulated in pulmonary vascular endothelial cells in fatal COVID-19 lungs compared with noninfectious controls, while ACE2 and TMPRSS2 expression remained unchanged.
TGFBR2 was significantly upregulated in vascular endothelial cells in fatal COVID-19 lungs, while its ligand TGFB1 was upregulated in monocytes.
Monocytes in fatal COVID-19 lungs showed significant upregulation of CCL2, a TGFB1-inducing chemokine.
VEGFA, the activating ligand for VEGF receptors, was produced and significantly upregulated by lung epithelial cells in fatal COVID-19.
Follicular lymphocytes in lymph nodes and spleen of fatal COVID-19 cases were NRP1-positive and NRP2-negative.
A subset of CD20-positive splenic B lymphocytes co-expressed NRP1 by CODEX, while CD8- and CD4-positive T lymphocytes were NRP1-negative.
Antisense SARS-CoV-2 RNA signals were detected in lymphocytes within the spleen and lymph nodes of fatal COVID-19 cases by RNAscope FISH.
CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells in lymph nodes were positive for NRP1 but negative for NRP2, and NRP1 transcripts (not NRP2) were detected in pDCs by transcript analysis.

Although NRP1 transcripts were present in mast cells, NRP1 protein was not detected in a subset of mast cells, which instead exhibited strong NRP2 protein expression by CODEX multiplex imaging in fatal COVID-19 lung tissue.
A subset of NRP2-positive mast cells also co-expressed NRP1 protein, while other mast cells remained NRP1-negative, indicating heterogeneous neuropilin expression within the mast cell population.
NRP2-positive mast cells in fatal COVID-19 lung tissue also expressed CD16 (FcγRIIIb), a marker previously linked to systemic mastocytosis.

Mast cells expressing NRP2 contained SARS-CoV-2 RNA yet were devoid of ACE2 expression, extending previous findings that neuropilins may serve as alternative entry factors in ACE2-negative cells such as mast cells.
The authors note that mast cell activation has been implicated in the pathophysiology of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC/long COVID).
Endogenous NRP1 on HEK293 cells bound the soluble SARS-CoV-2 S1 spike fragment but did not bind the S1' spike fragment.
Only HEK293 cells recombinantly expressing NRP2 were able to bind the soluble S1' spike fragment, while S1 binding was preserved, demonstrating that S1' binding requires NRP2.
Contrary to a previous report describing NRP1 as a Treg surface marker co-regulated with Foxp3, this study did not detect relevant NRP1 mRNA expression in regulatory T cells in COVID-19 lungs.
No overlap was observed between SARS-CoV-2-infected lung cell types and cell clusters co-expressing ACE2 and TMPRSS2, suggesting alternative entry factors such as neuropilins in infected cells.
Sarcoidosis affects the lungs in over 90% of patients and extrapulmonary organs in up to 70% of patients.
Systemic non-organ-specific symptoms of sarcoidosis, including fatigue and small fiber neuropathy, substantially impair quality of life.
Soluble IL-2 receptor is described as a biomarker that has improved diagnostic accuracy, risk stratification, and monitoring in sarcoidosis.
Cardiac MRI and 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging modalities are highlighted as advances improving diagnostic accuracy in sarcoidosis, though histological confirmation is almost always still required.
Steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, azathioprine, and leflunomide are widely used as alternatives to the classical glucocorticoid-centered step-up approach in sarcoidosis.
Biologics, particularly anti-TNF agents, and emerging small-molecule JAK and mTOR inhibitors offer additional therapeutic options for refractory sarcoidosis.
Efzofitimod is named as a new investigational therapy currently under evaluation for sarcoidosis.
Digital health tools, telemedicine, and mindfulness-based interventions show promise in supporting patient-centered care for sarcoidosis.
Biologics, particularly anti-TNF agents, are used as additional treatment options in refractory sarcoidosis.
Emerging small-molecule JAK inhibitors are described as offering additional treatment options for refractory sarcoidosis.
Emerging small-molecule mTOR inhibitors are described as offering additional treatment options for refractory sarcoidosis.
Efzofitimod is cited as a new investigational therapy currently under evaluation for sarcoidosis.
Digital health tools, telemedicine, and mindfulness-based interventions are highlighted as promising for supporting patient-centered sarcoidosis care beyond pharmacologic treatment.
Artificial intelligence and multi-omics approaches are proposed as future tools to enhance diagnostic accuracy, phenotyping, and precision medicine in sarcoidosis.
Despite advances in imaging and biomarkers, histological confirmation is almost invariably still required for diagnosing sarcoidosis.

Among 80 patients with myofibrillar myopathy (MFM) or MFM-gene-associated myopathy, 21 had peripheral neuropathy, comprising 13 with axonal large fiber neuropathy and 8 with small fiber neuropathy, mostly mild in severity.
Patients with desminopathy (DES-related myopathy) had a significantly lower prevalence of peripheral neuropathy compared with patients with other MFM-related genotypes.
Patients with desminopathy showed earlier onset and higher rates of cardiac involvement compared with other MFM-related genotypes.
Desminopathy was associated with more frequent respiratory involvement than other MFM-related genotypes.
Desminopathy patients required gait aids earlier than patients with other MFM-related genotypes, despite reaching loss of ambulation at a similar age.
Mortality rate did not differ significantly between desminopathy patients and those with other MFM-related genotypes.
Nearly two-thirds of patients eventually required mobility support, with 46 of 80 patients needing gait aids at a median of 10 years after symptom onset.
A subset of patients progressed to wheelchair dependence, with 17 of 80 patients becoming wheelchair-bound at a median of 19 years after symptom onset.
By age 60, patients with desminopathy had substantially higher rates of gait aid and wheelchair use than those with myotilinopathy or LDB3-related myopathy.
Cardiac involvement occurred in 31 of 80 patients, manifesting at a median of 7 years after myopathy onset.
Respiratory involvement occurred in 33 of 80 patients, manifesting at a median of 9 years after myopathy onset.
Seven patients died during follow-up, mainly due to cardiopulmonary complications, including 2 with DES, 1 with ACTA1, and 4 genetically uncharacterized patients.
Patients with DES-related myopathy (desminopathy) showed earlier onset and higher rates of cardiac involvement compared with patients with other MFM-related gene variants.
Patients with desminopathy had more frequent respiratory involvement than patients with other MFM-related gene variants.

Seven of the 80 patients died during the study period, primarily from cardiopulmonary complications, including two patients with DES variants, one with an ACTA1 variant, and four without a confirmed genetic diagnosis.
Patients with desminopathy had earlier onset and higher rates of cardiac involvement compared with patients carrying other MFM-related gene variants.
Forced swimming induced significantly greater immobility time in the model control group than in the untreated control, confirming successful induction of fatigue.
L-arginine at 1200 mg/kg/day showed a non-significant trend toward reduced immobility time in the forced-swimming test compared to the model control.
Serum LDH and CPK, markers of muscle injury, were significantly elevated in the model control group compared with the untreated control after forced swimming.

L-arginine supplementation at 600 and 1200 mg/kg/day reduced serum LDH and CPK levels in the forced-swimming test, suggesting attenuation of muscle damage, and serum lactate decreased across all L-arginine dose groups.

Blood glucose was significantly increased in the 1200 mg/kg L-arginine group, while NEFA decreased at doses of 600 mg/kg and above, serum nitric oxide was reduced at 600 mg/kg and above, and cortisol decreased at 1200 mg/kg in the forced-swimming test.

Skeletal muscle glycogen, reduced in the model control, was significantly restored by L-arginine (p<0.05 at 300 mg/kg; p<0.01 at ≥600 mg/kg), and liver glycogen increased across all L-arginine doses in the forced-swimming test.
Hepatic catalase, elevated in the model control, was significantly reduced by L-arginine at 600 mg/kg (p<0.05) with a similar decreasing trend at 1200 mg/kg.
In the treadmill endurance test, mice receiving L-arginine at 1200 mg/kg/day exhibited a significant increase in exercise duration to exhaustion compared with both control and model control groups.
In the treadmill test, LDH and CPK levels tended to decrease in L-arginine groups but did not reach statistical significance.
In the treadmill test, blood glucose increased at ≥600 mg/kg L-arginine, NEFA decreased significantly at 1200 mg/kg, and ammonia levels were significantly reduced at 1200 mg/kg.

In skeletal muscle after treadmill exercise, lactate content was increased in mice treated with L-arginine at ≥600 mg/kg, interpreted as reflecting lactate's role as an energy substrate and signaling metabolite, in contrast to the decreased serum lactate seen in the swimming test.

In the treadmill test, hepatic NEFA decreased significantly at ≥300 mg/kg and hepatic catalase activity was reduced at 1200 mg/kg, suggesting lower oxidative stress; muscle glycogen was also slightly elevated, particularly at 1200 mg/kg.

L-arginine treatment (100-500 μg/mL) significantly increased cell viability of undifferentiated C2C12 myoblasts challenged with H2O2 compared with H2O2-only treatment, indicating cytoprotective effects.
L-arginine significantly reduced H2O2-induced intracellular ROS levels in undifferentiated C2C12 cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
L-arginine significantly enhanced hexokinase (HK) activity in differentiated C2C12 myotubes compared with controls, suggesting improved glucose utilization.
Myogenin expression was increased in L-arginine-treated differentiated C2C12 myotubes, reflecting promotion of myogenic differentiation.

FPPS and CTGF protein levels in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) were significantly increased after stimulation with angiotensin II (Ang II) or TGF-β1 for 24, 48, or 72 hours, with no significant difference between the timepoints.
Lentiviral shRNA knockdown of FPPS (50 MOI) suppressed Ang II- or TGF-β1-induced upregulation of FPPS and CTGF mRNA and protein in VSMCs, restoring levels to those of untreated controls.
Activity of the small G proteins Rac, RhoA, and Ras was significantly elevated in VSMCs after 30 minutes of incubation with Ang II or TGF-β1.
FPPS knockdown via sh-FPPS lentivirus reduced Ang II- or TGF-β1-induced activation of RhoA and Rac in VSMCs, whereas Ras activity was not clearly affected.
Ang II- or TGF-β1-induced phosphorylation of p38, ERK1/2, and JNK increased at 6 hours, and FPPS knockdown reduced p-P38 and p-JNK levels but did not affect p-ERK1/2.
Lenti-FPPS shRNA significantly reduced Ang II- or TGF-β1-induced VSMC migration in scratch-wound assays, with migration inhibition rates of 4.3% (Ang II) and 11.6% (TGF-β1).

In the rat carotid balloon injury model, CTGF and FPPS protein levels in the carotid artery were elevated at all injury timepoints (7, 14, 21, 28 days) compared with uninjured controls, with the highest levels at 7 days.
Masson's trichrome staining showed that collagen fibrosis in the injured carotid arteries progressively increased with the duration of balloon injury (7 to 28 days).
Lenti-FPPS shRNA significantly reversed vascular remodeling (restenosis) in the rat carotid artery, reducing the neointimal-to-medial area ratio compared with the injury (Lenti-GFP) group.
FPPS and CTGF protein levels, elevated after 28 days of balloon injury, were decreased following Lenti-FPPS shRNA transfection in vivo.

GLISA assays showed RhoA, Ras, and Rac activity increased after carotid balloon injury; Rac and RhoA activity decreased following Lenti-FPPS shRNA transfection, while Ras activity was not clearly reduced.
Immunohistochemical staining for α-SMA showed that Lenti-FPPS shRNA transfection inhibited VSMC proliferation within the neointima of injured carotid arteries.

A novel heterozygous 280-298nt deletion in TGFB2 (c.280_298del, p.(Ser94Profs*7)) was identified in the proband and classified as likely pathogenic per ACMG criteria (PVS1, PM2), causing Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 4 (LDS4).
The frameshift caused by the deletion results in a truncated TGFB2 protein that lacks biological activity.

The 12-year-old proband presented primarily with pes planus and no thoracic aortic aneurysm or major vascular complications despite carrying the pathogenic TGFB2 variant, illustrating variable clinical expressivity of LDS4.
A carrier of the familial TGFB2 variant (IV.2) presented with joint laxity and bilateral pes planovalgus, consistent with the musculoskeletal features of LDS4.
Family members carrying the TGFB2 variant showed markedly variable clinical expression, ranging from asymptomatic carriers to severe outcomes including sudden death and fatal aortic aneurysm rupture.
The proband was started on a prophylactic antihypertensive regimen with sartans and periodic vascular imaging surveillance, alongside lifestyle measures to reduce cardiovascular risk.

A targeted NGS gene panel covering 21 connective-tissue/aneurysm-related genes (including ACTA2, FBN1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2, TGFB3) was used to identify the causative TGFB2 variant in this family.

LDS4, caused by TGFB2 mutations, is described as having milder symptoms than other LDS subtypes, with aneurysms typically presenting in the fourth decade and slower disease progression, most closely resembling Marfan syndrome.
The empirical 14-day omeprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin triple therapy regimen achieved H. pylori eradication in 90.7% of patients.
Smoking was significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure in simple logistic regression, with current smokers having eight-fold higher odds of treatment failure.
In multiple logistic regression, smoking remained the only independent factor significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure.
Fibromyalgia was associated with H. pylori eradication failure in simple regression analysis but did not remain significant after adjustment in the multiple regression model.

Irritable bowel syndrome, present in 4.1% of the cohort, was not identified as a factor associated with H. pylori eradication failure (0% prevalence in the failure group vs 4.5% in the eradicated group), and was not included among the significant factors in regression analysis.
Female sex was not significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure in simple regression.
Obesity (BMI≥30 kg/m²) was not significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure.
Diabetes mellitus was not significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure.
Anxiety and/or depression disorder was not significantly associated with H. pylori eradication failure.
Cirrhosis showed a numerically elevated but statistically non-significant odds ratio for H. pylori eradication failure.

The authors propose that chronic cigarette smoke exposure impairs H. pylori eradication through increased gastric acid/pepsin secretion, reduced gastric mucosal blood flow, decreased antibiotic bioavailability, and enhanced CYP2C19-mediated PPI metabolism, alongside behavioral effects such as poor treatment adherence and infection with higher-virulence strains.

A prior Brazilian study evaluating H. pylori treatment failure factors found no correlation with age, smoking, or alcohol consumption, but identified associations with clarithromycin resistance, cagA-negative status, and male gender, contrasting with the present study's finding of smoking as the sole significant factor.
Intrinsic cholinergic nerve fibers (hpChAT-labeled) in sigmoid mucosa were decreased by 39% in IBS patients compared to healthy controls, significant after controlling for sex.
hpChAT-labeled nerve fiber density was reduced by 50% in IBS-C patients compared to healthy controls.
hpChAT nerve fiber density was reduced by 31% in IBS-D compared to healthy controls but this did not reach statistical significance.
Extrinsic cholinergic (VAChT) and sympathetic (TH, NPY) nerve fiber densities in sigmoid mucosa were similar between healthy controls and IBS (including bowel habit subtypes).
Intrinsic primary afferent nerve fibers labeled by calbindin were reduced by 17% in IBS overall compared to healthy controls, a nonsignificant trend.
Calbindin-labeled intrinsic primary afferent nerve fiber density was significantly reduced by 26% in IBS-C compared to healthy controls.
VIP-labeled intrinsic secretomotor nerve fiber density was 1.5-fold lower in IBS-C compared to IBS-D.
Densities of SP nerve fibers, tryptase-labeled mast cells, and S100β-labeled enteric glial cells did not differ significantly between HCs and IBS, IBS-C, or IBS-D.
Overall proximity of mast cells to total, extrinsic primary afferent, and intrinsic primary afferent nerve fibers did not differ between HCs and IBS, IBS-C, or IBS-D.
In IBS patients, VIP nerve fiber density was negatively correlated with overall IBS symptom severity score.
NPY nerve fiber density was negatively correlated with overall IBS symptom severity score in IBS patients.
TH nerve fiber density was negatively correlated with the abdominal pain subscore of the IBS-SSS.
Proximity of mast cells to substance P nerve fibers was positively correlated with overall IBS symptom severity score.
Proximity of mast cells to calbindin-labeled intrinsic sensory nerve fibers was positively correlated with overall IBS symptom severity score.
Mast cell proximity to SP and calbindin nerve fibers positively correlated with abdominal pain intensity within 24 hours of biopsy in IBS patients.
MC-Calb proximity was positively correlated with the abdominal pain subscore of the IBS-SSS.
In IBS-C patients specifically, VIP nerve fiber density was strongly negatively correlated with IBS symptom severity score.
In IBS-C patients, mast cell proximity to SP and calbindin nerve fibers was positively correlated with IBS symptom severity, and MC-Calb further correlated with the abdominal pain subscore.
In IBS-D patients, NPY nerve fiber density was negatively correlated with IBS symptom severity and abdominal pain subscore.
In IBS-D patients, mast cell proximity to total (PGP9.5) and substance P nerve fibers was correlated with abdominal pain intensity over the preceding 24 hours.
In a prior study by this group, CALB2 gene expression in the sigmoid colonic mucosa was downregulated in IBS-C compared to healthy controls.

Addition of the JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor baricitinib to a regimen of corticosteroids, tacrolimus and nintedanib led to rapid clinical and radiologic improvement and discontinuation of oxygen therapy in a patient with RA-associated ILD refractory to prior therapies.
Prior treatment with tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor with a similar mechanism to baricitinib, achieved low RA disease activity but failed to prevent progression of interstitial lung disease.
Serum KL-6 rose progressively with worsening interstitial lung disease, peaking at 2830 U/mL despite corticosteroid, tacrolimus and nintedanib therapy, before declining after baricitinib was added.

The authors propose that IL-6 activates JAK1/JAK2-STAT3 signalling which crosstalks with Smad3, the downstream mediator of TGF-β, implying that STAT3 inhibition may suppress TGF-β-mediated pulmonary fibrosis.

A cited clinical trial of nintedanib plus tocilizumab (an IL-6 receptor antagonist) in 12 patients with progressive, treatment-refractory systemic sclerosis-associated ILD showed HRCT disease stabilisation in all cases and marked improvement in two.
Qualitative analysis of tweets from people with severe ME/CFS or their caregivers found profound functional debilitation as a core theme of daily life.
Individuals with severe ME/CFS and their caregivers reported emotional isolation as a major aspect of their lived experience.
People with severe ME/CFS described systemic exclusion from medical care and disability support systems.
The study identifies contested legitimacy and gendered stigma as structuring forces shaping the daily realities of people with severe ME/CFS.
The authors argue that ME/CFS as a medically contested illness renders patients, particularly those with severe disease, both physically incapacitated and socially invisible.

The TPOT AutoML pipeline achieved the highest classification performance for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls using plasma metabolomic/lipidomic data, with AUC 92.1%, accuracy 87.3%, sensitivity 85.8%, and specificity 89.0%.
Auto-Sklearn showed moderate diagnostic performance for ME/CFS classification (AUC 83.7%), lower than TPOT.
H2O AutoML had the lowest diagnostic performance among the three AutoML frameworks for ME/CFS classification (accuracy 70.1%, AUC 75.6%).

PLS-DA modeling of plasma metabolomic/lipidomic data showed a moderate but statistically significant separation between ME/CFS patients and controls, explaining 49.8% of the variance in disease status.
Fold-change analysis of 888 plasma metabolites/lipids identified 28 significantly altered compounds between ME/CFS patients and controls, 14 upregulated and 14 downregulated.
Several phosphatidylcholine species, including pc(32:2) and pc(p-34:2)/pc(o-34:3), were significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients.
Plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamine species pe(p-34:2)/pe(o-34:3) and pe(p-36:2)/pe(o-36:3) were significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients.
The sphingolipid sm(d36:0) was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients, part of complex changes in sphingolipid metabolism.
Ceramide species showed mixed dysregulation in ME/CFS, with cer(d34:1) and cer(d42:2)a upregulated and cer(d42:2)b downregulated.
Glycosphingolipids were consistently elevated in ME/CFS, with GlcCer(d42:2) showing the strongest significance among the fold-change analysis.
Cholesterol ester profiling revealed decreased polyunsaturated species ce(18:2) and ce(18:3), and increased omega-3 fatty acid esters ce(20:5) and ce(22:6) in ME/CFS.
Lysophosphatidylcholines containing polyunsaturated fatty acids, lpc(18:2) and lpc(18:3), were significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients.

Succinic acid, a TCA cycle intermediate, was significantly upregulated in ME/CFS patients, and was among the top SHAP-important metabolites for TPOT predictions and a discriminatory feature in PLS-DA and univariate ROC analysis.
Threonic acid levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients, consistent with altered energy/carbohydrate metabolism.

Leucine, a branched-chain amino acid, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients across FC analysis, PLS-DA VIP scoring, SHAP importance, and univariate ROC, suggesting impaired BCAA metabolism and neuromuscular fatigue.
Aminomalonate levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients.

Pyruvic acid was increased in ME/CFS patients per PLS-DA VIP scoring and SHAP analysis, indicating impaired glycolysis-to-TCA cycle transition and metabolic inflexibility; univariate ROC gave AUC 0.618.
Glutamine levels were increased in ME/CFS patients based on PLS-DA VIP scoring, consistent with immune activation and gut-brain axis dysregulation.

SHAP analysis of the TPOT model identified decreased prostaglandin D2, a pro-inflammatory lipid mediator, as increasing the probability of ME/CFS classification, suggesting a suppressed or shifted inflammatory response.

SHAP analysis identified increased 11,12-EET, an anti-inflammatory/vasodilatory arachidonic acid-derived epoxide, as increasing the probability of ME/CFS classification, potentially reflecting a compensatory vascular protective response.
SHAP analysis identified increased pc(35:2)a as one of the top predictors of ME/CFS, reflecting adaptive or dysfunctional cell membrane phospholipid remodeling.
SHAP analysis identified increased glycocholic acid, a bile acid, as one of the top predictors of ME/CFS, pointing to impaired gut microbiota-bile acid-brain axis interactions.

SHAP analysis identified decreased pseudouridine, a modified nucleoside linked to RNA turnover, as a top predictor of ME/CFS, suggesting suppressed RNA catabolism and weakened gut-brain axis communication.

Univariate ROC analysis showed that individual top SHAP metabolites (succinic acid, pyruvic acid, leucine) had only moderate standalone discriminatory power for ME/CFS, all with AUC values above 0.60 but below 0.80, whereas the integrated TPOT model achieved much higher discrimination (AUC 92.1%).

Females were disproportionately represented among long COVID patients with ME/CFS, comprising ~74% of the LC cohort with a female-to-male ratio of 2.9:1, despite age- and sex-matching efforts with recovered controls.

Female LC/ME-CFS patients showed increased absolute neutrophil and monocyte counts and decreased lymphocyte counts relative to recovered females, consistent with a shift toward myelopoiesis at the expense of lymphopoiesis; this pattern was absent in males.

Absolute numbers of naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were significantly reduced in whole blood of both female and male LC/ME-CFS patients compared to sex-matched recovered controls, with no change in central/effector memory subsets.

Terminal effector (TE) CD4+ and CD8+ T cell frequencies were significantly increased in PBMCs of both male and female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered controls, indicating persistent T cell activation regardless of sex.
The proportion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) in PBMCs was significantly reduced in female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to other groups, suggesting compromised immunoregulation specific to females.
The frequency of CD39-expressing Tregs and CD39 expression intensity were significantly reduced in female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to other groups.
CD71+ erythroid cells (CECs) were significantly expanded in the peripheral blood of female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered females, but not expanded in males.
RBC distribution width (RDW) was significantly increased in whole blood of female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to other groups, consistent with dysregulated erythropoiesis.

A broad panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines (IL-1α, IL-6, IL-12/23p40, IP-10, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17a, PlGF, MCP-1, MIP-1α, MDC, sFlt-1, VCAM-1, ICAM-1, CRP, SAA) was significantly elevated in plasma of female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered females.
TGF-β1, IL-16, eotaxin-3, and VEGF-C were significantly reduced in plasma of female LC/ME-CFS patients versus recovered females, suggesting weakened immunoregulatory capacity.

In males, a more limited and balanced set of cytokines/chemokines (IL-1α, IL-10, TNF-α, IL-17a, PlGF, MCP-1, MIP-1α, MDC, ICAM-1, sFlt-1, CRP, SAA) was elevated in LCM vs RM, with IL-10 elevation suggesting stronger anti-inflammatory signaling in males.
Plasma markers of gut barrier dysfunction and microbial translocation (I-FABP, LPS-BP, sCD14) were significantly elevated in female LC/ME-CFS patients vs recovered females but not in males.
Plasma Galectin-9, ARTN, and Reelin were significantly elevated in both female and male LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered controls, with significantly higher levels in females than males.
Plasma testosterone levels were significantly reduced in female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered females, with no change in males.
Plasma estradiol levels were significantly reduced in male LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered males.
Plasma cortisol levels were substantially lower in both male and female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered controls, suggesting a dysregulated stress response.
Plasma growth hormone (GH) levels were significantly elevated in female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to other groups.

Plasma testosterone levels were inversely correlated with multiple pro-inflammatory biomarkers (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1α, IFN-γ, MCP-1, IL-17a, IP-10, Reelin, VCAM-1, RDW) and with clinical symptom scores in female LC/ME-CFS patients.
Whole-blood bulk RNA-seq identified 1,088 significantly upregulated and 1,522 significantly downregulated genes in female LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered females.

Whole-blood bulk RNA-seq identified 662 significantly upregulated and 749 significantly downregulated genes in male LC/ME-CFS patients compared to recovered males; 290 upregulated and 458 downregulated genes were shared with females.

The most highly upregulated genes in female LC/ME-CFS patients (ZNF469 >6.7-fold, BRINP2 >5.8-fold, FEZF2 >5.5-fold, HOXC12 >5.1-fold, ZFHX3 >4.8-fold, RELN >4-fold, SKOR2 >3.7-fold, RPL17-C18orf32 >3.4-fold, MEIS2 >3.2-fold, EGR3 >3.1-fold) were predominantly linked to neuronal injury response, neurodevelopment, and cognitive dysfunction.

The most highly upregulated genes in male LC/ME-CFS patients (FcγR1-binding protein, PALB2, DSC2, MEIS2, EPSTI1, SCAF8, CLEC4D, CASP5, LYZ, TSNAX-DISC1) were enriched for innate immune activation, interferon signaling, and inflammation, contrasting with the neuroinflammatory profile seen in females.

CIBERSORTx deconvolution of whole-blood RNA-seq showed significantly increased memory B cells, activated memory CD4+ T cells, and neutrophils, alongside significantly reduced Tregs in female LC/ME-CFS patients versus recovered females; no significant immune cell proportion differences were seen in males.
FOXP3 gene expression was significantly reduced in female LC/ME-CFS patients, consistent with the observed reduction in Treg proportion and CD39 expression.

Hematopoiesis-associated genes GYPA (CD235a), TFRC (CD71), HBG2, and ARTN were significantly increased in female LC/ME-CFS patients versus recovered females; in males, CD71 and ARTN but not GYPA were upregulated, consistent with CEC expansion being female-specific.

Eighteen olfactory receptor (OR) genes were upregulated (and one downregulated) in female LC/ME-CFS patients, compared to only six OR genes upregulated in males, suggesting broader sensory/neuroinflammatory dysregulation in females.

Genes encoding estrogen receptor alpha/beta (ESR1, ESR2), estrogen-related receptor gamma (ESRRG), androgen receptor (AR), and glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) were upregulated in female LC/ME-CFS patients, potentially indicating heightened hormone receptor sensitivity.
LASSO regularized regression identified low testosterone plus high CEC frequency, high GH, and high CD4+ TE T cell frequency as the top biomarkers distinguishing female from male LC/ME-CFS patients.
Whole-blood RNA-seq identified 1,088 significantly upregulated and 1,522 significantly downregulated genes in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
Whole-blood RNA-seq identified 662 significantly upregulated and 749 significantly downregulated genes in long COVID males compared to recovered males.
290 upregulated genes and 458 downregulated genes overlapped between LCF-vs-RF and LCM-vs-RM comparisons, indicating a shared but sex-divergent transcriptional signature.
ZNF469 was the most upregulated gene in long COVID females versus recovered females, at greater than 6.7-fold, and is implicated in neuronal differentiation.
BRINP2 was upregulated more than 5.8-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females and is associated with neurological development and disorders.
FEZF2, essential for deep-layer neuron development, was upregulated more than 5.5-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
HOXC12, involved in hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell renewal and differentiation, was upregulated more than 5.1-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
ZFHX3, involved in neuronal differentiation and ECM remodeling, was upregulated more than 4.8-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
RELN gene expression was upregulated more than 4-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females, and also trended upward in males but below the fold-change cutoff.
SKOR2, linked to cerebellar Purkinje cells, was upregulated more than 3.7-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
RPL17-C18orf32, a ribosomal protein gene associated with Alzheimer disease, was upregulated more than 3.4-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.

MEIS2, associated with neuronal dysfunction and intellectual impairment, was upregulated in both LCF (>3.2-fold) and LCM (>2.8-fold), making it one of the few genes commonly upregulated in both sexes.
EGR3, linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, was upregulated more than 3.1-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
WDR62, involved in neurodevelopment, was among the most downregulated genes (>-2.7-fold) in long COVID females versus recovered females.
Neurexin2 (NRX2), linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, was downregulated more than -2.6-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
GMPR, which affects Rho-GTPase activity, was downregulated in both long COVID females (<-2.3-fold) and long COVID males (>-2.3-fold) versus their respective recovered controls.
MUC12, linked to ulcerative colitis, was downregulated more than -2.3-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
SYCE1 (<-1.7-fold) and SYCE1L (<-1.6-fold), genes expressed in the meiotic synaptonemal complex, were both downregulated in long COVID females versus recovered females.
FOXO4, a transcription factor involved in cell survival, proliferation, and apoptosis, was downregulated more than -1.2-fold in long COVID females versus recovered females.
FcγR1-binding protein was the most upregulated gene in long COVID males versus recovered males (>3.2-fold), implicated in antibody-mediated immune responses.
PALB2, involved in DNA damage repair, was upregulated more than 3.1-fold in long COVID males versus recovered males.
Desmocollin-2 (DSC2), involved in desmosome integrity that may cause cardiomyopathy when dysregulated, was upregulated more than 2.9-fold in long COVID males versus recovered males.
EPSTI1, involved in monocyte-endothelial adhesion and linked to atherosclerosis, was upregulated more than 2.7-fold in long COVID males versus recovered males.

CLEC4D, a C-type lectin receptor expressed by neutrophils/monocytes involved in respiratory burst and inflammatory cytokine production, was upregulated more than 2.5-fold in long COVID males versus recovered males.
Caspase-5, involved in NF-κB activation upon microbial sensing, was upregulated more than 2.4-fold in long COVID males versus recovered males.
CIBERSORTx deconvolution of whole-blood RNA-seq showed significantly increased memory B cells, activated memory CD4+ T cells, and neutrophils, alongside significantly reduced Tregs, in LCF versus RF.
No significant differences in immune cell subset proportions were found between LCM and RM by CIBERSORTx deconvolution.
FOXP3 gene expression was significantly reduced in LCF compared to RF, consistent with CIBERSORTx Treg reduction.
Multiple immune-cell surface marker genes (CD3e, CD14, CD7, CD320, CD101, CD82, CD81, CD6, CD68) were significantly downregulated in LCF versus RF.
CD69, CD302, CD226, and CD200R1 marker genes were significantly upregulated in LCF versus RF.
In LCM, CD36, CD48, and CD164 genes were significantly upregulated versus RM.
CD7, CD82, CD320, CD14, and CD79A genes were significantly downregulated in LCM versus RM.

Whole-blood RNA-seq showed significant upregulation of IL-33, IFNG, IFNA20P, IFNGR1, CXCL-8, GZMA, and VEGF-B transcripts in LCF versus RF, indicating a type 2/type II interferon-skewed signaling profile.
Several cytokine/chemokine receptor genes (CXCR3, IL-32, IL-15RA, IL-27, IL-9RP3, IL-2RB, IL-12RB1, IL-11RA) were significantly downregulated in LCF versus RF.
In LCM, only TGF-R1 was upregulated versus RM, whereas IL-27RA, IL-2RA, IL-11RA, and CXCR3 were downregulated, a markedly more limited cytokine/receptor gene signature than in LCF.
Hematopoiesis-associated genes GYPA (CD235a), TFRC (CD71), HBG2, and ARTN were significantly upregulated in LCF versus RF, consistent with expansion of CD71+ erythroid cells and elevated plasma ARTN.
In LCM, CD71 (TFRC) and ARTN transcripts were upregulated versus RM, but GYPA was not, mirroring the absence of CD71+ erythroid cell expansion seen by flow cytometry in males.

Eighteen olfactory receptor (OR) genes were upregulated and one downregulated in LCF versus RF, compared to only six OR genes upregulated in LCM versus RM (including OR10H1), suggesting more prominent ectopic OR dysregulation in females.

Estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1), estrogen receptor beta (ESR2), estrogen-related receptor gamma (ESRRG), androgen receptor (AR), and glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) genes were upregulated in LCF, suggesting heightened sensitivity to estrogen/androgen/glucocorticoid signaling.
ZNF469 was the most upregulated gene in LCF (>6.7-fold vs RF), a zinc-finger gene implicated in neuronal differentiation.
BRINP2 was upregulated >5.8-fold in LCF versus RF, a gene associated with neurological development and disorders.
FEZF2, essential for deep-layer neuron development, was upregulated >5.5-fold in LCF versus RF.
HOXC12, involved in hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell renewal and differentiation, was upregulated >5.1-fold in LCF versus RF.
ZFHX3, involved in neuronal differentiation and extracellular matrix remodeling, was upregulated >4.8-fold in LCF versus RF.
The RELN (Reelin) gene was upregulated >4-fold in LCF versus RF, and also upregulated in LCM (below the study's fold-change cutoff), consistent with previously reported elevated Reelin protein in LC.

MEIS2, associated with neuronal dysfunction and intellectual impairment, was upregulated in both LCF (>3.2-fold) and LCM (>2.8-fold) versus respective recovered controls, making it a shared upregulated gene between sexes.
EGR3, linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, was upregulated >3.1-fold in LCF versus RF.
WDR62, involved in neurodevelopment, was among the most downregulated genes in LCF (>−2.7-fold) versus RF.
Neurexin2 (NRXN2), linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, was downregulated (<−2.6-fold) in LCF versus RF.
WDR62, a gene involved in neurodevelopment, was among the most downregulated genes in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
Neurexin2 (NRX2), linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, was significantly downregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
Membrane-bound mucin 12 (MUC12), previously linked to ulcerative colitis, was downregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
SYCE1 and SYCE1L, expressed in the synaptonemal complex of meiotic chromosomes, were both downregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
Forkhead box O4 (FOXO4), involved in cell survival, proliferation, and apoptosis, was downregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
FcγR1-binding protein, involved in antibody-mediated immune responses, was the most upregulated gene in long COVID males compared to recovered males.
PALB2, involved in DNA damage repair, was upregulated in long COVID males compared to recovered males.
MEIS2, associated with neuronal dysfunction and intellectual impairment, was upregulated in both long COVID females and males relative to their respective recovered groups.
Epithelial-stromal interaction 1 (EPSTI1), involved in monocyte-endothelial adhesion and linked to atherosclerosis, was upregulated in long COVID males.
CLEC4D, a C-type lectin receptor on neutrophils/monocytes involved in respiratory burst and inflammatory cytokine production, was upregulated in long COVID males.
Lysozyme (LYZ), which can elicit pain via TLR-4 activation during neuroinflammation, was upregulated in long COVID males.
TSNAX-DISC1, located upstream of DISC1 and associated with bipolar disorder and major depression, was upregulated in long COVID males.
MCC (Mutated in colorectal cancer), a negative regulator of cell-cycle progression, was the most downregulated gene in long COVID males.
HLA-DRB5 was highly downregulated in long COVID males, suggesting dysregulated antigen presentation or autoimmune response.
KIR3DL2, an inhibitory ligand associated with reduced IFN-γ and NK cell cytotoxicity, was downregulated in long COVID males.

CIBERSORTx deconvolution of whole-blood RNA-seq showed significantly increased memory B cells, activated memory CD4+ T cells, and neutrophils, alongside significantly reduced Tregs, in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
No significant differences in CIBERSORTx-deconvoluted immune cell proportions were observed between long COVID males and recovered males.
FOXP3 gene expression was significantly reduced in long COVID females, consistent with reduced Treg proportions seen by flow cytometry.
Multiple immune cell surface marker genes (CD3e, CD14, CD7, CD320, CD101, CD82, CD81, CD6, CD68) were significantly downregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.
CD69, CD302, CD226, and CD200R1 immune marker genes were significantly upregulated in long COVID females compared to recovered females.

In long COVID males, CD36, CD48, and CD164 genes were significantly upregulated while CD7, CD82, CD320, CD14, and CD79A were significantly downregulated compared to recovered males, a distinct pattern from that seen in females.

RNA-seq analysis showed significant upregulation of IL-33, IFNG, IFNA20P, IFNGR1, CXCL8, GZMA, and VEGF-B, along with downregulation of CXCR3, IL-32, IL-15RA, IL-27, IL-9RP3, IL-2RB, IL-12RB1, and IL-11RA, in long COVID females versus controls.

In long COVID males, only TGF-R1 was upregulated, while IL-27RA, IL-2RA, IL-11RA, and CXCR3 were downregulated compared to recovered males, a much more limited transcriptional cytokine signature than seen in females.

RNA-seq showed significant upregulation of hematopoiesis-associated genes GYPA (CD235a), TFRC (CD71), HBG2, and ARTN in long COVID females compared to controls, consistent with expansion of CD71+ erythroid cells and elevated plasma ARTN.
CD71 (TFRC) and ARTN were upregulated in long COVID males, but GYPA was not, consistent with flow cytometry data showing CEC expansion occurs exclusively in long COVID females.

Eighteen olfactory receptor genes were upregulated and one downregulated in long COVID females, whereas only six ORs were upregulated in long COVID males, with mostly non-overlapping specific receptors between sexes.
No individual plasma proteins differed significantly between ME/CFS patients and sedentary controls at baseline or immediately after either exercise bout once FDR correction was applied.
AHSG (Fetuin-A/Alpha-2-HS-glycoprotein) plasma levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus controls at the 24-hour recovery timepoint (D2PRE).
CBLN4 (Cerebellin-4), a synaptic organizer protein, was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus controls at D2PRE (24h recovery).
MYBPC1 (Myosin-binding protein C, slow type) plasma levels were significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients relative to controls at D2PRE (24h recovery).
KLHL41 (Kelch-like protein 41), critical for skeletal muscle development, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients relative to controls at D2PRE.
MYL3 (Myosin light chain 3), a component of the myosin complex in cardiac and skeletal muscle, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients relative to controls at D2PRE.

T cell receptor signaling was the only KEGG pathway showing persistent alteration across all three GSEA timepoints assessed (D1PRE, D1POST/D2PRE window, D2POST), indicating sustained immune dysregulation in ME/CFS.
The glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway showed a positive normalized enrichment score at D2PRE, the only pathway upregulated in ME/CFS, suggesting a shift toward anaerobic metabolism during recovery.

T cell receptor signaling, B cell receptor signaling, and IL-17 signaling pathways were all significantly downregulated post-exercise (D2POST) in ME/CFS, suggesting impaired resolution of adaptive immune activation during PEM recovery.
The mTOR signaling pathway, a regulator of nutrient sensing and immune activation, was highly significantly affected at D2PRE, supporting impaired metabolic recovery in ME/CFS.

During the 24-hour recovery period, 13.5% of measured proteins changed significantly in the control cohort versus only 4.9% in the ME/CFS cohort, with 241 proteins altered in both groups, indicating a blunted recovery response in ME/CFS.

In female participants, an extensive 3425 proteins (47% of the dataset) changed significantly during the 24-h recovery period in the ME/CFS group compared to only 21 proteins in female controls, showing broad proteomic disruption specific to ME/CFS females.

In male participants, only three proteins changed significantly during the 24-h recovery period in the ME/CFS group, versus 2544 proteins (35%) in male controls, indicating a blunted or absent proteomic recovery response in ME/CFS males.
Immediate post-exercise blood draws (30-40 minutes after exercise) showed minimal proteomic change, affecting fewer than 1% of measured proteins in any group.

Temporal clustering of exercise-responsive proteins in controls identified a cluster enriched for striated muscle contraction along with interleukin, tyrosine kinase, and EPH-ephrin signaling pathways, which showed divergent dynamics when the same proteins were examined in ME/CFS.

Temporal clustering of the 378 significantly exercise-responsive proteins in ME/CFS identified a cluster enriched for immune system, integrin cell surface interactions, and iron uptake and transport pathways, showing strong dysregulation relative to controls.
HNF4A, a transcription factor essential for hepatic metabolism and circadian regulation, was negatively associated with both VO2max1 and VO2max2 at all four timepoints in ME/CFS patients.

TREM2, an immune-related lipid receptor, was consistently negatively associated with VO2max in controls but was not a significant VO2max predictor in ME/CFS, indicating dysregulation of this protein-fitness relationship specific to ME/CFS.
FABP3, involved in lipid metabolism, was negatively associated with VO2max across all timepoints and both CPETs in controls, replicating a prior independent study's finding in sedentary adults.
ANTXR2 was positively associated with VO2max1 at baseline in both ME/CFS and control participants, replicating findings from a prior independent study of 650 sedentary adults.
Age was a significant predictor of low intra-subject t-SNE proteomic similarity across Day1 exercise, with an odds ratio of 1.52 per 10-year increase.
BMI was a significant predictor of low intra-subject t-SNE proteomic similarity at ΔDay2, with an odds ratio of 1.58 per 5 kg/m2 increase.

Cardiorespiratory fitness measures VO2max2 and AT2 were significantly associated with low intra-subject t-SNE proteomic similarity at ΔDay2, with odds ratios of 1.13 and 1.23, respectively, per mL/kg/min increase.

Test site significantly influenced proteomic group assignment: participants tested in Los Angeles were 3.14 times more likely to have low intra-subject t-SNE similarity at ΔDay1 and 3.67 times more likely during recovery, compared to Ithaca.
Higher baseline (D1PRE) SHISA2 levels correlated with better SF-36 general health scores in ME/CFS patients, an association not seen in controls.
D2PRE levels of BAGE3 were inversely correlated with MFI-20 total fatigue score at D2PRE in the ME/CFS cohort.
Within-subject increases in MICU3 and NDRG3 levels over the full exercise protocol correlated with better SF-36 general health scores in ME/CFS patients.
Decreasing OXLD1 levels tracked with reduced sore throat severity in ME/CFS patients.
In female ME/CFS patients, lower SOSTDC1 and SUSD3 levels at D1PRE were negatively associated with recent PEM severity.
In female ME/CFS patients, YJEFN3 levels at D1POST were negatively associated with recent PEM severity.
Changes in SERPINB1 and MMP8 levels following the first exercise bout were negatively associated with SF-36 general health scores in female ME/CFS patients.
MICB, a stress-induced immune ligand, was positively associated with recent average fatigue from D1PRE to D2POST in female ME/CFS patients, the only protein among 16 with a positive correlation.

Proteins correlated with general health, sore throat, and unrefreshing sleep in female ME/CFS patients were enriched for interleukin/cytokine signaling, immune system, angiogenesis and extracellular matrix pathways (GH, sore throat), and plasma lipoprotein pathways (unrefreshing sleep).

Prior work cited in the discussion reported TRPM3 channel dysfunction in NK cells from ME/CFS patients leading to reduced calcium influx, potentially contributing to immunological, muscular, and neurological symptoms.
The discussion cites an in vitro study indicating that naltrexone, sometimes prescribed to ME/CFS patients, may help restore TRPM3 channel function.

The authors' own prior pilot proteomics study (SomaScan 5K Assay, 40 participants) had identified nine proteins elevated in ME/CFS at baseline using a less stringent statistical test, a result not replicated in the current, larger, FDR-corrected analysis showing no baseline differences.
A prior NIH-funded proteomics study using a smaller 1305-analyte SomaScan assay in 21 controls and 17 ME/CFS subjects found no significant proteomic differences between groups.

The authors' prior 5K SomaScan pilot study identified disruptions in Ephrin-Eph and immune system signaling between ME/CFS patients and controls, consistent with pathway findings in the current study.

Of six proteins significantly associated with VO2max in this study's sedentary control cohort, three (ANTXR2, FABP3, INHBC) overlapped in direction with associations reported in a prior larger 650-adult SomaScan VO2max study.

MYBPC1 and MYL3, previously positively associated with baseline VO2max in a larger prior study, did not replicate this VO2max association in the current dataset, although both showed significantly reduced levels in ME/CFS versus controls at D2PRE.

A prior transcriptomic study of PEM-inducing exercise challenges reported immune-cell signaling and NK cell cytotoxicity activation in a 13-male ME/CFS cohort but no significant stress-induced transcriptional changes in a 20-female ME/CFS cohort, contrasting with the current study's proteomic finding of a stronger response in females.

Using t-SNE of the whole proteomic dataset, only 22 of 132 participants showed close (stable) grouping of all their timepoint samples, 62 had one or more dispersed timepoints, and 28 had all three timepoint-transitions separated, unlike the tighter within-subject grouping seen in the group's matched metabolomics dataset.

Logistic regression of t-SNE-derived proteomic similarity groups showed age was a significant predictor at ΔDay1 (OR 1.52 per 10-year increase) and BMI a significant predictor at ΔDay2 (OR 1.58 per 5 kg/m2 increase), independent of ME/CFS status.

Higher cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max2, AT2) was associated with greater likelihood of low intra-subject proteomic similarity after the second exercise bout (ΔDay2), and test site (Los Angeles vs. Ithaca) significantly predicted group assignment at ΔDay1 and during recovery.

In healthy controls, roughly 20% of proteins significantly associated with anaerobic threshold at D1POST were enriched for Reactome immune system, cytokine regulation, and interleukin signaling pathways.

The commentary notes that the reported plasma SMPDL3B threshold of 30 ng/mL and its association with ME (OR = 3.0) in the Canadian cohort were derived and validated on the same dataset, creating circularity that likely inflates the apparent association.

The diagnostic accuracy of the plasma SMPDL3B threshold dropped substantially (AUC 0.84 to 0.73) when applied unmodified from the Canadian cohort to the Norwegian cohort, which used a different physician-based severity classification.

Vildagliptin and saxagliptin inhibited PI-PLC-mediated cleavage of membrane-bound SMPDL3B in vitro, but only at a supraphysiological concentration of 100 µM, roughly 250-fold higher than therapeutic plasma levels in diabetic patients.

Vildagliptin at 100 µM significantly reduced SMPDL3B gene expression, an effect the commentary suggests may reflect cytotoxicity rather than a specific pharmacological action, since viability controls were not reported.

Linagliptin at 100 µM paradoxically increased SMPDL3B expression, an effect attributed by the original authors to structural differences among DPP-4 inhibitors, but the commentary notes this was not validated against cytotoxicity or stress-response markers.
Individual face-to-face CBT produced a statistically significant reduction in fatigue compared to non-CBT comparators.
Group CBT did not significantly reduce fatigue compared to non-CBT comparators.
Self-directed CBT showed a non-significant trend toward reduced fatigue compared to non-CBT comparators.
When all CBT modalities were pooled together, CBT was not statistically significant in reducing fatigue overall.
CBT efficacy for fatigue at six months post-treatment was not statistically significant, indicating a lack of sustained long-term benefit.
Self-directed CBT significantly improved physical functioning compared to non-CBT comparators, with a large effect size.
Individual face-to-face CBT did not significantly improve physical functioning, though the p-value approached significance.
Pooled analysis of all CBT modalities together did not show statistically significant improvement in physical functioning.
Group CBT did not significantly improve physical functioning.
CBT did not show statistically significant improvement in physical functioning at six months post-treatment follow-up.
CBT did not significantly reduce anxiety symptoms in patients with CFS.
CBT did not significantly reduce depressive symptoms in patients with CFS.
CBT's effect on pain in CFS patients was borderline but did not reach statistical significance.
CBT did not significantly improve quality of life in patients with CFS.
In one trial, patients receiving group CBT had poorer physical functioning and bodily pain scores than the comparator group.
Adverse effects such as increased fatigue, pain, and distress were reported by approximately 15% of the CBT intervention group and 26% of the control group in one trial.
In another trial, 2% of the intervention group and 5% of the comparator group reported increased fatigue, nausea, and pain as adverse effects.
Across included RCTs, average dropout rate was 18.8% in CBT intervention groups versus 12.5% in comparator groups, with dropout ranging 8-43.4%.

PSQI sleep quality scores significantly decreased after treatment in both groups, with the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group showing significantly lower post-treatment PSQI scores than the eszopiclone-alone group.

The clinical overall response rate (basic recovery, significant improvement, some improvement, no change) trended higher in the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group (61.40% basic recovery) than the eszopiclone-alone group (38.00%), but the overall between-group difference did not reach statistical significance.

Serum 5-HT levels increased significantly after treatment in both groups compared to baseline, with a greater post-treatment increase in the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group than the eszopiclone-alone group.
Serum BDNF levels increased significantly after treatment in both groups compared to baseline, with a greater rise in the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group than the eszopiclone-alone group.
When assessed as percent change from baseline, the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group showed a lower percentage increase in 5-HT than the eszopiclone-alone group.

When assessed as percent change from baseline, BDNF increase differed significantly between groups, though the reported observation-group value (17.47 ± 9.95%) was numerically lower than the control-group value (51.19 ± 23.61%) despite being described as higher.
The incidence of total adverse reactions was significantly lower in the acupuncture-plus-eszopiclone group than in the eszopiclone-alone group.

The authors propose that acupuncture raises peripheral tryptophan levels and accelerates its transport across the blood-brain barrier, promoting central 5-HT synthesis and thereby improving sleep in CFS patients.

The authors propose that acupuncture enhances BDNF expression, promoting endothelial proliferation, neurovascular regeneration, and neuronal survival, thereby facilitating recovery of neurological function.
Achilles tendon stiffness was significantly lower in individuals with HSD/hEDS compared to matched controls.
Individuals with HSD/hEDS had a significantly higher metabolic energy cost of walking compared to controls.
Individuals with HSD/hEDS reported increased pain during walking trials compared to controls.
Muscle fascicle shortening and shortening velocity of the medial gastrocnemius were similar between HSD/hEDS and control groups.
Muscle energy cost and mechanical efficiency of the plantar flexors were similar between HSD/hEDS and control groups.
Greater muscle activation and antagonist coactivation, particularly during early stance, were observed in HSD/hEDS participants, likely reflecting compensation for joint instability.
The elevated cost of walking in HSD/hEDS appears driven not by increased plantar flexor work but by a redistribution of joint work to more proximal joints.
Significant left common iliac vein compression was more prevalent in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (68.0%) than in healthy controls (35.0%), with nearly fourfold higher odds.
Significant left common iliac vein compression was more prevalent in patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder (65.6%) than in healthy controls (35.0%), with over threefold higher odds.
There was no statistically significant difference in the prevalence of significant LCIV compression between the hEDS and HSD groups.
Across all three groups, significant LCIV compression prevalence differed overall, being higher in hEDS and HSD than in healthy controls.
Patients with HSD self-reported experiencing muscle pain more frequently than patients with hEDS.
Fibromyalgia comorbidity was substantially more common in patients diagnosed with HSD than in those with hEDS, indicating more widespread pain in HSD prior to treatment.
Over roughly one year of clinic care, patients with hEDS reported no change in their worst joint pain score.
Over roughly one year of clinic care, patients with HSD reported a modest improvement in their worst joint pain score.
Patients with HSD reported using muscle relaxers and other (unspecified) medications more often than patients with hEDS.

There was no significant difference between hEDS and HSD patients in the percentage using any of the 17 assessed treatment modalities, with rest, heat therapy, massage, oral medication, and exercise being the top 5 used by both groups.

Only a minority of patients perceived any of the 17 treatment modalities as improving their hypermobility, joint, or muscle pain, indicating limited overall perceived benefit from self-directed treatments.
Exercise was reported to significantly reduce hypermobility pain in patients with HSD.
Physical therapy was reported to significantly reduce hypermobility pain in patients with HSD.
In patients with hEDS, no treatment modality significantly improved hypermobility pain, though exercise showed a borderline trend.
Exercise significantly improved joint pain in patients with hEDS.
Exercise significantly improved joint pain in patients with HSD.
Physical therapy significantly improved joint pain in patients with HSD.
Injections were reported to significantly worsen joint pain in patients with HSD.
Exercise was the only modality self-reported to improve muscle pain in patients with hEDS.
Topical medications were reported to significantly worsen muscle pain in patients with hEDS.
Oral medications showed a borderline significant trend toward worsening muscle pain in patients with hEDS.
Exercise and physical therapy significantly improved muscle pain in patients with HSD.
Referrals to acupuncture, optometry, or genetics were perceived as beneficial by roughly three-quarters of both hEDS and HSD patients.
Perceived benefit from psychology referral differed substantially by diagnosis, with more hEDS patients reporting benefit than HSD patients, a substantial minority of whom reported worsening.
Perceived benefit from the pain rehabilitation program referral differed by diagnosis, with more HSD patients reporting benefit than hEDS patients.

Referrals to allergy/immunology and rheumatology were the most negatively perceived referrals, with a substantial proportion of both hEDS and HSD patients reporting that these referrals worsened their symptoms.
Patients with hEDS/HSD are described in the literature as having local anesthetic (lidocaine) resistance, with a high proportion reporting complete, partial, or rapidly waning anesthetic effect.
Patients with hEDS/HSD are reported in the literature to have elevated mast cell activity, which may increase risk of adverse reactions to topical medications.

The hypermobile group showed significantly greater absolute angular errors (worse proprioceptive accuracy) than the non-hypermobile group on elbow and knee joint position sense testing at both 30° and 60°.
Grip strength did not differ significantly between hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups.
Functional performance measures (CKCUEST and CKCLEST) did not differ significantly between hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups.
Higher Beighton scores were moderately, positively correlated with greater grip strength within the hypermobile group.
Higher Beighton scores were moderately, positively correlated with greater knee joint position sense error (worse proprioception) at both 30° and 60° flexion.
Beighton score showed no significant correlation with closed kinetic chain upper or lower extremity stability performance (CKCUEST, CKCLEST).
Just over half of patients with EDS or G-HSD reported clinically significant pain severity (55%) and pain interference (57%).
Alcohol use was reported by 59% of the sample, and 18% reported prescription opioid use.
Cannabis use was reported by 48% of patients, with 69% of cannabis users consuming it four or more times per week.
14% of patients used cigarettes, smoking a median of 8.0 cigarettes per day (IQR = 4.0-12.0).
Greater pain severity and interference were positively correlated with more frequent and higher quantity cannabis use.
Greater pain severity and interference were positively correlated with prescription opioid use.
Greater pain severity and interference were positively correlated with cigarette use.
Greater pain severity and interference were associated with lower alcohol use among EDS/G-HSD patients.

A Welsh healthcare records study reported EDS prevalence of approximately 1 in 500 (0.2%), higher than earlier estimates of 1 in 5,000, suggesting prior figures underestimated true prevalence, particularly for hEDS.
Classical EDS, driven by COL5A1/COL5A2 mutations, is estimated to occur in approximately 1 in 20,000 to 40,000 individuals.
Vascular EDS, caused by COL3A1 mutations, is estimated to affect about 1 in 100,000 to 200,000 people.
Arthrochalasia EDS is an exceptionally rare subtype with approximately 42 documented cases worldwide.
EDS patients are more prone to recurrent headaches than the general population, with 75% of the EDS population affected.
POTS and gastrointestinal disturbances such as gastroparesis frequently co-occur in EDS patients.
Small fibre neuropathy in EDS subtypes (hEDS, vEDS, cEDS) is confirmed by reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density on skin biopsies and drives neuropathic pain and autonomic symptoms.
Periventricular heterotopia (misplaced neurons from faulty migration) occurs in some EDS cases and is associated with epilepsy, developmental delay, and cognitive impairment.

Periodontal EDS shows white matter abnormalities and small vessel disease (leukoencephalopathy) on MRI, suggesting microvascular fragility, with variable clinical penetrance ranging from minimal symptoms to cognitive decline, ataxia, or seizures.

Neuroimaging in individuals with joint hypermobility shows reduced grey matter volume in midline cortical regions including the anterior cingulate cortex, a region implicated in pain and emotional regulation.
In anxious patients with JHS/hEDS, insular volume was found to be larger and linked to peak heart rate on standing.
Amygdala volume was found to be related to both degree of hypermobility and interoceptive accuracy in anxious JHS/hEDS patients.
Participants with hypermobility exhibited reduced neural responses to emotional faces in the inferior frontal gyrus and anterior cingulate cortex.
Individuals with both hypermobility and generalised anxiety disorder showed increased activity in the left amygdala and mid-insula, regions associated with threat processing and interoception.
The severity of hypermobility in anxious individuals correlated with heightened anterior insula activity.
Garcia Campayo et al. found a high prevalence of hEDS (61.8%) among subjects with panic disorder compared with 10.9% among healthy controls.
A meta-analysis found that individuals with hEDS experience significantly greater fear intensity and a higher probability of agoraphobia and panic disorders.
A large-scale Swedish study found a higher risk of mood disorders, anorexia nervosa, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and addiction among individuals with EDS.

Pasquini et al. observed a higher rate of depressive symptoms in JHS/hEDS patients compared to controls, but anxiety was not controlled for, raising the possibility that elevated depression scores partly reflect underlying anxiety.
Hershenfeld et al. reported a 42.5% prevalence of psychiatric disorders, especially depression and anxiety, in a retrospective sample of JHS/hEDS subjects.
Individuals with hEDS show markedly reduced muscle endurance and strength despite normal muscle mass, suggesting intrinsic neuromuscular inefficiency.
A 30-year study by Pepin et al. identified vascular complications, including arterial dissections and ruptures, as a primary cause of death in vEDS patients.
Despite elevated risk of vascular anomalies, vEDS patients exhibit a paradoxically lower incidence of ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes compared to the general population.

Hallam et al. noted increased amygdala activation in response to auditory stressors combined with reduced inhibition from the orbitofrontal cortex, suggesting a breakdown of automatic emotional modulation.
A novel splice-donor site variant in COL3A1 (c.2337+2T>G) was identified and confirmed the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this patient.

The patient experienced three metachronous arterial dissection/aneurysm events (right common iliac artery dissection, carotid-cavernous fistula from a dissecting left internal carotid aneurysm, and right internal iliac artery dissection) over 41 months, ultimately dying of sudden cardiac arrest the day after the third intervention.

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in AEBP1, encoding ACLP, are the known cause of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Classic-Like, 2 (clEDS2), a connective tissue disorder with joint laxity, skin hyperextensibility, osteoporosis and scoliosis.
ACLP interacts with the Wnt receptors FZD8 and LRP6 to activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, establishing a mechanistic link between ACLP and this pathway.
Conditional deletion of Aebp1 in Osx+ osteoprogenitor cells (Aebp1OsxCre mice) produced reduced bone mass and shorter body stature, phenotypically resembling human clEDS2.

With age, Aebp1OsxCre mice developed shortened limbs, reduced trabecular bone volume, bone mineral density, trabecular number and thickness, alongside increased trabecular separation, versus WT littermates.
