Cranial bones of Aebp1OsxCre mice were smaller than WT and OsxCre controls, with more pronounced hypomineralization at the coronal suture and occipital bone.

Aebp1OsxCre mice showed an enlarged Col10a1+ hypertrophic chondrocyte zone at P0 and persistent Col10a1+/Safranin O+ cartilage-like tissue in bone marrow at P3 and in the secondary ossification center at P21, indicating delayed endochondral ossification.
At 6 weeks of age, Aebp1OsxCre femur showed fewer osteoblasts and reduced cortical thickness compared with littermate controls.
Expression of the osteoblast transcription factor Osx (Sp7) and osteopontin (OPN) were markedly diminished in calvaria and long bones of Aebp1OsxCre mice.

Mineral apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate per bone surface (BFR/BS) were significantly diminished in Aebp1OsxCre mice compared with littermate controls, confirming impaired bone formation.

siRNA-mediated Aebp1 knockdown in osteoblasts reduced Sp7, Col1a1, and Runx2 mRNA and ACLP/Col1a1/RUNX2/OCN protein, decreased ALP activity, and completely abrogated mineralized nodule formation in vitro.
Osteocytes in Aebp1OsxCre mice showed reduced dendrite number and length, consistent with disrupted osteocyte connectivity and impaired mechanosensing.
Serum levels of the bone resorption markers CTX-1 and TRAP were significantly higher in Aebp1OsxCre mice than in littermate controls.
Aebp1OsxCre mice showed increased osteoclast number per bone perimeter and osteoclast surface area, with a larger TRAP+ area in whole-mount skull staining, compared with controls.
Osteoclast-related genes Ctsk, Acp5, Nfatc1, and Tnfsf11 (RANKL) were significantly upregulated in bone from Aebp1OsxCre mice.

Expression of Tnfrsf11a (RANK) and Tnfrsf11b (OPG) was unchanged between Aebp1OsxCre and control bone, suggesting mechanisms other than the classical RANK/OPG axis contribute to increased osteoclastogenesis.

In osteoblast-osteoclast coculture, osteoblasts derived from Aebp1OsxCre mice showed an enhanced ability to support osteoclastogenesis, evidenced by increased giant multinucleated TRAP+ osteoclast formation.

scRNA-Seq of Aebp1OsxCre osteoblasts revealed downregulated genes enriched in cartilage development, chondrocyte differentiation, bone development, endochondral ossification, and type I collagen formation.
Pseudotime analysis showed Aebp1OsxCre osteoblast-lineage cells enriched in early differentiation states (1-3) while WT cells predominated in later states (4-6), suggesting a differentiation block.

Csf1r+Tnfrsf11a+ monocyte/osteoclast-precursor cluster in Aebp1OsxCre mice showed upregulated Type I interferon signaling genes, raising the hypothesis that an IFN-I-primed precursor state contributes to increased osteoclast indices.

Bulk RNA-Seq of humeral and femoral bone showed downregulation of genes involved in skeletal system formation, ossification, osteoblast differentiation, and Wnt signaling in Aebp1OsxCre mice, with GSEA showing Wnt gene sets enriched in Aebp1fl/fl controls.

Wnt signaling genes Ctnnb1, Tcf7, Lrp5, and Fzd5 were markedly diminished in cranial bone RNA-Seq of Aebp1OsxCre mice, alongside downregulation of osteoblast markers Alpl, Sp7, Runx2, Col1a1, and Ibsp.
β-Catenin protein was markedly reduced in P0 long bones of Aebp1OsxCre mice, with reduced Axin2 and Ccnd1 (canonical Wnt readouts) and reduced Lrp5/Lrp6 expression.
Treatment of MC3T3-E1 osteoblast cells with recombinant ACLP increased β-catenin protein levels compared with control, supporting a direct role for ACLP in sustaining Wnt/β-catenin signaling.

Pharmacological GSK3β inhibition with BIO to stabilize β-catenin substantially ameliorated skeletal abnormalities, restored trabecular bone mass, osteoblast numbers, cortical thickness, mineralization, and reduced osteoclast hyperactivity and hypertrophic chondrocyte expansion in Aebp1OsxCre mice.
Biallelic mutations in the human AEBP1 gene are established as the genetic cause of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Classic-Like, 2 (clEDS2).
ACLP has previously been shown to bind the Wnt receptors FZD8 and LRP6, activating canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
Aebp1OsxCre mice showed a significant reduction in both the number and length of osteocyte dendrites compared with littermate controls, consistent with disrupted osteocyte connectivity.

The authors hypothesize that disrupted osteocyte dendritic morphology in Aebp1OsxCre mice may lead to dysregulated sclerostin (SOST) production, further impairing Wnt/β-catenin signaling, though this remains untested.

Csf1r+Tnfrsf11a+ osteoclast-precursor monocytes from Aebp1OsxCre mice showed significant upregulation of Type I interferon signaling genes (Bst2, Irf7, Irf9, Ifit1, Ifit2, Isg15, Mx2) compared with controls.
In cranial tissue bulk RNA-Seq, Wnt signaling genes Ctnnb1, Tcf7, Lrp5, and Fzd5 exhibited markedly diminished expression in Aebp1OsxCre mice compared with Aebp1fl/fl controls.
Deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-Seq using the scRNA-Seq reference indicated a higher proportion of osteoblasts in humeral and femoral samples of Aebp1fl/fl mice compared with Aebp1OsxCre mice.

Unlike other osteoclast-related genes, expression levels of Tnfrsf11a (RANK) and Tnfrsf11b (OPG) remained unchanged in Aebp1OsxCre mice, suggesting other mechanisms underlie enhanced osteoclastogenesis.

In wild-type mice, the same BIO treatment regimen produced no discernible alteration in basal bone formation, suggesting Wnt pathway activation is most effective under conditions of existing signaling deficit.

ACLP has also been identified in prior work as a liver-expressed ligand that activates the canonical Wnt pathway and exacerbates nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) pathology, indicating Aebp1's Wnt-amplifying role extends across tissue contexts.

Prior global Aebp1 knockout mouse studies showed embryonic lethality due to abdominal fissures and curled tails, leaving the precise skeletal phenotype of ACLP deficiency previously unclear due to widespread expression in muscle and ligament.

The study did not observe overt scoliosis in the Aebp1OsxCre colony, but this negative observation is interpreted cautiously since the bone-focused Osx-lineage model does not directly probe soft-tissue contributions to axial deformity.
Arthroscopic all-inside repair of popliteomeniscal fascicle tears significantly improved subjective IKDC scores from a mean of 60.2 preoperatively to 83.1 at two-year follow-up.
The Tegner Activity Scale score significantly improved from a preoperative mean of 2.9 to 6.5 at two-year follow-up after PMF repair.
The Lysholm knee score significantly improved from a preoperative mean of 56.72 to 89.8 postoperatively after PMF repair.

Post-traumatic injury of the popliteomeniscal fascicles is described as one of the most frequent causes of a hypermobile lateral meniscus, producing knee pain and a locking sensation during deep flexion.
The paper reports that popliteomeniscal fascicle tears co-occur with ACL/posterolateral corner injury in a high proportion of cases and with lateral meniscal tears in about a fifth of patients.

In this cohort, all four patients found to have chondral lesions of the lateral femoral condyle had a delay of more than 12 months between symptom onset and surgery, suggesting delayed repair may be associated with chondral damage.
The majority of patients returned to their pre-injury level of sports activity after arthroscopic all-inside repair of popliteomeniscal fascicle tears.
Both spiral stabilization and core stabilization exercise programs produced significant within-group improvements in Cobb angle, trunk aesthetics, and clinical outcomes after treatment.
Spiral stabilization exercises produced significantly greater improvement in Cobb angle than core stabilization exercises.
Spiral stabilization exercises led to significantly greater improvement in trunk rotation (angle of trunk rotation) compared with core stabilization exercises.
Spiral stabilization exercises resulted in significantly greater improvement in clavicle angle compared with core stabilization exercises.
Spiral stabilization exercises produced significantly greater improvement in pelvic obliquity than core stabilization exercises.
Spiral stabilization exercises produced significantly greater improvement in self-image (measured by the SRS-22 questionnaire) than core stabilization exercises.

Joint hypermobility, as measured by the Beighton score, correlated positively with the degree of Cobb angle correction, suggesting greater flexibility is modestly associated with better treatment response in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
HRV coherence was significantly lower in children/adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia compared to healthy controls, suggesting impaired autonomic regulation.
A family history of fibromyalgia was significantly more common among JFM patients than among healthy controls.
Chronic disease among family members was significantly more frequent in the JFM group than in controls.
Anxiety symptom severity, measured by the MASC-2, was significantly higher in JFM patients than in controls, with two-thirds of JFM patients scoring in the elevated range.
Within the JFM cohort, HRV coherence was negatively correlated with MASC-2 anxiety scores, indicating that more severe anxiety was associated with poorer autonomic regulation.
Logistic regression showed that reduced HRV was a significant predictor of JFM diagnosis even after adjusting for age and sex, suggesting potential diagnostic utility.
JFM patients showed a mean symptom onset around 8.9 years of age, mean diagnosis age of 10.8 years, and a diagnostic delay of nearly 2 years.
In the JFM cohort, mean Widespread Pain Index and Symptom Severity Scale scores exceeded diagnostic thresholds, and mean pain intensity on the NRS was 6.47.
There were no significant differences in age or sex distribution between the JFM group and healthy controls, confirming adequate matching.

Across the combined sample of functional motor disorder and fibromyalgia patients and controls, lower prepulse inhibition was significantly associated with higher fibromyalgia symptom severity scores.
In patients with functional motor disorder, prepulse inhibition magnitude was not associated with objectively rated motor symptom severity.

The authors propose that impaired early subcortical sensory processing, indexed by abnormal prepulse inhibition, may serve as a transdiagnostic marker of fibromyalgianess across functional motor disorder and fibromyalgia.
There was no significant difference in harmonised locus coeruleus MRI signal intensity between participants with fibromyalgia and healthy controls.
In healthy controls, LC signal intensity was significantly positively correlated with age, replicating prior literature, but this age relationship was not observed in fibromyalgia participants.

Participants with fibromyalgia had significantly higher scores than healthy controls on measures of fibromyalgia impact, cognitive complaints, central sensitization, depression, anxiety, and insomnia.
Within fibromyalgia patients, LC signal intensity was not associated with time since symptom onset or time since diagnosis, controlling for age.

Within fibromyalgia participants, LC signal intensity was not correlated with fibromyalgia symptom severity (FIQR total), pain intensity (FIQR item 12), central sensitization symptoms (CSI), insomnia (ISI), anxiety (GAD-7), or depressive symptoms (QIDS-SR), controlling for age.

LC signal intensity showed no significant association with subjective cognitive complaints (CFQ) or objective cognitive performance (THINC-it subtests) in fibromyalgia participants, healthy controls, or the pooled sample, controlling for age.
There was no significant group by age interaction on LC signal intensity between fibromyalgia and healthy controls, though a trend-level main effect of age on LC signal was observed across the model.
Urinary percentage excretion of lactulose (%Lac) was significantly higher in FM+IBS patients than in FM or IBS patients alone.
The Lac/Man ratio, a marker of paracellular intestinal permeability, was significantly higher in FM+IBS patients compared to IBS patients alone.
Urinary sucrose excretion, a marker of gastric/proximal small intestinal permeability, did not differ between FM, IBS, and FM+IBS groups.
Serum zonulin levels did not differ significantly between the FM, IBS, and FM+IBS groups.
Fecal zonulin levels were significantly higher in FM+IBS patients than in FM or IBS patients alone, indicating the most severe paracellular barrier disruption in the comorbid phenotype.
Serum I-FABP, a marker of enterocyte/epithelial injury, was significantly elevated in FM+IBS patients compared to FM patients.

Urinary indole, a marker of gut dysbiosis, was significantly higher in FM+IBS patients than IBS patients, and non-significantly higher than in FM patients despite a stated p-value below 0.05, indicating an inconsistency in the reported statistics.
Lac/Man ratio was positively correlated with urinary indole levels across the combined patient sample, supporting a link between dysbiosis and paracellular permeability.
%Lac, but not %Man, correlated positively with urinary indole levels, supporting the idea that dysbiosis specifically alters the paracellular pathway and compromises tight junctions.
Body mass index (BMI) was positively correlated with CRP levels across the sample, suggesting a link between adiposity and systemic inflammation.
BMI was inversely correlated with the Global Physical Capacity Score, linking higher adiposity to lower physical capacity.
In multivariable regression, membership in the higher Global Physical Capacity Score group was significantly associated with lower serum zonulin levels, independent of BMI.

When stratified by physical capacity, patients in the low physical capacity group had significantly higher serum zonulin levels than those in the high physical capacity group, across all diagnostic groups combined.
IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS) was significantly lower in the FM-only group compared to both the IBS and FM+IBS groups, which showed moderate severity.
Fibromyalgia symptom severity (FIQ-R) did not differ significantly between the FM-only and FM+IBS groups.
Baseline Global Physical Capacity Score did not differ significantly among the FM, IBS, and FM+IBS groups.

Fibromyalgia syndrome affects roughly 2-4% of the adult population worldwide, with women constituting 80-90% of diagnosed cases in North American and European registries, though referral/diagnostic bias may underestimate cases in men.

In the authors' previous study, twice-daily prickly pear consumption by women with fibromyalgia was associated with significant reductions in reported pain severity and improvements in quality-of-life indices.

Betalain pigments from prickly pear (betanin, indicaxanthin) downregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, which are central to nociceptor sensitization and immune-driven pain amplification.

Indicaxanthin, the dominant yellow betaxanthin in prickly pear, crosses the blood-brain barrier and modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and redox balance in neural tissue, suggesting a potential role in reducing central sensitization in fibromyalgia.
Coenzyme Q10 has shown potential as an adjunctive nutraceutical to alleviate pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia by enhancing mitochondrial function and attenuating inflammatory pathways.

Small randomized trials suggest that nutraceutical blends such as olive-based supplements combined with anti-inflammatory dietary strategies may reduce pain and fatigue severity in women with fibromyalgia.
Pregabalin, duloxetine, and milnacipran are the only FDA-approved medications for fibromyalgia, but their effectiveness is limited and varies among patients.
Red prickly pear cultivars are generally richer in betacyanins, while yellow cultivars contain higher levels of indicaxanthin, the betaxanthin shown to cross the blood-brain barrier.
Gastrointestinal disturbances including nausea, bloating, altered bowel habits, and abdominal discomfort are frequent among individuals with fibromyalgia.
Patients with chronic kidney disease may be at risk from regular prickly pear intake due to potential disruptions in potassium homeostasis and related electrolyte imbalances.

Cold storage of prickly pear fruit preserves bioactive compounds and antioxidant activity, though it may reduce fruit mass, underscoring the importance of standardized post-harvest handling for clinical use.

A single sublingual dose of THC significantly reduced spontaneous pain ratings on the McGill Pain Questionnaire compared with placebo in fibromyalgia patients, with no significant effect of time or treatment order.
THC significantly enhanced offset analgesia (OA) magnitude compared with placebo, indicating stronger cortically-mediated central pain modulation.
The OA index (normalized magnitude of offset analgesia) was significantly higher after THC than placebo, with a greater pre-to-post increase under THC (Treatment × Time interaction).

THC administration did not significantly alter conditioned pain modulation (CPM) magnitude compared with placebo, indicating no effect on brainstem-mediated descending pain inhibition in fibromyalgia.

Baseline offset analgesia (OA) magnitude was significantly and positively correlated with the reduction in McGill pain scores following THC treatment, suggesting OA as a predictive biomarker of THC analgesic response.
Baseline OA index similarly correlated significantly with the change in McGill scores after THC treatment, with higher OA index values corresponding to greater pain reduction.

Baseline OA magnitude did not significantly predict the change in McGill scores following placebo treatment, indicating that the predictive relationship is not simply a general placebo-response marker.

Baseline OA magnitude did not significantly predict the net THC effect (ΔMcGill THC minus ΔMcGill placebo), suggesting OA does not exclusively capture the isolated pharmacological component of THC analgesia once placebo effects are removed.
Baseline CPM magnitude showed a non-significant negative correlation with THC-induced pain reduction (ΔMcGill), contrasting with the significant predictive relationship found for OA.
Three participants withdrew from the study after their first THC session due to non-severe but intolerable side effects, while no significant side effects were reported after placebo administration.
Pain-related stigma was significantly associated with worse physical functioning across youth with JIA, JFM, and NSCP.
Pain-related stigma was significantly associated with worse social functioning across youth with JIA, JFM, and NSCP.
Pain-related stigma was associated with worse emotional functioning specifically among girls, indicating a gender-moderated effect.
Girls with chronic musculoskeletal pain reported worse overall emotional functioning and greater symptoms of anxiety and depression than boys.

Youth with Juvenile Primary Fibromyalgia Syndrome (JFM) and non-specific chronic pain (NSCP) showed lower functioning across domains compared to youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), regardless of stigma level.
Despite high-intensity warfarin dosing with a supratherapeutic INR of 6.0, the patient developed a new acute right upper extremity DVT, indicating anticoagulation failure in high-risk APS.
The patient had previously failed multiple direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, fondaparinux) for prevention of recurrent thrombosis related to APS.
The patient experienced bleeding complications while on enoxaparin (Lovenox) therapy.

Skewed or incomplete X chromosome inactivation can cause overexpression of X-linked immune genes such as TLR7, CD40L, and IRAK1, enhancing innate and adaptive immune responses and potentially contributing to female predominance in autoimmune and mast cell disorders.
Mast cell activation is proposed to contribute to vascular instability and medication hypersensitivity, complicating individualized treatment planning in this patient.

Hereditary angioedema, caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency/dysfunction, produced visceral edema and GI dysmotility that led to enteral feeding intolerance and prolonged central venous access dependence, increasing thromboembolic risk.
The patient had a documented history of dysautonomia with inappropriate sinus tachycardia as part of her complex comorbid presentation.
The patient's gastroparesis required chronic total parenteral nutrition, necessitating long-term central venous access that contributed to thrombotic and infectious risk.
Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus epidermidis, consistent with recurrent line-associated infection related to the patient's chronic central venous access for TPN.

Complement inhibitors such as eculizumab have been reported as salvage therapy for APS or recurrent thrombosis unresponsive to standard treatment, with case reports and small series suggesting benefit, though this was not administered to the described patient.
Endoscopic placement of a Corpak feeding tube failed due to intragastric looping and the tube was subsequently removed, leaving the patient dependent on TPN via a temporary catheter.
The patient experienced six episodes of green-brown diarrhea over 24 hours during hospitalization, attributed to prolonged nil per os status rather than infectious colitis.

The case describes overlapping treatment-refractory APS, hereditary angioedema, mast cell activation syndrome, dysautonomia, gastroparesis, and bilateral venous compression syndromes (TOS/SVCS) in a single patient, requiring multidisciplinary management.
APS-related thrombosis is described as being driven by endothelial activation, complement-mediated injury, and upregulation of tissue factor expression, sustaining a chronic hypercoagulable state.

The authors state that systemic autoimmune and prothrombotic disorders have higher prevalence and severity in females, likely influenced by hormonal, genetic, and epigenetic factors modulating immune tolerance and vascular reactivity.
Allergen-IgE complexes crosslink FcεRI receptors on mast cells, triggering calcium influx and mediator release, the classical mechanism of anaphylaxis.
Non-IgE-mediated mast cell activation in anaphylaxis can arise from direct pharmacologic triggers (opioids, vancomycin, radiocontrast media) or complement activation and pseudoallergic mechanisms.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, marked by loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and excess ROS, amplify mast cell mediator release during anaphylaxis.

Experimental data link cardiomyocyte mitochondrial impairment to left ventricular dysfunction and lipid peroxidation during anaphylactic shock, indicating a systemic metabolic and inflammatory process.

Galectin-9 regulates mast cell degranulation, and endogenous sulfur dioxide inhibits this process by sulfenylating Gal-9 at cysteine 74, a mechanism reversible by SO2 supplementation in experimental models.
Short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate and valerate suppress IgE-mediated mast cell activation via GPR109A signaling and enhanced PGE2 release.
Mast cells release mediators via compound exocytosis, a process where secretory granules fuse before releasing histamine, tryptase, heparin, and cytokines.
Mast cell-derived heparin provides negatively charged surfaces that facilitate factor XII binding and auto-activation, linking mast cell degranulation to the contact and coagulation pathways.

Intramuscular epinephrine at 0.01 mg/kg (1:1,000, max 0.5 mg) into the anterolateral thigh is the only medication proven to reduce mortality in pediatric anaphylaxis, but underuse and delayed administration remain problems.

Updated 2023-2024 guidelines recommend weight-tiered epinephrine autoinjector doses: 0.1 mg for 7.5-14 kg, 0.15 mg for 15-29 kg, 0.3 mg for 30-49 kg, and 0.5 mg for ≥50 kg to achieve age-appropriate plasma levels.
About 30-40% of children with anaphylaxis require more than one dose of epinephrine, supporting the need for access to multiple autoinjectors.

Refractory anaphylaxis, occurring in roughly 1% of severe cases despite two IM doses, requires intravenous epinephrine infusion (1 mg in 1,000 mL saline, 0.1 µg/kg/min titrated) under continuous cardiac monitoring.

Sublingual 30 mg epinephrine tablets achieved bioequivalent peak plasma concentrations to IM 0.15 mg epinephrine (16.7±1.9 vs 18.8±1.9 ng/mL) but reached therapeutic levels faster (~21 vs 36 minutes) with improved acceptability in children.
Biphasic anaphylactic reactions occur in 5-20% of cases, usually within four to six hours of initial symptom resolution, informing post-epinephrine observation duration.
Serum tryptase, though the most established biomarker for anaphylaxis, may remain normal in food-related cases or in those treated early with epinephrine, limiting its diagnostic sensitivity.
Cannabidiol significantly inhibits IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation by suppressing FcεRI downstream signaling and calcium mobilization, independent of cannabinoid receptors.
Probiotic Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains attenuate mast cell degranulation and reduce total IgE levels in experimental models.
Vancomycin-induced DRESS syndrome, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, carries mortality rates approaching 10%.
β-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins) account for most drug-induced anaphylaxis cases via IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to hapten-protein conjugates.
Epinephrine bioavailability in neonates is about 49% of adult levels, gradually reaching full adult equivalence by approximately two years of age.
Population PK/PD modeling predicts children aged 2-4 years require roughly 40% of adult exposure and those aged 5-9 years require ~70% for therapeutic epinephrine levels.

Recent trials in adolescents demonstrate superior plasma levels and hemodynamic responses with 500 μg versus 300 μg epinephrine autoinjectors, suggesting current pediatric dosing may be inadequate for older children approaching adult weight.
β-blockers can blunt epinephrine's therapeutic effect in anaphylaxis, while antihypertensive agents may modify hemodynamic responses.

Pediatric anaphylaxis incidence and hospital admissions have risen sharply across regions (often a five- to seven-fold rise), with food allergens the dominant trigger, higher rates in boys, and regional/sociodemographic variation.

Age-specific immune and mast cell distribution differences produce different clinical presentations: infants/toddlers show gastrointestinal symptoms while older children show respiratory and cardiovascular manifestations.
Anti-TIM-4 monoclonal antibody administered during the effector phase significantly inhibited airway hyperreactivity to methacholine in an OVA-induced allergic airway inflammation mouse model.

Anti-TIM-4 mAb reduced eosinophil accumulation and IL-13 production in BAL fluid, and eosinophilic infiltration with mucus overproduction in lung tissue, during the effector phase of allergic airway inflammation.

Anti-TIM-4 mAb treatment did not alter serum OVA-specific IgG1, IgG2a, or IgE levels, nor OVA-specific Th2 cytokine (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) production by lymph node cells, indicating TIM-4 blockade acts independently of T or B cell responses.

In a mast cell-dependent airway inflammation model, anti-TIM-4 mAb significantly inhibited eosinophil accumulation, eosinophilia, mucus overproduction, and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) in BAL fluid, without affecting serum OVA-specific antibodies.

Soluble TIM-4 was detected in the culture supernatants of TIM-4-transfected murine cell lines (L5178Y and NRK) but not untransfected cells, and this shedding was blocked by the MMP inhibitor BB-94, indicating MMP-dependent proteolytic generation of sTIM-4.

Primary mouse peritoneal macrophages showed decreased surface TIM-4 and increased sTIM-4 in culture supernatants after 24h, an effect blocked by BB-94, indicating macrophages are a physiological source of sTIM-4.
Mice with allergic airway inflammation had significantly higher levels of sTIM-4 in BAL fluid and sera than naïve mice.
sTIM-4-containing supernatant from TIM-4-transfected cells significantly enhanced FcεRI-stimulated IL-6 and IL-13 production by bone marrow-derived mast cells, an effect blocked by anti-TIM-4 mAb.

TIM-4-Fc fusion protein induced IL-6 and IL-13 production by mast cells in the absence of IgE and further enhanced FcεRI-stimulated cytokine production, but PD-L2-Fc and mouse IgG2a controls had no effect.

TIM-4-Fc did not induce β-hexosaminidase release (degranulation marker) from IgE-sensitized mast cells, and anti-TIM-4 mAb pretreatment did not inhibit passive cutaneous anaphylaxis, indicating sTIM-4 regulates cytokine production without promoting degranulation.
Bone marrow-derived mast cells expressed CD300b and TIM-3 but not TIM-1, TIM-2, or TIM-4, and bound TIM-4-Fc in a manner blocked by anti-TIM-4 mAb.

Cd300lb (CD300b) siRNA knockdown in BMMCs reduced surface CD300b expression and significantly decreased TIM-4-Fc-induced IL-6 and IL-13 production, and Cd300lb-/- BMMCs also produced less cytokine in response to TIM-4-Fc than wild-type, without affecting normal mast cell development.
TIM-4-Fc bound to NRK cells transfected with either C57BL/6- or BALB/c-type TIM-3, and this binding was inhibited by anti-TIM-4 mAb, identifying TIM-3 as a novel TIM-4 receptor.

Knockdown or knockout of TIM-3 in BMMCs significantly increased TIM-4-Fc-induced IL-6 and IL-13 production compared with controls, indicating TIM-3 normally inhibits TIM-4-CD300b-mediated cytokine production; this enhancement was reversed by anti-TIM-4 mAb.

The enhanced cytokine production seen in Tim3-/- BMMCs stimulated with TIM-4-Fc was significantly reduced by Cd300lb siRNA knockdown, indicating that CD300b is the dominant signaling pathway mediating TIM-4-induced mast cell cytokine production even in the absence of TIM-3.

Human TIM-4-transfected K562 cells generated soluble TIM-4 in culture supernatants via metalloproteinase-dependent cleavage, suppressed by BB-94, and human LAD2 mast cells (which express CD300b) produced significantly more IL-6 when cultured with TIM-4/K562 supernatants than mock supernatants, an effect blocked by anti-TIM-4 mAb.
In 124 asthma patients, serum sTIM-4 levels correlated positively with age, age at asthma onset, and V50/V25 ratio, and negatively with measures of airflow limitation (FVC, FEV1, PEF, V50, V25, MMF).
Serum sTIM-4 was significantly higher in patients with severe asthma (GINA step 4-5) than moderate asthma (step 3), but not significantly different between severe and mild asthma (step 1-2).

Serum sTIM-4 levels were significantly higher in asthma patients receiving high-dose inhaled corticosteroids compared with low-dose, and in patients previously treated with omalizumab compared with those not treated.
Oral minocycline (100 mg/day) for acne caused delayed-onset symptomatic dermographism, with recurrence confirmed on prolonged rechallenge at the therapeutic dose after nine consecutive days.
Doxycycline was tolerated without cross-reactivity, as shown by negative prick and intradermal skin tests and an uneventful 10-day oral challenge.
A 2-day course of oral cetirizine along with drug discontinuation led to resolution of the minocycline-induced dermographism symptoms.
The authors hypothesize that mast cell activation may underlie the immunopathogenesis of minocycline-induced delayed symptomatic dermographism.
A superantigen-like effect of minocycline is proposed as an alternative possible mechanism for the delayed dermographism reaction.
Participants with intracranial atherosclerosis (ICAS, 55.8% of cohort) were older and had higher systolic/diastolic blood pressure, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia compared to those without ICAS.

Lower heart rate variability, measured as abnormal SDNN on 3-minute ECG dispersion mapping, was independently associated with the presence of intracranial atherosclerosis after adjustment for age, gender, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Atrial myocardial oxygen deficiency, detected via ECG dispersion mapping, was more prevalent in participants with ICAS and remained independently associated with ICAS after adjustment for confounders.
No significant association was found between frequency-domain HRV parameters (high frequency, low frequency, and LF/HF ratio) and the presence of intracranial atherosclerosis.
Abnormal SDNN was not significantly correlated with distinct atherosclerotic plaque imaging features (eccentricity, irregularity, diffuse thickening) on high-resolution MRI.
Participants in the lowest SDNN tertile were older, more likely to have hypertension, and had higher prevalence of intracranial atherosclerosis compared with the highest SDNN tertile group.

The authors propose that reduced short-term daytime HRV and atrial myocardial hypoxia reflect autonomic nervous system dysfunction that disrupts cerebral blood flow autoregulation and endothelial homeostasis, contributing to intracranial atherosclerosis development.
The patient developed isolated small fiber neuropathy with sparing of large nerve fibers following chemotherapy for gastric adenocarcinoma.
The patient experienced progressive cognitive slowing consistent with chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment ('chemobrain') concurrent with small fiber neuropathy.
Autonomic testing revealed severely abnormal sudomotor and microcirculatory responses despite normal nerve conduction studies and brain MRI.
Nerve conduction studies were normal, indicating sparing of large nerve fibers despite small fiber pathology.
Betweenness centrality of pain-associated brain regions was significantly higher in SFN-SCN9A patients compared to healthy controls.
Betweenness centrality of pain-associated brain regions was significantly higher in SFN-SCN9A patients compared to idiopathic SFN patients.
Eigenvector centrality of pain-associated regions was not significantly different in SFN-SCN9A patients compared to healthy controls or idiopathic SFN patients.
The combined SFN group (iSFN and SFN-SCN9A) did not show significant differences in betweenness or eigenvector centrality of pain-associated regions compared to healthy controls.
No significant differences in nodal centrality of pain-associated regions were found between idiopathic SFN patients and healthy controls.
Eigenvector centrality of pain-associated regions showed a trend toward positive correlation with self-reported current pain (VAS) in the combined SFN group.
The relationship between eigenvector centrality of pain-associated regions and current pain differed significantly between iSFN and SFN-SCN9A groups (interaction effect).
Betweenness centrality of pain-associated regions did not show a significant relationship with current pain (VAS score) in either the iSFN or SFN-SCN9A group.
The SFN-SCN9A group had significantly more patients with abnormal intraepidermal nerve fiber density than the idiopathic SFN group.

A gain-of-function variant in SCN9A, encoding the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7, causes dorsal root ganglion neuron hyperexcitability and results in small fiber neuropathy in approximately 5% of SFN patients.

The SENT protocol, incorporating the empirically measured 11% perception threshold noise, could classify Nav1.7 conductance alterations with 92% accuracy at the group level (n=30) but only 50% accuracy at the individual level.
Overall group-level classification accuracy for sodium channel alterations decreased from 91% to 82% to 73% as simulated noise increased from 10% to 20% to 30%.
At the individual (single-patient) simulation level with 10% noise, total accuracy for classifying which sodium channel was altered was only 60%, and accuracy dropped rapidly with higher noise.
Downregulation of Nav1.7 and upregulation of Nav1.9 were harder for the SENT to correctly classify than other sodium channel conductance alterations.

In automated patch-clamp recordings from Nav1.7-expressing HEK293T cells, the SENT pulse shapes produced a very small peak current for the fourth and fifth (long ramp) pulses, matching the in silico model's prediction that Nav1.7 generates little current during slow ramps.
Perception thresholds for the SENT pulse shapes measured in 9 healthy participants were consistent with the in silico predicted AP initiation thresholds, with an average standard deviation of 11%.

The adaptive Psi-marginal method used to estimate perception thresholds produced a much lower standard deviation (11%) than the 85% reported using the conventional Method of Limits in a prior study by Pia et al.

During McGill Pain Questionnaire assessment after SENT stimulation, most healthy participants described the sensation as throbbing, shooting, stabbing, sharp, hot-burning, or tender, regardless of which pulse shape was used.

In silico modeling predicted that the three sodium channel subtypes each produce a unique peak-current pattern across the five SENT pulse shapes, providing the basis for the test's ability to discriminate which channel is altered.

The in silico model's predicted Nav1.7 current in response to the SENT voltage-clamp protocol closely resembled the peak current and current shape measured experimentally in Nav1.7-expressing HEK293T cells.

Among 138 evaluable patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, 79.7% scored ≥11 on the SFNSL (suspected SFN) and 6.5% scored ≥49 (certain SFN), indicating a high burden of small fiber neuropathy-associated symptoms.
72.3% of evaluable patients (107/148) had FAS scores ≥22 indicating fatigue, and 20.9% had scores ≥35 indicating extreme fatigue.
The KSQ general health status score in this Japanese cohort was lower than in a German outpatient cohort and a study of milder cases, indicating worse HRQoL in this population.
Patients taking ≥5 mg/day prednisolone-equivalent OCS had significantly lower KSQ Medication scores than those taking <5 mg/day, indicating greater treatment burden at higher doses.
The proportion of patients with extreme fatigue (FAS ≥35) was significantly higher among those currently receiving OCS compared with those not receiving OCS.
There was no significant difference in the proportion of patients with FAS ≥22 (fatigue) between those receiving and not receiving OCS.
The proportion of patients with SFNSL scores ≥11 (suspected SFN) was significantly higher among those currently receiving OCS compared with those not receiving OCS.
No statistically significant difference was found in the proportion of patients with SFNSL scores ≥49 (certain SFN) between OCS and non-OCS groups, likely due to small numbers.

KSQ general health status score correlated with FAS, SFNSL, KSQ Lung, and KSQ Medication scores, and FAS correlated with KSQ Lung and SFNSL, and SFNSL correlated with KSQ Lung, indicating interrelated systemic symptom burden and HRQoL domains.
Among 117 patients with OCS experience, about half discontinued OCS, most commonly due to symptom improvement, while some discontinued due to concerns about side effects.
Slightly more than half of patients were currently receiving oral corticosteroids for pulmonary sarcoidosis, with about a quarter having previously received them and a quarter never treated.

Compared to a prior Japanese study, this cohort had a higher mean FAS score and greater proportion using OCS, suggesting greater fatigue burden and disease severity in this patient-association-recruited sample.
This cohort showed higher SFNSL scores and a greater proportion of patients with probable/highly probable or certain SFN compared with a prior Japanese study.

Cardiac involvement was more frequently reported in this cohort than in a prior nationwide epidemiological survey, along with a high proportion holding intractable-disease medical certificates and pacemakers, suggesting the study population represents a more severe disease subset.
Adults with type 1 diabetes and lower eGDR (higher insulin resistance) had significantly lower feet ESC values than those with higher eGDR.
Hand ESC was also significantly lower in participants with lower eGDR (higher insulin resistance) compared to those with higher eGDR.
Feet ESC showed a positive Spearman correlation with eGDR, meaning greater insulin sensitivity was associated with better sudomotor function.
Hand ESC also correlated positively with eGDR, though the correlation was weaker than for feet ESC.
In a multiple linear regression model adjusting for age, sex, and diabetes duration, eGDR remained independently associated with feet ESC.
Hypertension was significantly and negatively associated with feet ESC in univariate regression.
HbA1c was significantly and negatively associated with feet ESC in univariate regression, indicating that poorer glycemic control correlates with worse sudomotor function.
Waist-hip ratio was not significantly associated with feet ESC in univariate regression, unlike hypertension, HbA1c, or composite eGDR.
The composite eGDR score showed the strongest positive association with feet ESC among all individual eGDR components, explaining the greatest proportion of variance.

Median eGDR progressively declined across stages of increasing sudomotor neuropathy severity, from no neuropathy to length-dependent to advanced neuropathy, indicating a dose-response relationship between insulin resistance and sudomotor dysfunction.

Multiple logistic regression confirmed a significant relationship between insulin resistance (eGDR) and impaired feet ESC (<70 µS) after adjusting for sex, diabetes duration, smoking, body weight, and skin autofluorescence.
Approximately half of the adult T1D cohort was classified as insulin-resistant using an eGDR cut-off of <7.4 mg/kg/min, consistent with prior reports of 25-50% prevalence in T1D populations.

Skin autofluorescence, reflecting long-term accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, had an independent impact on sudomotor dysfunction in the regression model, suggesting AGEs may mechanistically link chronic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance to nerve impairment.
Among 128 patients evaluated for peripheral neuropathy, 31 had elevated serum neurofilament light chain (27% excluding TTRv carriers), none of whom were asymptomatic TTRv carriers.

The odds of having elevated sNfL were substantially higher in patients with treatable causes of peripheral neuropathy (CIDP, ATTRv pre-treatment) compared to non-treatable causes (CMT, idiopathic, remote CIPN).
In treatment-naïve ATTRv-PN patients with elevated sNfL, levels decreased after starting TTR silencer therapy in all but the most advanced patient, and normalized in four of six.
In treatment-naïve CIDP patients, sNfL levels improved with IVIG treatment and normalized in four of six treated patients.

Three clinically stable CIDP patients had sNfL levels slightly above the age-adjusted normal range, potentially attributable to age-decade transition or mild subclinical activity rather than true elevation.
In a patient with active vasculitic peripheral neuropathy, sNfL dropped from 7.56 to 2.03 pg/mL after treatment.
None of the patients with MMN, anti-MAG neuropathy, or POEMS in this cohort had elevated sNfL, though most were already treated.
In the CMT subgroup, only two patients with CMTx had moderately elevated sNfL while the remainder had normal levels.
None of the patients with idiopathic polyneuropathy had elevated sNfL.
Serum NfL measured with the Roche Elecsys ECLIA assay used in this study correlates strongly with the Quanterix Simoa assay used in most prior published research.

Independent studies show that the Roche Elecsys assay yields NfL concentrations approximately 85% lower than the Quanterix Simoa, Siemens AtellicaIM, and Fujirebio Lumipulse assays despite strong correlation among all four.

Per prior literature cited by the author, sNfL is elevated in many GBS patients at diagnosis, peaks around 14 days, then decreases, though some GBS patients may have normal levels early in the disease course.
PD patients with pain showed significantly lower corneal nerve fiber density compared to both healthy controls and PD patients without pain.
Corneal nerve fiber length was significantly reduced in PD-P patients compared to HC and PD-NP groups.
Corneal nerve fractal dimension was significantly reduced in PD-P patients compared to HC and PD-NP groups.
Corneal nerve parameters showed significant negative correlations with pain severity and anxiety (HAMA) scores in PD patients.
Mediation analysis indicated that anxiety partially mediates the relationship between corneal nerve loss and pain in PD patients.
A principal component combining nerve parameters explained 81.58% of variance and strongly correlated with pain scores.
Logistic regression identified low corneal nerve fiber density (CNFD) as an independent risk factor for pain in Parkinson's disease.
A combination of CNFD, CNFL, and CNFrD effectively discriminated PD patients with pain from those without pain, with an AUC of 0.80.
Polymorphisms of HLA class II genes are identified as genetic risk factors for the development of connective tissue diseases.
The TRAF1-C5 locus is cited as a genetic risk factor for connective tissue diseases.
TNFSF4 gene polymorphisms are cited as genetic risk factors for connective tissue diseases.
Antibodies to MDA5 are highlighted as a genetic/serologic risk marker associated with connective tissue diseases, particularly relevant to dermatomyositis.
Insolation, smoking, and vitamin D deficiency are identified as epigenetic risk factors triggering the onset of connective tissue diseases.
Antibodies to MDA5 have been identified as a genetic/immunologic risk marker associated with connective tissue diseases.
Vitamin D deficiency, along with insolation and smoking, was identified as an epigenetic risk factor contributing to the onset of connective tissue diseases.
Physical therapy, supported by high-level evidence (I, A), improves joint and lung function and reduces fibrosis severity in connective tissue diseases.
UVA-1 phototherapy is the treatment of choice for improving skin elasticity in scleroderma and skin forms of connective tissue disease by inhibiting TGF-beta and collagen synthesis.
Autologous stem cell transplantation has demonstrated effectiveness in refractory forms of connective tissue diseases.
Ultrasound therapy combined with hyaluronidase is indicated for reducing vascular disorders in tissues affected by connective tissue disease.
Pulmonary hypertension develops as a major comorbid complication in 30-40% of patients with systemic scleroderma.
Paraneoplastic syndromes are recorded in 40% of patients with dermatomyositis, representing a major oncological comorbidity.
Epigenetic/environmental factors including insolation, smoking, and vitamin D deficiency were identified as risk factors triggering onset of connective tissue diseases.
Development of targeted drugs inhibiting TGF-β and interleukin-6 is recognized as a promising future direction for treating connective tissue diseases.
The gut microbiome is highlighted as a promising area of future research for connective tissue disease pathogenesis and therapy.
Major treatment challenges identified include resistance to therapy and increased infection risk during immunosuppressive treatment of connective tissue diseases.
Personalization of biomarker-based therapy was reported to improve quality of life in patients with connective tissue diseases.
History of sexual assault was associated with a 69% increased risk of incident functional somatic disorder over 5 years.
Sexual assault was associated with increased risk of single-organ functional somatic disorder.
Sexual assault was strongly associated with a markedly increased risk of multiorgan functional somatic disorder, though the estimate had wide confidence intervals reflecting small case numbers.
Sexual assault was associated with increased risk of functional somatic syndromes (FSS) overall.
Sexual assault was associated with increased risk of incident chronic widespread pain.
Sexual assault was not significantly associated with incident irritable bowel syndrome.
Sexual assault was not significantly associated with incident chronic fatigue.
Individuals exposed to sexual assault reported a significantly higher frequency of incident somatic symptoms across multiple body systems compared to unexposed individuals.
Baseline emotional distress (e.g., anxiety or depression) did not modify the association between sexual assault and functional somatic disorder.

A sensitivity analysis using diagnostic interview-based ascertainment of functional somatic disorder cases, rather than questionnaire-based ascertainment, confirmed the main study results linking sexual assault to incident functional somatic disorders.
8 weeks of high-fat diet increased body weight in both WT (+28%) and TLR4-knockout (+10%) mice compared to standard diet.
TLR4-knockout mice showed delayed onset of HFD-induced weight gain (beginning at week 5) compared to WT mice, which gained weight from the start of HFD exposure.
WT mice fed HFD showed elevated plasma glucose (+20%), triglycerides (+48%), and cholesterol (+40%) compared to SD-fed WT mice.
TLR4-knockout mice on HFD showed increased triglycerides (+58%) and cholesterol (+25%) but no change in glucose, unlike WT mice.
HFD increased TNFα, IL-1β, and IL-6 mRNA and protein levels in the small intestine of WT mice compared to SD-fed WT mice, indicating gut inflammation.
TLR4-knockout mice showed elevated baseline pro-inflammatory cytokines compared to WT under standard diet, but these were unaffected by 8 weeks of HFD.
Under standard diet, TLR4-knockout mice had a significantly lower geometric center (delayed GI transit) than WT mice, with delayed gastric emptying and reduced fecal output/water content.
HFD prolonged GI transit time (reduced geometric center) only in WT mice, not in TLR4-knockout mice.
WT mice fed HFD showed reduced gastric emptying, stool expulsion frequency, and fecal water content compared to SD-fed WT mice.
HFD reduced stomach and caecum weight and small intestine/colon length in both WT and TLR4-knockout mice.
HFD reduced carbachol-induced maximal contractility (Emax) by 32% in WT ileal segments compared to SD-fed WT mice.
TLR4-knockout mice had lower baseline CCh-mediated contraction than WT mice, and this was not further altered by HFD.
HFD attenuated electrical field stimulation-evoked contractions at 40 Hz in both genotypes, by 42% in WT and 34% in TLR4-knockout mice.
HFD caused a 33% reduction in EFS-evoked (10 Hz) cholinergic contraction in WT ileum, indicating impaired enteric cholinergic neurotransmission.
HFD significantly reduced ChAT immunofluorescence (-14%) and disrupted myenteric cholinergic network architecture in WT mice only, with no changes in TLR4-knockout mice.

Under baseline standard diet, TLR4-knockout mice showed NANC relaxation mediated by both iNOS and nNOS (1.3-fold increase sensitive to 1400W and L-NAME), whereas WT relaxation was almost entirely nNOS-dependent.
HFD significantly reduced the inhibitory NANC relaxation response in WT mice compared to WT SD (-26±1%).
HFD also reduced inhibitory NANC response in TLR4-knockout mice (-24±2%), but 1400W (iNOS inhibitor) did not further alter the response, unlike in WT.
TLR4-knockout mice on standard diet had significantly fewer nNOS+ myenteric neurons than WT SD mice (-26±1%).
HFD decreased the number of nNOS+ neurons by 23% in WT myenteric ganglia, with only minor, non-significant changes in TLR4-knockout mice.
Neuronal loss in the myenteric plexus following HFD was evident exclusively in WT mice, not in TLR4-knockout mice.
TLR4-knockout mice on standard diet showed increased S100β (+79±2%) and GFAP (+15±1%) density indices compared to WT SD mice, indicating a baseline reactive gliosis phenotype.
TLR4-knockout mice showed a reduction in total HuC/D+ myenteric neurons compared to WT SD mice, in addition to reactive gliosis.
HFD induced reactive gliosis in WT mice, shown by a 2.4-fold increase in S100β and 1.2-fold increase in GFAP immunoreactivity.
In TLR4-knockout mice, HFD reduced (normalized) S100β (-25±2%) and GFAP (-33±2%) immunoreactivity, in contrast to the increase seen in WT.
HFD increased the total number of SOX10+ glial cells in the myenteric plexus in all experimental groups regardless of genotype.
Ileal 5-HT levels were significantly higher in TLR4-knockout mice compared to WT controls at baseline.

Under standard diet conditions, TLR4-deficient mice showed higher S100β and GFAP density indices in myenteric ganglia than wild-type SD mice, indicating a baseline reactive gliosis phenotype in enteric glial cells associated with loss of TLR4 signaling.
TLR4-deficient myenteric ganglia showed a modest reduction in total HuC/D+ neuron numbers compared with WT SD mice, indicating a baseline difference in enteric neuron density between genotypes.
High-fat diet induced reactive gliosis in wild-type mice, shown by large increases in S100β and GFAP immunoreactivity in myenteric ganglia compared with WT standard-diet mice.
In contrast to wild-type mice, high-fat diet appeared to normalize enteric gliosis in TLR4-deficient mice, reducing S100β and GFAP immunoreactivity relative to TLR4-/- standard-diet controls.
High-fat diet led to an overall increase in the total number of SOX10+ enteric glial cells in the myenteric plexus in both wild-type and TLR4-deficient mice.
At baseline, ileal 5-HT tissue levels were significantly higher in TLR4-deficient mice than in wild-type controls.

High-fat diet significantly increased ileal 5-HT levels in wild-type mice, whereas no significant change occurred in TLR4-deficient mice, suggesting TLR4-dependent modulation of diet-induced serotonergic changes.

Ileal segments from HFD-fed wild-type mice showed significantly enhanced contractile responses to low-dose (0.3 μM) exogenous 5-HT compared with SD-fed controls, while responses to higher concentrations were unchanged.
At baseline, TLR4-deficient ileal segments showed an overall increase in 5-HT-induced contraction compared with wild-type, shown by an upward shift of the concentration-response curve.
High-fat diet significantly reduced the 5-HT-mediated contractile response in TLR4-deficient ileal segments compared with TLR4-deficient standard-diet controls.
Blood TGFB1 gene expression was significantly lower in RA-ILD patients compared with RA-nonILD patients.
Blood TGFB2 gene expression was significantly lower in RA-ILD patients compared with RA-nonILD patients.
Blood TGFB1 gene expression was significantly lower in SSc-ILD patients compared with SSc-nonILD patients.
Blood TGFB2 gene expression was significantly lower in SSc-ILD patients compared with SSc-nonILD patients.
Blood PDGFA gene expression was significantly lower in RA-ILD patients compared with RA-nonILD patients.
IM-ILD and IM-nonILD patients showed similar blood expression of PDGFA, TGFB1, and TGFB2.
TGFB3 blood gene expression did not differ significantly between any CTD-ILD group and their respective CTD-nonILD comparators (RA, SSc, IM).
IM-ILD patients had significantly higher blood PDGFA and TGFB2 expression than IPF patients.
TGFB1 and TGFB3 blood expression did not differ significantly between IM-ILD and IPF patients.
RA-ILD and SSc-ILD patients showed similar blood expression of PDGFA, TGFB1, TGFB2, and TGFB3 compared with IPF patients, unlike IM-ILD.
ROC analysis showed PDGFA blood expression discriminates RA-ILD from RA-nonILD patients with acceptable accuracy (AUC 0.7345).
ROC analysis showed TGFB1 blood expression discriminates RA-ILD from RA-nonILD patients with acceptable accuracy (AUC 0.7300).
ROC analysis showed TGFB2 blood expression discriminates RA-ILD from RA-nonILD patients with satisfactory accuracy (AUC 0.8021).
ROC analysis showed TGFB2 blood expression discriminates SSc-ILD from SSc-nonILD patients with acceptable accuracy (AUC 0.7518).
Although TGFB1 expression differed significantly between SSc-ILD and SSc-nonILD by ANOVA, ROC analysis found it lacked sufficient discriminative capacity to serve as a diagnostic biomarker.
ROC analysis showed PDGFA blood expression can differentiate IM-ILD from IPF patients, though with limited discriminative capacity.
ROC analysis showed TGFB2 blood expression accurately differentiates IM-ILD from IPF patients (AUC 0.7064).

In RA-ILD patients, PDGFA blood expression was lower in those with a more fibrotic radiological pattern (UIP/probable UIP/indeterminate) than those with NSIP/non-NSIP patterns, suggesting a prognostic role.
TGFB2 blood expression was significantly lower in RA-ILD patients positive for anti-CCP antibodies compared with those negative, linking it to a marker of more severe RA-ILD.
In SSc-ILD patients, lower blood TGFB2 expression correlated with lower FEV1 (% predicted), indicating an association with poorer lung function.
In SSc-ILD patients, TGFB3 blood expression was elevated in those with a UIP/probable UIP/indeterminate radiological pattern compared to non-UIP patterns.
TGFB3 blood expression was higher in SSc-ILD patients who developed progressive fibrosing pathology than in those who did not.
In IM-ILD patients, no significant associations were found between PDGFA, TGFB1, TGFB2, or TGFB3 expression and any of the clinical characteristics evaluated.

The patient had persistently low C4 with normal C3 and was confirmed to have acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, attributed to immune-mediated consumption secondary to an underlying low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.
Serum mast-cell tryptase measured during an acute airway swelling episode was within the normal range (6.1 µg/L), arguing against IgE-mediated mast-cell-driven anaphylaxis as previously assumed.

A cited prospective study of 102 patients with suspected anaphylaxis found that a peak tryptase value exceeding 11.4 µg/L strongly supported an anaphylaxis diagnosis, whereas normal tryptase results were not compatible with systemic mast-cell activation.

In the FAST-2 active-comparator trial, icatibant shortened median time to symptom relief to 2.0 hours versus 12.0 hours with tranexamic acid, while the placebo-controlled FAST-1 trial did not meet its primary endpoint though secondary measures favored icatibant.

Randomized controlled trials in hereditary C1-INH deficiency demonstrated that plasma-derived C1-INH produced faster clinical resolution of angioedema attacks than control, supporting extrapolated use in acquired C1-INH deficiency.
Ecallantide, a plasma kallikrein inhibitor, showed benefit in placebo-controlled trials for acute hereditary angioedema attacks.

Case series report that rituximab-based regimens targeting the underlying B-cell clone achieved biochemical normalization and sustained remission of angioedema in autoantibody-mediated acquired C1-INH deficiency.

In B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders, circulating anti-C1-INH autoantibodies or increased consumption of the inhibitor can produce functional C1-INH deficiency and recurrent bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
Acquired C1-INH deficiency (AAE-C1-INH) has an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 100,000 people and accounts for fewer than 10% of all C1-INH deficiencies.

In a multicenter review, almost one-third of patients with acquired C1-INH deficiency were initially treated for recurrent allergic or idiopathic angioedema before the underlying mechanism was identified.
The WAO/EAACI guideline recommends the pattern of low C4 with normal C3 as the initial screening clue for C1-INH deficiency, prior to measuring C1-INH concentration and function.

At an exploratory uncorrected threshold, PCC patients showed a trend toward reduced CBF in the right angular gyrus compared to COVID-recovered controls.
At an exploratory uncorrected threshold, PCC patients showed a trend toward reduced CBF in the right middle occipital gyrus compared to controls.

Reduced CBF in the right inferior occipital gyrus was significantly associated with higher total fatigue scores (WEIMuS) in PCC patients.
The association between right middle and inferior occipital gyrus hypoperfusion and fatigue was more pronounced for physical fatigue than for mental fatigue subscores.
Mental fatigue subscores were not significantly associated with CBF in the right middle or inferior occipital gyrus.
No significant associations were found between regional CBF and MoCA cognitive performance, olfactory performance, or GDS-15 depression scores in PCC patients.
Nearly one third (31%) of PCC patients scored below the cutoff on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, indicating cognitive impairment.
More than half (56%) of PCC patients had impaired olfactory performance on Sniffin' Sticks testing.
The large majority (81%) of PCC patients reported fatigue symptoms on the WEIMuS questionnaire.
Fatigue severity (WEIMuS) was strongly correlated with the degree of current disability in PCC patients.
Fatigue severity (WEIMuS) was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms (GDS-15) in PCC patients.

Current disability grade was significantly correlated with depressive symptoms (GDS-15) in PCC patients.
Compared to COVID-recovered controls without lasting symptoms, PCC patients performed significantly worse on olfactory testing.
PCC patients had significantly higher depressive symptom scores (GDS-15) and fatigue (WEIMuS) than COVID-recovered controls.
FreeSurfer-based cortical morphometry showed no measurable volume loss or cortical thinning in PCC patients compared to COVID-recovered controls.

No significant association was found between structural cortical parameters (cortical thickness, surface area, gray matter volume) and PCC-related symptoms including cognition, olfaction, and fatigue.

In sputum, 85% of ME/CFS patients released high EBV viral loads compared with 50% of age-matched healthy controls.

Herpesviruses (HHV-6, HHV-7, EBV) and papillomaviruses were detected at similar frequency in saliva of ME/CFS patients and healthy controls with no significant difference in prevalence.
Sputum HHV-6 and human cytomegalovirus viral loads did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Saliva HHV-6 and HHV-7 viral loads did not differ between CFS patients and healthy controls in one study.

GI biopsy analysis found Parvovirus B19 DNA markedly higher across all biopsy sites in CFS patients compared to controls.

Elevated antibody responses to EBV/HHV-6/HERV-K after SARS-CoV-2 infection were more prominent in saliva and not detectable systemically in plasma, highlighting mucosal-specific immunity.

Long COVID patients with herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6, or coinfection) experienced more severe COVID-19, including higher rates of pneumonia and longer hospital stays, than patients without viral reactivation.
A Norwegian study found that individuals infected during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic had more than a two-fold increased risk of developing ME/CFS compared to non-infected individuals.
Enterovirus RNA has been detected in stomach biopsies and throat swabs of CFS patients.
In three patients with documented acute enterovirus infection who developed ME/CFS, stomach biopsies taken years later revealed persistent, low-abundance enteroviral RNA and capsid protein.

HAdV was detected in sputum from one patient with severe ME/CFS and one non-ME/CFS immunosuppressed individual, but not in other ME/CFS patients or healthy controls.
HERV-K transcript levels in PBMCs did not differ between healthy controls and ME/CFS patients, and no correlation was observed between HERV-K18 transcript levels and HHV-6 or HHV-7 viral copy number.
Differential expression of HERV-K, but not HERV-W, has been reported in the blood of patients with moderate ME/CFS.

Overexpression of HERV-H, -K, and -W types was detected in a small cohort of fibromyalgia patients with or without comorbid ME/CFS, correlating with interferon-β and interferon-γ expression.
Duodenal biopsies from 8 of 12 ME/CFS patients showed presence of HERV-K, HERV-FRD and HERV-R.

In the authors' own GI faecal virome study, virome and bacterial diversity were similar between ME/CFS patients and controls, but HHV-6A, papillomaviruses, coronavirus NL63, and adenovirus 54 were detected exclusively in ME/CFS samples.

Vulnerability to post-EBV fatigue is more strongly associated with pre-existing symptoms and functional limitations than with initial immune or infection indicators, which may explain why only a subset of EBV-infected individuals develop ME/CFS.
Dysfunctional breathing during cardiopulmonary exercise testing was significantly more common in ME/CFS patients (42.1%) than in sedentary controls (16%).
Persistent hyperventilation during low-level exercise (hypocapnia at rest that continued through 25W) occurred in 31.6% of ME/CFS patients compared to 4% of sedentary controls.
58% of ME/CFS patients showed either persistent hyperventilation or dysfunctional breathing compared to 16% of normal controls.
PETCO2 was significantly lower at rest, anaerobic threshold, and maximal exercise in ME/CFS patients with hyperventilation compared to those without.

Resting respiratory exchange ratio was significantly higher in the ME/CFS hyperventilation subgroup than the non-hyperventilating subgroup, consistent with excess CO2 elimination from hyperventilation.
An elevated VE/VCO2 slope, reflecting excessive/inefficient ventilation, was found in ME/CFS patients and overlapped substantially with hyperventilation and dysfunctional breathing.
Breathing patterns observed on Day 1 CPET were reproducible on Day 2 in 93% of ME/CFS patients, supporting the reliability of the breathing-pattern classification.
Among ME/CFS patients with persistent hyperventilation, 50% also had dysfunctional breathing, indicating substantial overlap between the two ventilatory abnormalities not seen in controls.

ME/CFS patients with both dysfunctional breathing and hyperventilation reported significantly greater symptom severity (dyspnea) than those with normal breathing, whereas either abnormality alone did not differ significantly from normal breathing.
ME/CFS patients with hyperventilation alone or dysfunctional breathing alone did not show significantly different symptom severity compared to those with normal breathing.
Peak VO2 as a percentage of predicted was comparable between ME/CFS patients (79±20%) and sedentary controls, though maximal heart rate was higher and perceived exertion (Borg) lower in controls.
The 42% prevalence of dysfunctional breathing in this ME/CFS cohort is substantially higher than the ~9% estimated in the general population.

The authors' prior work found dysfunctional breathing in 49% of patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), with other investigators reporting a 29.4% incidence in long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea, compared to 42% in this non-COVID ME/CFS cohort.
In the early months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, PCS-ME/CFS patients had a higher prevalence of hyposmia/anosmia than PCS-only patients.
By more than 20 months post-infection, all evaluated PCS and PCS-ME/CFS patients had recovered normal olfactory function (normosmia).
Between 10 and 20 months post-infection, the majority of both PCS and PCS-ME/CFS patients still had hyposmia.
Six of 13 patients assessed beyond 20 months post-infection reported parosmia despite testing as normosmic on the TDI test, four of whom had PCS-ME/CFS and two PCS, all female.

Odor threshold detection was the most impaired olfactory sub-property early after SARS-CoV-2 infection but improved significantly by more than 20 months, along with discrimination and total TDI score, while identification did not improve.

Odor identification did not improve significantly over the study period; in the PCS-ME/CFS group it worsened during the first 20 months before returning to baseline, whereas the PCS group showed continuous, non-significant improvement.
No significant differences were found between PCS and PCS-ME/CFS patients in overall olfactory function or in the dynamics of improvement over the study period.

Patients vaccinated against COVID-19 prior to infection had no diagnosed hyposmia or anosmia and showed greater olfactory capability at initial assessment compared to unvaccinated individuals, though the vaccinated group was too small for firm conclusions.
Patients vaccinated after infection but before their first olfactory assessment showed superior odor discrimination compared to unvaccinated patients.
Patients infected with the SARS-CoV-2 wildtype variant showed a higher rate of hyposmia at initial assessment than those infected with later variants (Alpha, Delta, Omicron).
Self-reported olfactory dysfunction during acute COVID-19 showed no significant association with objectively measured normosmia at follow-up.

In PCS patients, early odor threshold recognition negatively correlated with subsequent muscle fatigability, while muscle recovery capacity positively correlated with total olfactory scores and odor discrimination, and hyposmia/anosmia negatively correlated with muscle recovery.

In PCS-ME/CFS patients, early odor threshold recognition and overall olfactory performance positively correlated with future handgrip strength, muscle fatigability negatively correlated with later threshold recognition, and poorer muscle recovery was linked to lower odor identification; these associations were not observed in PCS-only patients.
Higher age was negatively correlated with odor identification scores across all participants during the second and third year post-infection, but not with other olfactory measures.
Sex was not associated with olfactory performance in this cohort.

In PCS-ME/CFS patients, more severe early fatigue (CFQ) was paradoxically linked to a lower frequency of hyposmia/anosmia, better early odor threshold results, and improved odor identification after 20 months, while better early olfactory performance was associated with improved emotional-role QoL despite lower Bell Score (worse daily functioning).

Higher total olfactory scores at the first assessment were positively correlated with better cognitive outcomes (SDMT) at the second assessment (and at a trend level at the third), across the cohort but especially in PCS patients.

In PCS-only patients, better olfactory outcomes at 10 and 20 months post-COVID were associated with improved cognitive performance (SDMT), daily functioning (Bell Score), and multiple HRQoL domains (SF-36), persisting into later assessment; the strongest correlation was between early odor discrimination and daily functioning and physical role/health-change QoL after 20 months.
In PCS-only patients, lower fatigue levels (CFQ) were linked to better olfactory outcomes, particularly odor discrimination, in the second and third year post-infection.
The 195-peptide urinary classifier PASC195 discriminated PASC cases from controls with an AUC of 0.949 using leave-one-out cross-validation in the training set.
In an independent validation set of 40 individuals, PASC195 distinguished PASC cases from controls with an AUC of 0.962 and 95% sensitivity/specificity at a threshold of -0.596.
In the external multicenter UriCoV cohort, PASC195 did not significantly differentiate PASC cases from controls.
The majority of PASC195 peptides (172 of 195, 88.2%) were derived from collagen alpha chains, predominantly collagen alpha-1 (76.7%) and collagen alpha-2 (16.9%) subtypes.
Peptide fragments of collagen alpha-1(I) (CO1A1) were the most abundant upregulated peptide species in PASC195.
Peptide fragments of collagen alpha-1(III) (CO3A1) were among the most abundant upregulated peptides in PASC195.
Peptide fragments of collagen alpha-2(I) (CO1A2) were among the abundant upregulated peptides in PASC195.

A small minority of PASC195 peptides were downregulated, including fragments of collagen alpha-2(IV), collagen alpha-1(XIV), clathrin, glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha, and Golgin subfamily A member 6-like protein 2.
Degradation products of alpha-1-antitrypsin (A1AT) were upregulated in the PASC urine peptidome, mirroring prior reports of A1AT elevation in acute COVID-19.
Peptide fragments of fibrinogen alpha (FIBA) and beta (FIBB) subunits were upregulated in the urine peptidome of PASC patients, consistent with prior plasma proteome findings.

Antithrombin-III (AT III) peptide fragments were among the dysregulated components of PASC195, possibly reflecting altered coagulation-related cleavage activity as reported in a prior serum proteome study of PASC.
Serotransferrin (TF)-derived peptides were upregulated in the PASC urine peptidome, aligning with prior reports of iron homeostasis disruption and inflammatory anemia in PASC.
CD99 antigen fragments were upregulated in the PASC urine peptidome, contrasting with the depletion of CD99 previously reported specific to severe acute COVID-19.
Peptides derived from calprotectin subunit S100A9 showed higher abundance in the PASC urine peptidome, consistent with immune dysregulation.

PGBM (perlecan), a basement membrane component including the glomerular basement membrane, was overexpressed in the PASC urine peptidome, potentially reflecting increased peptide leakage or endothelial barrier alterations.

An in silico simulation applying six candidate interventions to PASC patient data predicted heterogeneous individual improvements in PASC195 scores, with physical activity, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and GLP-1 receptor agonists predicted to be most beneficial.

Higher PASC195 classification scores were significantly associated with self-reported concentration impairment/short-term memory consolidation problems and exertional dyspnea among all questionnaire respondents.

In a subgroup analysis restricted to PASC cases, higher PASC195 scores were significantly associated with word retrieval difficulty, concentration impairment/short-term memory consolidation, and exertional dyspnea.
Concentration impairment and short-term memory consolidation problems were the most frequently reported symptoms overall and were even more prevalent among PASC cases specifically.

A minority of the overall cohort and of PASC patients met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS at baseline, indicating that most PASC patients did not meet formal ME/CFS diagnostic criteria despite symptom overlap.

IgG positivity against HHV-6 was a significant predictor of an extreme hypertensive reaction during HUTT in the Lyme disease group.

Patients in the late-stage Lyme disease group had a significantly higher proportion with a history of syncope compared to the other three post-infectious groups.

The prevalence of POTS during HUTT ranged from 5.4% to 13.7% depending on the post-infectious syndrome group.
