Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 activation was reduced in EDS patients, driven by decreased talin-1 phosphorylation, leading to aggregation and spreading defects.
Decreased phosphorylation of talin-1 was identified as the proximate mechanism underlying reduced integrin activation in EDS platelets.
Platelets from people with EDS showed defective aggregation and spreading.
Col5a1+/- mice, a model of classical EDS, showed increased tail bleeding time compared to wild-type controls.
Col5a1+/- mice exhibited decreased susceptibility to FeCl3-induced carotid artery thrombosis, consistent with a prothrombotic-to-hemorrhagic shift due to platelet dysfunction.
Overall platelet dysfunction observed across multiple EDS subtypes and the Col5a1+/- mouse model likely contributes to the hemorrhagic complications seen in EDS patients.
Decreased phosphorylation of talin-1 was identified as an upstream mechanism leading to reduced integrin αIIbβ3 activation in EDS platelets.

Overall, 80% of patients treated with compression garments met at least one component of the composite effectiveness endpoint (pain reduction, reduced analgesic use, improved QoL, or reduced fatigue).
At follow-up, 80% of patients reported a subjective reduction in pain following compression garment use.
About half of patients with available data reported reduced analgesic consumption (excluding acetaminophen) after starting compression garments.
Only 40% of patients reported an improvement in quality of life after compression garment use, with the majority reporting QoL as stable.
Only 15% of patients reported a reduction in fatigue after compression garment use, reflecting the multifactorial nature of fatigue in this population.
Altered visceral proprioception (including autonomic/orthostatic features such as orthostatic intolerance and POTS) was significantly more common in patients with hEDS than in those with HSD.
The proportion of patients achieving the composite clinical response endpoint did not differ significantly between HSD and hEDS groups (85.7% vs 76.9%).
Intolerance to compression garments was significantly associated with absence of clinical benefit, with only 20% of intolerant patients improving versus 100% of tolerant patients.
Patients who met the composite treatment response endpoint had a significantly higher BMI than nonresponders.
Longer daily wearing time of compression garments was significantly correlated with a better treatment response.

A modest inverse correlation was observed between the duration of chronic pain prior to compression garment initiation and the treatment response, approaching but not reaching statistical significance.
The Beighton hypermobility score was not significantly correlated with treatment response to compression garments, suggesting hypermobility severity alone does not predict benefit.

Patients reporting an immediate 'on-off' symptom relief effect with compression garment wear/removal showed a trend toward greater overall treatment response, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Mast cell activation syndrome was present as a comorbidity in 20% of the hEDS/HSD cohort, with no significant difference between subgroups.
Altered visceral proprioception, encompassing autonomic/orthostatic features (e.g. orthostatic intolerance, POTS, bladder/bowel dysfunction), was present in 60% of the overall hEDS/HSD cohort.
Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous 8-nucleotide duplication in the polypyrimidine tract upstream of COL5A1 exon 22 in a 9-year-old girl with clinical features of classical EDS.

Minigene splicing assays in Flp-In-293 cells confirmed that the duplication causes exon 22 to begin 8 base pairs earlier, introducing a premature termination codon and validating the bioinformatic splice-site predictions.
Segregation testing showed both parents were negative for the variant, confirming it arose de novo in the patient.

The patient presented with a constellation of clinical features consistent with classical EDS, including generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton 8/9), soft doughy hyperextensible skin with delayed wound healing (but no atrophic scarring), malocclusion, epicanthal folds, blue sclera, hernias, pes planus, unexplained abdominal pain, a Baker's cyst, and growth parameters below the 10th percentile.

Combining functional splicing evidence (PS3) with the de novo occurrence (PM6), the variant initially classified as likely pathogenic (PVS1, PM2) was reclassified as pathogenic per ACMG-AMP guidelines.

Approximately 50% of classical EDS patients carry a variant in COL5A1 or COL5A2, and about one-third of individuals with classical EDS have nonsense or frameshift variants leading to a non-functional COL5A1 allele.
According to the ClinVar database, 249 COL5A1 variants have been classified as pathogenic and 102 as likely pathogenic.

In a rabbit model of surgically-induced TMJ hypermobility, autologous blood injection produced a higher fibrosis grade than dextrose prolotherapy, with more than 75% fibrosis observed in half of the treated joints.

CD68 immunostaining, a marker of macrophage infiltration, was stronger in joints treated with autologous blood injection than in those treated with dextrose prolotherapy, indicating a more pronounced inflammatory response.
Control joints treated with saline showed no fibrosis grading and negative CD68 staining, indicating that the fibrotic and inflammatory responses were specific to the active prolotherapy treatments.
Pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene cause abnormal type III collagen synthesis, reducing tissue resistance to mechanical stress and leading to pulmonary vascular and parenchymal fragility in vEDS.
In this case series, pulmonary hemoptysis-type vEDS occurred predominantly in young males (8 of 9 patients), with a mean age of 22.22 ± 5.72 years.
All 9 patients presented with repeated cough and hemoptysis, with daily hemoptysis volume of about 10-50 ml, and 3 cases experienced paroxysmal massive hemoptysis up to 100-200 ml.

Chest CT in this cohort showed patchy ground-glass opacities in 9/9, fibrous strip shadows in 8/9, non-cavitary nodules in 9/9, cavitary nodules in 7/9, consolidation in 3/9, emphysema with bullae in 3/9, calcified nodules in 2/9, and liquid pneumothorax in 2/9.

Pathological examination of resected or biopsied lung tissue showed diffuse erythrocyte exudation into alveolar spaces, abundant hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and fibrous/hyaline nodules corresponding to imaging abnormalities.

Eight of 9 patients were initially misdiagnosed with infectious lung disease and treated with anti-infective therapy, including 4 who received diagnostic anti-tuberculosis treatment, which was ineffective at preventing recurrent hemoptysis.
18F-FDG PET-CT in 3 patients showed light-to-moderate uptake of lung lesions with maximum SUV values of 3.9, 6.5, and 9.2, and excluded systemic tumor involvement.
Family genetic screening identified asymptomatic COL3A1 mutation carriers among relatives of 2 of the 9 patients.
In a French cohort of 144 genetically confirmed vEDS patients, arterial events occurred in 51.4%, gastrointestinal events in 22.9%, and pulmonary events in 10.4%.
In a UK cohort of 180 vEDS patients, vascular events occurred in 40%, intestinal perforations in 13.88%, and pneumothorax in 5.55%.
A cohort study of 136 vEDS patients found that 57.4% had lung abnormalities, most commonly emphysema (32.3%), often asymptomatic.

Hemoptysis is a rare complication of vEDS lung involvement compared with pneumothorax/hemopneumothorax, occurring in only 2.2% of Frank's cohort and 5 of 180 patients with lung disease in the Sheffield cohort.
Among vEDS patients with pulmonary involvement, hemoptysis was reported in 12.5% according to the Boussouar study.
Long-term use of angiotensin II receptor blockers and/or beta blockers has been reported to reduce the occurrence of vascular events in vEDS, although this lacks randomized controlled trial support.

vEDS patients treated with celiprolol showed higher survival rates and lower rates of arterial complications than other treatment groups, but the study lacked a placebo control, limiting assessment of absolute efficacy.

The authors recommend that lung tissue biopsy, whether surgical or interventional, be avoided as far as possible in patients with suspected vEDS due to high risk of severe complications and the possibility of non-diagnostic pathology.
Three of 9 patients had skin changes (systemic thinning in 1, multiple scars in 1, hyperelasticity in 1), while none had joint changes.
The time from symptom onset to definitive diagnosis of vEDS ranged from 0.36 to 5.07 years, averaging 2.19 ± 1.77 years, reflecting frequent initial misdiagnosis.
Crystal structure of human B3GalT6 (PDB 9SP7) reveals a homodimer covalently linked by an intermolecular disulfide bond between Cys206 of each monomer.
SEC-MALS analysis showed that the fully deSUMOylated recombinant transferases B4GalT7, B3GalT6, and B3GlcAT-1 all remained dimeric in solution.
The B3GalT6 Cys206Ser mutant remained dimeric but showed enzymatic activity reduced to about 60% relative to the disulfide-linked wild-type enzyme.

Thermal unfolding by CD spectroscopy showed the Cys206Ser mutant (21S) had a lower melting point (53°C) than wild-type B3GalT6 (20S, 59°C), indicating the interchain disulfide contributes to thermal stability; B4GalT7 (18S) melted at 55°C.
The catalytic Mn2+ ion in B3GalT6 is coordinated in a tripodal manner by Asp156, Asp158 (DXD motif) and the NE2 nitrogen of His279.
B3GalT6 contains two intramolecular disulfide bridges, Cys271-Cys300 and a rare vicinal disulfide Cys321-Cys322 with a trans backbone configuration.

Human GlcAT-I unexpectedly glucuronylates complex N-glycans in vitro, with preferential transfer onto the 1,6-arm over the 1,3-arm, showing it can act on β1,4-linked galactosides at a lower rate than its natural β1,3-linked acceptor.
B3GalT6 shows unexpected promiscuity by synthesizing poly-β1,3-galactose extensions (1-13 additional Gal residues) on complex N-glycans under stringent enzyme/substrate conditions.
GlcAT-I can slowly and directly glucuronylate the truncated Gal-Xyl disaccharide (bypassing B3GalT6), converting most substrate (~85%) into the non-canonical GlcA-Gal-Xyl trisaccharide glycopeptide.

Patients with pathogenic loss-of-function B3GalT6 variants (causing spondylodysplastic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) show severely impaired GAG biosynthesis initiation and highly increased levels of the truncated linkage region trisaccharide, consistent with the paper's in vitro bypass mechanism.

In bikunin from healthy individuals, only a small amount (0.1%) of the truncated linkage region trisaccharide is detectable, consistent with GlcAT-I's slow bypass activity being a minor pathway under normal conditions.
A zebrafish double-knockout study of B3GalT6 (cited) showed results similar to the paper's in vitro biosynthetic bypass findings, supporting the salvage pathway concept.

N-terminal His6-SUMO fusion tags markedly improved solubility and yield of active recombinant B4GalT7, B3GalT6, and B3GlcAT-1 when expressed in E. coli, which otherwise gave largely insoluble protein.
A stepwise chemoenzymatic cascade using B4GalT7, B3GalT6, and B3GlcAT-1 produced the canonical linkage region tetrasaccharide glycopeptide 16 from bikunin 1-25 in 81% isolated yield after RP-HPLC.

Alignment of 19 mammalian, avian, fish, amphibian, nematode, and insect B3GalT6 sequences showed Cys206 is conserved in nearly all species, except two Drosophila species where it is a serine, indicating the disulfide-linked dimer is broadly conserved in higher animals.

The B3GalT6 dimerization interface calculated with PISA has a buried surface of 1256 Å2 and a total surface of 13,897 Å2 per monomer, is predominantly hydrophobic, and features Trp203 as a key interlocking residue within the Val192-Leu205 loop.

In 51 patients with hereditary thoracic aortic disease (HTAD) treated with frozen elephant trunk (FET) hybrid prostheses, overall 30-day survival was 98.0% (50/51), with one in-hospital death due to stroke after emergency surgery.
Elective surgery (including reoperations) achieved 100% 30-day survival compared to 87.5% (7/8) in patients undergoing emergency surgery for acute aortic syndrome.
Reoperative FET procedures (previous sternotomy, n=26) performed electively yielded 100% 30-day survival.
Mid-term overall survival following FET hybrid prosthesis in HTAD patients was 93.9% at 1 year, 90.6% at 3 years, and 90.6% at 5 years over a median follow-up of 48 months.
Intraluminal thrombosis within the FET stent graft occurred in 4 of 51 patients (12.5%) postoperatively, all successfully managed conservatively or with TEVAR.
Distal stent graft-induced new entry (dSINE) occurred early in 3 of 51 patients (9.4%) and in an additional 2 patients (4.3%) during mid-term follow-up, all successfully treated with TEVAR.

Subsequent thoracic aortic interventions after FET implantation were required at increasing rates over time, with freedom from reintervention at 1, 3, and 5 years of 32.7%, 44.9%, and 47.0% respectively, most commonly TEVAR.
Despite a relatively high frequency of subsequent aortic reinterventions, mid-term survival was not adversely affected, with no deaths occurring after reintervention in this cohort.

Neurological complications after FET were infrequent, with permanent stroke in 3.9% (2/51) of patients (one mRS 2, one mRS 1 recovering fully), no cases of paraplegia, and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy in 17.6% (9/51).
Marfan syndrome patients (n=31, 60.8% of cohort) all harbored pathogenic FBN1 variants, and were the most prevalent HTAD subtype undergoing FET.

The single vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) patient in the cohort, harboring a pathogenic COL3A1 variant, underwent FET as primary surgery, survived to 30 days and mid-term follow-up with no subsequent aortic intervention required.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients (n=11) carried pathogenic variants in TGFBR1 (n=2), TGFBR2 (n=6), SMAD3 (n=2), or TGFB2 (n=1).
Non-syndromic HTAD patients (n=8) had pathogenic variants in ACTA2 (n=5), MYH11 (n=2), or MYLK (n=1).

Overall mid-term mortality was 8.0% (4 patients), with deaths attributed to heart failure, acute pancreatitis, unknown cause (all MFS), and cerebral hemorrhage (LDS); no deaths occurred in nsHTAD or the single vEDS patient.
Since 2015, the FET distal anastomosis was proximalized from arch zone 3 to zone 2 using a 'simplified technique,' which was applied in 74.5% (38/51) of the cohort thereafter.

The article describes MCAS as a distinct clinical entity requiring systemic symptoms, objective biochemical evidence of mast cell mediator release, and response to targeted therapy for diagnosis.

The authors note that increased referrals for suspected mast cell activation disorders are partly driven by unverified internet/social media information, leading to incorrect self- or provider-suggested diagnoses.

The paper states that diagnostic criteria for MCAS and other mast cell activation disorders have been proposed but are inconsistently known, applied, or accepted by providers, and stringent criteria must be fulfilled to confirm mast cell involvement.

Although some authors have proposed a link between MCAS and POTS, hypermobile EDS, or long COVID, this association has never been demonstrated in patients who unambiguously meet ECNM-AIM consortium diagnostic criteria for MCAS.
Proponents of broader (non-ECNM-AIM) MCAS diagnostic criteria claim that chronic aberrant mast cell activation may affect up to 17% of the population.
The ECNM-AIM consortium's preferred biochemical criterion for MCAS is an acute increase in serum tryptase to at least 120% of baseline plus 2 ng/mL.
An elevated baseline serum tryptase level, seen in about 6% of the population, should not itself be interpreted as evidence of mast cell activation.

In an observational study of 31 patients with idiopathic MCAS, all were treated with H1-antihistamines and all reported a positive response.
