Two small RCTs of omalizumab in systemic mastocytosis (30 and 16 patients) found no anaphylaxis events in either arm during the study period.

Kaminsky et al.'s systematic review plus retrospective cohort found that among 35 idiopathic anaphylaxis patients treated with omalizumab, 62% had a complete response, 29% a partial response, and 9% were nonresponders.
Only a small minority of MCAS patients require omalizumab, as shown in a case series where 1 of 31 idiopathic MCAS and 2 of 13 clonal MCAS patients received it.

Most patients with systemic mastocytosis have elevated baseline urinary NMH, 2,3dPGF2α, and LTE4, whereas patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia typically have normal baseline levels despite elevated tryptase.
A recent study suggested an acute increase as low as 30% above baseline in any urinary mast cell mediator metabolite could correlate with a 20% + 2 ng/mL acute increase in serum tryptase.
Currently, only a small minority of patients referred for suspected MCAS are ultimately diagnosed with the condition.
Diagnosis of mast cell activation disease (MCAD) takes on average more than 5 years to reach a definitive conclusion.
MCAS prevalence in the Northern Hemisphere is estimated at 4%-17%.
Up to 80% of patients with MCAD report cardiovascular symptoms, attributed to the high density of mast cells in the cardiovascular system.
Mast cell chymase converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II independently of ACE, contributing directly to cardiac fibrosis via fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation.
Mast cell tryptase and chymase activate TGF-ß, driving fibroblast differentiation to myofibroblasts and collagen deposition, contributing to cardiac fibrosis.
Dysrhythmias are frequently reported by MCAD patients, with about 29% prevalence in systemic mastocytosis and at least 20% in MCAS.
Mast cell activation increases norepinephrine release from cardiac sympathetic nerves via ANGII acting on presynaptic AT1 receptors, leading to arrhythmias and potential sudden cardiac death.
Mast cell-derived histamine stimulates H2 receptors on sinoatrial node cardiomyocytes, increasing heart rate and contractility and eliciting sinus tachycardia.
Prostaglandin D2, a major mast cell mediator, has been shown to induce tachycardia in humans.
Ivabradine effectively reduces heart rate in MCAD patients with sinus rhythm without altering blood pressure, and is preferred when renin/AT1 blockade is contraindicated due to hypotension.
The calcium channel blocker verapamil is frequently ineffective for treating mast cell mediator-induced tachycardia in MCAD.
ß-adrenoceptor antagonists should be avoided in MCAD because ß-adrenoceptors normally inhibit mast cell mediator release, so blockade disinhibits mediator release and aggravates MCAD symptoms.
Epinephrine used for anaphylactoid reactions should be given with particular caution in tachycardic MCAD patients as it has been reported to precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
Catheter ablation for recurrent ventricular tachycardia in MCAD patients was performed but VT reappeared after weeks or months, likely due to complex underlying pathophysiology.
Histamine's most prominent effect on the AV node is slowing of conduction, which can progress up to third-degree AV block.
In a Danish retrospective cohort of 548 adults with systemic mastocytosis, 12 patients had congestive heart failure.
In a prospective study of 18 MCAS patients, diastolic left ventricular dysfunction was found via Doppler imaging in 12 patients, and left ventricular hypertrophy was observed in 5 of those 12.
ACE inhibitors should be avoided in MCAD because ACE degrades bradykinin, a mast cell activator, so ACE inhibition increases mast cell mediator release and worsens MCAD.

SGLT-2 inhibitors should be considered for heart failure in MCAD patients as they may also possibly have a beneficial effect on MCAD itself, though allergic reactions warrant close monitoring during introduction.
Hypotension with lightheadedness or syncope is reported by 22%-55% of MCAD patients versus 5% in a control group.
Acetylsalicylic acid (80-325 mg orally once or twice daily) may benefit MCAD patients with high levels of vasodilating prostaglandins, if NSAID tolerance is confirmed.
Preliminary data from systemic mastocytosis patients suggest omalizumab is efficacious in preventing spontaneous episodes of systemic hypotension.
Marked recurrent or sustained elevation in arterial blood pressure due to mast cell activation has been observed in up to 31% of MCAD patients.
The vasodilator prostaglandin D2 can be metabolized by 11-ketoreductase into 9α,11ß-PGF2, a biologically active vasopressor, linking PGD2 metabolism to hypertension in MCAD.
Cholesterol and triglycerides are diet-independently increased in the blood of approximately 75% of MCAD patients, contributing to atherosclerotic plaque formation.
Systemic mastocytosis has been proven to be associated with a higher incidence of acute coronary syndrome even when plasma lipid levels are low.
Mast cells have been detected at the site of vasospasm in patients with variant angina, indicating a role in coronary artery spasm.
Clinical signs of bleeding diathesis occur in approximately 50% of MCAD patients, though severe or fatal bleeding is rare.
Increased mast cell-derived heparin release can reach circulating concentrations comparable to therapeutic thromboprophylaxis levels, potentially contributing to bleeding diathesis in MCAD.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV given 30 minutes before surgical incision, continued for 12-24 hours (total 2-3 g/24h), is recommended to manage perioperative bleeding tendency in MCAD patients.

Mast cells accumulate within atherosclerotic plaques and release mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, cathepsins, TNFα, IFNγ, CCL2, IL-6, IL-8) that promote plaque progression, instability, rupture, and thrombosis.
Statins, beyond their lipid-lowering effect, are proposed to have a pleiotropic mast cell-inhibiting effect, supporting their use as first-line lipid therapy in MCAD.
Cholesterol and triglycerides are diet-independently increased in the blood of approximately 75% of MCAD patients.
Systemic mastocytosis is associated with a higher incidence of acute coronary syndrome even in patients with low plasma lipid levels.

Mast cells have been detected at sites of coronary vasospasm in variant angina, and their release of vasoconstrictive mediators such as serotonin, leukotrienes, and endothelin is proposed to trigger coronary artery vasospasm in MCAD.
Non-cardiac angina pectoris in MCAD is hypothesized to reflect neuropathic pain caused by mast cell mediator activation of nearby sensory C-fibers, which the brain interprets as anginal pain.
Acute mast cell mediator release can cause focal gas accumulation and GI dysmotility that displaces the cardiac axis, producing cardiac-type pain known as the Roemheld symptom complex.

Clinical signs of bleeding diathesis (hematoma, bruising, prolonged bleeding after biopsies, gingival bleeding, epistaxis, GI hemorrhage, menorrhagia) occur in approximately 50% of MCAD patients, though severe or fatal bleeding is rare.
Increased mast cell release of heparin can reach circulating concentrations comparable to thromboprophylactic exogenous heparin dosing, potentially contributing to bleeding diathesis in MCAD.
The main cause of bleeding diathesis in MCAD is proposed to be a serious hyperfibrinolysis rather than heparin excess alone.

Tranexamic acid administered intravenously before and after invasive procedures is recommended to control bleeding in MCAD patients, given at 1 g pre-incision and continued at 2-3 g/24h for 12-24 hours.
Raynaud's phenomenon prevalence in MCAD has not been formally determined but is estimated at up to 10% based on clinical experience.
Propofol is recommended for short-term anesthesia during procedures such as cardiac catheterization and pacemaker implantation in MCAD patients because it also inhibits mast cell activity.
Patients with MCAD have a reduced ability to dissolve absorbable suture material, so its use should be avoided to prevent impaired postoperative wound healing.
Pacemakers implanted in MCAD patients should be MRI-compatible up to 3 Tesla, since these patients require repeated MRI scans for their multisystem symptoms and comorbidities.
Aprocitentan, a non-selective endothelin receptor antagonist approved by the FDA in 2024 for resistant hypertension, has no published studies in MCAD patients to date.

Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine, and clonidine if insufficient, are recommended treatments for hypertension in MCAD patients, with careful titration required during hypertensive crises due to mismatched mediator/drug half-lives.
Pediatric mastocytosis typically begins in infancy and often follows a transient course with spontaneous resolution by adolescence.
Monomorphic maculopapular skin lesions in children, the pattern typically seen in adults, may indicate rare persistent mastocytosis into adulthood and are often associated with systemic disease.
Children with cutaneous mastocytosis typically carry KIT mutations located in various regions of the gene, distinct from the single hotspot seen in systemic disease.
Children with systemic mastocytosis predominantly carry the KIT D816V variant, distinct from the more heterogeneous KIT mutations seen in cutaneous-limited disease.
Diagnosis of pediatric mastocytosis relies on noninvasive measures including skin inspection, Darier's sign, and analysis of serum tryptase and KIT variant in blood.
Symptomatic management of mast cell activation in children encompasses trigger avoidance plus H1 and H2 antihistamines, cromolyn, and omalizumab.
In children with systemic mastocytosis, tyrosine kinase inhibitors tailored to the specific KIT variant may be considered as treatment.
Duodenal mast cell density (by tryptase and CD117 staining) was increased in patients with suspected MCAD-GI compared with an asymptomatic control cohort.
Colonic mast cell density was also increased in patients with suspected MCAD-GI compared with the asymptomatic control cohort.
GI mast cell density (high vs low) did not correlate with specific GI symptoms in either the duodenum or colon.
Local GI mastocytosis (high vs low MC density) was not associated with clinical response to mast cell-targeted therapies.
MCAS diagnosis requires a rise in serum tryptase during an acute episode of at least 20% above basal serum tryptase plus an absolute increase of at least 2 ng/mL.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) is caused by duplication or amplification of the alpha-1 allele of TPSAB1 and results in basal serum tryptase greater than 8 ng/mL.
HαT genotypes are highly prevalent in Western populations, ranging from 4.4% to 5.6% depending on cohort, making HαT the most common cause of elevated basal serum tryptase.
HαT prevalence in patients with clonal mast cell activation disorders (cMCADs) is estimated at 12.2%-17.2%, higher than the general population.

HαT prevalence varies by cMCAD subtype: 12% in cutaneous mastocytosis, 12% in indolent systemic mastocytosis, 20% in bone marrow mastocytosis, and 33% in monoclonal MCAS, with higher prevalence in non-cutaneous forms.
HαT is consistently associated with increased baseline serum tryptase levels in both healthy individuals and those with cMCADs.
HαT is associated with an increased risk of anaphylaxis, particularly severe episodes, in patients with clonal mast cell activation disorders.
A higher prevalence of HαT has also been found among patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis (Adv-SM).
Baseline serum tryptase levels are significantly higher in advanced systemic mastocytosis compared with non-advanced disease, reducing the influence of HαT status on triggering diagnosis.
Patients with HαT and irritable bowel syndrome show increased mast cell counts in gastrointestinal biopsies compared to HαT-negative patients.
In HαT-positive patients with MCAS, bone marrow mast cells may show abnormal morphology, including spindle-shaped cells and hypogranulation, resembling that seen in mastocytosis.
The authors hypothesize an estimated threefold increased risk of developing clonal MCADs in HαT-positive individuals if a true pathophysiological link exists.
Peripheral blood ddPCR/ASOqPCR detection of the KIT D816V mutation has significantly lower sensitivity than bone marrow testing, estimated around 50%-60%, in patients without skin involvement.
Individuals with both HαT and clonal MCADs are at increased risk of anaphylaxis, particularly from hymenoptera venom, with a higher likelihood of grade IV reactions.
Recent data suggest mastocytosis prevalence is approximately 1 in 3,500 individuals, implying the true prevalence of clonal MCADs may be about twice current estimates.

The prevalence of clonal MCADs among individuals with HαT is estimated to be low, between 1 in 1,100 and 1 in 3,500, which the authors state does not warrant routine genetic counseling or family screening.
CEREMAST now routinely prescribes epinephrine auto-injectors as a preventive measure to patients with both HαT and cMCADs, particularly those in remote areas with limited emergency access.
No therapeutic studies have demonstrated a differential treatment response to mediator-targeted therapies or tyrosine kinase inhibitors based on HαT status.

The WHO/ICC minor criterion for systemic mastocytosis requires basal serum tryptase >20 ng/mL, but this threshold must be adjusted for alpha-tryptase gene copy number, for which CEREMAST uses an online calculator.

EC-specific expression of dominant-negative TRF2 induced endothelial senescence in dermal microvasculature of transgenic mice, confirmed by colocalization of endothelial markers with senescence markers.
TRF2DN transgenic mice showed significantly delayed wound healing compared with wild-type mice, with open wounds still visible at day 5 when WT wounds were nearly healed.
Dermoepidermal junction surface area was significantly reduced (flatter) in Tg mice at both 10 and 40 weeks compared to age-matched WT controls.

Dermal thickness, second-harmonic-generation collagen signal intensity, and hydroxyproline-measured collagen content were all significantly reduced in Tg mice, with 10-week-old Tg mice resembling 40-week-old animals.

Ki67+ proliferating cells were significantly fewer in Tg mouse skin compared to WT, while phospho-H2AX+ DNA damage cells and SA-β-Gal+ senescent cells were significantly increased in dermis and epidermis.
SASP-associated cytokines IL-1α, IL-1β, and IL-6, along with CDK inhibitors p19 and p21, pERK1/2, and NFκB activation, were elevated in Tg mouse skin.

Dermal vascular area fraction, vessel density on intravital imaging, and HIF-1α gene expression were comparable between Tg and WT mice, indicating no gross anatomical change in vasculature despite EC senescence.

Mast cell density and the proportion of degranulated mast cells were significantly increased in the dermis of TRF2DN mice at both 10 and 40 weeks compared to WT, confirmed by toluidine blue and tryptase staining.
Serum IgE levels did not differ significantly between WT and Tg mice at 10 weeks, indicating that mast cell activation in aged skin occurs via a non-IgE-dependent pathway.

Intraperitoneal quercetin (mast cell stabilizer) reduced mast cell density and degranulation in Tg mice, and improved dermoepidermal junction surface area and dermal thickness toward WT levels, along with reduced inflammatory markers and serum IL-1β.

Quercetin did not prevent endothelial cell senescence or reverse fibroblast senescence markers, and did not change increased Edn1 expression, indicating mast cells act as intermediaries rather than primary initiators of skin aging.

Fibroblasts exposed to conditioned media from senescent TRF2DN endothelial cells showed only slight changes in IL-1α and FGF2 and no significant differences in p16, p19, and p21, suggesting SASP alone insufficiently drives direct fibroblast senescence in vitro.
CGRP protein expression was significantly higher in skin of 4-week-old Tg mice, preceding full manifestation of SASP and senescence phenotypes, and remained elevated at 10 weeks.

Transcription of Tac1, which encodes substance P and related neuropeptides, was comparable between Tg and WT mice, indicating the mast cell activation is specifically CGRP-mediated rather than mediated by other neuropeptides.

Unilateral surgical axotomy of dermal nerves significantly reduced CGRP expression in denervated Tg skin, confirming dermal neurons as the primary source of excess CGRP, independent of any change in neuron density.

Intradermal atogepant (CGRP receptor antagonist) significantly reduced mast cell degranulation and improved dermoepidermal junction surface area compared to vehicle-treated skin, with lower phospho-NFκB and p19 levels, despite CGRP itself remaining elevated.

Ex vivo, isolated peritoneal mast cells exposed to recombinant CGRP (but not TRF2DN-EC conditioned media, which lacked detectable CGRP) showed degranulated morphology and secreted tryptase, demonstrating that CGRP alone is sufficient to directly activate mast cells.

Isolated dermal endothelial cells from 2-week-old Tg mice showed significantly increased IL-1α and IL-6 expression (with reduced Edn1 and comparable TNF-α), suggesting these early EC-derived SASP factors may induce neuronal CGRP expression.

Daily intraperitoneal dexamethasone (SASP inhibitor) reduced mast cell degranulation, improved DEJ surface area, and lowered CGRP, phospho-NFκB, p16, IL-6, and TNF-α levels in Tg mice, supporting SASP as the driver of CGRP induction.

Intradermal tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor inhibitor) reduced CGRP expression, mast cell degranulation, and improved dermoepidermal junction surface area in Tg mice, implicating IL-6 as a specific SASP mediator upstream of CGRP.

c-kit+ mast cells were located near, but did not directly colocalize with, β-gal+ senescent cells in Tg dermis, and CGRP colocalized with synaptophysin+ axons but not with CD117+ mast cells despite spatial adjacency.

At 4 weeks of age, before full SASP manifestation, Tg mice already showed significantly higher mast cell density and degranulation rates than WT, with only dermal p19 elevated among SASP/CDKI markers, indicating mast cell activation precedes overt senescence phenotypes.
Zingerone showed no significant cytotoxicity in mast cells (BMMCs, RBL-2H3) at concentrations of 1-50 μM after 8h, with viability above 95% and confirmed non-toxic even after 24h exposure at 50 μM.
Zingerone dose-dependently increased LKB1-mediated phosphorylation of AMPKα (Thr172) and downstream ACC phosphorylation in IgE-sensitized bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Zingerone-induced AMPK activation suppressed FcεRI proximal signaling, significantly inhibiting phosphorylation of PLCγ1, Akt, MAPKs (p38/ERK/JNK), and IKK in BMMCs and RBL-2H3 cells.
Zingerone significantly suppressed IgE/Ag-triggered β-hexosaminidase release, a marker of mast cell degranulation, in BMMCs.
Zingerone significantly reduced synthesis of the lipid mediators LTC4 and PGD2 in IgE/Ag-stimulated BMMCs.
Zingerone significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine (TNF-α and IL-6) secretion from IgE/Ag-stimulated BMMCs.
Zingerone significantly inhibited FcεRI-mediated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.

Mast cell activation induced nuclear translocation of AMPK (increased nuclear, decreased cytoplasmic signal), and Zingerone treatment attenuated this translocation, promoting cytoplasmic AMPK retention.
Genetic silencing of AMPKα2 in BMMCs abolished Zingerone's suppression of FcεRI proximal signaling and downstream effector functions, restoring signaling and mediator release to control levels.
Genetic silencing of LKB1 in BMMCs prevented Zingerone-mediated LKB1/AMPK/ACC phosphorylation and abrogated its inhibition of FcεRI signaling cascades.
Zingerone enhanced LKB1 phosphorylation even in AMPKα2-silenced mast cells, indicating that LKB1 (or an upstream regulator) rather than AMPK itself is the primary molecular target of Zingerone.

In a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, oral Zingerone (25 and 50 mg/kg) dose-dependently reduced Evans blue extravasation at the ear compared to vehicle, comparable in direction to the H1-antihistamine fexofenadine.
In a passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) mouse model, oral Zingerone dose-dependently reduced serum levels of histamine, LTC4, and PGD2 following DNP-HSA challenge.

Propionate showed strong predicted binding affinity for the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), identified via bioinformatics as a key target mediating its effects in intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Propionate increased AhR expression during intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury, which was associated with inhibition of mast cell activation.
Propionate reduced mast cell activation (assessed by inflammatory factor and trypsin expression and flow cytometry) during intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Propionate attenuated intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury by inhibiting mast cell activation through regulation of the AhR-Notch1 pathway.
Propionate treatment enhanced expression of intestinal tight junction proteins, contributing to reduced mucosal damage in the ischemia-reperfusion mouse model.
Propionate treatment improved survival rate and histological outcomes in mice subjected to intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Intradermal LL-37 injection induced significant skin redness/lesions in wild-type mice, which were reduced by GE1111 treatment and absent in vehicle control and MRGPRB2 knockout mice.
Serum MCP-1 was significantly elevated in LL-37-treated wild-type mice compared to vehicle control and LL-37-treated MRGPRB2 knockout mice, and was reduced by GE1111 treatment.
Epidermal thickness was significantly increased in LL-37-treated mice compared to vehicle control and LL-37-treated MR K/O mice, and was significantly reduced by GE1111 treatment.
Percentage of degranulated mast cells in skin was significantly increased in LL-37-treated mice, and was significantly reduced in mice treated with 10 mg/kg or 20 mg/kg GE1111.
Epidermal barrier protein Involucrin expression was significantly lower in LL-37-treated mice compared to vehicle control and LL-37-treated MR K/O mice, and GE1111 treatment restored its expression.
Claudin-1 protein was reduced and TSLP protein was increased in skin of LL-37-treated mice, both reversed by GE1111 treatment.
STIM1 protein expression, involved in MRGPRX2/B2-mediated mast cell activation via store-operated calcium entry, was elevated in LL-37-treated mouse skin and reduced with GE1111 treatment.
Gene expression of the inflammatory cytokines IL-13, IL-33, MCP-1, IL-1β and TNF-α was elevated in LL-37-treated mouse skin, and GE1111 treatment dose-dependently decreased their expression.

Compound 48/80 significantly increased scratching number and duration in wild-type mice versus vehicle control and C48/80-treated MR K/O mice; GE1111 reduced scratching number and duration but not average scratch length.

C48/80 induced a significant increase in degranulated mast cells in skin compared to vehicle control and C48/80-treated MR K/O mice, which was significantly reduced by GE1111 treatment; epidermal thickness was unchanged.
GE1111 inhibited LL-37-induced mast cell degranulation with an IC50 of 6.271 µM and inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated calcium flux in transfected HEK-293 cells with an IC50 of 12.31 µM.

GE1111 significantly right-shifted the EC50 of LL-37 from 4.542 µM to 60.320 µM in the mast cell degranulation assay and from 7.163 µM to 26.680 µM in the calcium flux assay, indicating inhibition of LL-37-induced mast cell activation.
GE1111 reduced STIM1 expression and ERK1/2 phosphorylation induced by LL-37 in LAD-2 mast cells, indicating inhibition of the MRGPRX2 downstream activation pathway.
GE1111 treatment significantly decreased LL-37-induced gene expression of IL-31, MCP-1, and TNF-α in LAD-2 mast cells.
Supernatant from LL-37-treated mast cells reduced claudin-1 and increased TSLP expression in HaCaT keratinocytes; GE1111-treated mast cell supernatant reversed these changes.

Keratinocytes challenged with LL-37-treated mast cell supernatant showed significantly increased gene expression of IL-8, IL-13, and IL-17 compared to negative control, which was significantly reduced when treated with LL-37+GE1111 mast cell supernatant.
Macrophages exposed to LL-37-treated mast cell supernatant showed significantly reduced phagocytic activity compared to control, and this decrease was reversed by GE1111 co-treatment.
A β-arrestin PRESTO-TANGO assay failed to detect a luminescence change for LL-37 activation of MRGPRX2, prompting the authors to instead use a calcium flux assay in MRGPRX2-transfected HEK-293 cells.
Molecular profiling of breast mucinous cystadenocarcinoma showed a high frequency of TP53 mutations.
Large panel sequencing of breast MCA cases revealed frequent alterations in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway.
Genomic profiling comparisons in the literature indicate that breast MCA shares molecular similarities with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).
Despite the prevailing view that breast MCA is indolent, the study's cases showed robust growth features including a relatively high Ki67 proliferation index and brisk mitotic activity.
One of the 5 breast MCA cases exhibited micrometastasis in an axillary lymph node.
The isogenic GLA knockout (p.S364del, hemizygous) iPSC line lacks AGAL enzyme activity, leading to accumulation of the sphingolipid Gb3, modeling Fabry disease.

Fabry disease sensory-like neurons showed dysregulation of axon guidance and other disease-related pathways at both the transcriptomic (RNA) and proteomic (protein) level compared to the isogenic healthy control line.
Microfluidic assays showed that Fabry disease sensory-like neurons had shorter neurite length compared to the healthy isogenic control neurons.
Supplementation with AGAL enzyme reduced Gb3 accumulation in Fabry disease sensory-like neurons.
AGAL enzyme supplementation did not restore the transcriptomic state of Fabry disease sensory-like neurons toward the healthy control profile.
AGAL enzyme supplementation lowered ephrin A5 protein level in Fabry disease sensory-like neurons.
AGAL enzyme supplementation lowered glycoprotein M6A protein level in Fabry disease sensory-like neurons.
AGAL enzyme supplementation lowered protein levels of ephrin A5 in FD sensory-like neurons.
AGAL enzyme supplementation lowered glycoprotein M6A protein levels in FD sensory-like neurons.
Burning pain caused by small fiber neuropathy is described as an early symptom of Fabry disease with a major impact on health-related quality of life.
The 2023 Japanese nationwide survey identified 87 cases of atopic myelitis (AM), a number similar to the 2006 survey when accounting for the different survey periods.
The survey additionally identified 11 plexin D1-IgG-positive patients who did not fulfill AM diagnostic criteria, with a preponderance of women (8 of 11).
AM patients frequently exhibited paresthesia/dysesthesia (>90%), hypesthesia, motor weakness, and neuropathic pain (>70%) during the illness course, along with pyramidal tract signs in about 70%.
EDSS disability scores significantly improved from peak illness to last examination in AM patients, consistent with beneficial treatment effects over the disease course.
In all AM patients, EDSS disability scores were significantly positively correlated with disease duration.

AM patients frequently showed central conduction abnormalities on motor- and somatosensory-evoked potentials and cervical spinal cord MRI lesions, whereas peripheral nerve conduction studies were largely normal, localizing the lesion to the cervical spinal cord.

Current perception threshold testing frequently showed abnormalities affecting Aβ, Aδ, and C fibers in AM patients, most often as increased sensory thresholds, suggesting frequent dorsal horn/DRG damage.
Most AM patients had preceding/concomitant atopic disorders (>90%) and elevated total serum IgE (median 683 U/mL), with about two-thirds showing hyperIgEemia, while eosinophilia was infrequent.
Intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP) pulse therapy was the most commonly used treatment in AM (87.1%) and was generally effective (86.4%), but less effective specifically for pain (71.1%).
Plasmapheresis, used in about half of AM cases, showed the best general and pain-specific effectiveness (≥90%) among treatments.
Anti-allergic drugs, used by half of AM patients, were generally effective for overall symptoms (80%) but not effective for pain specifically (35.7%).
Among 31 AM patients tested for plexin D1-IgG, 6 (19.4%) were positive.

The underlying diseases associated with plexin D1-IgG positivity included AM and small fiber neuropathy (SFN) in 6 patients each (35.3%), NMOSD with aquaporin-4-IgG in 2 (11.8%), and painful trigeminal neuropathy, erythromelalgia, and multiple sclerosis in 1 patient each (5.9%).
Patients with plexin D1-associated neuropathic pain syndrome (PANPS) had a significantly older age at onset than plexin D1-IgG-negative AM patients, with a much higher frequency of onset at age ≥50.
Neuropathic pain at onset was significantly more common in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM, whereas motor weakness at onset was significantly more frequent in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM.
Facial pain was much more frequently encountered in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM patients, and the overall distribution of pain sites differed significantly between the two conditions.

Allodynia and erythromelalgia were significantly more frequent in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM, whereas motor weakness and pyramidal tract signs were significantly more common in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM.

Peak and final EDSS disability scores were significantly lower in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM patients, and EDSS did not significantly change from peak to last exam in PANPS (unlike AM-negative).

In PANPS, EDSS scores showed a strong positive correlation with disease duration, whereas plexin D1-IgG-negative AM patients showed no significant correlation, suggesting a chronic progressive, undertreated course in PANPS.

Decreased C-fiber thresholds on current perception threshold testing were more frequent in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM, while decreased thresholds were absent in AM-negative patients across all fiber types.

Atopic diathesis was markedly less prominent in PANPS than in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM, with significantly lower frequencies of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, total serum IgE, and hyperIgEemia, while eosinophil counts and specific IgE profiles did not differ.

Immunotherapies (oral corticosteroids, IVMP, immunosuppressants, plasmapheresis, IVIg) were used significantly more often in plexin D1-IgG-negative AM than in PANPS, but when administered, oral corticosteroids, IVMP, and plasmapheresis were similarly effective in both conditions; anti-allergic drugs were used more in AM-negative and were less effective in PANPS.

Comparing AM patients with vs without plexin D1-IgG, neuropathic pain at onset, allodynia, and facial pain were significantly more frequent in those with plexin D1-IgG, while total IgE and anti-allergic drug use were significantly lower.

This nationwide survey confirmed a female preponderance in PANPS, consistent with the authors' earlier single-institution study and with reports of plexin D1-IgG-positive small fiber neuropathy in Korean, Singaporean, and North American cohorts.
Tight junction protein ZO-1 was significantly reduced/disrupted in colonic mucosa of IBS patients compared to healthy controls.
Mucosal mast cells (tryptase-positive) in IBS patients showed elevated Tβ4 expression compared to healthy subjects.
Colonic mucus Tβ4 levels, quantified by ELISA, were significantly higher in IBS patients (n=38) than in healthy subjects (n=38), supporting its use as a diagnostic biomarker.
In a water avoidance stress (WAS) rat model of IBS, mast cell numbers and Tβ4 secretion were markedly increased in the colon after 10 days of psychological stress.
Serum markers of intestinal permeability (diamine oxidase, D-lactate, bacterial endotoxin) were significantly elevated in stressed rats compared to controls, confirming increased gut permeability.
MLCK, which promotes tight junction opening via MLC phosphorylation, was significantly increased in colon mucosa of stressed rats compared with controls.
Bacterial infiltration into the submucosa, assessed by FISH, was markedly increased in stressed rats, confirming intestinal barrier damage and dysbiosis.
IBS colonic mucus decreased TEER and increased FD4 permeability in Caco2 monolayers, and this effect was abolished by pre-neutralizing the mucus with a Tβ4-neutralizing antibody but not IgG control.
Synthetic Tβ4 applied directly to Caco2 monolayers caused a concentration-dependent decline in barrier impedance (Cell Index) and reduced ZO-1 and Occludin protein levels.
Tβ4 treatment of Caco2 cells increased MLCK expression while decreasing protein and mRNA levels of IL22RA1 and its downstream effector Reg3γ in a dose-dependent manner.
Pretreatment with the MLCK inhibitor ML-7 alleviated the Tβ4-induced decrease in ZO-1 levels, indicating MLCK mediates Tβ4's effect on tight junctions.

Intraperitoneal injection of Tβ4 in C57BL/6 mice increased intestinal permeability, disrupted tight junctions, enhanced MLCK activation, reduced IL22RA1, and increased bacterial infiltration beneath the mucosa.
Tβ4 induced intestinal permeability and dysbiosis even in mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice, showing its barrier-disrupting effect occurs independently of mast cells.

Tβ4 knockout rats were protected from stress-induced intestinal barrier damage, maintaining intact tight junctions and normal MLCK levels, and reintroduction of Tβ4 restored susceptibility to stress-induced injury.
In Tβ4-/- rats, stress did not reduce IL22RA1 and Reg3γ expression, but reduction occurred only when Tβ4 was administered exogenously, confirming Tβ4's necessity for immune barrier disruption.

Transplantation of IBS patient colonic mucus into rat colons disrupted tight junctions and caused bacterial infiltration in wild-type rats but not in Tβ4 knockout rats, demonstrating that mucus-induced barrier damage requires Tβ4.
Reconstitution of Tβ4-/- rats with wild-type peritoneal mast cells (PMCs) restored serum and intestinal Tβ4 to normal levels, indicating mast cells are a major source of circulating and tissue Tβ4.

CRH treatment increased epithelial cell shedding and barrier permeability (FD4 flux, TJ disruption, bacterial infiltration) more strongly in Tβ4-/- rats reconstituted with wild-type mast cells than in controls, confirming MC-derived Tβ4 mediates CRH-induced barrier damage.

CRH treatment of wild-type HMC-1 mast cells, but not Tβ4-knockdown HMC-1 cells, disrupted tight junctions in co-cultured Caco2 monolayers, confirming that MC-derived Tβ4 is required for barrier damage.
The mast cell stabilizer DSCG blocked CRH-induced degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release) but did not inhibit CRH-induced Tβ4 secretion, showing Tβ4 release is independent of degranulation.
The CRHR1 antagonist R121919 inhibited CRH-induced Tβ4 secretion from mast cells, identifying CRH/CRHR1 signaling as the specific trigger for Tβ4 release.

Intraperitoneal R121919 treatment in stressed rats blocked FD4 permeability, reduced intestinal mucosal Tβ4 levels, normalized tight junctions, and blocked stress-induced submucosal bacterial infiltration, indicating therapeutic potential for stress-induced IBS.
RNA sequencing of Tβ4-treated Caco2 cells identified 243 upregulated and 186 downregulated genes, with KEGG pathway enrichment in HIF-1, PI3K/Akt, TNF, and JAK/STAT signaling pathways.
Tβ4 significantly suppressed phosphorylation of JAK1 and STAT3 in Caco2 cells, confirmed by GSEA, western blot, and immunofluorescence.

Co-culture of CRH-activated Tβ4-knockdown HMC-1 (vs wild-type) increased JAK1/STAT3 phosphorylation and ZO-1 while reducing MLCK in Caco2 cells; these effects were reversed by the JAK1/STAT3 inhibitor SHR0302, demonstrating Tβ4 acts via JAK1/STAT3 inhibition to regulate MLCK/ZO-1.
IBS patients showed significantly worse current anxiety scores (HADS-A) compared to healthy controls.
IBS patients showed significantly worse depression scores (HADS-D) compared to healthy controls.
IBS patients had significantly worse physical (SF-12 PCS) and mental (SF-12 MCS) quality of life scores compared to healthy controls.
IBS patients had significantly higher GI symptom-related anxiety (Visceral Sensitivity Index) compared to healthy controls.
IBS patients had significantly higher perceived stress levels (PSS) compared to healthy controls.
IBS patients had significantly higher somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) compared to healthy controls.
Across all participants, those with high ACE total scores had worse somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) than those with low ACE scores.

IBS patients with high ACE scores did not significantly differ from IBS patients with low ACE scores in clinical/behavioral symptom measures, although IBS-SSS and IBS-QOL trended worse in the high ACE group.
Among healthy controls, those with high ACE scores reported worse somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) than those with low ACE scores.
Among those with high ACE scores, IBS patients scored higher than HCs on the 'parents treated violently' ACE subscale, anxiety/depression, VSI, PSS, PHQ-15, and had poorer SF-12 PCS/MCS.
Among high-ACE participants, healthy controls scored higher than IBS patients on the emotional and physical abuse ACE subscales.

A stacked ensemble XGBoost/SVM model integrating clinical, metagenomic, structural, diffusion, and resting-state connectivity data classified the four IBS/ACE subgroups with a Cohen's kappa of 0.67 and overall accuracy of 78.19%.
The multi-omic model achieved AUCs of 0.70 for HC-high ACE, 0.82 for IBS-low ACE, and 0.87 for IBS-high ACE classification.

The top clinical predictors of subgroup classification, ranked by model gain, were VSI Score, PHQ-15 Score, ACE Parental Divorce/Separation, and IBS-QOL Social Reaction, all associated with IBS-related classes.
IBS participants showed a stronger negative correlation between Bifidobacterium abundance and ACE parental divorce/separation score compared to healthy controls.
In IBS participants with high ACE scores, Akkermansia abundance was more strongly negatively associated with somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) than in other groups.

In IBS participants with high ACE scores, Bifidobacterium was more negatively associated with ACE parental divorce/separation and with cortical thickness of a central autonomic/salience network region (left lateral orbital sulcus) than in other groups.

In participants with high ACE, GI symptom-related anxiety (VSI) was positively associated with functional connectivity between the postcentral sulcus and parahippocampal gyrus, regions involved in interoception and emotional processing.

In healthy controls with high ACE, salience network cortical thickness was negatively associated with several beneficial gut bacterial genera (Akkermansia, Subdoligranulum, Intestinimonas, Christensenella).
In low-ACE IBS participants, the butyrate-producing genus Subdoligranulum was negatively linked to a default mode network brain region (lateral superior temporal gyrus microstructure).
Prior literature cited in the paper reports higher IBS prevalence in women than men, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.67.
Cited literature indicates individuals with a history of adverse childhood experiences are twice as likely to have IBS as those without ACE exposure.

The individual neuroimaging and metagenomic base models had much lower standalone predictive power (kappa 0.07-0.18) than the clinical model (kappa 0.67), suggesting subtle, context-dependent brain and microbiome alterations in IBS.
Intracerebroventricular (ICV) Angiotensin II significantly increased mean arterial pressure compared to ICV saline.
ICV Angiotensin II significantly decreased renal sympathetic nerve activity (RSNA) compared to ICV saline, without affecting heart rate.

Blocking AT2 receptors with PD123319 during Ang II infusion produced a further significant increase in MAP with no change in HR or RSNA, consistent with AT2 receptors normally buffering the AT1-mediated pressor effect.
Selective AT2 receptor activation with CGP42112 increased heart rate without changing MAP or RSNA.
Combining Ang II with AT1 blockade (losartan) significantly increased heart rate, unmasking an AT2-mediated chronotropic effect.
Central losartan alone did not significantly alter MAP, HR, or RSNA, suggesting AT1 receptors do not exert tonic effects under baseline conditions.
NOS inhibition with L-NAME significantly increased MAP and HR, without altering RSNA, indicating a tonic vasodilatory role for central nitric oxide.
Adding L-NAME to ongoing Ang II infusion further increased MAP with no change in HR or RSNA, suggesting nitric oxide normally restrains the central pressor effect of Ang II.
Combining the AT2 agonist CGP42112 with L-NAME significantly increased MAP and HR, indicating that the cardiovascular effects of central AT2 receptor stimulation are NO-dependent.
ICV Ang II expanded the baroreflex range (A1) and increased sensitivity (maximum response and maximum gain) of the RSNA-MAP baroreflex curve compared to saline.

CGP42112 (AT2 agonist) alone produced only minor baroreflex changes: expanded range (A1) and a drop in the lowest point of the curve (A4), with no other baroreflex parameter changes compared to saline.

Central losartan increased baroreflex sensitivity (slope A2) and maximum gain compared to saline, but lowered MAP saturation and operating range, indicating AT1 receptors normally dampen baroreflex sensitivity.
AT2 receptor blockade with PD123319 lowered baroreflex sensitivity (A2), MAP threshold, and maximum gain, but increased MAP saturation and operating range compared to saline.
ICV L-NAME increased the baroreflex mid-point pressure (A3) but did not change other baroreflex gain curve parameters compared to saline.

Baroreflex gain curve parameters following Ang II plus losartan were comparable to Ang II alone, indicating the Ang II-induced baroreflex enhancement persists despite AT1 receptor blockade and is thus AT2-mediated.

AT2 receptor blockade with PD123319 during Ang II infusion reduced baroreflex sensitivity (A2) and maximum gain but increased mid-point pressure (A3), MAP saturation and operating range, indicating that the baroreflex-enhancing effect of Ang II is partly mediated via AT2 receptors.
Baroreflex gain curve parameters during Ang II plus L-NAME were similar to Ang II alone, indicating the pressor and baroreflex effects of ICV Ang II itself are independent of NOS.

Combining the AT2 agonist CGP42112 with NOS inhibitor L-NAME increased baroreflex sensitivity (A2), maximum gain, and elevated the lowest point (A4) of the curve, reversing the CGP42112-induced lowering of A4 and demonstrating that AT2-mediated baroreflex facilitation is nitric oxide-dependent.
Prior literature cited in the introduction associates autonomic nervous system dysfunction with visceral pain in IBS.
The introduction cites prior work indicating IBS is associated with unchecked sympathetic nervous system predominance and desensitized parasympathetic activity.
Prior studies cited by the authors report that abdominal muscle EMG can serve as a metric of visceral pain distinguishing IBS patients from controls.
Skin conductance level rose from baseline to the Stroop, Contraction, and Combo stress tasks in both the prototype and reference EDA devices, with minimal change during Tilt.
NS.SCRs increased from baseline to stress task in both devices during Stroop, Contraction, and Combo conditions, tracking closely between the prototype and reference devices.
The frequency-domain EDASympn index was nearly identical between the prototype and reference devices across all four stress tasks, indicating strong device agreement.
TVSymp values increased from baseline during Stroop, Contraction, and especially the Combo condition, with close agreement between the prototype and reference devices.
EMG envelope correlations between the prototype and reference devices averaged 0.79 across channels, confirming strong agreement in temporal signal shape.
PSD correlations between prototype and reference EMG signals exceeded 0.72 across channels, indicating consistent spectral agreement.

The prototype device showed a lower signal-to-noise ratio but a higher signal-to-motion ratio than the reference device, indicating better robustness against motion artifacts despite modestly worse noise performance.
Both the prototype and reference ECG devices showed consistent decreases in mean RR interval (i.e., increased heart rate) from baseline to the Tilt and Stroop stress tasks.
The LF/HF ratio, an index of sympathovagal balance, increased from baseline to task during both Tilt and Stroop tests, with comparable patterns between the prototype and reference devices.

Adaptive NLMS denoising using EMG and accelerometer signals as noise references restored accurate R-peak detection in ECG recordings that were heavily contaminated by motion and muscle interference during the Contraction and Combined stress tests.

Under full-load continuous operation, the wearable belt operated for approximately 7 hours and the wristband for approximately 10 hours before battery voltage decay disrupted Bluetooth signal transmission.

Impedance spectroscopy showed stainless-steel electrodes had the lowest overall electrode-skin impedance compared to Ag/AgCl and CB-PDMS electrodes, though direct comparison is limited by differing placements and sizes.
No participants reported itching or skin irritation during or after use of the belt and wristband across all experimental tasks, supporting device wearability.
Gastric electrical stimulation produced significant relief of nausea, vomiting, and upper GI symptoms at one-year follow-up in patients with drug-refractory gastroparesis.
Patients with gastroparesis symptoms receiving jejunostomy tube feedings responded similarly to gastric electrical stimulation as those without tube feedings.
Patients treated with GES maintained their weight regardless of whether they had a jejunostomy tube, indicating the tube is not a contraindication to GES.
Both the tube-fed and non-tube-fed treatment arms experienced considerable improvement in tolerability of a regular diet after GES.
GzmB knockout mice developed significantly smaller collagen-1+ subretinal fibrotic lesions than wild-type mice overall.
In older mice specifically, GzmB knockout resulted in significantly smaller fibrotic lesions than wild-type, but the difference did not reach significance in younger mice.
TSP-1 immunolabeling within subretinal fibrotic lesions was lower in GzmB KO mice compared to WT mice, contrary to initial expectation.
GzmB knockout mice showed increased decorin (DCN) immunolabeling within subretinal fibrotic lesions compared to wild-type mice.

GzmB deficiency increased macrophage density and macrophage-to-myofibroblast transition within subretinal fibrotic lesions, without changing total macrophage numbers in the overlying subretinal space.
GzmB knockout mice exhibited a greater number of CD206+ α-SMA+ M2 macrophages within fibrotic lesions and in the choroid beneath the lesions than wild-type mice.
GzmB knockout mice had fewer mast cells within subretinal fibrotic lesions than wild-type mice, confirmed by fluorescein-avidin D labeling and toluidine blue staining.

TUNEL staining revealed significantly fewer dying photoreceptor cells in the outer nuclear layer above fibrotic lesions in GzmB knockout mice compared to wild-type mice, while GFAP macroglial reactivity did not differ between genotypes.

Exogenous recombinant GzmB treatment significantly delayed ARPE-19 wound closure compared to control and TGF-β2 treatments at 24, 48, and 72 hours, with co-administration of GzmB and TGF-β2 delaying closure further.

The small-molecule GzmB inhibitor VTI-1002 significantly enhanced ARPE-19 wound closure when co-administered with GzmB or GzmB+TGF-β2, and also rescued delayed wound closure when added after sequential GzmB then TGF-β2 exposure.

Bulk RNA sequencing of ARPE-19 cells after acute 6-hour GzmB stimulation identified 713 differentially expressed genes, with downregulation of TGF-β signaling, angiogenesis, and cell-junction genes, and upregulation of junction, EMT, and inflammation-related genes.

qPCR validation showed VEGF-A, BMP4, and IL-33 gene expression were significantly increased only at 18 hours after GzmB stimulation, while GJA1 was elevated at both 6 and 18 hours and SOX4 was unchanged.
Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analyses of GzmB-stimulated ARPE-19 DEGs showed enrichment for angiogenesis, cell migration, cell proliferation, TGF-β signaling, apoptosis, and EMT-related pathways.

Acute GzmB stimulation followed by TGF-β2 treatment induced loss of tight junction protein ZO-1 and expression of EMT markers (α-SMA, TSP-1, Col1, fibronectin) in ARPE-19 cells, consistent with partial epithelial-mesenchymal transition rather than full myofibroblast differentiation.
Sex-based differences in fibrotic lesion area were observed among wild-type mice, but not among GzmB knockout mice, likely reflecting an unequal male/female cohort composition in the WT group.

Older wild-type mice developed significantly larger fibrotic lesions than younger wild-type mice, whereas lesion area did not differ by age in GzmB knockout mice, supporting an age-dependent role of extracellular GzmB accumulation in fibrosis.
Serum IgE levels were significantly reduced in mice treated with chlorogenic acid or quercetin compared to the positive allergic group.
Serum IgG1 levels were significantly reduced by CA and QR treatment compared to the positive allergic group.
Serum IgG2a levels were significantly increased in CA and QR treated mice compared to the positive allergic group.
IL-4 levels were reduced by 11.62% in the CA group and 29.02% in the QR group compared to the allergic group.
IFN-gamma levels were significantly higher in CA and QR treated mice than in the allergic group.
IL-10 levels were significantly higher in CA and QR treated mice than in the allergic group.
IL-10 mRNA expression in the jejunum was significantly elevated in CA- and QR-treated mice compared to the allergic group.
FOXP3 mRNA expression in the jejunum was significantly elevated in CA- and QR-treated mice compared to the allergic group, indicating increased regulatory T-cell activity.
Protein expression of PPAR-gamma in the jejunum was significantly increased following CA and QR treatment compared to the allergic group.
Protein expression of CD36 in the jejunum was significantly increased following CA and QR treatment, consistent with enhanced fatty acid oxidation downstream of PPAR-gamma activation.
Protein expression of CPT1 in the jejunum was significantly increased following CA and QR treatment, indicating upregulated fatty acid oxidation.
The authors conclude that CA and QR alleviate food allergy responses in mice by boosting PPAR-gamma activity, which upregulates CD36/CPT1-mediated fatty acid oxidation.
Long COVID participants showed no significant differences from healthy controls on pulmonary function tests or 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures.
Long COVID participants reported significantly reduced perceived cognitive function in everyday life compared to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated fatigue symptoms relative to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated anxiety symptoms relative to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated depression symptoms relative to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated sleep disturbance relative to normative expectations.
Average dyspnea severity and pain interference in Long COVID participants did not significantly differ from normative expectations.

Despite significant subjective cognitive complaints, most Long COVID participants had objective NIHTB-CB total cognitive composite, executive function, processing speed, and language scores within normal limits.
Memory domain t-scores on NIHTB-CB were significantly elevated relative to normative expectations in the Long COVID sample.
Lower 129Xe MRI RBC:membrane gas exchange ratio was correlated with higher cerebral perfusion measured via arterial spin labeling.
Lower 129Xe MRI RBC:gas ratio was correlated with higher cerebral perfusion measured via arterial spin labeling.
RBC:mem showed an inverse trend with severity of sleep disturbance that did not reach statistical significance.
Lower RBC:gas was significantly correlated with greater sleep disturbance severity.
Cerebral perfusion measured via ASL showed a strong positive correlation with sleep disturbance severity.
Higher RBC:mem gas exchange was positively correlated with better executive function performance on objective cognitive testing.
RBC:mem showed a non-significant trend toward positive correlation with total cognitive composite score.
129Xe pulmonary MRI measures were not associated with subjective report of cognitive difficulties in everyday life.
Initial significant relationships between lobar brain volumes and 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures were no longer significant after adjusting for age.
White matter hyperintensity volume and diffusion tensor metrics (FA, MD, RD) were not significantly related to 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures after controlling for age.
Pre-existing comorbidities reported among the Long COVID cohort included hypertension, asthma, fibromyalgia, depression, neuropathy, diabetes mellitus, and sleep apnea.
The most commonly reported Long COVID symptoms in the cohort were fatigue, dyspnea, and headache.
Elevated plasma neurofilament light chain levels were found in ME/CFS patients and correlated with cognitive deficit and autonomic dysfunction.
Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ have been consistently observed in ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients show a Th1/Th2 imbalance with reduced Th1 functionality and disrupted Th2 responses, contributing to autoimmune-like features and immune dysregulation.
A subset of ME/CFS patients displayed B cell hyperactivity, suggesting a role in autoimmune-mediated disease pathogenesis via pathogenic autoantibody production.
NK cell dysfunction in ME/CFS compromises antiviral immunity, potentially permitting reactivation of viruses like EBV and cytomegalovirus.
ME/CFS patients exhibit significantly diminished glutathione levels, with a specific GSH peroxidase 1 gene variant associated with reduced cerebral GSH levels.

Activity of key antioxidant enzymes SOD, CAT, and GPx is attenuated in ME/CFS patients, aggravating oxidative stress; a shared oxidative stress signature with PACS shows diminished SOD activity and GPx4-mediated lipid peroxidation.
ME/CFS patients show significantly reduced ATP synthesis rate by Complex V in PBMCs, along with increased mitochondrial proton leak diverting energy from ATP synthesis.

A metabolic profiling study of 200 ME/CFS patients found diminished serum amino acids for oxidative metabolism and elevated PDK expression in PBMCs inhibiting PDH, with patient serum inducing excess lactate in myoblasts, implicating PDH dysfunction in PEM and impaired ATP generation.

dUTPase protein encoded by EBV and HSV-1 is transported to the brain via exosomes, inducing pro-inflammatory cytokine release from endothelial cells, astrocytes, and pericytes, degrading tight junction proteins and disrupting blood-brain barrier integrity.
A meta-analysis of 65 neuroimaging studies on ME/CFS revealed hypoactivity in the insula and thalamus, disrupting limbic connections and contributing to symptoms.

ME/CFS patients exhibited higher levels of fibroblast growth factor 21 and N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide than healthy controls, along with elevated oxidative stress markers and inflammatory cytokines.

A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 99 CFS patients found no dose-dependent efficacy for IVIG (0.5, 1, or 2 g/kg monthly for 3 months) and did not support its use as standard therapy.
An uncontrolled case series of 17 infection-related ME/CFS patients receiving low-dose subcutaneous Ig showed decline in composite symptom scores and improved quality of life and working capacity.
In a Phase III trial of 208 ME/CFS patients, 51.2% of a severely debilitated subgroup experienced ≥25% improvement in exercise treadmill test duration with rintatolimod.
In a second Phase III trial of 234 severe CFS patients, rintatolimod yielded 21.3% placebo-adjusted improvement in exercise tolerance by Week 40, with improved Karnofsky scores and ADL.
NAC supplementation (1800 mg/day for 4 weeks) in 16 ME/CFS patients increased cortical GSH levels and significantly reduced ME/CFS symptoms.
In a study of 15 ME/CFS, 15 PACS, and 16 healthy controls, NAC did not significantly reduce T-cell hyperproliferation in female patients with ME/CFS or PACS.
An 8-week trial combining CoQ10 (400 mg) and selenium (200 µg) significantly reduced fatigue and improved quality of life in ME/CFS patients.
A 12-week trial in 207 ME/CFS patients found CoQ10 (200mg) plus NADH (20mg) resulted in significant reductions in fatigue and improvements in quality of life and sleep parameters.
A 28-day pilot randomized blinded trial in 23 ME/CFS patients found daily hydrogen water supplementation did not improve self-reported fatigue compared to placebo.

Four ME/CFS patients receiving hydrogen gas inhalation (6-7%, 3-5 h/day) showed progressive symptom improvement over 20 weeks, with total symptom scores decreasing from 43 to 13 on the Canadian Consensus Criteria.

Neither 2400 IU/week nor 1200 IU/week vitamin D3 supplementation effectively relieved pain, and high-dose vitamin D3 (100,000 IU every 2 months for 6 months) failed to improve vascular function markers or fatigue in ME/CFS patients.

Coadministration of weekly high-dose vitamin D (cholecalciferol 50,000 IU) with antidepressant therapy was associated with significantly improved fatigue scores at weeks 4, 8, and 12 in a case-control study.
In 38 female CFS patients, 2 months of multivitamin-mineral supplementation increased SOD activity with alleviation of fatigue, sleep disturbances, autonomic symptoms, and headache burden.
36-week supplementation with yeast beta-glucan, vitamin D3, vitamin B6, and zinc significantly alleviated cognitive fatigue in 65 ME/CFS patients in an RCT.

Studies have identified low carnitine levels in ME/CFS patients, suggestive of underlying mitochondrial impairment, and L-carnitine supplementation reduced fatigue in a systematic review, with oral L-carnitine restoring serotonin levels and reducing fatigue in ME/CFS with comorbid hypothyroidism.

Daily supplementation with 2000 mg oxaloacetate for 3 months significantly reduced fatigue levels by over 25% from baseline compared to placebo, with a dose-response relationship observed in a 6-week trial.

A 30-day pilot trial of sodium DCA-based supplement in 22 ME/CFS patients resulted in a 42.7% reduction in fatigue severity scores among 10 participants; a separate prospective trial identified pretreatment characteristics predicting DCA responders with ROC AUC of 0.92.

ME/CFS patients show dysfunction of the TRPM3 calcium channel critical for NK cell calcium permeability, resulting in diminished NK cell activity; low-dose naltrexone reversed this via mu-opioid receptor blockade.
In a study of 218 ME/CFS patients, LDN demonstrated significant improvement in 73.9% of cases, with notable benefits in alertness and overall function.

In a pilot study of 55 ME/CFS patients, a 41-day course of oral minocycline resulted in favorable symptom improvements for 80% of treatment completers, with 90% success when initiated within six months of onset.

A pooled analysis of 1298 ME/CFS patients from eight trials revealed CBT was associated with significant reductions in fatigue severity and functional impairment, alongside improved physical function.

GET research shows divergent outcomes, with some trials showing improvement but recent findings associating GET with symptom exacerbation including increased fatigue, pain, and PEM in a significant proportion of patients; a pragmatic trial in 241 adolescents found no significant difference vs activity management on physical function at 6 months; updated NICE guidelines classify GET as harmful and advise against its use.

A systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated pacing interventions led to significant reduction in fatigue (Hedges' g = -0.52) and improvement in physical function compared to no treatment or routine care.
A meta-analysis of 16 studies with 1346 participants confirmed manual and electroacupuncture are effective in alleviating ME/CFS symptoms.
In an uncontrolled case series of 17 patients with infection-related ME/CFS, low-dose subcutaneous immunoglobulin improved composite symptom scores, quality of life, and working capacity.
A double-blind RCT of 99 CFS patients found no dose-dependent efficacy of IVIG across three dose regimens compared to placebo.
In a Phase III RCT of 208 ME/CFS patients, 51.2% of a severely debilitated subgroup showed ≥25% improvement in exercise treadmill test duration with rintatolimod.
A second Phase III RCT of 234 severe CFS patients found rintatolimod produced a 21.3% placebo-adjusted improvement in exercise tolerance by Week 40, with improved Karnofsky scores and ADL.
A study of 16 ME/CFS patients found NAC supplementation (1,800 mg/day, 4 weeks) increased cortical GSH levels and significantly reduced ME/CFS symptoms.
NAC did not significantly reduce T-cell hyperproliferation in female patients with ME/CFS or PACS, suggesting increasing GSH alone may be insufficient.
A pilot study in older adults found GlyNAC (glycine plus NAC) supplementation improved GSH, mitochondrial function, and reduced oxidative stress, with benefits in cognitive and muscle function.
An 8-week trial found CoQ10 (400 mg) combined with selenium (200 µg) significantly reduced fatigue and improved quality of life in ME/CFS patients.
A 12-week trial in 207 ME/CFS patients found CoQ10 (200 mg) plus NAD (20 mg) significantly reduced fatigue and improved quality of life and sleep.
In healthy participants, a randomized double-blind trial found pre-exercise hydrogen water consumption improved endurance capacity and reduced subjective fatigue scores.
A 28-day pilot RCT in 23 ME/CFS patients found daily hydrogen water supplementation did not improve self-reported fatigue compared to placebo.
Four ME/CFS patients receiving hydrogen gas inhalation (6-7%, 3-5 h/day) showed progressive symptom improvement over 20 weeks, with total symptom scores decreasing from 43 to 13.
A cross-sectional survey of 38 ME/CFS patients on long-term B12 injections and oral folic acid found higher injection frequency/dose and folic acid intake associated with improved clinical outcomes.
In a 3-month open trial of vitamin B12 nasal drops in 51 ME/CFS patients, 34 responders showed improved physical activity and fatigue scores correlated with serum B12 rising from 328 to 973 pmol/L.
Wepner et al. found neither 2,400 IU/week nor 1,200 IU/week vitamin D3 supplementation effectively relieved pain in ME/CFS patients.
Witham et al. reported high-dose vitamin D3 supplementation (100,000 IU every 2 months for 6 months) failed to improve vascular function markers or reduce fatigue in ME/CFS patients.

Coadministration of weekly high-dose vitamin D (cholecalciferol 50,000 IU) with antidepressant therapy was associated with significantly improved fatigue scores at weeks 4, 8, and 12 in a case-control study.

In a prospective study of 38 female CFS patients, 2 months of multivitamin-mineral supplementation increased SOD activity and alleviated fatigue, sleep disturbances, autonomic symptoms, and headache burden.
A 36-week RCT of 65 ME/CFS patients found daily supplementation with yeast beta-glucan, vitamin D3, vitamin B6, and zinc significantly alleviated cognitive fatigue.
Studies have identified low carnitine levels in ME/CFS patients, suggestive of underlying mitochondrial impairment.
A systematic review identified L-carnitine as one of the few dietary supplements showing significant efficacy in reducing fatigue in ME/CFS patients, though with methodological limitations.
Oral L-carnitine administration was associated with restored serotonin levels and reduced fatigue in patients with ME/CFS and hypothyroidism.
A 6-week oxaloacetate supplementation trial produced marked improvements in physical and mental fatigue with a dose-response relationship.
Cash et al. found daily supplementation with 2,000 mg oxaloacetate for 3 months significantly reduced fatigue levels by over 25% from baseline compared to rice flour placebo.
An analysis of 200 ME/CFS patients versus 102 healthy individuals revealed reduced amino acids involved in oxidative metabolism, indicative of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) dysfunction.
A 30-day pilot trial of a sodium DCA-based nutritional supplement in 22 ME/CFS patients resulted in a 42.7% reduction in fatigue severity scores among 10 participants.
In a prospective trial of 35 ME/CFS patients, a logistic regression model identified six pretreatment characteristics that predicted DCA responders vs non-responders with ROC AUC of 0.92.
In a mouse model of ME/CFS-like manifestations induced by repeated forced swimming, DCA administration rescued locomotor deficits and elevated PDH activity.
Dysfunction of the TRPM3 calcium channel, critical for NK cell calcium signaling, results in diminished NK cell activity in ME/CFS patients; naltrexone restores calcium influx.
In a study of 218 ME/CFS patients, low-dose naltrexone demonstrated significant improvement in 73.9% of cases, with notable benefits in alertness and overall function.
Experimental study demonstrates that low-dose naltrexone induces a phenotypic shift in BV-2 microglial cells from a pro-inflammatory to a quiescent, anti-inflammatory M2 state.

Oral minocycline (100 mg twice on day 1, then 100 mg daily for 41 days) improved ME/CFS symptoms including disequilibrium, orthostatic intolerance, and neuropathic pain, most pronounced in early-stage patients.
A registered clinical trial (NCT06952413) is evaluating rituximab in ME/CFS to target immune dysfunction, B cell abnormalities, and autoimmune components.
The Low-dose Naltrexone for Post-COVID Fatigue Syndrome trial (NCT05430152) is exploring LDN's potential to reduce fatigue and inflammation in a mechanistically grounded approach.
ME/CFS patients show significant alterations in T cell metabolism and function, including mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced glycolytic activity, and upregulated exhaustion markers.
ME/CFS patients frequently show gut dysbiosis with diminished microbial diversity and depletion of health-promoting Firmicutes and butyrate-producing species.
The Brain-Gut Interaction Mechanism in CFS study (ChiCTR2200056530) uses fMRI and 16S rRNA sequencing to investigate immune, neuroinflammatory, and metabolic interactions underlying ME/CFS.
A registered yoga trial (NCT06978582) is evaluating yoga, breathing exercises, and body awareness for reducing fatigue in ME/CFS using HRV and the Chalder Fatigue Scale.
Studies show that yoga can significantly reduce fatigue, pain, anxiety, and depression, and improve subjective well-being and personality traits in ME/CFS patients.

Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS), under investigation in two registered trials, is proposed to mitigate cognitive deficits, improve autonomic function (e.g., HRV), and reduce POTS-related symptoms by modulating vagus nerve activity.
The Hydrogen Water Intervention trial (NCT07009691) is investigating hydrogen water as a supplemental ME/CFS therapy, using HRV monitoring to predict individual treatment responses.

The Solve Together platform (NCT04806620) collects multidimensional phenotypic data from electronic medical records, patient-reported outcomes, and wearables to identify ME/CFS disease endotypes and monitor progression.
The Long COVID-19 Wearable Device Study (NCT05741112) uses continuous monitoring of sleep, activity, heart rate, and HRV to objectively quantify PEM and fatigue severity.
The Multi-Center Registry for ME/CFS (NCT05778006) is building a large-scale registry to standardize epidemiological data collection, phenotypic stratification, and longitudinal outcome monitoring.

Ongoing CFS trials integrating photobiomodulation and biofeedback with remote monitoring platforms (NCT06145867, NCT05397626) aim to enhance patient engagement and adherence to potentially improve treatment outcomes.
Overall frequencies of major T cell subsets and NK cells in ex vivo PBMCs did not differ between mild/moderate and severe ME/CFS groups.

MR1-tetramer confirmed that CD3+ MAIT cells and CD8+ MAIT cells were present at elevated frequency in severely affected ME/CFS (ME-SA) compared to mild/moderate (ME-MM), consistent with a prior report.
CD4+ MAIT cell frequency was significantly higher in the mild/moderate ME/CFS group compared to the severe group, consistent across all staining panels.
CD8 surface expression (MFI) on CD8+ T cells was significantly lower in the mild/moderate group compared to the severe group.
Frequency and CD8 expression in the CD8intermediate subpopulation were higher in ME-MM, while the CD8upper subpopulation was more frequent in ME-SA.
The early-senescence-associated CD57-CD28- subset within CD4+ central memory T cells was significantly more frequent in the mild/moderate group than the severe group.
The senescence-associated CD57-CD28- subset within CD8+ effector memory and TEMRA T cells was significantly elevated in mild/moderate compared to severe ME/CFS.
Frequency of CD28 expression on double-negative MAIT cells was reduced in mild/moderate ME/CFS compared to severe.
A strong negative correlation between CD28+ MAIT frequency and CD57-CD28- T cell frequency (CD4+ and CD8+) was seen only in the mild/moderate group, not the severe group.
NK cell granzyme B expression (MFI) was reduced in severe ME/CFS compared to mild/moderate, while perforin MFI did not differ.
MFI of both granzyme B and perforin in CD8+ T cells was significantly reduced in the severe ME/CFS group compared to mild/moderate.
Ex vivo granzyme B-positive MAIT cell frequency was higher in severe ME/CFS, but upregulation after stimulation was greater in mild/moderate ME/CFS.
Perforin-expressing MAIT cell frequency was significantly lower in severe ME/CFS than mild/moderate, and the CD4-CD8- double negative MAIT subset was identified as the main perforin source.
Ex vivo CD69 expression was significantly higher on CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells and MAITs in severe compared to mild/moderate ME/CFS, indicating global increased lymphocyte activation status.
Frequency of CD38+CD69+ cells within CD4+, CD8+ T cells and MAITs was significantly increased in severe compared to mild/moderate ME/CFS.
PD-1 expression level (MFI) within PD-1+ subsets of CD4+, CD8+ T cells, MAITs and NK cells was lower in severe compared to mild/moderate ME/CFS, despite no difference in the frequency of PD-1+ cells.
Frequency of HLA-DR and CD38 co-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was significantly higher in mild/moderate compared to severe ME/CFS.
After PMA/ionomycin stimulation, TNF production was higher in severe ME/CFS across CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells and MAITs, with a significant difference in MAITs.
After stimulation, IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells and MAITs were significantly elevated in severe compared to mild/moderate ME/CFS.
The proportion of IFNγ and TNF co-producing bifunctional MAIT cells was significantly higher in severe ME/CFS, while double-negative (non-cytokine-producing) MAITs were reduced.
Both frequency and MFI of T-bet expression in MAIT cells were significantly increased in severe ME/CFS, without a corresponding difference in EOMES.

The COL1A1 missense variant c.934C>T p.(Arg312Cys) is a known rare cause of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and was identified in both mother and infant in this family.
This case represents the first reported association of COL1A1-related classical EDS with congenital diaphragmatic hernia in a newborn.
The infant's postoperative recovery from diaphragmatic hernia repair was complicated by chylothorax, diagnosed on day 10 of life, which resolved with reduced long-chain triglyceride enteral feeding.
A small muscular ventricular septal defect was detected antenatally at 20 weeks gestation in the fetus but was clinically undetectable after birth.

The COL1A1 p.(Arg312Cys) variant is associated with vascular complications such as mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, vertebral artery tortuosity, iliac artery aneurysm/dissection and coeliac trunk aneurysm/dissection, though with incomplete penetrance and usually manifesting in adulthood.

The COL1A1 c.934C>T p.(Arg312Cys) variant is absent from gnomAD v4.1.0, segregates with disease including one de novo case, and functional studies show it disrupts fibrillogenesis, supporting pathogenic classification per ACGS guidelines.

Serial imaging showed progression from mild odontoid protrusion through the foramen magnum at age 5 to severe basilar invagination with brainstem impingement by age 7, necessitating urgent surgical decompression.

The patient underwent occipital-to-C5 fusion with suboccipital decompression and C1 laminectomy using an occipital keel plate and pedicle screws, achieving adequate brainstem decompression and craniocervical junction stabilization while preserving neurological function.

For progressive early-onset scoliosis unresponsive to casting, the patient underwent posterior spinal fusion (T2-T4, L3-L4) with magnetically controlled growing rods (MAGEC system), enabling non-invasive outpatient lengthening.

At age 8, mechanical failure of the MAGEC rod's internal lengthening mechanism occurred, with inability to achieve further distraction despite appropriate external magnet application, necessitating surgical rod exchange.

Despite appropriate initial screw placement, compromised bone mineralization associated with EDS led to hardware loosening around the C3-C5 facet screws, though solid bony fusion prevented clinical consequence or need for revision.

Following multiple spinal surgeries, the patient retained reduced but functional strength (4/5 upper extremities, 3/5-4/5 lower extremities), developed a scissoring gait, and requires wheelchair assistance for mobility.

The majority of reported FKBP14-EDS cases (65%) were managed conservatively or with less extensive procedures, in contrast to the index patient's extensive surgical course beginning at 15 months.

GDNF, CaMKII RNAi, and the Ca2+ chelator each suppressed the elevated p-JNK protein levels seen in activated RBL-2H3 cells; RET inhibition alleviated GDNF's suppressive effect, while the Ca2+ chelator further enhanced GDNF's effect on p-JNK, and GDNF had no additional effect when combined with Ca2+ chelator or CaMKII RNAi.

mRNA and protein expression levels of total JNK, JNK isoforms (JNK1, 2, 3), GFRα1, RET, and CaMKII showed no statistically significant differences between treatment groups, indicating GDNF modulates JNK phosphorylation status rather than expression of these components.
Immunofluorescence showed GDNF and GFRα1 co-localize on the cell membrane of RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Immunofluorescence showed CaMKII and JNK co-localize in the cytoplasm of RBL-2H3 mast cells.

A GST pull-down assay demonstrated direct binding between CaMKII and JNK.
