Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that CaMKII and JNK physically interact with each other in RBL-2H3 cells.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density at the distal calf was significantly reduced in SFN patients compared with healthy controls, while proximal thigh IENFD was normal.
Plasma 1-deoxysphingosine, 1-deoxysphinganine, and total 1-deoxysphingolipids were higher in the low fiber density (LFD) subgroup compared to the high fiber density (HFD) subgroup.
In the LFD group, plasma 1-deoxysphingosine and 1-deoxysphinganine were inversely correlated with IENFD, an effect not observed in the HFD group.
Body mass index was higher in the low fiber density subgroup compared to the high fiber density subgroup.

In the LFD group, 1-deoxysphingosine and total 1-deoxysphingolipids showed a weak positive correlation with cold pain threshold, and all sphingolipid parameters positively correlated with paradoxical heat sensation.

In the LFD group, the ala/ser ratio correlated with 1-deoxysphingolipid levels, an association not seen in the HFD group, though no significant difference in ala/ser ratio itself existed between subgroups.
No association was found between IENFD and the ala/ser ratio in either the LFD or HFD groups.
Plasma glutamic acid levels were higher in patients with LFD compared to patients with HFD, while other amino acids showed no group differences.
Fasting plasma glucose was higher in the LFD group compared to the HFD group, though it was not correlated with IENFD within LFD.
HDL was lower in the LFD group compared to the HFD group and positively correlated with IENFD in the LFD group.

IENFD was lower in patients with previously diagnosed arterial hypertension or hypercholesterolemia compared to those without, while plasma 1-deoxysphingolipid levels did not differ between these subgroups.

Multivariate stepwise linear regression identified plasma 1-deoxysphingolipid levels and male sex as independent predictors of reduced IENFD, explaining 24% of variance, while BMI, glucose metabolism, lipid parameters, and ala/ser ratio were not significant predictors.

Genetic analysis in this cohort revealed a single SPTLC1 variant in one patient without clinical signs of HSAN1 or relevant family history, suggesting no pathogenic relevance of SPTLC1/SPTLC2 variants in this idiopathic SFN cohort.

In a mouse model of Marfan syndrome, TGF-beta neutralizing antibody treatment reduced elastic fiber fragmentation, and losartan was found to be as effective as TGF-Nab in reducing aortic media fragmentation.

The first human trial of 18 MFS patients treated with losartan (17 patients) or irbesartan (1 patient) showed a dramatic reduction in annual aortic root diameter growth rate from a baseline of 3.54±2.87 mm/year to 0.46±0.62 mm/year on treatment.

A meta-analysis combining individual patient data from approximately 18 MFS studies (1442 participants after exclusions) found that ARB therapy nearly halved the annual rate of aortic root Z-score progression compared with controls, with no significant difference between ARBs and beta-blockers.
Among ARB-treated MFS patients, subgroup analysis showed that those harboring pathogenic FBN1 variants experienced significantly greater benefit from ARB therapy than non-variant carriers.

In a COMPARE trial substudy of 233 patients (186 with pathogenic FBN1 mutations: 79 dominant-negative, 37 haploinsufficient), patients with haploinsufficient FBN1 mutations showed a greater reduction in mean aortic root diameter on losartan over 3 years, whereas dominant-negative mutation carriers showed no significant change.

The Pediatric Heart Network trial compared losartan (mean 1.3 mg/kg/day) with high-dose atenolol (mean 2.7 mg/kg/day) and found similar reductions in aortic root dilatation between the two treatments.

The LOAT trial randomized 140 MFS patients (ages 5-60) to losartan versus atenolol and followed 128 participants open-label for a mean of 5.9±2.0 years, finding identical aortic root growth rates (0.4 mm/year) between groups and similar total clinical events (21 total: 9 losartan, 12 atenolol).

In a mouse model with pre-existing aneurysmal degeneration, combination therapy with doxycycline and losartan, but not either monotherapy alone, improved aortic contractility, attenuated TGF-beta activity, and lowered the risk of aortic dilatation and aneurysm formation.

A retrospective pediatric study found that children treated with ARBs (mean age 8.1±4.7 years) had a significant aortic Z-score reduction of -0.20±0.41, whereas those treated with beta-blockers (mean age 9.9±5.6 years) had a Z-score increase of 0.20±0.33, favoring early ARB treatment.

In the extended (8-year) COMPARE trial of 153 participants randomized to losartan or control (over half on adjunctive beta-blockers), the losartan arm had fewer deaths (0 vs 5) and fewer aortic dissections (3 vs 11) than controls, though the difference in aortic root replacements (10 vs 13) was not statistically significant.
Mullen et al.'s RCT demonstrated that irbesartan reduced aortic root growth compared to placebo (0.53 mm/year vs 0.74 mm/year, p=0.030), although the trial faced substantial recruitment shortfalls.

Studies show higher angiotensin II concentrations in the aorta of MFS mice, which enhances thrombospondin-1 (TSP1) expression, a strong TGF-beta stimulator, suggesting that elevated TGF-beta signaling in MFS may result from Ang II signaling rather than solely mutant fibrillin.

Losartan reduces SMAD2 phosphorylation and connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) accumulation induced by angiotensin II signaling, suggesting an additional unidentified mediator within the AT1R pathway.

ARBs have demonstrated anti-inflammatory properties across studies of angina, type II diabetes, and hypertension, including suppression of TNF-alpha and IL-6, reduction of oxidative stress and C-reactive protein, and decreased vascular hypertrophy.
Losartan's low oral bioavailability (33%) and short half-life (2 hours) may explain inconsistent clinical outcomes relative to promising preclinical results.
Research by Stark et al. showed that ARBs reduced TGF-beta levels in pediatric MFS patients, suggesting potential benefit of TGF-beta receptor blockade initiated at an early age.

Daugherty et al. showed that losartan mitigates angiotensin II-mediated abdominal aortic aneurysm development, whereas angiotensin II type-2 receptor blockers worsen aortic pathology, indicating that AT1R activation negatively impacts aneurysm development while AT2R signaling may be protective.

Cardiovascular, dermatological, ear-related, muscular, digestive, endocrine, and hematological symptoms were less common, each occurring in 3-7% of ECM disorders.

A heterozygous ABL1 variant c.199T>C (p.Trp67Arg) was identified in the patient via a 70-gene connective tissue disorder panel, initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance.
Parental testing was negative for the variant, confirming it arose de novo in the patient, supporting its pathogenicity (PM6 criterion).

The variant was reclassified as probably pathogenic per ACMG/AMP criteria (PM2, PM5, PM6), given absence in gnomAD, a prior pathogenic ClinVar variant at the same amino acid, and de novo occurrence, leading to a diagnosis of ABL1-associated CHDSKM.

The patient exhibited connective-tissue-suggestive features including joint hypermobility, mandibular hypoplasia, pectus excavatum, clinodactyly and camptodactyly of the 4th/5th fingers, and thin translucent skin.
The patient had multiple episodes (five total) of spontaneous pneumothorax associated with bilateral subpleural apical bullae seen on CT.

Esophageal manometry with impedancemetry showed severe ineffective esophageal motility, with 90% of swallows showing failed peristalsis, 10% fragmented peristalsis, and 100% incomplete esophageal bolus transit.
Chronic gastritis and GERD symptoms showed only partial response to pharmacotherapy on long-term follow-up.
At birth the patient presented right renal agenesis, unilateral cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and umbilical/epigastric hernia, and at age 14 was diagnosed with hypothyroidism.
Unlike most reported CHDSKM patients who present cardiac defects (septal defects, aortic root dilation) from birth or early childhood, this patient has no current cardiac involvement.

In the previously reported Wang et al. (2017) cohort of CHDSKM patients from 4 unrelated families, three patients showed joint hypermobility along with dysmorphic facial features, congenital heart defects, skeletal abnormalities, GI conditions, and genital abnormalities in males.

Chen et al. reported two CHDSKM patients (30-year-old male, 20-year-old female) with spontaneous pneumothorax onset at age 16; the male had 2 episodes resolved by bullectomy with talc, compared to this patient's 5 episodes resolved by VATS.

TENS electrotherapy provided the patient with only partial and momentary relief of chronic joint/temporomandibular/cervical pain, while conventional therapy (daily exercises, hot compresses, infrared radiation) was ineffective.
Muscle de-escalation and lidocaine infiltration improved the patient's cervical joint pain.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with excision of bullae was effective, with no recurrence of pneumothorax for 3 years post-surgery, though surveillance CT continued to show persistent bilateral apical bullae.
Patients with chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) showed significantly higher normalized peak plantar force in the medial midfoot region during single-leg stance compared to healthy controls.
Patients with concomitant CLAI and osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT) showed a larger increase in medial midfoot plantar pressure compared to healthy controls than CLAI alone.
Patients with isolated CLAI showed increased normalized peak plantar force in the third metatarsal (M3) region compared to healthy controls.
Patients with CLAI and concomitant OLT had significantly lower absolute anterior-posterior time-to-boundary during single-leg stance than healthy controls, indicating greater postural instability.
Both the CLAI group and the CLAI+OLT group showed significantly greater anterior-posterior COP variance on the affected side compared to healthy controls, indicating postural instability.
In the CLAI group, normalized peak force in the medial midfoot was significantly higher on the affected side than the unaffected side.

In the CLAI+OLT group, the unaffected side showed significantly lower posterior heel pressure and significantly higher fifth metatarsal pressure compared to the affected side, indicating bilateral compensatory adaptation.
In patients with CLAI, mean medial-lateral time-to-boundary was significantly lower on the affected side compared to the unaffected side.
In patients with CLAI+OLT, both absolute and mean anterior-posterior time-to-boundary were significantly lower on the affected side compared to the unaffected side.

For patients with CLAI, COP variance in both medial-lateral and anterior-posterior directions was significantly greater on the affected side than the unaffected side, indicating increased postural instability.
Normalized peak force in the third metatarsal region discriminated between CLAI and CLAI+OLT patients with an AUC of 0.700, sensitivity 45.8%, and specificity 89.5% at a cut-off of 15.80.
There was no significant difference in Beighton score (a measure of generalized joint hypermobility) between the CLAI and CLAI+OLT groups.
In the subgroup with Beighton score <5 (lower joint hypermobility), normalized peak force in the M3 region was significantly higher in the CLAI group than in the CLAI+OLT group.
In the subgroup with Beighton score >5 (greater joint hypermobility), no significant differences in plantar pressure were found between the CLAI and CLAI+OLT groups.
In the male subgroup, normalized peak force in the M3 region of the affected side was significantly higher in the CLAI group than in the CLAI+OLT group.
In the female subgroup, normalized peak force in the T1 (first phalanx) region was significantly lower in the CLAI group compared to the CLAI+OLT group.
In the BMI ≥25 subgroup, normalized peak force in the posterior heel region was significantly lower in the CLAI group than in the CLAI+OLT group.
There were no significant differences in plantar pressure characteristics between medial talus and lateral talus lesion locations in the CLAI+OLT group.
Fibromyalgia and IBS frequently co-occur, with 28-59% of FM patients developing IBS and 32-77% of IBS patients developing FM.

Mast cells activated early in FM and IBS pathogenesis produce pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-8, IL-6, IL-17, TNF-α) that affect the intestinal mucosa in IBS and produce systemic widespread pain in FM.
Colonic leptin released by mast cells is significantly increased in IBS patients with severe diarrhea-predominant symptoms.
Fibromyalgia severity is associated with increased levels of monocyte chemotactic protein 1 (CCL2).
Plasma TNF-α levels in IBS patients positively correlate with fatigue, a symptom shared with FM.
The TNFSF15 gene, which encodes TL1A involved in intestinal mucosal immune activation, is cited as genetic evidence for IBS susceptibility.
Elevated TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR9, LPS, and anti-flagellin antibodies correlate with IBS symptoms.
Raised β-defensin 2 levels in IBS patients suggest immune activation in the absence of gross inflammation.
IBS patients show abundant Ruminococcus gnavus and Lachnospiraceae with lower levels of Barnesiella intestinihominis and Coprococcus catus.
IBS patients show an increased Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio, increased Clostridia/Clostridiales, and decreased Bacteroidia/Bacteroidales.
IBS patients show lower levels of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and higher levels of E. coli and Enterobacter.
No substantial difference was detected in fecal Bacteroides or Enterococcus levels between IBS patients and healthy controls.
IBS patients show lower alpha diversity and altered beta diversity of the gut virome, with Siphoviridae, Myoviridae, and Podoviridae the most abundant families.
Both FM and IBS patients show reduced populations of Bifidobacteria (GABA producers) and Ruminococcaceae (butyrate producers) compared to healthy controls.
Clostridium scindens, which converts primary to secondary bile acids potentially involved in nociception, is increased in both FM and IBS patients.
Butyrate-producing Eubacteria are reduced in FM patients but increased in IBS patients.
Lachnospiraceae are reduced in FM patients but variably increased or decreased in IBS patients.
Rikinellaceae, fiber-digesting bacteria, are increased in FM patients but reduced in IBS patients.
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is common in FM patients and may translocate endotoxins through a compromised intestinal barrier, contributing to inflammation and pain sensitization.
Upregulation of vasoactive intestinal peptide and its receptor VPAC1 enhances migration of E. coli and Salmonella to the lamina propria in IBS patient biopsies.
Blockade of VPAC1 receptors decreased bacterial migration to the lamina propria and produced clinical improvement in IBS symptoms.
Eubacteria, which produce butyrate, are reported to be reduced in fibromyalgia patients but increased in IBS patients.
Lachnospiraceae, which produce butyric acid, are reduced in fibromyalgia patients while showing variable increases or decreases across IBS patients.
Reduced butyrate and SCFA synthesis may compromise gut and blood-brain barrier integrity, permitting systemic LPS release and enhanced pain perception.
Lachnospiraceae levels are especially low in IBS patients who report anxiety and depression, suggesting a role in the psychological aspects of IBS and FM.
Clostridium scindens, which converts primary to secondary bile acids potentially involved in nociception, is increased in both FM and IBS patients.
Reduced bile acid levels create a favorable environment for gram-negative bacteria, promoting a pro-inflammatory microbial population.
Butyrate-producing Eubacteria are reduced in FM patients but increased in IBS patients.
Butyric-acid-producing Lachnospiraceae are reduced in FM patients, while showing variable increases or decreases in IBS patients, possibly reflecting population heterogeneity.
Reduced butyrate lowers SCFA synthesis, compromising gut and blood-brain barrier integrity and allowing systemic LPS release that enhances pain perception.
Rikenellaceae, which help digest crude fiber, are increased in FM patients but reduced in IBS patients.

Many FM patients have SIBO, supporting the hypothesis that expanded microbe populations translocate endotoxins through a compromised intestinal barrier, causing inflammation and pain sensitization; SIBO is also hypothesized to contribute to IBS.

Bednarska et al. found increased migration of E. coli and Salmonella to the lamina propria in IBS patient biopsies, enhanced by upregulated VIP/VPAC1 signaling, and blockade of VPAC1 reduced bacterial migration and improved clinical symptoms.
Increased mast cells and decreased tight junction efficiency in intestinal mucosal cells disturb gut barrier integrity in FM and IBS.

Zhao et al. described that distinct gut bacterial taxa modulate intestinal permeability, hypersensitivity, and motility through diverse pathways, including IL-22 signaling (Lactobacillaceae), 5-HT pathways (Corynebacterium, Streptococcus, Enterococcus), the indole pathway (E. coli, Achromobacter liquefaciens, Bacteroides spp.), Wnt/beta-catenin and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling (Limosilactobacillus reuteri, L. delbrueckii, Alistipes onderdonkii), and TLR2 signaling (Akkermansia muciniphila, Clostridium butyricum).

Labus et al. found that gut microbe-brain somatosensory network associations, particularly involving Clostridiales such as Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae that stimulate EC 5-HT release, are protective in healthy controls but diminished in IBS patients (65 IBS patients, 46 female; 21 healthy controls, 16 female).
Lachnospiraceae incertae sedis connectivity to the primary somatosensory cortex, linked to rectal pain processing in healthy controls, was not prominent in IBS patients.

Clostridium XIVa and Coprococcus subnetworks show connectivity with subcortical and somatosensory GI sensorimotor regions in healthy controls that is not evident in IBS patients, with only Clostridium XIVa retaining a positive subcortical association in IBS.

Clos-Garcia et al. reported augmented populations of Dorea, Roseburia, Papillibacter, and Subdoligranulum in FM patients, alongside reduced Bifidobacteria, Eubacterium, Lachnospiraceae, Clostridium, and Firmicutes.

Depletion of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus (GABA producers) may shift the glutamate-to-GABA ratio toward glutamate, which may enter systemic circulation via a compromised gut and blood-brain barrier, potentially explaining elevated CSF glutamate in FM patients.

Valencia et al. reported abnormal serotonin and dopamine secretion in IBS patients attributable to dysbiosis, and raised the possibility of genetic polymorphisms in serotonin, dopamine, and catecholamine pathway genes in FM.

Alfaro-Rodriguez et al. found significantly lower 5-HT levels and 5-HT transporter in the CSF of FM patients, with lower serotonin associated with heightened pain sensitivity via reduced suppression of substance P release.
Downregulation of serotonin receptors 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C may contribute to chronic hyperalgesia in FM.
Diminished tryptophan and kynurenine levels in FM patients correlate with the severity of FM symptoms.
Cortisol released in response to emotional stress activates the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway, reducing tryptophan availability for serotonin synthesis and contributing to pain in FM.

Increased kynurenine levels raise quinolinic acid in the CNS, potentially elevating glutamate activity and causing cellular stress and neural inflammation, contributing to pain and sleep disturbance in FM.

Singh et al. reported that 90% of total body serotonin is produced by gut microbiota, and this serotonin binds 5-HT receptors on microglia, activating inflammatory cytokines that contribute to gut inflammation.

Amplified levels of gut mucosal serotonin have been found in IBS patients, linked to disturbed gut motility resulting in abdominal pain and altered stool frequency; 5-HT3A antagonism alleviates mucosal inflammation, gut permeability, and IBS-like symptoms.
A positive correlation exists between lamina propria mast cells and spontaneous release of 5-HT in IBS patients, and mast-cell-derived histamine causes diarrhea when overproduced.
Chen et al. reported that 5-HT and 5-HT3 receptor levels in the intestinal mucosa are substantially higher in IBS patients compared to healthy controls, suggesting an impaired serotonergic system.

Studies show that IBS-C predominant patients have increased dopamine, while IBS-D patients show no difference; levodopa, dopamine agonists, metformin, butyrate, losartan, and imipramine are potentially useful for relieving IBS symptoms via gut-brain axis modulation.
IBS patients display decreased GABA, GABA receptors, and glutamate decarboxylase 2, but increased GABA transporter 2.

Elevated histamine levels in the colon and urine of IBS patients correlate with symptom severity, particularly abdominal pain, with H1 and H4 receptors implicated in visceral hypersensitivity and pain.

Chen et al. noted increased indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (which degrades tryptophan) in IBS, while neuroprotective kynurenic acid and the KynA-to-kynurenine ratio were diminished, findings that parallel reduced tryptophan and kynurenic acid reported in FM.
Colonic leptin released from mast cells is significantly increased in patients with severe symptoms of diarrhea-predominant IBS.
Increased levels of monocyte chemotactic protein 1/chemokine C-C motif ligand 2 are associated with greater severity of fibromyalgia.
High plasma TNF-α levels in IBS patients positively correlated with patient-reported fatigue, a symptom shared with fibromyalgia.
The TNFSF15 gene, which encodes the TL1A protein involved in immune-mediated intestinal inflammation, was cited as genetic evidence for a component of IBS pathogenesis.
Elevated TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR9, lipopolysaccharide, and anti-flagellin antibodies correlate with IBS symptoms.
Raised β-defensin 2 levels were recorded in IBS patients, suggesting immune system activation in the absence of overt inflammation.
IBS patients show lower alpha diversity and altered beta diversity of the gut virome, with Siphoviridae, Myoviridae, and Podoviridae as the most abundant families.
Clostridium scindens, which converts primary to secondary bile acids potentially involved in nociception, is increased in both FM and IBS patients.
Butyrate-producing Eubacteria are reduced in fibromyalgia patients but increased in IBS patients.
Fiber-digesting Rikinellaceae are increased in fibromyalgia patients but reduced in IBS patients.

Many fibromyalgia patients have been found to have small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, supporting endotoxin translocation through a compromised intestinal barrier as a mechanism of inflammation and pain sensitization; SIBO is similarly hypothesized to play a role in IBS.

Upregulation of vasoactive intestinal peptide and its receptor VPAC1 enhanced bacterial migration (E. coli, Salmonella) into the lamina propria in IBS biopsies, and blocking VPAC1 reduced bacterial migration and improved clinical symptoms.

In healthy controls, Lachnospiraceae incertae sedi connectivity with the primary somatosensory cortex is linked to rectal pain processing, but this association is not prominent in IBS patients, and Clostridium XIVa/Coprococcus subnetwork connectivity with subcortical gastrointestinal sensorimotor regions is diminished or absent in IBS patients.

Depletion of GABA-producing Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in FM patients may shift the glutamate-to-GABA ratio toward glutamate, potentially explaining elevated glutamate observed in the cerebrospinal fluid of FM patients.
IBS with constipation predominance is associated with increased dopamine, whereas diarrhea-predominant IBS patients show no significant difference in dopamine.
Levodopa, dopamine agonists, metformin, butyrate, losartan, and imipramine were noted as potentially useful for relieving IBS symptoms via gut-brain axis modulation.
IBS patients display decreased GABA, decreased GABA receptors, and decreased glutamate decarboxylase 2, but increased GABA transporter 2.
Elevated colonic and urinary histamine levels correlate with symptom severity, particularly abdominal pain, in IBS patients, with H1 and H4 receptors implicated in visceral hypersensitivity.
Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, which degrades tryptophan, is increased in IBS, while neuroprotective kynurenic acid and the KynA-to-kynurenine ratio are both reduced.
Reduced kynurenic acid levels were documented in both IBS and fibromyalgia patients, highlighting a shared metabolic feature between the two conditions.

Lowered SCFAs in IBS patients contribute to inflammation, impaired tryptophan metabolism, and altered acetylcholine receptor activity, potentially resulting in visceral hypersensitivity, with SCFAs also exerting influence via the vagus nerve on pain and anxiety symptoms.
Elevated 5-HT levels have been noted in diarrhea-predominant IBS patients alongside reduced serotonin transporter expression.
Certain probiotics including Lactobacillus, Enterococcus, and Bifidobacterium bifidum were reported to alleviate the severity of IBS symptoms.
Lactobacillus acidophilus increases cannabinoid receptor 2 and colonic μ-opioid receptor expression, decreasing pain sensation.

In fibromyalgia patients, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei and Bifidobacterium longum infantis improved cognitive functions including decision-making, but did not impact pain, quality of life, or mood disorders.

A combination probiotic of L. rhamnosus, L. paracasei, L. acidophilus, and Bifidobacterium bifidus reportedly improved cognitive and emotional symptoms in fibromyalgia, but findings were inconsistent due to short treatment durations.

A case study reported that FMT substantially benefited a patient with fibromyalgia, IBS, and chronic fatigue syndrome, normalizing elevated Candida and streptococci and resolving fatigue and depression with improved insomnia and touch/noise hypersensitivity.
Studies show 28-59% of fibromyalgia patients develop IBS, while 32-77% of IBS patients develop fibromyalgia.
Diagnostic delays average two to five years for fibromyalgia and one to three years for IBS.
Both fibromyalgia and IBS show a two to three times higher prevalence in women compared to men.
FM patients reported significantly higher pain intensity scores than healthy controls on the Numeric Rating Scale.
FM patients had significantly lower muscle mass than healthy controls.
FM patients showed poorer nutritional status than controls as measured by the Mini Nutritional Assessment.
